name: Florida Phoenix
title: One death reported in Florida as Hurricane Isaias moves through
description: Note: The Phoenix will update this story as it develops. With Hurricane Isaias making landfall on the Florida Panhandle and now moving through Alabama, Gov. Ron DeSantis said Saturday morning that Florida came through the storm relatively well, compared to other storms that have hit the state. One death had been reported due to a […]
text:
A view from atop a downtown Pensacola parking garage as Hurricane Isaias passed through on Oct 9, 2026. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)Note: The Phoenix will update this story as it develops.
With Hurricane Isaias making landfall on the Florida Panhandle and now moving through Alabama, Gov. Ron DeSantis said Saturday morning that Florida came through the storm relatively well, compared to other storms that have hit the state.
One death had been reported due to a falling tree in Escambia County, he noted. Another was reported in Alabama.
But flooding was receding, DeSantis said during a news conference in Tallahassee, and bridges and major highways were open.
It had been “a significant storm,” he acknowledged.
“There’s obviously damage. There’s obviously debris,” he continued.
“But in terms of some of the other storms we’ve had, [when] we’ve had to really mobilize, massive search and rescue, and bring people out of very perilous situations — fortunately, that has not been something that’s been requested of us. And my sense is, from talking to some of the local officials, that they’ve been able to fulfill needs and requests through their ordinary course of business.”
Moreover, although search and rescue teams have been mobilized, “we have not yet received any request for search and rescue deployment, and I take that as an optimistic sign. But our resources are prepared in the event that the need arises. Particularly with respect to any flooding that may occur on the back end of this storm — and we’re likely to continue to see in some areas water levels continue to rise.”
A downed tree lies on a street in downtown Pensacola on Friday Oct. 9, 2026, as Hurricane Isaias approaches. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)
Landfall
Isaias made landfall near Destin, around 50 miles east of Pensacola, about 8:30 p.m. Central time Friday with maximum sustained winds of 105 mph.
During the storm, in downtown Pensacola debris like fast food containers, sticks, and even sheet metal roofing flew down the streets.
As the sun set, the wind died down with it. An orange and pink haze covered the skyline as wind ripped through and power went out. At one point, Pensacola police informed reporters that they were stopping patrol due to the conditions.
As of 4 a.m., the National Hurricane Center placed Isaias roughly 25 miles south-southwest of Montgomery, Alabama, with maximum sustained winds of 35 mph, moving north at 14 mph.
“Through the weekend, Isaias is expected to produce rainfall amounts of 4 to 8 inches across southern Alabama, the Florida Panhandle and Big Bend, and southwest Georgia,” the center reported. “Localized totals up to 15 inches are possible, particularly within banding across the Florida Panhandle and Big Bend.
The National Hurricane Center says the remnants of Hurricane Isaias will move over the Tennessee Valley, Southern Appalachians and the Southeast today with “considerable flash and urban flooding” possible. (National Hurricane Center)
 
Here’s how DeSantis described the situation in Florida:
More than 16,000 power line workers had staged before the storm, and they began repairs as soon as it was safe. “Cut and toss” operations for downed trees and other debris and bridge inspections kicked off at around 3 a.m.
“As of this morning, all state-owned bridges are safe and have been reopened for travel. Crew finished inspecting all the coastal bridges by 0600 this morning,” the governor said. Also cleared were Interstate 10 and U.S. Highway 98, which follows the coast. Smaller roads still had debris.
As of 7 a.m., 448,000 electricity customers in Florida were without power. Officials were inspecting the grid, DeSantis said.
Some 90% of customers in Santa Rosa County lacked power; in Holmes County, it was 89%; in Washington, 86%; Walton, 85%; Escambia, 75%; and Okaloosa, 53%.
The Northwest Florida Beaches International Airport near Panama City Beach was reopened, but Destin-Fort Walton Beach and Pensacola International airports remained closed.
Caution urged
Attorney General James Uthmeier cautioned against hiring unlicensed contractors to clear debris or make repairs. Often, these are fly-by-night operators from out of state, he said.
“They come in wanting to take advantage of the situation and market themselves as there to do roof repairs, other repairs. They’re often not licensed, not competent. They just want to take your money and run.”
Jared Purdue, Florida’s transportation secretary and emergency management director, also urged caution.
“Even though the storm has made landfall, dangerous conditions could remain,” he said. “Please avoid unnecessary travel to allow first responders, utility crews, and debris removal teams to work safely. Always assume downed lines are energized, stay away from damaged electrical equipment, and standing water near power lines. If there is standing water or flowing water on top of a road, please do not drive through it. It can be very dangerous.”
Jay Waagmeester reported from Pensacola.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: One person killed as Hurricane Isaias brings heavy rain, wind to Alabama
description: Hurricane Isaias caused severe damage in parts of southern Alabama Saturday and led to the death of at least one person in Birmingham. The storm made landfall as a Category 2 hurricane near Destin, Florida, at approximately 8:30 p.m. CST Friday evening, bringing high winds and heavy rains throughout the state. Jefferson County Emergency Management […]
text:
Emily Bradley of Murfreesboro, Tennessee, looks out at the water before the arrival of Hurricane Isaias in Orange Beach, Alabama, on Oct. 8, 2026. The hurricane made landfall as a Category 2 storm Friday night. (Dan Anderson for Alabama Reflector)Hurricane Isaias caused severe damage in parts of southern Alabama Saturday and led to the death of at least one person in Birmingham.
The storm made landfall as a Category 2 hurricane near Destin, Florida, at approximately 8:30 p.m. CST Friday evening, bringing high winds and heavy rains throughout the state.
Jefferson County Emergency Management Agency confirmed that a person was killed in Birmingham around 5 a.m. on Saturday when a tree fell on a house.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
National Weather Service stations in Birmingham and Mobile said they received reports of damage throughout the evening.
“Significant trees and powerline damage,” said Jason Beam, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Mobile. “Many of our inland counties were at a 100% power loss, and there was some heavy damage to the power infrastructure. Monroe County is one example of that.”
The storm Saturday morning had been downgraded to a post-tropical cyclone whose center is located between Birmingham and Montgomery, according to the National Weather Service. A high wind advisory remained in effect for most of central and northern Alabama.
Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey said in a statement early Saturday morning that the major concern was “strong winds, heavy rain and possible spinoff tornadoes in certain parts of the state.”
According to the website poweroutage.us, which tracks power outages in the U.S., about 275,000 Alabamians were without power as of 9:48 a.m. Saturday morning. The number represented almost 11% of the more than 2.6 million customers in the state, though it was down from about 300,000 people earlier Saturday morning. The website reported Houston, Mobile and Baldwin counties with the highest number of outages.
In five counties — Wilcox, Conecuh, Monroe, Geneva and Coffee — a majority of residents were without power, according to the website.
Some parts of the state experienced heavy rainfall, with counties in southwest Alabama getting about 2 inches of rain while the areas east of that received about 8 inches.
Thus far, no tornadoes have been reported in the state.
FEMA announced in a news release Friday evening that President Donald Trump approved an emergency declaration for the state, which makes available federal disaster assistance.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: A quote for the age of revolution, in 1968 and today
description: John Glenn, American hero for being the first U.S. citizen to fly into space, decided to stay at the hotel instead of going to the victory speech of Robert F. Kennedy, who had just won the 1968 California presidential primary. He sat there, watching the candidate complete his remarks, sharing the room with his wife, […]
text:
David Russell sat holding an American flag on the steps of the Iowa Capitol as part of the "No Kings" protest in Des Moines March 28, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)John Glenn, American hero for being the first U.S. citizen to fly into space, decided to stay at the hotel instead of going to the victory speech of Robert F. Kennedy, who had just won the 1968 California presidential primary.
He sat there, watching the candidate complete his remarks, sharing the room with his wife, other members of the Kennedy family, and five of the Kennedy children. Glenn heard the speech and wrote, “Then came the madness and chaos after his shooting.”
President Lyndon Johnson flew the Kennedy family and the Glenns back to Washington, D.C. on Air Force One. The following night, RFK died. Glenn and Susie Markham, a neighbor close to the children, told them that their father had passed.
He said later, “It was one of the hardest things, I have ever had to do.”
The next day, Glenn walked into the senator’s study and found on the desk speeches and writings, and a book by Ralph Waldo Emerson. One quote from Emerson, which RFK had marked in the book’s margin as being of interest, captured Glenn’s attention and seemed so relevant then and to today’s times as well. We will come to that quote, but first a few observations from someone who’s been watching elections since before 1968.
I am not sure to how to describe this election season. Sometimes, with all the anger, rage and hostility, it almost seems like we are having a national temper tantrum. Negative ads attack the character the candidate’s opponent more than a difference on issues. There is something deeper behind the storm clouds than just another routine election.
The current president is a skilled in-fighter when confronting his political opponents. In this election, indeed, he is extraordinary in his ability to provoke his adversaries in responding to his allegations. For example, he will tear down the Kennedy Center and build arches that block the view from Arlington Cemetery and put a sniper’s nest and a national defense center in it, as well as commencing a tariff war with Canada. To these assertions and others, national Democrats respond, demand action or explanation, accomplishing two of his political goals. First, President Trump fires up his own supporters to turn out to vote and, second, he muddles the opposition’s reasons for calling for change by talking about his issues, not theirs.
Today, at best, the Democrats want to focus on inflation and affordability. Trump sees a danger of ultra liberals (read communists) taking over the government and ruining an already strong economy.  In one form or another, these four issues are what we will decide in November.
While all of those or some of them may cause a tilt to the red or swing to the blue, the impact of a decision by our voters will weigh heavily on the form and function of the very future of our government. Ratification or disapproval of the president’s economic and war powers will be seen as approval or disapproval of the way President Trump has shaped and utilized the power of the government.
Should the president’s desire to modify or even change the concept of sharing functions between three different branches of government, the Congress, the Judiciary and the Executive Branch, be affirmed and further power drained from the legislative branch flowing to him? Should we retain the concept of the separation of powers, with three co-equal branches of government?
Which side is seen as prevailing in the election when the results are tabulated will, in large measure, provide an answer to the question. Trump’s candidates do well, his stock rises and his leadership is confirmed.  Perform poorly, Democrats advance and a challenging Congress awaits him.
What makes Emerson’s quote, which Glenn located that solemn morning almost 60 years ago in Kennedy’s study, somewhat astounding is its applicability to the choice in front of us, we the keepers of this democracy in our time.
“If there is any period one would desire to be born in, is it not the age of revolution, when the old and the new stand side-by-side and admit of being compared? When the energies of all men are searched by fear and by hope, when the historic glories of the old can be compensated by the rich possibilities of the new era, this time like all times is a very good one if we but know what do with it.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Time for term limits? Dems in majority could have familiar faces in key roles
description: FILE - Rep. Bennie Thompson, D-Miss., speaks during a voting rights town hall at the historic Farish Street Baptist Church in Jackson, Miss., Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026. (AP Photo/Sarah Warnock)
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
WASHINGTON (AP) — Democrats hope to bring a new agenda to the House next year if they take the majority, but they will most likely do so with many of the same faces that have steered their party’s legislative work for a decade or more.
Potential committee chairs in the next Congress include Rep. Bennie Thompson of Mississippi, who has served as top Democrat on the House Homeland Security panel since 2005. Then, there’s Adam Smith of Washington, who began serving as top Democrat on Armed Services in 2011, and Rep. Maxine Waters of California, who became the lead Democrat on Financial Services in 2013.
FILE – Rep. Frank Pallone, Jr., D-N.J., attends a hearing, April 21, 2026, on Capitol Hill in Washington. (AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin, File)
Other longtime committee leaders include Reps. Frank Pallone at Energy and Commerce and Bobby Scott at Education and Workforce, who assumed their leadership posts in 2015. Rep. Richie Neal became the top Democrat on the Ways and Means Committee in 2017.
None would be able to continue in that position under the rules used by House Republicans, which generally limit lawmakers to three terms as chairman or ranking member.
For Democrats, the question is whether to stick with their current system, which emphasizes seniority, or move closer to the one that Republicans have established. It’s a discussion that some Democrats say they are having behind the scenes.
“I think that the idea of term limits could be appealing to the American people, to the Democratic base. It sounds Democratic,” said Rep. Eugene Vindman, D-Va. “I’m open to the idea. I’ve spoken to a number of folks who are open to the idea.”
“I personally think it makes for a more vibrant Congress, but I know I’m in the minority in the minority,” said Rep. Chrissy Houlahan, D-Pa.
Party leaders are playing down the issue for now. Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said seniority has always been a factor when it comes to committee leadership, but not the only one.
“The caucus is going to work its will as we move forward,” Jeffries told reporters. “At the end of the day, we can’t put the cart before the horse. We’ve got to still go out and win this thing in November.”
House Rules Committee Ranking Member Jim McGovern, D-Mass., left, and Chairman Tom Cole, R-Okla., attend a markup hearing. (AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin)
Democrats have been here before
Term limits are not a new discussion for Democrats. When they were weighing whether to return Nancy Pelosi as speaker in 2018, those opposing her bid wanted her to commit to limiting how long lawmakers could serve as House party leaders or committee chairs. She eventually agreed to serve in the post for no more than four more years.
No such restrictions were added for committee chairs. In 2022, Democrats voted overwhelmingly against a six-year term limit for committee leaders.
Rep. Jim McGovern, D-Mass., who has served as top Democrat on the House Rules Committee since 2018, called term limits an “artificial, random mechanism that doesn’t always serve the best interest of the institution.”
“I want people in chairs who are going to fight to get things over the finish line and make a real difference,” McGovern said. “Some of those people may have been around for a long time and some of them may be relatively new.”
Pallone said he intends to be the next Energy and Commerce chairman or ranking member. He called term limits for chairs “very undemocratic.”
“If people want to vote for somebody they should be allowed to,” Pallone said.
He also said that term limits can lead to short-term thinking from chairs looking at their next opportunity in the private sector.
“People serve for a couple years, then they go work for some lobbying firm,” he said. “What they do when they’re here is very much influenced by what lobbying firm they’re going to work for.”
Thompson also said he would like to serve again as top Democrat on Homeland Security if he wins reelection. He dismissed the way Republicans limit committee leaders to three terms.
“I don’t want to be like Republicans. I’m a Democrat,” Thompson said.
House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., says term limits have served Republicans well.
“It’s been really good to show younger members that you’re always going to have a path to leadership if you keep working hard, if you do your job really well,” Scalise said. “We definitely lose some good chairmen along the way, but we also get new leaders who otherwise would not have been able to rise up.”
Democrats have broken with seniority on occasion
Democrats don’t always stick with seniority. One recent exception is Rep. Jamie Raskin, the lead Democrat on the Judiciary Committee. He challenged Rep. Jerry Nadler for the job in late 2024, prompting Nadler, then 77, to step aside.
Similarly, Democrats selected Rep. Angie Craig to become the top Democrat on the Agriculture Committee after she challenged the late Rep. David Scott for the post. Scott had been the panel’s top Democrat for the previous two sessions, but was in poor health.
Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., speaks during a Congressional spotlight hearing on Capitol Hill, Tuesday, Sept. 22, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein)
Democrats also elected Rep. Robert Garcia last year to succeed Rep. Gerry Connolly on the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee. Connolly died after a battle with esophageal cancer. Garcia defeated veteran Rep. Stephen Lynch of Massachusetts for the job.
“He has done, by everybody’s measure here, an incredible job,” said Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas. “We would not have all of the Epstein files that we’ve gotten so far without his leadership on that committee.”
Casar called next steps for Democrats on committee chairs an “internal conversation.”
“I think at a minimum we should go to a system where it’s about who the right person is, and then have discussions about how we make sure that new blood comes in,” Casar said.
Rep. Brad Schneider, D-Ill., said he hears less talk about term limits than past years, and he credits some of the changes Democrats already made.
“Last cycle, there was a lot of clamor, and you saw some changes,” Schneider said. “I’m not hearing similar angst this time.”
Rep. Pramila Jayapal of Washington said she favors term limits, but emphasized that her view is no reflection of the current leaders. It’s more about helping Democrats develop a deeper bench.
“I just think it’s really smart policy and it’s really smart strategy to make sure that we keep building people skills, opportunities and leadership,” Jayapal said.
She said she understood when she first served in Congress a decade ago the longstanding concerns voiced by the Congressional Black Caucus about term limits hurting members who had just earned chairmanships, but believes Democrats have done a better job of diversifying the caucus.
“And we need to do more, but we are taking away opportunities from a lot of those newer members,” Jayapal said.
Some Democrats have talked about a hybrid approach that sets some limits, but not at the three-term threshold set by House Republicans.
“I don’t know what the magic number is, but endless is not the magic number,” Houlahan said.

title: State suspends enforcement of dyed fuel for some vehicles
description: Montana is temporarily expanding the usage of dyed diesel fuels for commercial vehicles engaged in work related to agriculture and logging. The expansion will not apply to noncommercial vehicles, like passenger cars and trucks. The move comes after President Donald Trump announced a federal executive order allowing for wider use of dyed diesel. It does […]
text:
A diesel pump at a gas station in Billings, Montana. It has options for different types of diesel for purchase, including red dyed diesel (Photo by Darrell Ehrlick of the Daily Montanan). Montana is temporarily expanding the usage of dyed diesel fuels for commercial vehicles engaged in work related to agriculture and logging. The expansion will not apply to noncommercial vehicles, like passenger cars and trucks.
The move comes after President Donald Trump announced a federal executive order allowing for wider use of dyed diesel. It does not change individual state taxes and Trump has said he issued the order to help ease soaring fuel prices.
Dyed diesel fuel is untaxed federally and allowed for off-road usage only.
The executive order, which was issued by Montana Lt. Gov. Kristen Juras, currently the acting governor as Gov. Greg Gianforte is not in the country, says it’s being issued due to “recent global events” that have disrupted the fuel supply chain.
“Uninterrupted operation of commercial motor vehicles engaged in agricultural and timber-related transport is necessary to maintain economic stability and support Montana’s resource-dependent communities during this emergency period,” the order states.
Dyed fuel is not sold at all gas stations and usually retails for around $1 per gallon cheaper than other diesel because it’s tax-exempt. Those taxes, state and federal, often go toward transportation projects, but since dyed diesel is used in vehicles that do not travel on roads, they’re exempt from paying those taxes.
The fuel is dyed so law enforcement can test for vehicles illegally using the fuel on roadways. There are penalties associated with using the fuel against its intended purpose which include fines and, on the third offense, the possibility of jail time.
It’s also not an uncommon offense, Montana Department of Transportation spokesperson Charity Burns said.
“Violations are mostly found in pickups, rather than large commercial motor vehicles,” Burns wrote in an email. Motor Carrier Services Officers enforce the law through probable cause stops, tips, and visual monitoring of dyed fuel pumps.
The order is good for 45 days and ends on Nov. 23. Farm advocacy organizations in other states have wondered about traces of dye in their fuel after the period ends.
“Montana farmers, ranchers, and timber industry workers are feeling the squeeze at the gas pump,” Gov. Greg Gianforte said in a press release. “This executive order will help bring relief for transporting essential goods including agricultural commodities, livestock feed, and timber products.”

name: VTDigger
title: For Vermont cell users, breaking up is easy to do
description:
It’s a familiar reality for many people in Lamoille County: The phone call dropped. The texts won’t send.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  For Vermont cell users, breaking up is easy to do.
text:
Jewett Brook Road in the Roy Mountain Wildlife Management Area in Barnet on Wednesday, May 1, 2024. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
This story by Liberty Darr was first published in the News & Citizen on Oct. 1, 2026.
It’s a familiar reality for many people in Lamoille County: The phone call dropped. The texts won’t send.
Even in the height of this digital age, there are people without cell phone service.
Most recent driving test data from the state show that large swaths of the county have limited to zero cell phone service, even from major providers like Verizon and AT&T. The maps show a trail of small, red hexagons — each representing a measurement of distance — following steadily through places like Wolcott, Elmore, Eden and Belvidere.
These driving tests are how the Vermont Department of Public Service’s telecommunications and connectivity division keeps track of connectivity data across the state.
They are done almost exactly as it sounds. Staff from the division gear up with a bank of mobile cellphones and drive between 6,000 and 7,000 miles of road to test where the service reaches.
Each hex on the maps, the most recent of which is the 2024 and 2025 data, represents roughly three quarters of a square kilometer.
It’s granular — and that’s intentional.
That’s partly because the map provided to the state by cellphone providers isn’t always entirely accurate, according to Hunter Thompson, director of the state’s telecommunications and connectivity division.
“They’re projections based on propagation from their towers,” he said. “They’re great to look at. They’re very colorful. They give people a wonderful idea of where you may get cell phone service. But they’re not entirely accurate at the granular level that we are testing at.”
The division is nearing a decade of collecting this sort of data and is spearheading the state’s “10-Year Telecommunications Plan.” The last iteration was completed in 2024 and will again be updated in 2029.

Four smartphones connected to a power strip charging inside a wooden drawer. Photo via News & Citizen

And the data is telling the state some useful information. For example, 77% of the tests that had any sort of results in 2022 saw an increase in the data speed in 2024. Within that same time frame, there was a 36% improvement across the state for tests that passed.
While these could be considered wins, for Thompson, the work doesn’t stop. Cell service, he said, is no longer a privilege. Not only is it a disservice to the state’s at-risk population, since cellular service is needed to access state services for addiction or recovery, he added, “It is a bare necessity to participate in the digital economy.”
Safety first
Cell service is also necessary to dial 9-1-1 in emergencies.
Trevor Braun, an Elmore resident and member of the town’s fire department, knows this situation well. He’s been actively involved in the local conversation around finding solutions while working closely with FirstNet, a nationwide cellular network designed specifically for first responders and public-safety personnel. It is operated by AT&T under a 25-year federal contract and overseen by the First Responder Network Authority, part of the U.S. Department of Commerce.
“It is, I would say, potentially the biggest public safety hazard or risk in the town,” Braun said. “Because there’s so little coverage and non-existent coverage in so much of the town, when there are emergencies or accidents, people in some cases have to drive 10 to 20 minutes to get to a place just to report a serious accident or emergency.”
He recalled a recent situation in which a multi-car accident in Elmore couldn’t be reported until the passerby drove to Morrisville to get service.
FirstNet recently provided equipment that acts as small cellphone repeaters, which the town was able to install in the emergency shelters, like the fire department and the town garage.
Connectivity is also top of mind for Lamoille County Sheriff Roger Marcoux, who Tuesday morning was just leaving a meeting with FirstNet, after switching to the provider just a few months ago. Marcoux also chairs the state’s Enhanced 911 board.
“Where it affects us mostly is when I’ve got deputies on the road and they can’t use the radio or they’re trying to call in on the cell that doesn’t work, or if we’re trying to get information from a complainant,” he said.
Tower talk
Some of those trouble spots include the well-traveled Route 15 and Route 100 corridors, largely mirroring the data compiled from the state division.
A large part of the difficulty of sustaining reliable coverage in the area is the region’s general topography: mountainous peaks with narrow river valleys. This makes it difficult to reach all the nooks and crannies in the state and, in part, describes why certain areas of towns may be covered but others are not.
Thompson’s division at the state uses the drive test data to interface directly with providers, who may not even know that the services aren’t providing coverage in the way that was intended.
A large part of this work is incentivizing providers to come to these areas. Thompson has made budget requests to the state to increase the pool of money to do this work, but those requests have not been funded in recent years.

READ MORE

“We also have what’s called an amenable landlord list, where people will get hold of us and say, ‘I have land that I would like to put a cell tower on,’” he said. “We pass that on to the providers so that they can add it to their amenable landlord list.”
Cell tower applications go through the state’s Public Utility Commission, leaving little room for town or resident input — some towns’ residents don’t favor the aesthetics associated with a tall tower.
That topic took up a large portion of Waterville’s most recent Town Meeting Day, revolving largely around a plan to install a cell tower. Some residents voiced passionate opinions against such a project, with many upset with how it might impact the landscape.
The Hyde Park selectboard also just recently held a public hearing regarding a possible tower proposed by Verizon on Crabapple Lane.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Recent razor-thin result is a reminder of the importance of voting
description: Sometimes voting in South Dakota can seem like a lost cause. With Republicans dominating every state and national elected office, it seems like a foregone conclusion that they will win again. It’s easy to make excuses for sitting out this election.  Part of the problem is the less than stellar job that members of the […]
text:
A ballot box at the South Dakota Military Heritage Alliance in Sioux Falls, as seen during a primary election on June 2, 2026. (Photo by John Hult/South Dakota Searchlight)Sometimes voting in South Dakota can seem like a lost cause. With Republicans dominating every state and national elected office, it seems like a foregone conclusion that they will win again. It’s easy to make excuses for sitting out this election. 
Part of the problem is the less than stellar job that members of the state’s Democratic Party have done in recruiting candidates. Their candidate for U.S. Senate decided to call it a day, and they didn’t field a candidate for state attorney general. In the state legislative races, Democrats are running for 44 of the 105 seats in the Legislature. That means 58% of those seats won’t have a Democrat on the ballot competing for your vote. In many districts, seats in the Legislature were decided in the Republican primary.
If every Democrat on the legislative part of the ballot is elected, Republicans will still ease their way into automatic majorities in the House and Senate. Fortunately for voters, there’s more to hold your interest on Election Day than just seeing which Republican will be elected to office for the next two, four or six years. Even in a blushingly red state like South Dakota, there may be reasons for some Republican candidates to feel uneasy. 
[Voter Guide: 2026 general election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
It wasn’t too long ago that the city of Sioux Falls almost elected a Democrat as its next mayor. City elections are supposed to be nonpartisan, but some of the Republican candidates in the gubernatorial primary felt like it was their job to endorse the Republican in that race. 
Democrats have every right to feel good about one of their own coming so close to running the state’s largest city. Republicans who have dominated state politics for so long will be forgiven for feeling a little queasy about that outcome and what it might mean for the general election. 
Nicole Gronli, the Democratic candidate for the U.S. House, and Brian Bengs, the independent candidate for the U.S. Senate, have been touting polls that show them closing in on their opponents. Any candidate’s polling has to be taken with a grain of salt, but, in a year when there is supposed to be a “blue wave,” Republicans Marty Jackley and Mike Rounds may not have the easy road to victory that candidates from their party have enjoyed in the past. How much more interesting the politics in this state would be if having an “R” next to your name didn’t ensure an automatic win. 
The political competition doesn’t stop at the top of the ballot. During this election, many county races will be decided, too. Races for sheriff, auditor and county commissioner have a direct bearing on your safety and how your local tax dollars will be spent. 
In some communities, the election for city council members will be held in conjunction with the general election. The candidates chosen by voters in those nonpartisan elections will have a direct influence on the spending of local tax dollars. 
South Dakota voters will also be making decisions about four state constitutional amendments. They’ll decide the fate of a trust fund for unclaimed property, a back door method for getting the state out of funding expanded Medicaid, a measure that mirrors a law that already bars noncitizens from voting in South Dakota elections and an amendment that makes it tougher to change the state constitution by requiring a 60% favorable vote. 


Let us know what you think...


 

No matter what you may think about the need for these particular amendments, it’s plain that they touch on important issues of our day — state funding, access to Medicaid, voting rights and citizen access to changing the state constitution. The amendments alone are reason enough to show up on Election Day. 
Or show up sooner. Early voting is going on now and absentee ballots are also available. If you’re not registered to vote, get registered. The deadline is Oct. 19.
Making what you consider to be the right choices on the ballot requires some work on your part. Get a sample ballot at your courthouse to look over the candidates and the issues. Attend candidate forums or debates. You’ll make an informed decision by spending some time studying the candidates and the issues. South Dakota Searchlight offers an extensive Voter Guide with explanations of the constitutional amendments, links to the candidates’ websites and links to past news coverage. 
There’s too much at stake in this election to just sit on the sidelines. As citizens, it’s our duty to play a part in the election process. Remember the outcome of the mayoral election in Sioux Falls. It was decided by a handful of votes. That’s a wonderful example of every vote counting. Make sure yours gets counted, too.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Prevention should not be a buzzword. It should be at the heart of Missouri’s child welfare system
description: The growing attention being given to Missouri’s child welfare system offers a critical opportunity to address not only the challenges with the system, but the circumstances that bring families to a point of crisis — and into contact with the system in the first place. Children’s Division Director Sara Smith has made significant strides within her […]
text:
Members of the Missouri Child Welfare Task Force discuss child safety standards in Jefferson City, Missouri, on Oct. 5. Pictured from left are St. Louis County Chief Juvenile Officer Rick Gaines, Missouri State Courts Administrator Kathy Lloyd, Christian County Circuit Judge Jessica Kruse, Audrain County Associate Circuit Judge Melissa Buckman Young, Children's Division Director Sara Smith and State Rep. Melissa Schmidt (Steph Quinn/Missouri Independent).The growing attention being given to Missouri’s child welfare system offers a critical opportunity to address not only the challenges with the system, but the circumstances that bring families to a point of crisis — and into contact with the system in the first place.
Children’s Division Director Sara Smith has made significant strides within her department to reduce the backlog of child abuse hotline investigations, stem the extraordinary rates of frontline staff turnover, and address gaps in the state’s foster care system.
Gov. Mike Kehoe also recently signed an executive order creating the Missouri Child Welfare Task Force, a panel charged with issuing recommendations for the Legislature ahead of the 2027 legislative Session.
These improvements are important steps forward, and the progress being made should be recognized.
But while improving the systems that support children and families is necessary, lasting change requires us to look upstream at the systemic conditions that contribute to family stress and instability.
Problems at Children’s Division are a direct reflection of the struggles that families in poverty and in crisis face.
The scale and scope of child abuse, neglect, and state intervention we currently see in our state is itself preventable—a problem entirely within our ability to understand and to solve.
Successfully tackling many of the longstanding challenges within the Children’s Division will require us to acknowledge some inconvenient truths:

Children’s Division and DSS frontline staff handling the emotional and mental burden of child abuse and neglect investigations need — and deserve — vastly improved or restructured pay and compensation;
As a state and as a society, we must invest in the basic supports that help children thrive- and keep them out of the system in the first place: healthcare, food security, stable housing, consistent access to diapers, formula, clothing, and child care from trusted providers;
Finally, and possibly the most important and most difficult truth of them all: we have to muster the political will to tackle the root causes of the child welfare problem and the willingness to rebuild the system from the middle out, at the community level.

As the newly-constituted Child Welfare Task Force begins its work to understand the full scope of what children, families, and frontline professionals are experiencing, we have to push to ensure that the most cost-effective and proven method for reducing and eliminating child abuse and neglect is not left out of the discussion altogether: prevention.
Why is prevention widely recognized as an effective, efficient, and attractive approach?
Preventing child abuse and neglect means meeting parents exactly where they are  while also putting the health and safety of children first. Prevention makes keeping children and families together—safely—the top priority in any child welfare system.
There is a common misconception that child welfare intervention is primarily about the most extreme and heartbreaking cases that make headlines. Those cases do require immediate action. But the reality is that many families who come to the attention of child welfare—and drive up unmanageable caseload numbers—are facing challenges that could have been addressed much earlier with the right supports in place: a parent overwhelmed by circumstances, a family without enough food, a child who needs medical care, or a caregiver without anyone to call for help.
The Saint Louis Crisis Nursery has served Missouri families for over 40 years, keeping nearly 150,000 children safe and healthy since 1986. Through our work, we have witnessed a simple but powerful truth: when families do not have the support they need, children are more likely to experience crises that can bring them into contact with the child welfare system.
But we have also witnessed the opposite: when families receive timely support—safe child care during moments of crisis, access to basic necessities, connection to resources, and ongoing community-based support—the outcome changes drastically. Families stabilize. Parents gain confidence and tools. Children remain safely connected to the people who love them and the child welfare system has no reason to get involved.
When a caseworker arrives at a family’s door and finds a child whose needs are not being met because a family is struggling, what should we want our system to do? We should want it to connect that family with food, health care, safe child care, and meaningful support. We should want it to strengthen families before a crisis escalates.
Doing so is not a failure to protect children; it is exactly what protecting children looks like.
Missouri children deserve more than they currently are getting from our child welfare system, and we must be willing to examine and change the systems, policies, and practices that stand between children and families and the support they need to thrive.
Now is the time to raise our voices together and demand better. Now is the time to place prevention — and compassion — at the very heart of our approach to child welfare.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraskan in Greece​: Voting connects citizens born abroad to US
description: I first registered to vote on my 18th birthday. Perhaps many people do that, but my birthday is in June, and the next election was more than a year away. My interest in politics started long before then, and that is why I’m interested in the story of Nebraska’s Republican Party suing to prevent voting […]
text:
I first registered to vote on my 18th birthday. Perhaps many people do that, but my birthday is in June, and the next election was more than a year away. My interest in politics started long before then, and that is why I’m interested in the story of Nebraska’s Republican Party suing to prevent voting by U.S. citizens who have never lived in Nebraska.
My family’s influence certainly shaped how I feel about voting and civics. My father was an active member of the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers. My grandfather and uncles were members, and my oldest brother became the union’s business manager. Another brother became a Nebraska state senator.  Political discussions and Labor Day marches were part of my childhood.
After finishing college, I moved to Greece, where voting is compulsory. If someone wasn’t able to make it to the polls, they had to file a paper with the police. The ancient Greeks considered participation in civic life an ethical and moral duty. I have continued to vote in every Democratic primary and general election in Nebraska by requesting my absentee ballot each time, printing it, voting and taking it to the post office in time. I take the time to read about the candidates and make the effort to vote. I also take the time to write to my representative and senators, giving them my opinion on a variety of topics.
Living abroad gives me a unique perspective on the United States. Seeing how other people regard my homeland has always been an eye-opener. Most people held it in awe. Even now, despite the anti-immigration policies this administration is encouraging, moving to the U.S. is a dream for many. Those who have managed to get there as college students or professionals rave about the standard of living, the opportunities and the salaries.
My three children are all U.S. citizens, but have never lived there. I encouraged them to register to vote in the U.S., but only my daughter did so. I recently asked her why she wanted to vote, and she replied that it is one of her only ties to the country. She visited Nebraska several times while growing up and has fond memories of our big family and the abundance she saw there. She said she sees stories on the news about ICE raids, the millions of Americans who don’t have health insurance, the income inequality and other issues, and says maybe her vote could make a small difference.
I do understand, up to a point, the objections to allowing U.S. citizens who have never lived in Nebraska the right to vote. Why should someone who has never lived in the U.S. be able to decide on school board members or whether a judge should retain their seat? To be honest, I don’t vote for those positions, and my daughter didn’t either. But the president of the United States and members of Congress actually do affect people all over the world. Just look at this administration’s trade policy, elimination of foreign aid and, of course, the war with Iran. There’s not a person on the planet who hasn’t been affected.
I find it appalling that so many millions of Americans do not make the effort to vote and that many more are being disenfranchised by this administration and the Republican Party. I feel it is the duty of every citizen to be as informed as possible and choose the leaders they see fit. The efforts of the Nebraskan Republican Party to deny the right of even so few U.S. citizens is despicable. We should be making it easier to vote by opening more polling places and allowing voting on Sundays so no one has to take the day off work to cast their ballot, and mail-in voting shouldn’t be demonized.
Why is the Republican Party afraid of informed and active citizens? If every vote is really so important, then let them be counted.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Officials take another look at hospital use of offshore captive insurance companies
description: State officials are taking another close look at how Maryland’s nonprofit hospitals store billions of dollars in “captive insurance” companies domiciled in the Cayman Islands to determine if those funds should be subject to state taxes.
text:
Maryland Insurance Commissioner Marie Grant sits on a panel to discuss insurance with Maryland legislators. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)State officials are taking another close look at how Maryland’s nonprofit hospitals store billions of dollars in “captive insurance” companies domiciled in the Cayman Islands to determine if those funds should be subject to state taxes.
Hospital representatives, a national whistleblower and Maryland Insurance Administration officials met virtually this week in first public information gathering session on the question: How can Maryland officials ensure that nonprofit hospitals are not skirting state tax laws through the offshore insurance accounts?
It’s a question that state officials studied more than 10 years ago, but renewed attention to the potentially billions in untaxed that could be owed to the state came after a national whistleblower revived the issue during the 2026 session.
Most hospitals believed they were not subject to the tax. But some other nonprofit organizations may have been paying that tax, raising questions on whether the insurance administration was enforcing the tax or might have been missing millions owed to the state.
“It is very hard for the MIA to detect these in-house transactions, and paying the tax is essentially on the honor system,” Jason Schupp, the whistleblower largely responsible for the awareness of nonprofit hospitals using captive insurance, said during his testimony Wednesday.
Economic policy experts, whistleblower urge House to oppose captive insurance tax pause

“While a handful of captive owners faithfully report their captive insurance transactions and pay the premium tax … most do not,” said Schupp, who was largely anonymous until he publicly testified in April on the issue before the House Ways and Means Committee. He asserts that as much as $3 billion of nonprofit hospital funds are sitting in those offshore captives.
Captive insurance is when a business forms its own insurance company — a captive — to help cover financial losses that are not covered by commercial insurance. Hospitals may form a captive for the purpose of covering the costs of medical malpractice claims and cybersecurity risks, for example.
Maryland is one of 15 states that do not have a regulatory framework to let companies establish captives within the state. That’s why decades ago Maryland nonprofit hospitals set up captives in offshore locations such as the Cayman Islands.
But in the years since, there have been questions about whether the Maryland Insurance Administration should have been collecting money from nonprofit hospitals with offshore captive insurance, under a statute that subjects other nonprofits to those taxes.
Most hospitals believed they were not subject to the tax.
“It is really the hospital setting aside their own money and the amount of money that they set aside is based on actuarial assessments of the hospital’s risks,” said Andrew Nicklas, senior vice president of government affairs and policy and general counsel at the Maryland Hospital Association, in Wednesday’s meeting.
Nicklas told state officials that hospitals did not gain a tax deduction advantage by using captives. He also said that because Maryland restricts their rates, hospitals have limited avenues to raise money for insurance coverage against unique risks that they face.
That’s why they funnel their own money into captive insurance accounts in the first place.
“This is not something that is necessarily new, or novel, or certainly not nefarious,” he said, suggesting that state officials could ensure hospitals register their captives with the state to give greater transparency to those operations.
But Schupp said that the use of captive insurance left him “a bit uncomfortable” during his years working within the insurance industry.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
He explained that there were “two major benefits” when nonprofits like Maryland’s hospitals create captive insurance accounts.
“One is that the money can be brought outside of the nonprofit perimeter, so that accountability that we normally think of in a nonprofit, around things like executive spending, on travel, all that disappears because that’s kept down in the Caymans,” he said. “The other reason that we see here is that the transactions are extremely difficult for tax enforcement authorities to identify, and so, effectively, reporting of a captive transaction is on the honor system.”
The Wednesday conversation will inform a future study due to lawmakers by Jan. 1, 2027, which will also include recommendations from MIA about how to settle the issue. Those recommendations could inform legislation if deemed necessary.
Wednesday’s meeting is not the end of the conversation, said Insurance Commissioner Marie Grant.
“This public meeting is part of our informational gathering and consultation,” Grant said. “It is not the exclusive mechanism by which we are gathering information or consultation.”
The study grew out of a bill that would have required nonprofit hospitals to pay the tax going forward. Senate Bill 890, sponsored by Sen. Dawn Gile (D-Anne Arundel), would originally have clarified the issue by making hospitals’ captives exempt from the tax. That was amended to require that hospitals pay a 3% tax going forward, but economic policy advocates pushed to require back taxes.
Lawmakers then amended the bill to pause tax collection completely for two years while the MIA studied the issue. After additional pushback, lawmakers agreed to remove the moratorium on the tax, solely requiring the Maryland insurance Administration to study the issue, formalizing in law efforts that state insurance officials said they were already leaning toward.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Sexual assault survivors’ stories may shift over time — but that doesn’t mean they’re lying
description: If a person’s story changes in the weeks following an alleged sexual assault, are they not telling the truth? It’s a criticism I’ve seen on social media and heard in the public conversation surrounding the lawsuit filed in September 2026 by a plaintiff known as Jane Doe, a former student at Cornell University, accusing seven […]
text:
A majority of rape survivors don’t immediately recognize what they experienced as rape. (Photo by Ryan Murphy/Getty Images)If a person’s story changes in the weeks following an alleged sexual assault, are they not telling the truth?
It’s a criticism I’ve seen on social media and heard in the public conversation surrounding the lawsuit filed in September 2026 by a plaintiff known as Jane Doe, a former student at Cornell University, accusing seven male students of rape.
Initially, Doe discussed events with a friend but reportedly didn’t identify them as assault. It wasn’t until weeks later, when her experience was labeled as a gang rape by others, that she came forward to authorities.
Survivors are often questioned about how they relay their stories. When societal expectations about how rape survivors should respond do not align with the victim’s experience, it’s easy to assume that the victim is lying and the assailant is innocent.
Research indicates 60% to 70% of female rape survivors do not identify their experience as rape. That’s especially true for college students. Instead, rape survivors often describe their experience in more general terms, referring to it as “bad sex” or “miscommunication.” That’s both because of how sexual assault affects a survivor’s mind, brain and body and because of how society thinks about rape.
In my experience as a psychologist doing crisis intervention work with rape and sexual assault victims, it is very common for survivors to prefer to continue as if the assault never happened and to be driven by a strong desire to return to normalcy. While this seems counterintuitive, understanding the biological and psychological survival processes that sexual assault can activate may help explain why this response is perfectly logical.
 
Trauma’s immediate impact
Immediately following a rape, survivors — whether they characterize their experience as rape or not — often experience myriad symptoms broadly referred to as rape trauma syndrome. These symptoms include self-blame, emotional dysregulation and feelings of fear and humiliation. These symptoms often lead to problems with sleep, headaches, muscle tension and fatigue.
Psychologists generally diagnose symptoms consistent with rape trauma syndrome as acute stress disorder. Acute stress disorder reflects the unique psychological reactions immediately following trauma, whereas the longer-term effects are characterized as post-traumatic stress disorder, or PTSD.
People with acute stress disorder experience at least nine symptoms across several categories, including avoidance of trauma reminders, persistent negative mood and dissociation — defined as a disconnection between thoughts, feelings and bodily sensations. Other symptoms include intrusive experiences like nightmares or flashbacks, feeling like they are reexperiencing the trauma, constantly being on high alert and having overly intense emotional reactions to reminders of the traumatic event.
 
The brain on trauma
During acute stress, the brain shifts into survival mode.
Two of the main bodily systems activated during this period are the limbic system and the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis. The limbic system controls emotions, memory and behavior. The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis controls how the body responds to stress by regulating hormones like cortisol.
These systems mobilize the body’s key survival responses — fight, flight, freeze and fawn.
When the limbic system and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis kick in following trauma, the internal commotion that ensues takes over the brain’s ability to control thinking, planning and decision-making. This effectively prevents the brain from making accurate sense of what happened and from coping with the trauma in a healthy way.
 
Self-blame and denial are protective

For rape survivors, a common outcome of this neurobiological storm is self-blame — a tendency to hold themselves responsible for the events that led to the trauma. Generally, people believe they live in a world that feels safe and predictable, and they tend to adhere to the just world hypothesis, which posits that good things happen to good people. To preserve the illusion of control, safety and predictability, survivors blame themselves in an effort to to restore order to a world that has been incredibly shaken by trauma.
Rape survivors often experience hindsight bias — the belief that they should have been able to predict or prevent an assault. This belief, which further reinforces self-blame, is fortified by a culture in which rape prevention programs tend to focus on women as opposed to men, leading women to believe they alone are responsible for and can prevent rape.
Then there’s denial, a defense mechanism that can take the form of avoidance of or dissociation from the trauma. Because the reality of what has happened is overwhelming to the brain and psyche, denying or ignoring it provides a defense from the flood of emotion that follows trauma and helps reestablish a sense of stability.
Common rape stereotypes — for example, that rape is mainly committed by strangers in a novel situation, not by acquaintances during everyday experiences — reinforce these feelings. In fact, statistics indicate that 80% to 90% of women are raped by someone they know.
 
Judging a changing story
A person assessing the reactions of a rape and trauma survivor generally does so in a calm and collected frame of mind. Yet the actions they are judging were made under extreme duress — under mental and physical hurricane conditions, you could say.
For a survivor of rape, an inability to clearly name the assault for what it was is a common outcome of the biological and psychological factors at play during acute stress. This denial functions to preserve their identity and sanity during acute stress, restore order to their world and help them make rational sense of what has happened to them.
Breaking through these self-preservation mechanisms often takes time — time that observers too often misinterpret as a false accounting of what actually happened.

This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.
Michele Patterson Ford is a practicing licensed psychologist and lecturer at Dickinson College with more than 20 years of experience working in academic and clinical settings addressing and treating mental health and mental illness. name: Georgia Recorder
title: How Trump’s gutting of the Endangered Species Act could hurt three iconic Georgia species
description: This coverage is made possible through a partnership between WABE and Grist, a nonprofit environmental media organization. The Supreme Court once billed the Endangered Species Act “the most comprehensive legislation for the preservation of endangered species ever enacted by any nation.” Federal protections have been key to saving nearly 300 U.S. species — in[...]
text:
Researchers at Fort Stewart have helped the endangered red-cockaded woodpecker thrive through their efforts to install cavities (bottom left) for the birds to live in (bottom right). Larry Carlile (top right) has been aiding this effort for more than 25 years. (Stephen B. Morton/WABE)This coverage is made possible through a partnership between WABE and Grist, a nonprofit environmental media organization.
The Supreme Court once billed the Endangered Species Act “the most comprehensive legislation for the preservation of endangered species ever enacted by any nation.” Federal protections have been key to saving nearly 300 U.S. species — including the bald eagle, American alligator, and grizzly bear — from extinction. 
The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, which is primarily responsible for implementing the law, evaluates species and lists them as “endangered” or “threatened.” When a federal project or private development has the potential to harm a listed species or its habitat, project developers are required to consult with the Fish and Wildlife Service or obtain a permit prior to construction.
For the last several decades, the interpretation of two words in particular — “take” and “harm” —  have formed the backbone of the Nixon-era act. The law’s prohibition of “taking” an animal criminalized any attempts to “harass, harm, pursue, hunt, shoot, wound, kill, trap, capture, or collect” at-risk species. And its provision on “harm” ensured that degrading the habitat of a listed species could be penalized. These definitions have been key to the success of the law. 
But that all changed last month when the Trump administration determined that razing the places where endangered or threatened species breed, feed, and shelter would no longer be subject to federal penalties. In a separate internal memo, the administration also reinterpreted the definition of “take,” limiting it to instances of intentional killing of an endangered species. The administration contends the changes will correct past overreach.
“For years, federal agencies abused the ESA to obstruct lawful land use and burden American families and businesses,” Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said in a statement to the Associate Press. 
Nearly two dozen attorneys general have sued over some of these changes.
“These rule changes, when you zoom out, are an assault on threatened and endangered species unlike we’ve ever seen before,” said Elizabeth Forsyth, a senior attorney in the biodiversity defense program with Earthjustice, a nonprofit environmental law organization. “It’s an effort to eliminate habitat protections, eliminate automatic protections for threatened species, and give industry power.”
Climate change is making matters worse, as species struggle to adapt to warming temperatures and changing ecosystems. 
Below, we look at how three iconic Georgia species might fare as the regulatory framework that has kept them afloat is weakened. 
North Atlantic right whale
North Atlantic right whales got their name perversely. Because they stick close to shore and to the surface, and float when killed, they were the “right whale” to hunt. So right that humans hunted them nearly to extinction before the practice was banned in the 1930s.
That’s not why right whales are dying today.
“Nobody goes out and says, I’m gonna hit a right whale with my ship,” said Delcianna Winders, director of the Animal Law and Policy Institute at Vermont Law and Graduate School. 
A dead 1-year-old female North Atlantic right whale calf rests on a beach in Savannah, Georgia. Experts found evidence of blunt force trauma consistent with a vessel strike. Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation / NOAA permit 24359
But it happens anyway.
Though it’s not always possible to determine the cause of death for a whale, research shows that the leading cause is human activity: Ships strike the whales, and fishing gear tangles them up, leading to injury and death. It happens often enough that North Atlantic right whales have been experiencing what the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration calls an unusual mortality event since 2017, in which 43 have died, and 133 have been spotted injured or in poor health. About 380 whales remain, only 70 of which are breeding females.
More about efforts to track and protect right whales off Georgia’s coast.
Well before the latest changes to the Endangered Species Act, the Trump administration had already begun rolling back protections for right whales. In March, NOAA announced plans to rescind ocean speed restrictions designed to reduce the risk of vessel strikes. The agency later declined to expand the whales’ designated critical habitat to include their migratory route. The Biden Administration had proposed expanding the speed restrictions after years of pressure from advocates, but withdrew the plan shortly before Trump took office the second time.
The administration will likely use its new definition of “take” to bolster those actions, Winders said. “Now they can point to this and say, ‘Look, we can’t have speed limits under the law because it only applies to intentional direct activities.’”
A memo describing the change, signed by Fish and Wildlife Service Director Brian Nesvik, directly referenced whales. “A vessel that inadvertently strikes a whale has not taken it, because the vessel’s course was not set against the whale,” it said.
A North Atlantic right whale and calf swim about 19 nautical miles off Little St. Simons Island, Georgia, in 2025. Clearwater Marine Aquarium Research Institute / NOAA permit 26919
Right whales are “particularly vulnerable” to the changes, Winders said, both because of their critically low population figures and because their primary causes of death are incidental takes. 
“Right whales don’t have two years or four years or six years” to wait for a new president or Congress to restore their protections, Winders said. “This is going to impact them immediately.”
Eastern hellbender
Wildlife advocates with the Center for Biological Diversity and other organizations have been trying to get the eastern hellbender listed as endangered for more than a decade. In 2024, they came close. After Hurricane Helene felled trees and kicked up sediment, disturbing the sensitive salamander’s habitat, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service finally proposed the hellbender for protection, with a decision expected at the end of 2025. But the decision never came. In fact, not a single endangered species has been listed since Trump took office. 
The head of a hellbender (Matthew Pearson/WABE)
The eastern hellbender has enjoyed state protection in places like New York and North Carolina, and isolated populations in Missouri are federally protected. It’s considered “threatened” by the Georgia Department of Natural Resources. However, unlike species that have been federally designated as “endangered” or “threatened,” most populations of hellbenders have had no federal protection, even as populations have dwindled dramatically. The salamander is a homebody — once it finds a place it likes to live, it often stays there its entire life. An ancient remnant of the Ice Age, it has lived in the same streams and rivers for just about 160 million years and has been called a living fossil.
See more about hellbenders in Georgia
According to the Fish and Wildlife Service, its roughly 600 known historical populations have endured narrowing margins over the past few decades. More than 40% of those populations have vanished, and another 36% are in active decline. The hellbender breathes through its skin, meaning water pollution and sedimentation can cause disease and death. It thrives best in the cold, clear streams of the higher mountains in the Appalachian region, and shade cover is vital.  
The Center for Biological Diversity filed a lawsuit in February, demanding the Fish and Wildlife Service complete its decisionmaking process. Since then, though, there’s been no movement, with the next regulatory step listed as “to be determined,” along with hundreds of other endangered species whose protections have been similarly delayed.
According to Michael Gangloff, who studies freshwater life at Appalachian State University, human development is the biggest threat to hellbenders. But, he said, they’re also fighters. 
“These things are tough, and the fact that they’re still here, attests to their toughness,” he said. “They’re an ancient, ancient group of salamanders.”
Red-cockaded woodpecker
The Southeastern United States used to be a red-cockaded woodpecker’s paradise, with longleaf pine forest stretching across much of the region. Unlike many other woodpeckers that hollow out dead trees to nest, these black-and-white-spotted birds live exclusively in the trunks of living pine trees. They spend months or years hollowing out a suitable cavity, and they prefer to do it in mature trees. 
But finding suitable trees has become much harder than it was a century ago. Much of the South’s longleaf pine forest was clear-cut for timber and replaced by faster-growing species of pine. Management practices vary, but commercial timber operations often cut and replant pines before the trees are mature enough for a red-cockaded woodpecker’s liking, according to Joe Burnham, a wildlife biologist with the Georgia Department of Natural Resources. 
“They have pretty specific habitat requirements,” Burnham said. “There are a whole suite of species, both plant and animal, that evolved with this ecosystem over time that really have a hard time surviving elsewhere.”
Wildlife Biologists Tommy Holland holds a captured red-cockaded woodpecker before he tags and release it back to the longleaf pine forest where the endangered birds thrive. (WABE Photo by Stephen B. Morton)
Development is booming in Georgia, with much of the state’s forested land at risk of conversion to housing or more profitable forms of agriculture. The Trump administration’s policy changes, particularly its new definition of “harm,” could put red-cockaded woodpeckers at greater risk by removing protections for their habitat. As a result, more forests could become vulnerable to conversion, further shrinking the mature pine forests the birds rely on. 
More about red-cockaded woodpecker conservation in Georgia
Still, red-cockaded woodpeckers have made substantial strides since their 1973 Endangered Species Act listing, thanks in large part to efforts to restore longleaf pine habitat and transplant birds to suitable forests so they can reestablish themselves. In 2024, the federal Fish and Wildlife Service downlisted them from endangered to threatened. Despite the change, state- and region-level restoration efforts continue, Burnham said, because the woodpeckers need them — as do the many other endangered and threatened species that rely on the same habitat, including gopher tortoises and indigo snakes.
“We’re managing these stands for a multitude of species,” he said. “We’ve invested a lot of conservation effort into these species.”
