name: Mississippi Today
title: Isaias makes landfall along the US Gulf Coast as a dangerous Category 2 hurricane
authors: By Sophie Bates, Emilie Megnien and John Seewer, Associated Press
description: An American flag flaps in the wind generated by the effects of Isaias on an empty beach on Friday, Oct. 9, loom overhead on Friday, Oct. 9, 2026, in Mon Louis Island, Ala. (AP Photo/Octavio Jones)
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
GULF BREEZE, Fla. (AP) — Hurricane Isaias crashed into the U.S. Gulf Coast as a dangerous Category 2 storm on Friday, lashing communities with wind and rain and threatening to flood low-lying areas where residents were advised to evacuate ahead of its arrival.
The first hurricane of the Atlantic season made landfall near Destin, Florida, the Miami-based National Hurricane Center said. It had maximum sustained winds of 105 mph (169 kph). The storm weakened to just below major hurricane status before it came ashore.
People sit outside an evacuation shelter as Hurricane Isaias approaches Pensacola, Fla., Friday, Oct. 9, 2026. (AP Photo/Gerald Herbert)
High winds whipped palm trees and thundering waves crashed along the beaches of the Florida Panhandle and Alabama on Friday as Isaias approached.
“The storm is here. Buckle down at this point. Don’t be getting out on the roads,” Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said at a news conference, adding that flash flooding would be a hazard “throughout the region.”
Forecasters warned of a significant storm surge, damaging winds, flooding and possibly even tornadoes before the storm loses steam as it moves inland and delivers strong winds and rain well north into Atlanta.
Hurricane-force winds lashed the Gulf shoreline in the low-lying coastal area known for powdery white sand beaches that are dotted with vacation homes, waterfront bars and seafood shacks.
In Mobile, Alabama, officials reported downed trees and power lines, while Emerald Coast Utilities Authority, which serves parts of Florida, issued a boil-water notice for its customers.
More than 400,000 customers in Florida and Alabama were without power Friday evening, according to poweroutage.com.
Residents in Panama City, Florida, braved the rain while filling sandbags Friday to protect their houses.
“I mean, it’s just the nature of the beast. It’s Florida,” said Corliss Stone, who works for the fire department.
Many will brave Isaias at home
One of the biggest concerns is a storm surge that could be as high as 6 to 9 feet (1.8 to 2.7 meters), according to the hurricane center. Places most at risk include Florida’s Pensacola Beach and the Gulf Islands National Seashore.
Daniel and Brand Harp, of Lebanon Tenn., here on vacation, pack their belongings to evacuate in the morning as Hurricane Isaias approaches Pensacola Beach, Fla., Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026. (AP Photo/Gerald Herbert)
Anne Petzold, who lives with her husband in the Florida beach community of Gulf Breeze, said everyone in their neighborhood planned to ride out the storm. The couple installed hurricane shutters and picked up anything in their yard that could turn into a projectile.
“Everybody does what they can do, everybody asks if they need help — they ask for help, they offer help. All good,” she said. “It’s just another adventure.”
Several counties announced mandatory evacuations while Mobile, Alabama, imposed a curfew beginning Friday evening until morning.
In a sign of how serious the warnings are, dozens of Waffle Houses in the Florida Panhandle were closed, according to the company’s website. The beloved Southern breakfast chain is known for staying open through severe weather and often is a measuring stick of a storm’s severity.
Kelsei Frazier, a Florida-native living in Pace who is no stranger to hurricanes, knows all about the Waffle House Index.
“We joke because if Waffle House is still open, then you know it’s not a bad hurricane, but all the Waffle Houses that I know of within at least a normal range from us are closed,” said Frazier. “Which is a pretty big deal.”
DeSantis warned residents to expect power outages, gasoline shortages and closures of bridges and highways.
The state’s National Guard deployed about 5,000 soldiers and airmen to help with the response, and search and rescue teams were ready to respond, while some prisons evacuated inmates.
The whole region could get soaked
Isaias is expected to weaken and be downgraded to a tropical storm by Saturday afternoon, the center said.
Still, heavy rain is forecast as it moves inland, with 4 to 8 inches (10 to 20 centimeters) or even more expected through the weekend from southern Alabama to southwestern Georgia.
Jason Coffey boards up a convenience store at a gas station as Hurricane Isaias approaches Pensacola Beach, Fla., Friday, Oct. 9, 2026. (AP Photo/Gerald Herbert)
Isaias, which is the first hurricane to hit the eastern U.S. since Milton tore up the Gulf Coast of Florida in 2024, also is expected to bring heavy rain and potential flooding to much of the Southeast over the weekend, and then to parts of the Midwest and Northeast into Monday.
Isaias grounds flights but likely to miss oil hubs
The storm grounded most Friday flights at several Panhandle airports, including all flights into and out of Destin-Fort Walton Beach Airport. President Donald Trump, meanwhile, scrapped his plans to attend Saturday’s football game between the University of Georgia and the University of Alabama in Tuscaloosa. He said he didn’t want to disrupt the emergency response.
Isaias was expected to miss the oil industry’s biggest hubs along the Gulf Coast, but fuel prices could rise if power outages shut down refineries for processing crude, industry experts said.
On Dauphin Island, a barrier island off the Alabama coast, Mayor Jeff Collier said he didn’t expect major damage, “but at the same time, these things are very fickle and a little jog here or there, or some last-minute increase in strength — we just have to be prepared for the worst.”
Meanwhile in the Pacific, Hurricane Simon became a Category 2 storm on Friday and was expected to strengthen further before making landfall in Mexico this weekend.
Tropical Storm Rachel was also expected to bring heavy winds and rain to northern Mexico and Southern California over the weekend.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: State report shows heating fuel prices are at a record high in rural Alaska
description: The average price of a gallon of heating fuel — No. 1 diesel — in rural Alaska reached a record $7.97 per gallon in August, according to the latest biannual survey conducted by the Alaska Division of Community and Regional Affairs. The rural average, based on a survey of 100 communities taken between July 15 […]
text:
Petty Officer 3rd Class Brandon Dawson, a U.S. Coast Guard Marine Safety Task Force member, chats with a community representative at a fuel facility in St. Michael in the Bering Strait region during an inspection conducted on July 28, 2022. (Photo by Petty Officer 1st Class Nate Littlejohn/U.S. Coast Guard)The average price of a gallon of heating fuel — No. 1 diesel — in rural Alaska reached a record $7.97 per gallon in August, according to the latest biannual survey conducted by the Alaska Division of Community and Regional Affairs.
The rural average, based on a survey of 100 communities taken between July 15 and Aug. 24, was up 23% from January and the highest nominal price on record since the survey began in 2005. 
Adjusted for inflation, prices were higher in 2008-2009 and 2011-2014. But Steve Colt, research professor at the University of Alaska’s Center for Energy and Power, noted that heating fuel prices have continued to climb since the state conducted the summer survey.
By the time the next survey takes place in January, prices could be at an inflation-adjusted record as well.
“I fear the worst is yet to come,” he said by email.
In July, rural Alaska diesel prices were 44 percent higher than the national average. 
On July 6, the U.S. average price of diesel was $4.58. That had risen to $6.20 by Oct. 5, indicating that rural Alaska prices may now be near $9 per gallon. 
That was already the average price in Western Alaska this summer; other rural areas, particularly in Southeast Alaska, had lower prices.
Local prices vary, depending on when the local community ordered its fuel and when it arrived by barge; only a handful of surveyed rural communities in eastern Interior Alaska have road connections. 
Ordinarily, rural Alaska sources its fuel from Asia, but the U.S. war on Iran has caused shortages in that region. At least one company supplying rural Alaska switched to fuel from the Gulf of Mexico instead, adding shipping costs. 
In July, DCRA’s survey found the average rural price of gasoline was $7.56 per gallon, up 14% from January.
Prices in some communities were well above that average, including in Kokhanok, which had the highest reported price, at $14.50 per gallon. Hughes reported $13 per gallon, Grayling $12.50 and Arctic Village $12 per gallon.
The new survey does not include Shungnak, where prices exceeded $26 per gallon in August due to a local shortage and the need to fly in fuel.

Some of those ordered to evacuate were University of West Florida students living in on-campus dormitories in Pensacola. UWF’s houses about 1,500[...]
text:
The entrance to University of West Florida, situated in the northwest corner of the state in Pensacola. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)PENSACOLA — Evacuation orders for coastal and low-lying areas have been issued for counties across the Florida Panhandle over the past two days as powerful Hurricane Isaias, fueled by warm Gulf waters, intensified.
Some of those ordered to evacuate were University of West Florida students living in on-campus dormitories in Pensacola. UWF’s houses about 1,500 students amid a student body of around 15,000.
UWF sent an email after 8 p.m. Wednesday telling students the campus, including dorms, would close Thursday at 7 p.m. Students were required to unplug their refrigerators and other electronics.
Students with “no safe alternative” were told a UWF shelter of last resort “may” be available. Those who wanted to take advantage of the offer were told they had a one-hour window to do so Friday morning.
The email warned, though, that it was an “emergency safety option” and “not a traditional shelter or an alternative housing arrangement.” Conditions would be basic and “potentially uncomfortable.”
Students were told they had to prepare for three days in the shelter and to bring their own bedding, toiletries, drinking water and nonperishable food. No pets would be welcome. And if students left the shelter, even for a short time, they wouldn’t be allowed back in.
Twenty-eight students were admitted to the shelter, UWF told the Phoenix Friday. The Phoenix was not allowed inside the facility to speak to any of the students.
Parental criticism
A look inside University of West Florida’s shelter of last resort in Pensacola. (Photo via UWF)
UWF’s action spurred criticism from some parents, who, on a Facebook page, voiced disappointment the university did not provide information sooner.
The Phoenix attempted to reach several parents who chimed in on the post for comment but was not successful.
Kristi Foley Kervaski, a Santa Rosa Beach resident and mother of a UWF student, told the Phoenix in a telephone interview Friday that she was touched by some of the parents’ comments on the group page.
“That’s why I opened my door, because my mom’s in New York and she’s freaking out and I’m 53 years old,” Kervaski said. “So, I can only imagine someone that doesn’t live in Florida sending their baby off to another state, and then having the fear of not knowing. I think that’s probably the worst: it’s the not knowing what to expect inside of a hurricane.”
Kervaski directed her son, Mason Kervaski, to make clear to other students that his family would take in students.
No one took Kristi or Mason Kervaski up on their offers.
Good Samaritans
It wasn’t just families of UWF students offering temporary shelter on the UWF FB page.
Olive Baptist Church coordinated a network of members to take in otherwise homeless UWF students. The gym at the church is host to power line workers coming to town.
Associate Pastor Tim Hunter told the Phoenix the church has banded together through its student ministry and older members to house students who needed a place to go.
Hunter said the church was working with the university to direct students to shelter, too, if the university shelter doesn’t work.
“For the most part, it seems like, within network, a relationship, students have been able to find housing if needed, so a lot of it will be organic, but I’m able and willing to help as students reach out,” Hunter said.
Hunter said the church’s membership and leadership is “ready to respond and love on the community and serve as needed.”
Pictures of the shelter provided by UWF show sandwiches and chips available.
The campus is to remain closed at least through Monday.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Want to take a stand for Banned Book Week? Start next time you’re at the ballot box
description: Maryland law has very specific rules for removing books from school library shelves, but that doesn't always stop a determined local school board, writes Sonia Kumar, which is why she says the fight against book banning begins with voting for our school boards.
text:
Banned and restricted books. (Photo illustration by Sarah Ladd/Kentucky Lantern)This Banned Books Week (Oct. 4-10), Marylanders should pay attention to what is happening on our local school boards. In Harford County, for example, a court will hear arguments later this month about the school board’s decision to yank “Flamer” from all library school shelves.
“Flamer” tells the story of Aiden, a Filipino American teenager spending the summer at Boy Scout camp before his first year of high school. He is struggling to figure out who he is. He’s embarrassed. He’s bullied. He prays. He tries to square his faith, which is central to him, with his realization that he is attracted to other boys. At one low point, he thinks about ending his life. Near the end, a letter arrives from his best friend back home, hand-lettered on the page: “There is nothing wrong with you.”
The semi-autobiographical, vividly illustrated graphic novel by Mike Curato has been lauded by critics as “a book that will save lives.” One Horn Book reviewer wrote that it speaks to kids going through exactly what Aiden does, adding, “I wish I had had this book fifty years ago.”
For a time, “Flamer” was available to Harford County students who might want to read it. No student was required to.  And any parent who didn’t want their kid to read it could say so.
Then a Harford parent asked that “Flamer” be removed from school libraries after seeing a Fox News report about it.  She hadn’t read the book but feared it might “plants seeds in the heads of children.”




Your opinion matters

We suggest a 750-word limit and reserve the right to edit or reject submissions. We do not accept columns that are endorsements of candidates, and no longer accept submissions from public officials, elected officials or political candidates.
Opinion pieces must be signed by at least one individual using their real name. We do not accept columns signed by an organization. Commentary writers must include a short bio and a photo for their bylines.
Views of writers are their own.




Under the 2024 Maryland Freedom to Read Act, schools to have a process for reviewing such objections. A committee including parents, school personnel and students was trained on legal standards. Every member read the book, took notes, and weighed the parent’s concerns against its content and literary value.  They discussed its age-appropriateness and community standards. Then they voted to keep it in high school libraries, noting the parent remained free to tell the school her child was not allowed to borrow the book. The superintendent agreed.
The parent — who still had not read “Flamer” — appealed to the local school board. She was not asking for the right to decide whether her child could read “Flamer.” She already had that right. She sought a ruling that no one else’s child could read it.
The local board granted her request. Unlike the committee — which read the book, considered the objection, applied legal standards and explained its reasoning — the board did none of those things. After a hearing held without public notice, it voted 5-3 to pull “Flamer” from every school library in the county. The decision called the book “pervasively vulgar” but didn’t say how members reached that conclusion. The record suggests members reviewed selected passages without context, but not who chose them or which ones. The board declined to release the record of its deliberations, claiming they were privileged.
Board members’ own words from other meetings are telling. One said the book should be removed because of its “demeaning reflection on the Church.” (The Freedom to Read Act forbids removing books “because of partisan, ideological, or religious disapproval.”) Another said that if the committee chose to keep the book, she would revisit the entire review process because “parents do not want their kids exposed to these books.”
Community members appealed to the State Board of Education, which took the rare step of reversing the local board’s decision as arbitrary and unreasonable. It found no evidence that board members had read the book, let alone engaged with the committee’s reasoning. The local board has challenged that decision in state court. A judge will decide the legal question.
The rest of us should ask a related one: Who is serving on our local school boards and what are their priorities? In 2024, the Maryland Library Association reported that book challenges in the state had risen more than 130% since 2019.  And in some local school boards, book challengers have found a receptive audience.
Most of us don’t follow school board races closely. It’s hard to know what a candidate stands for, and the stakes can feel small. They aren’t. Local boards decide whether a teenager in a small town can find a book about someone like him, or a book about someone nothing like him, which may be just as important.
Parents can decide what their own kids should read. But that is different from deciding for everyone else. When we vote for school board members, we are choosing who understands the difference.

name: Mississippi Today
title: MVSU basketball player was reportedly warned about his expired immigration status years before ICE detained him
description: Qingfang Pang played forward as a sophomore in 2025 for the Mustangs basketball team at Monroe University in New York before transferring to Mississippi Valley State University.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Years before immigration officers arrested a Mississippi Valley State University basketball player last week, the school he previously played for said it warned him to correct his immigration status — contradicting his attorney’s earlier claim that the student athlete didn’t know his visa had expired.
But Qingfang Pang, the 6-foot-9-inch player born in China, received warnings as early as two years ago — when his previous college, Monroe University in New York, advised him to restore his status after learning it had lapsed in September 2024, spokesperson Jacqueline Ruegger told Mississippi Today.
His attorney, former professional basketball player Marcus Session, said Friday the information was news to him. 
“It doesn’t seem like they’re forthcoming with the right information because they continue to allow a student who’s on an expired visa to attend for two years after they supposedly warned him,” Session told Mississippi Today. “This doesn’t make sense.”
Pang previously met with another attorney at Monroe’s recommendation to discuss his expired status, Ruegger said. But Session said Pang told him that he didn’t know his visa had expired until MVSU recently alerted him of the issue.
In the years since Monroe reportedly warned Pang to correct his immigration status, he continued to play basketball for the Monroe University Mustangs, before joining the Delta Devils this academic year.  Under federal immigration law, if Pang were on the main international F-1 student visa, his records should have listed that he had officially transferred to MVSU before classes started.
Although MVSU’s semester kicked off in August, Ruegger and Session said the university didn’t contact Monroe for Pang’s international-student records until this week — after immigration authorities had already arrested him. MVSU did not communicate a reason for the potential delay in its request, according to Ruegger. Mississippi Valley did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Before Mississippi Today learned of the potential delay, MVSU spokesperson Donnell Maxie said the school’s international student office “wouldn’t delay” on paperwork.
“We’re not going to play with that,” Maxie said. “I mean, we’re not a big university with a lot of resources, so we’re just getting by as it is.”
Pang is now in the custody of Immigration and Customs Enforcement at the Richwood Correctional Center in Louisiana, according to the agency’s website. Session previously told WJTV that Pang was detained last week after MVSU alerted him that his visa had expired. When Pang tried to fly to New York to meet with his sponsor, a family friend, to correct his status, ICE arrested and detained him, Sessions said.
The Department of Homeland Security wrote in an email Friday that Pang’s immigration status expired in September 2024, a day after he started his first year playing basketball at Monroe.
“He legally entered the U.S. on November 17, 2023 on a temporary basis not to exceed September 5, 2024, but illegally overstayed,” DHS wrote. “This administration will not ignore the rule of law.”

title: University of Northern Iowa fundraising campaign ends with more than $340 million
description: The University of Northern Iowa’s fundraising campaign garnered a record amount of donations that put it more than $90 million ahead of its original goal. The Cedar Falls university’s “Our Tomorrow: The Campaign for UNI” initiative, publicly announced in 2022 but “quietly launched” in 2018, according to a Friday news release, has raised $342,842,222 from […]
text:
The University of Northern Iowa announced Friday it has raised more than $340 million through its years-long fundraising campaign. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)The University of Northern Iowa’s fundraising campaign garnered a record amount of donations that put it more than $90 million ahead of its original goal.
The Cedar Falls university’s “Our Tomorrow: The Campaign for UNI” initiative, publicly announced in 2022 but “quietly launched” in 2018, according to a Friday news release, has raised $342,842,222 from more than 34,000 donors.
“Throughout my time at UNI, I have been continually inspired by the Panther Family’s commitment to our students’ success,” UNI President Mark Nook said in the release. “A total of 34,031 alumni, employees and friends demonstrated that commitment by choosing to invest in UNI’s future, making the Our Tomorrow campaign the most successful fundraising campaign in UNI history.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Officially announced during homecoming celebrations Friday evening, the campaign lasted eight years before closing June 30. The campaign began with a $250 million goal, which the university surpassed two years ahead of schedule in 2024. The goal was then raised to $300 million.
More than 147,900 gifts, 58 of which topped $1 million, made up the fundraising total, the release stated, with a median gift of $100 and 47% of donations representing the donors’ first gift to the institution. UNI saw donations from all 50 states and 17 countries.
Through the campaign, the release stated the university has established 556 new scholarship funds with $108 million in donations, 72% of which was endowed. Endowed support through the campaign totaled $159 million, and UNI’s endowment grew during the Our Tomorrow campaign from $113 million to $267 million.
Around one-third of the raised funds went to supporting academic programs, including nursing, business, engineering and more, and faculty saw $41 million in donations to support their work. Other student supports, including internships, clinical work, career preparation and other experiences received $7 million in donations, and undergraduate research received $2.1 million.
Panther Athletics at UNI received $74 million in campaign support, including $18 million for athletic scholarships, and $50 million went to capital projects on campus, the release stated.
Nook said in the release that all UNI community members should feel proud of the impact the campaign is making on students and the institution, now and in the future.
“Our donors have helped UNI meet the needs of students today while building resources that will support generations to come,” said Jim Jermier, vice president for university advancement and president of the UNI Foundation, in the release. “At the beginning of this campaign, we asked, ‘What does the world need from us tomorrow?’ Our alumni and friends answered with a belief in our students and investments that will shape the future of UNI.”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah group says there’s a faster way to block Flock cameras  — without legislation
description: A group opposed to Flock cameras says Utah transportation managers hold the keys to the future of the technology on state roads.
text:
Flock Safety cameras are mounted on a pole in the parking lot of the Home Depot in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)A group opposed to automated license plate readers in Utah says state transportation managers largely hold the keys to the future of the technology on state roads, even though they don’t use it themselves.  
The nonprofit Utah Civic Compact is urging the Utah Department of Transportation to cut its contract with the company, a move they say would sharply limit the number of cameras and the surveillance they conduct. 
Members of the group are lobbying state lawmakers for tighter restrictions on license plate data, but they told reporters Friday that immediate intervention from UDOT would be faster and easier than an act from the Legislature.
Utah lawmakers are eyeing new Flock camera regulations amid misuse controversies

They found the workaround by reading line-by-line through the agency’s contract with Flock Group Inc., which allows it to end the agreement centered on installations in the event it “determines that the public does not support the Company’s activities,” according to a copy provided to Utah News Dispatch.
Utah Civic Compact members say widespread public outcry in recent months shows Utahns disapprove of the technology, noting in some cases the cameras have been vandalized or cut down. 
“They do not trust this new technology, and they do not feel safe when they are being surveilled, cataloged, and surveilled and and watched,” said Clark Dice, a spokesperson for the group, at Friday’s news conference at the Capitol in Salt Lake City.
The devices and the vast trove of data they collect have met strong public outcry centered on privacy concerns and cases of police throughout the country improperly using them to stalk people they know. 
Flock Safety cameras are mounted on a pole in the parking lot of the Home Depot in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
While Utah’s transportation department is a third party granting permits for the cameras along state highways at the request of law enforcement agencies, it’s also a party with the ability to help restore trust in government that’s been damaged by misuse use of the cameras, Dice said. 
At the Department of Transportation, attorneys were looking over the contract Friday, said spokesperson John Gleason. He said the department’s focus right now is on verifying the cameras bordering state roads have the proper permits, and it’s still working to count them all. 
“We wouldn’t be determining the big-picture questions of whether these cameras should be out there or, you know, what the purpose is,” Gleason said. “So those types of questions would have to go to the law enforcement agencies that put them out there.” 
He said the department considers matters of equipment, highway safety and paperwork instead. It cannot access the information obtained by the devices and doesn’t determine the location, number of cameras or how they operate, Gleason said. 
Flock Safety cameras are mounted on a pole in the parking lot of the Home Depot in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
While the state agency is required by law to permit cameras designated for official police use, Gleason said he didn’t know under which circumstances, if any, the department could pull a particular permit. 
The cameras have long been a tool for law enforcement across the country, with police saying it’s a major help in solving crimes. Last month at the Capitol, law enforcers urged lawmakers to keep the technology in Utah, pledging to use it responsibly. 
For its part, the Flock network says its platform helps to solve about 2,000 crimes per day. 
Utah governor says he’s ‘deeply troubled’ by Flock cameras, calls for review to protect privacy

State leaders have expressed their own misgivings about the technology, with Gov. Spencer Cox saying in August he thinks Americans “should be deeply concerned” about police combing through the data for personal reasons. 
He directed the Utah Privacy Governing Board and the Utah Privacy Commission to review the state’s rules and regulations for the cameras, he said, “especially how they’re being used with local agencies to make sure that they are not being abused, to make sure that the public understands how and when they can be used, and if there are abuses taking place, people are held accountable.”
Existing state law restricts use of the cameras to law enforcement for an active criminal investigation, to arrest someone with an outstanding warrant, find a missing or endangered person, or track down a stolen car. 
Using or sharing the data for another reason is a misdemeanor offense, but Utah Civic compact says there’s a gap in the law because there’s no way to ensure out-of-state agencies are following Utah’s requirements.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Two Alaska governor candidates advocate lower minimum wage, rollback of sick leave law
description: If elected, Republican governor candidates Dave Bronson and Bernadette Wilson said they would seek to roll back Alaska’s mandatory sick leave law and eliminate a minimum wage increase approved by voters in 2024.  The two spoke at a forum hosted Wednesday in Juneau by the Juneau Chamber of Commerce, which is in favor of rolling […]
text:
Alaska gubernatorial candidates Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins (left), and Republicans Bernadette Wilson (center) and Dave Bronson (right) attend a forum hosted by the Juneau Chamber of Commerce in Juneau on October 7, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)If elected, Republican governor candidates Dave Bronson and Bernadette Wilson said they would seek to roll back Alaska’s mandatory sick leave law and eliminate a minimum wage increase approved by voters in 2024. 
The two spoke at a forum hosted Wednesday in Juneau by the Juneau Chamber of Commerce, which is in favor of rolling back the sick leave law.
Four candidates are running for governor in this year’s general election — Wilson, Bronson, Democratic candidate Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, and Republican candidate Treg Taylor. All except Taylor attended Wednesday’s event.
Seasonal employers — particularly in the seafood and tourism industries — are seeking to roll back the law because they said some seasonal workers have begun using sick leave as terminal leave at the end of the summer.
This spring, the Alaska House voted 22-18 on a bill to end sick leave immediately for seasonal workers and employers with nine or fewer workers. The rollback bill failed to pass the Senate before the end of the legislative session but is expected to return in 2027.
“I absolutely support an exemption for seasonal workers,” said Wilson.
“I would support introducing legislation to go back and repeal that ballot measure. It did not have the effect that it needed,” she said.
The 2024 ballot measure included both mandatory sick leave and a minimum wage increase. Under the law, Alaska’s minimum wage increased from $11.73 per hour to $13 per hour in 2025, and $14 this year. It will rise to $15 per hour in 2027, then rise with inflation each year after that.
Wilson said after Wednesday’s event that she does support repealing both the sick leave requirement and the minimum wage increases prescribed by the 2024 ballot measure.
So did Bronson, who said that while he isn’t proposing to eliminate the state’s minimum wage altogether, he wouldn’t mind doing so.
“In most small businesses, as you know, there’s no greater cost really than your employees, and to raise the cost of your greatest cost is prohibitive. My belief is that government shouldn’t be in the business of telling small business and private enterprise what to be doing in this regard, in the first place,” he said. “Mandatory sick leave, minimum wage — I would repeal them both because small business will figure this out.”
Kreiss-Tomkins, sharing the stage with Wilson and Bronson, was more moderate on the sick leave issue but said he does support changes to what voters enacted.
“Broadly speaking, I support paid sick leave,” Kreiss-Tomkins said. He added that he has heard from seafood and tourism trade organizations, “and I do think it is appropriate to look at amendments to the paid sick leave law.”
“I don’t know if that’s a wholesale exemption, but certainly making adjustments to the law that recognize the unique dynamics around seasonal industries and seasonal businesses is something that makes sense,” he said.
After the debate, Kreiss-Tomkins said he opposes lowering the minimum wage.
Taylor, by text message afterward, said he also supports amending the sick leave law.
“Yes, I agree!” he said in a text message sent through his campaign manager, April Gettys, “139,534 Alaskans work for small businesses, and I want to fix this law so those businesses can keep hiring and keep their doors open – Alaska should lead the nation in job opportunities. That means working with the Legislature to adjust the statute so it works for the corner café, the seasonal operator and the rural business. More jobs, more paychecks, more families staying in Alaska.”

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: LDS Church makes $1 million donation to anti-Prop 1 PAC ahead of Idaho’s general election
description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints has donated $1 million to an Idaho political action committee, or PAC, opposing the abortion rights initiative on the ballot this November.  The donation went to the Too Extreme for Idaho Political Action Committee, which opposes the initiative. “While The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints […]
text:
The Boise Temple of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints as seen on Feb. 5, 2025. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun)The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints has donated $1 million to an Idaho political action committee, or PAC, opposing the abortion rights initiative on the ballot this November. 
The donation went to the Too Extreme for Idaho Political Action Committee, which opposes the initiative.
“While The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints remains neutral toward political candidates, it actively addresses ballot initiatives it believes carry significant moral consequences,” the church said in a statement. “Accordingly, the Church has joined a coalition of like-minded organizations and individuals in Idaho to dedicate resources toward defeating Proposition 1.”
Supporters and opponents of Idaho’s abortion rights initiative, Prop 1, have raised millions

If passed, the voter initiative would repeal Idaho’s abortion laws, enumerate rights related to reproductive health, and create liability protections for healthcare providers who provide abortion and other reproductive healthcare. 
The Idaho Falls radio station NewsTalk 107.9 first reported the donation on Thursday. The Idaho Capital Sun confirmed the donation with a spokesperson for the church on Friday. 
The large donation comes after Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador published an opinion in August that says churches are allowed to donate money to political campaigns — including for and against Proposition 1 — without disclosing their donors, as long as they don’t ask members to donate specifically for the campaign, Boise State Public Radio reported. 
Leaders from the church, widely known as the Mormon church, issued a letter against Prop 1 in September, the Salt Lake Tribune reported. The letter was read to congregations last month, the church’s assistant communications director Brian Whitlock said in an email. 
“Our long-held stance on abortion remains clear and unchanged,” the four-member U.S. Central Area Presidency of the LDS Church wrote in the letter.
The church, which opposes elective abortions, posted its stance on abortion online. It allows for possible exemptions in cases of rape and incest, if a “competent physician determines that the life or health of the mother is in serious jeopardy,” or a “competent physician determines that the fetus has severe defects that will not allow the baby to survive beyond birth.”
“Even these exceptions do not automatically justify abortion,” the statement said. “Abortion is a most serious matter. It should be considered only after the persons responsible have received confirmation through prayer.” 
Idaho’s abortion ban allows the procedure to prevent the death of the mother and in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester with a police report. Doctors who provide abortions outside of those exemptions face felony penalties, including minimum prison time, and potential civil lawsuits brought by family members of the aborted fetus. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Other churches, faith-based groups have contributed to campaigns for and against Prop 1 

The LDS Church isn’t the first or only faith-based organization to contribute to the campaigns related to the ballot measure, but it is the largest reported donation from a church-affiliated group. 
Groups attached to Catholic organizations have contributed $7,161 to the Too Extreme for Idaho PAC, campaign finance reporting shows. The Roman Catholic Diocese of Boise contributed $2,000, and Catholic fraternal groups, called Knights of Columbus Councils, contributed the rest, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported.  
The image above is overhead view of the Cathedral of St. John the Evangelist. The Catholic Cathedral is the seat of the Diocese of Boise. (Photo courtesy of Deacon Gene Fadness)
The Catholic Diocese of Boise could not be reached for comment for this story after multiple emails and phone calls. The diocese has publicly opposed the initiative. 
Bishop Peter Christensen in late July posted a statement in opposition to the ballot measure and encouraged other members of the church to voice their opposition. 
“I strongly encourage you to vote NO this November. Our response must not be rooted in anger or fear, but in steadfast faith, charity, and an unwavering commitment to the truth about human life,” Christensen wrote. 
He said the diocese will be encouraging parishes to offer “pro-life themed Masses” and pastors to communicate “awareness raising information in bulletins and parish communications provided by the Diocese.” 
The Boise Unitarian Universalist Fellowship contributed $5,000 in September to the PAC created by the initiative’s authors and supporters, Idahoans United for Women and Families. The Boise fellowship’s leaders could not be reached for comment after multiple emails and a phone call. 
The Boise Unitarian fellowship is part of a group of progressive churches and faith-based groups in Idaho called Interfaith Justice Idaho — which supports Prop 1. 
The Rev. Josh Lee poses for a portrait at Boise’s First Congregational United Church of Christ on Feb. 3, 2025. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger for the Idaho Capital Sun)
“We recognize that both the LDS Church and the Roman Catholic Church have taken public positions and had statements read in many of their pulpits opposing this, Proposition 1,” said the Rev. Josh Lee, a spokesperson for Interfaith Justice Idaho and senior pastor at Boise First United Church of Christ. 
“And so we felt the need to speak up as progressive faith leaders here in Idaho to say not all people of faith think that Prop 1 is bad, and that we should vote no and that you can’t be a person of faith and support women’s choice.” 
He said many of the group’s members made their churches available for signature-gathering for the voter initiative and different leaders have started releasing videos on Facebook sharing why they support the measure. 
The Boise synagogue Congregation Ahavath Beth Israel had a reported donation to the Idahoans United PAC. However, that donation was made in error by a former employee and has since been refunded, according to Congregation Ahavath Beth Israel President Betsy Russell. 
Campaign donations go against the congregation’s policy, Russell said, but many of the members do support Proposition 1. 
“Regardless of what Raúl Labrador says, we don’t believe it’s right for a tax-exempt religious organization to funnel dark money into political campaigns; we don’t do that and won’t do that,” Russell said in a statement. “That said, this proposition is one of huge interest to our members, in part because Idaho’s current abortion ban directly conflicts with Jewish law.”
“Judaism does not hold that life begins at conception. Instead, Jewish law requires prioritizing the life and health of the mother over that of the fetus, though the potential life of the fetus is increasingly valued in the later stages of pregnancy,” she continued. “Idaho’s current ban has no health exception for the mother.”
She said that individual members have differing views, but the Union for Reform Judaism, with which the Boise synagogue is affiliated, “holds that reproductive rights are a Jewish value.”

text:
Glacier National Park's Going-to-the-Sun Road saw a 41 percent increase in traffic on opening day compared to 2019, according to the park. (Keila Szpaller/The Daily Montanan)With temperatures drastically lowering, Glacier National Park is expecting rain and possible snowfall this weekend, the park said in a news release.
Beginning at 7 p.m., Oct. 9, a temporary road closure in the alpine section of Going-to-the-Sun Road will be implemented, the park said. The closure will extend from Avalanche to Jackson Glacier Overlook.
According to the National Weather Service forecast, winter weather may extend through Oct. 11, with rain, snow, and gusting wind expected in higher elevations of the park.The closure area of Going-to-the-Sun Road may change as needed for visitor and staff safety, the park said.
“Glacier National Park will evaluate and re-open the alpine section of Going-to-the-Sun Road when conditions improve,” the news release said.
Visitors are reminded that weather conditions can change quickly, and park travelers should always be prepared for inclement weather.
The park recommended visitors check the park website for the most up to date information and sign up for Glacier National Park notifications to receive road status updates by texting GNPROADS to 333111.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Summit pipeline ruling in North Dakota called a win for local control
description: A North Dakota judge ruled Friday that state rules on where infrastructure such as pipelines can be built do not automatically trump local zoning ordinances.  The ruling comes from a case in which a group of landowners and Emmons and Burleigh counties sued the Public Service Commission and pipeline developer Summit Carbon Solutions.  Bismarck attorney […]
text:
The Public Service Commission holds a public hearing April 22, 2024, in Mandan on the Summit Carbon Solutions pipeline. (Photo by Kyle Martin/For the North Dakota Monitor)A North Dakota judge ruled Friday that state rules on where infrastructure such as pipelines can be built do not automatically trump local zoning ordinances. 
The ruling comes from a case in which a group of landowners and Emmons and Burleigh counties sued the Public Service Commission and pipeline developer Summit Carbon Solutions. 
Bismarck attorney Derrick Braaten, who represented Emmons County, said the ruling is a win for local government authority and its ability to set rules on how far a pipeline route must be from homes and other buildings, which is known as a setback.
“It’s really significant because what the judge is saying is that he agrees with the local government that the statute preserves local control and there’s still a place for local control,” Braaten said.
Bismarck attorney Derrick Braaten updates landowners on the status of pore space litigation against the state of North Dakota on Feb. 2, 2026. (Photo by Jacob Orledge/North Dakota Monitor)
Braaten said the ruling goes beyond pipelines. The Legislature in 2025 copied the language that had applied to pipelines and used it to give the PSC authority over power lines as well. 
Preemption of local zoning was an issue during PSC hearings on the JETx power line that is to run from Jamestown to Ellendale. 
South Central District Court Judge Jackson Lofgren’s order says the pipeline route permit that the PSC issued to Summit in November 2024 remains in place. However, the court says the PSC must address problems identified in the ruling. 
Issues the PSC need to address include: 
Public welfare: The PSC must better explain why it thinks the pipeline route will not impair public welfare. An attorney for the PSC argued in July it was not responsible for safety, with pipeline safety standards enforced by a federal agency. But Braaten said the judge’s ruling is clear that the state agency can and should address safety when considering the effect of a pipeline route on public welfare. 
Alternate route: The judge said the PSC did not adequately address why it felt an alternate route through southern Burleigh County had been sufficiently analyzed. 
Plume model: Summit created a model for how carbon dioxide might disperse if there were a rupture in its high-pressure pipeline. The PSC agreed with Summit that the information should not be made public. The judge ruled that a redacted version of the model should be made public or the PSC should better explain why the information should not be made public in light of evidence that Summit had given some members of the public access to the model.
Local ordinances: The PSC must make a determination on whether setbacks set by Emmons and Burleigh counties were unreasonable. If deemed unreasonable, then state rules apply. 
Safety not a factor in determining North Dakota pipeline routes, attorney says

A spokesperson for the PSC said Friday its legal team was reviewing the judge’s findings but would need time to determine the agency’s next steps. 
Summit Carbon Solutions did not return an email Friday afternoon seeking comment. 
The future of Summit’s project in North Dakota remains unclear. The Iowa-based company’s original plan was to gather carbon emissions from ethanol plants in five states and use a network of pipelines to bring the CO2 to western North Dakota for permanent underground storage. 
But the company has been unable to obtain a permit for a pipeline through South Dakota to get to North Dakota.
In addition, Lofgren ruled a North Dakota law allowing the underground storage was unconstitutional, echoing a ruling in a different court. An appeal seeking to retain access to some of that storage is pending with the North Dakota Supreme Court. 
Summit has developed an alternative plan to use underground storage in Wyoming.

title: Trump may backtrack on livestreamed execution of Fort Hood shooter
text: President Donald Trump on Friday appeared to leave open the possibility that the federal government won’t livestream a military execution planned for December that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had said would be public.But Trump also told reporters at the White House that he had “absolutely” approved livestreaming the execution.The apparently contradictory comments came as the Trump administration faced a wave of criticism over plans to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, a former Army major convicted of killing 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009. Hegseth announced Thursday that Hasan’s death by firing squad would be public.“I'm going to make a determination about that, but he will be killed,” Trump first told reporters when asked about the livestream.A short time later, Trump was asked whether he had approved livestreaming the execution. He replied, “Did I approve? Absolutely.”Plans for the public execution came under bipartisan condemnation from lawmakers, along with numerous religious figures, Thursday and Friday. Sen. Thom Tillis, a North Carolina Republican, wrote on social media that public executions are “what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do.” He called the plans “beyond disgusting.”Sen. Patty Murray, a Washington Democrat, on social media urged the Pentagon to reverse course.“We are long past the days of public hangings in the town square,” Murray wrote. “Kids watch what our leaders do and say, is this kind of bloodshed really what we want them seeing?Even Vice President JD Vance cast doubt on whether the execution would be broadcast. He told reporters that if it’s ultimately livestreamed, “I’m not gonna be watching it.”

title: Hurricane Isaias expected to make landfall Friday evening
description: Hurricane Isaias is expected to make landfall near Pensacola, Florida on Friday evening as a Category 3 storm.  As of Friday afternoon,  the storm system was 90 miles south of Pensacola, moving at about 17 mph toward the Gulf Coast with sustained winds of 115 mph. The storm is expected to travel north through Alabama […]
text:
Double red flags wave near a beach entrance as a warning before the arrival of Hurricane Isaias in Orange Beach, Alabama on October 8, 2026.  Hurricane Isaias strengthened into a Category 3 storm on Friday and was expected to make landfall late Friday or early Saturday. (Dan Anderson for Alabama Reflector)Hurricane Isaias is expected to make landfall near Pensacola, Florida on Friday evening as a Category 3 storm. 
As of Friday afternoon,  the storm system was 90 miles south of Pensacola, moving at about 17 mph toward the Gulf Coast with sustained winds of 115 mph. The storm is expected to travel north through Alabama on Friday and Saturday. 
Hunter Richardson, a meterologist with the National Weather Service in Birmingham, said the storm would go “straight across the state line and generally up through the Interstate 65 corridor.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“We are expecting pretty high winds related to the tropical system across most of central Alabama,” he said.
Isaias was a Category 2 storm as late as Thursday, but the National Hurricane Center upgraded it to Category 3 Friday morning after it reached sustained winds of 120 mph. The system is expected to cause tornadoes and bring rain to the area.
Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey Friday urged Alabamians to “remain vigilant.”
“We remain concerned about strong winds, heavy rain and possible spinoff tornadoes,” the statement said. “Downed trees and power outages are certainly likely, but our power companies have assured me they are prepared to efficiently respond.” 
Ivey’s office said Uber announced it will offer free round trip rides, up to $40 each way and that Comcast made its WiFi Hotspot available to help residents and first responders in Baldwin, Houston and Mobile counties. 
President Donald Trump canceled his scheduled trip to Tuscaloosa to watch the Alabama v. Georgia football game on Saturday. The game was still scheduled to take place as of late Friday afternoon, though the university has cut back on pregame activities.
A hurricane warning was in effect for Mobile, Baldwin, Conecuh, Escambia, Covington, Coffee and Geneva counties Friday afternoon, with central and north-central Alabama under tropical storm warnings. 
Isaias is expected to bring 3 to 4 inches of rain in the southern part of the state with some parts receiving as much as six inches of rain. Central Alabama is forecast to get 2 to 3 inches of rain with some getting as much as four inches of rain. The northern part of the state is estimated to get 2 to 3 inches of rain while the most northern areas will get 1.5 to 2 inches of rain.
“The wind, it is going to be much stronger near the state line,” Richardson said.
Winds may gust as high as 70 mph near the eye of the storm, and could reach 60 mph in southern and central Alabama.

title: Coloradans prepare to monitor polls for voter intimidation, election issues during midterm
description: Around 50 Coloradans gathered in a conference room down the street from the state Capitol on Friday morning to become trained poll monitors ahead of the midterm elections, a subset of the 1,000 volunteers statewide who plan to observe polling sites and dropboxes as part of a pro-democracy effort. “We’re obviously nonpartisan. We’re there to […]
text:
Aly Belknap with Colorado Common Cause leads a poll monitor training in Denver on Oct. 9, 2026. (Photo by Sara Wilson/Colorado Newsline)Around 50 Coloradans gathered in a conference room down the street from the state Capitol on Friday morning to become trained poll monitors ahead of the midterm elections, a subset of the 1,000 volunteers statewide who plan to observe polling sites and dropboxes as part of a pro-democracy effort.
“We’re obviously nonpartisan. We’re there to report any issues,” Luana Charnes, a senior organizing manager with Common Cause, told trainees. “We’re also there as a community. You’re most likely going to volunteer in a county you live in, your local library, your neighborhood school down the road, and be that friendly face.”
Colorado Common Cause is part of the Just Vote Colorado assistance project that is seeking to station volunteers at polling locations around the state. The goal is to support voters, maintain a positive environment and report and document any issues at the site, such as lengthy lines, inaccessible entrances, high numbers of provisional ballots or students being told they can’t vote.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Organized, nonpartisan poll monitoring in the state is nothing new, but organizations say they are training more volunteers than before. Participation in Colorado Common Cause’s program is up from 300 volunteers two years ago.
“Just Vote Colorado is prepared to protect every eligible person’s right to vote from unfair barriers and intimidation so they have an equal say in decisions impacting their lives,” Aly Belknap, Colorado Common Cause’s executive director, said in a statement. “We’re here to send a clear message to the federal administration desperately trying to prevent people from voting to hang on to their power: Hands off our vote.”
People at the training learned about Colorado’s election laws, how to help voters facing issues using a national hotline and how to report concerning activity, such as intimidation or federal immigration enforcement. The goal isn’t for poll monitors to de-escalate conflict, Belknap said, but to have resources and confidence on how to navigate specific situations.
It is Judith White’s first time volunteering as a poll monitor, though the Denver resident has previously done other election-related activities like phone banking and is part of the left-leaning Indivisible movement. She said she’s alarmed by reports of armed guards at postal facilities and conflicting announcements from the federal government over whether U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement will be near polling sites.
“This feels like it’s adding a presence of force, rather than supportive protection,” she said. “We have to understand that maybe it’s all for the drama, but even the announcement that there’s this forceful presence is enough for people to say ‘Maybe not this year.’ Anything that disrupts your planned vote means you’re less likely to vote.”
She recalls experiences growing up in the American South and the region’s history of racial voter suppression.
“It can happen in lots of ways,” she said. “You can distort an election by keeping eligible voters from voting.”
‘They want to silence our voices’
As Friday’s training session started, Charnes asked people to share what a healthy democracy could look like for everyone. Participants shouted out responses like increasing the time window for people to vote, lessening anxiety around voting and removing corporate money from campaigns. Everyone agreed that trusting the election process in the face of misinformation is important for democracy. One man, a former election judge from Broomfield, said he wished every citizen could know the careful process of sorting, counting and double-checking ballots.
Vita Lantz-Brown of Arapahoe County said she has done some type of poll monitoring and election volunteering for the past two decades. A grandmother of 25 and great-grandmother of 10, she said she wants to safeguard democracy for future generations and make sure everyone who wants to vote feels empowered.
“I feel right now that we are not in a safe space for democracy,” she said. “This administration has attacked us at every level, and they want to silence our voices. How we can be heard is to vote.”
President Donald Trump and other federal officials have repeatedly shared falsehoods about widespread fraud and security concerns with mail-in ballots, including persistent false claims casting doubt on Trump’s defeat in the 2020 presidential election. Tina Peters, the former Mesa County clerk who was convicted of multiple felonies for her role in a failed attempt to breach secure elections equipment to prove Trump’s claims of fraud, reportedly met with the president this week to talk about federal involvement in the November midterm elections.
The U.S. Supreme Court recently blocked Trump’s bid to restrict mail-in ballots in November. Colorado is a universal vote-by-mail state with systems in place to ensure ballots are counted accurately. There is no evidence of widespread fraud in the election system.
Lantz-Brown worries that some people, especially naturalized citizens, won’t vote because they are afraid to be targeted by federal immigration enforcement at the polls.
“We have people who want to vote, but may be afraid,” she said. “That’s why it’s important to volunteer and that we’re seen in these places, so people know it’s ok. They’ll have someone to stand up for them and protect them.”
County clerks have mailed ballots to Colorado voters. The state recommends sending a ballot back via mail by Oct. 26 to ensure it gets counted. Otherwise, voters can drop it at a polling site or drop box until 7 p.m. on Nov. 3.

title: Standing Rock Sioux Tribe files lawsuit to shut down Dakota Access Pipeline
description: The Standing Rock Sioux Tribe on Friday filed a new lawsuit to try to shut down the Dakota Access oil pipeline, continuing a decadelong battle over the project. The tribe filed the case in U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia against the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, the U.S. Pipeline and Hazardous Materials […]
text:
Standing Rock Tribal Chairman Steve Sitting Bear speaks during a meeting of the Tribal and State Relations Committee in Fort Yates on July 22, 2026. The tribe filed a new lawsuit challenging the Dakota Access Pipeline. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)The Standing Rock Sioux Tribe on Friday filed a new lawsuit to try to shut down the Dakota Access oil pipeline, continuing a decadelong battle over the project.
The tribe filed the case in U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia against the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, the U.S. Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration and three federal officials of those agencies. The lawsuit seeks to overturn the Army Corps’ May record of decision granting an easement for the pipeline’s river crossing upstream of the tribe’s reservation, among other actions.
“For ten years, Standing Rock’s concerns about this pipeline have not changed, and for ten years we have fought to protect our water, our Treaty rights, and our people,” Standing Rock Sioux Tribal Chairman Steve Sitting Bear said in a statement. “The Army Corps has now chosen to move forward without addressing those concerns. Until this pipeline is shut down, we will continue to defend what generations before us protected for our children.” 
In 2016 and 2017, thousands of people gathered near the project’s Missouri River crossing to demonstrate against the pipeline, which the tribe views as a threat to its water supply from a potential rupture. 
In 2020, a federal judge ordered a more rigorous environmental review of the pipeline’s river crossing. In May, the Army Corps issued its record of decision granting the crucial easement for the pipeline, which has continuously operated since mid-2017.
Army Corps grants final approval for Dakota Access Pipeline, 9 years after oil began flowing

The tribe said the final environmental impact statement issued by the Army Corps in December 2025 does not resolve issues surrounding the safety of the pipeline, spill response, threats to the tribe’s sole source for drinking water, treaty rights and the federal government’s obligations to the tribe. 
The tribe also expressed concerns about the pipeline potentially increasing capacity to 1.1 million barrels of oil per day which the tribe said would change operational risks related to spill volume and emergency shutdown, according to court papers.
“We should not have to live with unanswered questions about the safety of our water,” Sitting Bear said.
The pipeline transports an average of 500,000 to 525,000 barrels of oil per day from North Dakota’s Bakken oil field to Illinois. The environmental review considered a capacity of up to 1.1 million barrels per day. The pipeline’s operational capacity is 750,000 barrels per day, North Dakota Pipeline Authority Director Justin Kringstad said.
The federal pipeline safety agency declined to comment on the lawsuit. Officials with the Army Corps and pipeline developer Energy Transfer did not return emails seeking comment Friday.
State and industry officials have said the pipeline is safe and needed infrastructure for transporting oil from North Dakota, the No. 3 oil-producing state in the U.S. Energy Transfer has said the pipeline is among the safest in the world, complies with regulations and crosses at least 95 feet below the riverbed.
The tribe argues a spill would threaten the health and welfare of the Standing Rock community. The lawsuit also seeks to rescind the federal pipeline safety agency’s approvals of spill response plans, and block the transport of oil through the river section until spill response plans meet federal law, according to court documents.
North Dakota Supreme Court orders judge to halt Dutch suit against Dakota Access Pipeline developer

“The Tribe files this action to require the defendant agencies to respect the Treaty rights and sovereignty of the Tribe and to protect the waters of the Missouri River and the ancestors resting at the water’s edge,” the tribe said in court papers. 
In 2024, Standing Rock filed a federal lawsuit against the Army Corps over its ongoing environmental review. In 2025, a judge dismissed the case. The tribe appealed, but dropped its appeal earlier this year.
Other court cases still linger in connection with the protests, including Energy Transfer’s lawsuit against several Greenpeace organizations and a Dutch lawsuit brought by Greenpeace International against the pipeline developer. 
Last month, tribal citizens, council members and others who were at the protests attended a first-time renewable energy event at Standing Rock and reflected on the decade since the demonstrations and how they have moved forward, despite not blocking the pipeline.
North Dakota Monitor reporter Michael Achterling contributed to this story. Mary Steurer also contributed to this story.

title: US Senate majority leader campaigns with Darline Graham in SC, saying GOP can’t ‘take any chances’
description: CHARLESTON — Following a fundraiser for her campaign, U.S. Sen. Darline Graham projected confidence while acknowledging a “close race” to keep the South Carolina seat her late brother held for almost 24 years. Appearing beside her for reinforcements were South Carolina’s now-senior senator, Tim Scott, who chairs the fundraising committee for Senate Republica[...]
text:
Sen. Darline Graham speaks to reporters alongside Sen. Tim Scott and Senate Majority Leader John Thune in Charleston on Friday, Oct. 9, 2026. (Photo by Katharine Wilson/SC Daily Gazette)CHARLESTON — Following a fundraiser for her campaign, U.S. Sen. Darline Graham projected confidence while acknowledging a “close race” to keep the South Carolina seat her late brother held for almost 24 years.
Appearing beside her for reinforcements were South Carolina’s now-senior senator, Tim Scott, who chairs the fundraising committee for Senate Republicans, and Senate Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota.
“It is going to be a close race, but I feel confident that we’re going to win,” Graham told reporters outside Hall’s Chophouse in downtown Charleston. “We’re going to hold the Republican seat here in South Carolina. That is so important.”
The fundraiser was held as polls show the Lexington Republican in a tighter-than-expected contest with Democrat Annie Andrews of Mount Pleasant. Two elections forecasters, Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball, have recently shifted the race from a solid to likely GOP win.
Andrews still faces an uphill battle but maybe not by much.
She’s trying to be the first Democrat to represent South Carolina in the U.S. Senate since Fritz Hollings retired in January 2005, ending his 38-year tenure. South Carolinians tend to keep their senators. Lindsey Graham was on track to win a fifth term when he died unexpectedly in July, creating an entirely different contest.
His younger sister, Darline Graham, ultimately won the special GOP primary to be on the Nov. 3 ballot, aided by the endorsement of President Donald Trump, who rallied for her in Myrtle Beach ahead of the runoff. But even in a state he won by 18 percentage points two years ago, there are questions of whether the first-time candidate can keep the seat in the GOP column another six years.
On Friday, Thune called Graham “battle-tested” after emerging from a 10-way GOP scramble in August. But with Senate Republicans trying to hold onto a slim majority in the midterms, he’s not “leaving anything to chance,” he said.
“I’m going places where if people are interested in having me come in and help, I’ll do what I can to help the team,” Thune said about why he’s in a state that’s supposed to be ruby red. “This is a team effort. It’s a team sport, and Sen. Graham is an important part of our team.”
‘Not presidential,’ SC Senate candidate says about Trump’s post others called cruel and offensive

Scott said South Carolina is not among the 10 toss-up states the National Republican Senatorial Campaign Committee, which he leads, is focused on.
“We are not having to use outside resources in South Carolina,” said the Charleston County Republican.
His remarks came days after reports that the separate Senate Leadership Fund, a leading political action committee for Senate Republicans, is sending $5 million to assist Graham’s campaign.
It’s unclear how much cash the candidates have on hand. The next campaign filings are due later this month.
The visit by Thune followed backlash this week after Trump used a slur for transgender people in a social media post about Andrews. A group that backs Democrats, 314 Action, sent $3.6 million to Andrews’ campaign in response.
Graham’s campaign has drilled into Andrews’ past public advocacy for transgender youth, using her own social media posts to call Andrews a radical who’s switching her positions. Andrews’ campaign has pushed back, releasing an ad where she says she opposes transgender women and girls playing in women’s sports. She also says she opposes gender-transitioning surgeries for minors, though the accusations include her previous opposition to ending transitioning hormone treatments and puberty blockers.
Asked specifically about that earlier this week, Andrews’ campaign told the SC Daily Gazette the prohibitions in state law are not something she’s working to change.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Deadly 2026 heat season shatters state records for heat-related emergency calls, fatalities
description: The annual Maryland heat season ended with record-breaking heat-related illnesses and deaths: The 61 fatalities shattered the 2012 record of 42 deaths, and 1,657 emergency calls topped last year's 1,634, the previous record. Health experts point to climate change.
text:
Maryland ends the official 2026 heat season with a record-breaking 61 fatalities, though public health advocates warn that there's still time for another heat wave this year. (Photo by Staff Sgt. Sheila deVera/U.S. Air Force)The annual Maryland heat season ended with a record-breaking year for heat-related illnesses and deaths, with the state reporting that 61 Marylanders died due to hyperthermia in the season that ended Sept. 30.
It shattered the previous record of 42 fatalities, set in 2012, according to available public data, and came close to doubling last year’s 34 deaths, continuing a troubling four-year rise in heat-related fatalities.
This heat season also saw the highest number of calls to emergency medical services for heat-related illnesses in a year, at 1,657, up from last year’s 1,634.
The 1,603 visits to emergency department or urgent care this summer were down slightly from the record 1,670 set last year, according to the final data update for the 2026 heat season released Wednesday by the Maryland Department of Health.
Public health advocates say climate change is leading to longer heat waves and hotter temperatures during the summers, which puts more Marylanders at risk of heat exhaustion, heat stroke and death.


Dr. Georges Benjamin, executive director of the American Public Health Association anticipates those dangerous conditions will continue.
“It’s right now being exacerbated and driven a lot by climate change,” Benjamin said. “This is going to get worse…. The heat waves we’re having now are higher heat but also persisting longer.”
Heat-related deaths have been on an upward trend in Maryland since 2022, when five heat-related deaths were reported for the summer.
The Maryland Department of Health notes that of the 61 deaths reported this year, 41 occurred from the last week of June into the first week of July, “where the high temperatures were consistently in between the high 90s to low 100s, and the lowest temperatures at night were in the upper 70s.”
“As the climate warms, we are seeing longer periods of hot weather and higher temperatures, and both of those are contributing to increased risk for Maryland residents,” Cliff Mitchell, environmental health bureau director for the state health department said in a written statement Thursday.
“In many cases, it’s not just about how hot it is during the day, but whether things cool off enough at night. If people don’t have a chance to recover from scorching afternoons, the physical toll on their body can be fatal,” he said.
There were 29 deaths that occurred indoors, representing 48% of all heat-related fatalities this summer. Of the remaining deaths, 26% occurred outdoors and 26% occurred in a vehicle.
Jamie Madrigano, associate professor with the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, who is researching the health impacts of climate change and extreme weather, said it’s not surprising that many fatalities occurred indoors.
‘Dangerous’ winter weather broke state records for cold-related deaths, ER visits

“A lot of the guidance is, ‘Seek shelters indoors. Try to get out of that extreme heat situation.’ That is important and correct guidance,” she said. “But a lot of these fatalities are occurring inside…. They’re occurring when people either don’t have access to air conditioning or are not running it because of the costs to their utility bills.”
Benjamin with APHA added that indoor infrastructure to combat hot weather may be lacking in regions that have not historically had high temperatures.
“We have hot weather in places that were not as hot as before, and so our fundamental infrastructure isn’t designed to address it,” he said. He noted that low-income areas may not have adequate air conditioning in their homes and even the lack of greenspace in those areas contributes to higher temperatures.
Certain populations, such as elderly residents, are vulnerable to heat-related illness and fatalities. Among the 61 people who died this summer, 62% were age 65 and older. Meanwhile, people from 45 to 64 accounted for 26% of heat-related deaths. Another 10% of fatalities were among people between the ages of 18 and 44. The department reports at least one child, age 4 or younger, also died due to heat-related illness this year.
While the “surveillance period” for the 2026 heat season ended and state officials will not continue weekly updates, Benjamin warns that there could still be another heat wave before the end of the year.
“We’re not out of the woods yet,” he said. “But we should begin planning. That means spending time identifying who are the high-risk people in the community, putting together plans so you can identify these folks, educating the community broadly about the risk.”
