name: WyoFile
title: Industrial development boom drives Laramie County’s new workforce housing requirement
description:
Wyoming’s most populous county has begun requiring temporary housing to prevent short-term construction workers from straining an already low housing supply.
The post Industrial development boom drives Laramie County’s new workforce housing requirement appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
CHEYENNE—Laramie County is moving toward a new standard for industrial developments that requires construction workers be housed outside the local housing market, whether it be through accommodations on the project site or through another arrangement approved by county officials.
The policy is emerging as the county works through permitting the Laramie Range Wind Project and anticipates a growing number of large-scale energy and data center developments.
Wyoming’s most populous county has begun requiring workforce accommodations for large projects on a case-by-case basis, according to Justin Arnold, director of Laramie County’s Planning and Development Department. That includes Project Latigo, a proposed data center development by Vantage Data Centers, located 12 miles south of Cheyenne.
The requirement is intended to prevent temporary construction workers from putting additional pressure on Cheyenne and Laramie County’s already low housing supply, Arnold said.
“It mitigates multiple impacts to the community from these large construction projects,” Arnold said, “from traffic sheds to inundating our local housing and rental markets.”
The city and county are seeing multiple large industrial projects proposed or under construction at the same time, he said. This includes data centers, wind farms and solar energy projects.
“Cumulative effects, we don’t have really any other option than to figure out housing outside of our local markets,” Arnold said. “And there’s multiple ways to do that.”
Developers could build workforce housing developments on the project site; build a general workforce housing camp that accommodates construction workers for multiple developers or contractors; or build an RV park on-site, he said.
The requirement would apply only to construction-period workers, rather than full-time employees once the development becomes fully operational.
“Data centers, when it’s all said and done, they’re looking at 250 (full-time) employees versus 2,500 (construction workers),” Arnold said. “… But usually with the wind farms and solar farms, you get them constructed and you have a handful, less than single digits for daily operations and maintenance.”
For wind and solar projects, Arnold said construction workforces generally have around 300 people.
“Three hundred people coming here is 300 less units that the locals have available to themselves from the local supply,” he said.
Laramie Range Wind Project
The housing issue became a more prominent discussion among county officials as the Laramie Range Wind Project makes its way through another round of the permitting process following its approval by the Wyoming Department of Environmental Quality’s Industrial Siting Council last month.
After previous denial from the Laramie County Board of County Commissioners in September 2025, developers announced in January their intention to submit an application to the council to permit the project on private and state lands.
The wind farm is expected to erect 139 turbines on 41,220 acres of Farthing Ranch Co. land and land managed by the Wyoming Office of State Lands and Investments roughly 20 miles northwest of Cheyenne. It’s being developed by ConnectGen Laramie County, an affiliate of Repsol Renewables North America.
Wind turbines near Cheyenne poke into a colorful sunrise in January 2025. (Tennessee Watson/WyoFile)
The Industrial Siting Council green-lit the permit after a two-day hearing on Aug. 31 and Sept. 1. It was approved with 26 conditions, which are not available to the public due to the document’s status as unfinalized. Jenny Staeben, Industrial Siting Council administrator, previously told the Wyoming Tribune Eagle that the list and all other relevant documents submitted as exhibits during the Sept. 1 hearing would be released approximately 45 days later.
The project is expected to have a peak of 305 workers during its construction period.
Even though the Industrial Siting Council approved the permit, there are still local conditions Repsol has to meet, such as county requirements regarding permits and studies, before construction of the wind farm can begin.
Arnold said county officials have told Repsol representatives that workforce accommodations will be required as part of that process. However, he said it’s not clear yet what form those accommodations will take.
Repsol representatives met with Arnold this week and told him that requiring on-site housing may conflict with existing contracts and agreements with the landowner, he said.
“So I said, ‘Here’s the deal. If you don’t want to renegotiate with the landowner and say everybody needs to stay on site, find alternative means,’” Arnold said. “I’ve been meeting with no less than three or four commercial entities that do workforce accommodation as their specialty. So in lieu of requiring it on-site, they could potentially just say, ‘OK, we’re (contracting) with this other entity who is doing workforce accommodation.’” 
Arnold said the project’s recent Industrial Siting Council approval included an unknown condition that Repsol representatives told him could make its current plans unworkable. The company could seek to amend that condition, request the county postpone its local proceedings, or withdraw and resubmit its county application after resolving the issue.
“So, at this point in time, we don’t know,” Arnold said. “… It’s going to be really important they receive that amendment. So let’s just say at this point in time, we don’t know what’s going to be submitted until they figure out what’s going on with the Industrial Siting Division, nor do we know if this application is going to have a public hearing and request postponement.”
The exact solution could also ultimately require approval from county commissioners.
Regardless, Arnold reiterated that the new workforce housing requirement will apply to all proposed industrial developments in the county from here on out.
“Basically, at the end of the day, we said no matter what … we need to just simply require workforce accommodation on-site, regardless of whether (developers) go through the Industrial Siting Division or whether they get a zone change from the county and go through the site plan process,” he said. “That’s just going to be the standard operating procedure on these moving forward.”

Denver City Council unanimously adopted the policy in March in response to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers wearing masks to conceal their identities. It applies to federal, state and local law enforcement, and says officers must show identification upon request.

In a statement announcing the lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court of Colorado, the Department of Justice said the law threatens the safety of federal officers “who are already facing an unprecedented wave of harassment, doxxing, and even violence.” 
“The Denver masking and identification ordinance directly regulates federal law enforcement operations and threatens severe consequences for officers and public safety alike,” Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate said in a statement. “The Federal Government gets to decide which equipment federal officers may or may not wear when performing their official duties.”
Jon Ewing, a spokesperson for Mayor Mike Johnston, said the city is prepared to defend the law in court. He said he is unaware of any incidents where the city has had to enforce the law since it passed, “and we’re hoping to keep it that way.”
“But other cities have had incidents with masked law enforcement and clearly, with this action from the Trump Administration, ICE would like to keep wearing them,” Ewing said in a statement.
A federal appeals court in April blocked California’s mask ban for law enforcement officers, saying it violates the U.S. Constitution’s supremacy clause, which prohibits states from regulating federal operations. Other states with laws that ban federal law enforcement officers from concealing their identities, including Oregon and Washington, have yet to be challenged by the Trump administration.
The administration is seeking a court order that declares the Denver law violates the supremacy clause, declares the city has “no authority” to enforce the law, and permanently prohibits the city from enforcing it.

name: WyoFile
title: Yellowstone wolves struggle to produce pups, again, but don’t blame disease this time
description:
Despite a continued lull in adding new wolves to the national park’s population, there are no ‘biological red flags’ that have biologists concerned. 
The post Yellowstone wolves struggle to produce pups, again, but don’t blame disease this time appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Yellowstone National Park’s wolf packs — arguably the world’s most visible and famous wild wolves — had another poor year of producing puppies and keeping the youngsters alive, according to a Park Service biologist. 
A paucity of pups being raised by park packs in 2026 comes on the heels of a year where canine distemper, a nonnative disease, took a significant toll on the wolf population in the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem. In Wyoming, numbers sank to levels not seen since the reintroduction era. Distemper especially affects juvenile wolves: In 2025, Yellowstone packs produced 17 pups that survived until the end of the year — a record low. 
Now, 2026 is shaping up to be another dismal year for pup production, according to Yellowstone Wolf Project leader Dan Stahler. 
“We might have another low year,” Stahler said. “Some of our wolf packs on the landscape just did not have any surviving pups.” 
When Stahler spoke with WyoFile in early September, there were “about 20” surviving pups spread amongst several packs. Ordinarily, there are about twice as many: On average, 37 pups survive until the end of the year and are tallied in Yellowstone’s annual wolf reports. 
Distemper is not the suspected culprit this time, Stahler said. Instead, there were a variety of non-disease related causes of litters failing or not happening. 
Eight gray pups born to the 8 Mile Pack lounge outside their den in 2025. Seven of these pups survived until the year’s end, making this pack the most successful contributor to Yellowstone’s pup recruitment in 2025. (M. Metz/NPS photo)
The 8 Mile Pack, for example, lost its alpha male, an animal that is atop the hierarchical ladder, during the breeding season — an old wolf that died of natural causes. 
“So the female didn’t get bred, and that pack did not produce pups,” Stahler said. 
The Bliss Creek Pack didn’t have pups for the second straight year for reasons that aren’t understood, he said. Meanwhile, the Junction Butte Pack did produce a litter, but the breeding female was young and the pups never emerged from the den. 
“We’re not sure if she just was inexperienced, or if something happened to the pups underground,” Stahler said. “She acted like she was denning and localized, and then nothing happened.” 
Pack by pack
Successful breeding packs included the Wapiti Lake Pack, which had seven surviving pups in early September. The Rescue Creek Pack also produced seven surviving youngsters. Yellowstone’s oldest wolf pack, Mollie’s Pack, also managed to produce a litter that included five surviving pups as of July. 
Because Mollie’s Pack left Yellowstone, its “breeding pair” might have counted as part of Wyoming’s population and not the park’s (there are minimum numbers for each jurisdiction). But then the pack returned to its historical territory in Pelican Valley — a movement that allowed the animals to avoid hunter gunfire that was a cause of considerable concern. 
“They moved back into the park with the pups,” Stahler said of Mollie’s Pack, “so it could very well be that they do count toward our population at the end of the year.” 





A map showing 2025 wolf pack territories within Yellowstone National Park. Aerial locations are not gathered outside of the park during wolf hunting seasons in surrounding states. Therefore, some wolf pack territory polygons do not represent all transboundary space use. (National Park Service)

Just this week, avid wildlife watchers rejoiced online about footage of Mollie’s Pack captured while the wolves were back in Yellowstone. 
Although Yellowstone’s experienced two straight years with far fewer than normal wolf pups, Stahler emphasized that he’s not worried about the population. 
“We still feel like we have a naturally functioning population and the ups and downs are well within the range that we’ve seen,” he said. “There’s not a biological red flag.” 
Yellowstone went into 2026 with 84 total wolves — 67 adults and 17 pups. Since stabilizing about 15 years ago, the average park population has remained just under 100 wolves. 
“It’s roughly a 16% drop from our average year-end count over the last 15 years, but it isn’t a new low,” Stahler said. “We had a count of 83 wolves in 2012, and we had a count of 80 wolves in 2018. After both those years, the population absorbed that hit and decline, and came back.” 
The lowest population recorded, in 2018, also aligned with a distemper outbreak, Stahler said. 
Last year, distemper was the suspected main cause of a “really low” 47% survival rate for Yellowstone wolf pups. Thirty six pups were documented emerging from the den, but only 17 were counted the following winter. Typically, about three in four pups survive to see the new year, Stahler said.
Yellowstone’s wolves in 2026 should be better equipped to prevent distemper from spreading through their ranks and killing pups, whose immune systems are especially vulnerable to the disease. The reason is because the population has the antibodies. A majority of the park wolves captured for research last winter had “high seroprevalence” for distemper, Stahler said.
Wait and see
Outside of Yellowstone, the picture of how wolves in the ecosystem are recovering from the distemper outbreak is somewhat less clear, Wyoming Game and Fish Department biologist Ken Mills said. 
“We’re just different than Yellowstone,” Mills told WyoFile. “They’re able to keep much tighter tabs on individual litters of pups. We can count pups in the middle of summer, but that doesn’t mean they survive through fall, and we don’t have real-time data because we back off monitoring during the hunting season.”
Wyoming’s wolf hunting opportunities were reduced significantly because of the distemper outbreak. The maximum number of wolves that could be killed in the state’s trophy game area — where the large canines are managed tightly — was reduced by 50% because the population was the lowest since around the turn of the century, when wolves were still reestablishing. (Conversely, hunting is unlimited and without seasons or restrictions on methods in the remaining 85% of Wyoming where wolves are classified as predators.)
Ken Mills checks a young wolf’s teeth for sign of canine distemper during a February 2018 collaring operation near Jackson. (Ryan Dorgan)
Although Wyoming wildlife managers are still assembling detailed wolf data, Mills said that anecdotally there were plenty of wolf pups outside the park this summer. Most of the packs that didn’t have litters last year produced pups in 2026, he said.
“Litters looked good and healthy,” he said. “We were documenting normal-sized litters, and even a few litters that were maybe a little larger than normal.” 
A couple of Wyoming packs even had multiple females give birth to litters, Mills said. Double litters are a rarity, he said, and usually only occur about once every four to five years outside of Yellowstone. 
While Yellowstone wolves have bounced back from widespread distemper outbreaks in the past, it’s uncharted territory outside of the national park. 
“We’ve never documented a population-level impact in Wyoming, and so this will be the first year we’re testing that response,” Mills said. 
But like Stahler, the Wyoming biologist wasn’t too worried about where the population is headed, both because of the nature of the disease and the species. 
“Distemper is mostly lethal to wolf pups, which are not the reproductive members,” Mills said. “Wolf packs have alternate breeders available at all times, essentially. Reproduction, we would expect to be responsive to population decline.” 
Wyoming’s wolves, in other words, might produce a lot of pups this year just because their population was lower. 
“But they still have to survive to the end of the year,” Mills said, “and they haven’t done that yet.” 
One common cause of death for wolf pups is hunting because they’re relatively naive and lack the savvy of older animals. But in 2026, there’s not much more hunting left to occur where Wyoming manages wolves as a trophy game species. As of Friday afternoon, 16 of the 22 wolves that hunters are permitted to kill have already been taken, according to Game and Fish’s online harvest report.

title: Idaho Gov. Little suspends dyed diesel inspection to ease costs for farmers as Iran War continues
description: Idaho Gov. Brad Little signed an executive order Friday to suspend state inspections of dyed diesel fuel in an attempt to lower costs for farmers and ranchers, according to the governor’s office.  Dyed diesel is diesel fuel with red dye in it and is exempt from federal and state motor fuel taxes. The tax-exempt fuel […]
text:
President Donald Trump signed an executive order to allow dyed diesel on highways and prohibit the Internal Revenue Service from imposing the typical penalties for doing so. Some state restrictions remain on the fuel, but on Friday, Idaho Gov. Brad Little relaxed the Gem State's inspections of the fuel during harvest. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)Idaho Gov. Brad Little signed an executive order Friday to suspend state inspections of dyed diesel fuel in an attempt to lower costs for farmers and ranchers, according to the governor’s office. 
Dyed diesel is diesel fuel with red dye in it and is exempt from federal and state motor fuel taxes. The tax-exempt fuel is only meant for certain approved off-road uses, such as for farming equipment, construction equipment and home heating. The dye helps regulators enforce this requirement. 
Idaho’s average diesel price was around $6.41 per gallon as of Friday, according to AAA fuel prices. Prices for oil products have risen this year largely because of restrictions on ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz amid the U.S. and Israel’s war with Iran, which have disrupted global supply chains. Diesel supplies have been in particularly short supply, NPR reported, and Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries have also affected global supplies. 
On Monday, President Donald Trump signed an executive order to allow dyed diesel on highways and prohibit the Internal Revenue Service from imposing the typical penalties for doing so. Some state restrictions remain on the fuel. 
President Donald Trump hands off a newly signed executive order waiving federal taxes on red-dyed diesel to aide Natalie Harp during a 2026 midterms rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Oct. 5, 2026, at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds with thousands in attendance. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Little’s order signed Friday directs Idaho State Police and the Idaho Transportation Department to suspend inspection for dyed diesel while the agencies review Idaho’s policies and procedures, his office announced in a press release. The review will consider other state’s approach to dyed diesel enforcement and the agencies will make recommendations to Little for “efficient, effective, and practical inspection,” the release said. 
Little said in the press release that the timing of the order is meant to ease costs during harvest season. 
“Idaho farmers and ranchers work hard to feed our families, our country, and the world,” Little said in the release. “President Trump has made cutting red tape a priority, and Idaho is doing the same. We will continue looking for ways to give our farmers, ranchers, and working men and women on the road more freedom to do what they do best.”
Legislative leaders in written statements said they supported the governor’s decision. 
“Idaho farmers and ranchers are facing high costs across the board, and expensive diesel is adding to the pressure during harvest,” Senate President Pro Tempore Kelly Anthon, R-Declo, said in the release. “This order provides some immediate relief while giving the state time to review these requirements and find a practical approach that supports our producers without adding unnecessary costs or red tape.” 
House Speaker Mike Moyle, R-Star, said suspending the inspections while the state reviews its policies “is a practical approach that puts common sense first and gives Idaho producers one less thing to worry about during harvest.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: El-Sayed talks corporate money, healthcare, artificial intelligence at Lansing town hall
description: Corporate influence in politics and its ripple effects on issues ranging from data centers to healthcare, was the focus of a town hall Friday in downtown Lansing hosted by Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who was joined by End Citizens United President Tiffany Muller.  “Because of Citizens United, because of the way that our […]
text:
U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and End Citizens United President Tiffany Muller discussed corporate influence at a town hall in Lansing on Oct. 9. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance) Corporate influence in politics and its ripple effects on issues ranging from data centers to healthcare, was the focus of a town hall Friday in downtown Lansing hosted by Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who was joined by End Citizens United President Tiffany Muller. 
“Because of Citizens United, because of the way that our politics works, we’ve also allowed these huge corporations to hop over the firewall that is supposed to protect our politics from the power of the biggest players in our economy to buy politicians too,” El-Sayed told a largely enthusiastic audience. “It’s hard for Congress to be that check on corporate power when they’re so busy cashing their checks, right?”
End Citizens United is a Democratic-aligned political action committee seeking to overturn the 2010 landmark U.S. Supreme Court decision Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission, which greatly expanded the ability of corporations, labor unions and other outside groups to spend money on political campaigns.
El-Sayed, whose campaign refrain often includes a call-and-response cheer of “money out of politics,” tied that to another key platform of his campaign — healthcare reform and Medicare for All. 
He explained to the crowd how he envisions Medicare for All — healthcare that covers individuals from birth to death with no premium, no copay and no deductible, eligible anywhere that is needed to get healthcare without limits based on in-network providers. 
“And it buys you out of ever having to worry about getting debt,” he said. “Because here’s the thing about it: almost everybody in this economy has this experience where you get sick and you’re like, ‘Damn, I have to see a doctor.’ You know why? Because you know it’s going to come with a bill, even if you’re insured.”
U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed speaks at a campaign town hall hosted alongside End Citizens United in Lansing on Oct. 9. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)
Muller also noted that, in response to a recent poll from End Citizens United, about 60% of respondents said that they had experienced government corruption — tying their rising health costs to the electoral influence of healthcare corporations.
“When we asked why, they said, ‘Well, my healthcare costs are going up, but members of Congress are cashing out to health insurance companies, they’re coming after Social Security all to pay off Wall Street banks’,” she said. “This tie between corruption and economic pressure is something that voters not only feel but deeply understand, and it’s something you talk about all the time.”
El-Sayed was also critical of his opponent, Republican Mike Rogers, for taking corporate money while serving in the U.S. House of Representatives and then “advising the very same corporations he was regulating just before.”
“He saw his boss Donald Trump make $2.2 billion while he was in office, and he says, ‘You know what? I might as well get while the getting is good’,” El-Sayed said of Rogers. “Well, who do you think gets got? We do. We’re the ones paying the higher prescription drug prices. We’re the ones paying the higher utility rates. We’re the ones paying the higher premiums for insurance. We’re the ones paying for gas. We’re the ones paying more for groceries.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
At a Thursday night debate, El-Sayed and Rogers traded barbs about their own respective stock holdings, especially in relation to companies funding data center development. 
El-Sayed noted at Friday’s town hall that his own retirement account is invested in a mutual fund, which is managed independently of him and his work — differently than stock trading that he seeks to ban for members of Congress. 
“It gets even more funky because if you’re personally trading stock and you have insider information, you can then start to short stocks or long stocks based on how regulations you vote on shape those stocks,” he said.
William Lawrence, the Democratic nominee for Michigan’s 7th Congressional District, which includes Lansing, opened the event by explaining how his refusal to take corporate money in his campaign allows him to be an effective check on policies promoted by major corporate donors. 
“It’s because I’m not taking any money from data center developers that I can afford to stand strong for a moratorium on data center development,” Lawrence said. “Because I’m not taking any money from health insurance corporations that I can afford to fight hard for Medicare for All. It’s because I’m not taking any money from Wall Street firms that I can afford to stand alongside our neighbors, fighting back against unjust evictions here in the Lansing area, pushed by those Wall Street firms. And you know what I’ve learned time and time again is that when you stand alongside people and fight for them, they will fight for you.”
U.S. Congressional candidate Will Lawrence speaks at an event with End Citizens United and Abdul El-Sayed’s Senate campaign on Oct. 9. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)
Artificial intelligence and the data centers that power them were also a hot topic at the town hall after an audience member said he is skeptical of El-Sayed’s anti-data center platform. 
“The issue with AI, the tech that is being built off the back of data centers, is that it is incentivized to pick the lowest hanging fruits, which is other people’s jobs, and the process by which it’s happening may not be sustainable on its own terms, and we are in the circumstance where we are watching a tech transition happen, even if this takes off faster than the whole time horizon of a work life, which could create massive technological changes in our society that we are not ready for,” El-Sayed said in response to the question. “AI shouldn’t be able to fire a weapon, shouldn’t be able to fire you, shouldn’t be able to prior authorize your healthcare and tell you what healthcare you don’t need or shouldn’t need.”
Muller again linked the issue of artificial intelligence to money in politics.
“What we have also seen is that AI right now is spending over 200 million dollars to influence the midterm elections because what they want are people in Congress who won’t bother putting in any of these regulations, any of this oversight, or making sure that the people are protected, or that any of this could happen,” she said. “They want people who will just rubber stamp so that they can keep lining their pockets and driving up their profits, and they think $200 million can buy it, and you know that’s a lot of money.”

name: VTDigger
title: Godnicks celebrates 100 years of furnishing Rutland
description:
A fourth generation of Godnicks celebrate the milestone.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Godnicks celebrates 100 years of furnishing Rutland.
text:
Owners Brent, left, and Brian Godnick stand in the showroom of Godnicks Grand Furniture recently. Photo by Gabby Blanchard/Community News Service

For Community News Service, a VTSU-Castleton internship, for Rutland HeraldIn 1926, Irving Godnick opened the first furniture store of a now 100-year-old family business.
“The business was started by Godnicks and is still run by Godnicks,” Brian Godnick said in a recent interview.
In a small space upstairs in the Tuttle Block on Center Street, the first store offered furniture and a small clothing section, and was known for letting customers pay weekly for their purchases.
“They could either go to the shop and pay or my grandfather had a guy who went around to people’s houses collecting a little bit of money every week,” Brian said.

The Godnick family celebrates the opening of Godnicks Grand Furniture in 1956. Provided photo

The business continued this unique payment style for about 50 years.
While the name and quality of service have remained consistent, there have been several different Godnicks furniture store locations over the years — and several generations of Godnicks running them.
Now in its fourth generation, Brian’s son, Brent Godnick, has been running the business since 2008, taking over from his father and uncle Jeff Godnick.
“I started working at the warehouse in high school and during summer vacations from college,” Brent said. “I’ve grown up in every part of the store, working every part of the store.”
In 1940, the business moved to Willow and Edson streets in downtown Rutland until 1950, when it moved to 82 West St., on the corner of West and Wales streets. During that time, the family also opened Furniture Fair, a lower-priced store located on South Main Street, a few years later changing its name to Furniture Warehouse.
The 1970s and ’80s saw more store openings, including the Economy Department, Godnicks Fine Furniture in Glens Falls, New York, and a water bed shop next to the current North Main Street location.

The Godnicks opened Grand Furniture on West Street in Rutland in 1950.

Brian noted the reputation of the family’s business helped his father, Gilbert Godnick, get elected mayor of Rutland City, a seat he held from 1973 to 1981.
“The main thing is reputations, and hard work put into the business,” he said.
In 1986, the family decided to consolidate the disparate businesses to make Vermont’s largest furniture store. At the time, the North Main Street store was one story but an addition more than doubled its size to the 85,000-square-foot building now known as Godnicks Grand Furniture.
The showroom spans two floors of retail space, separating different sections for specific types of furniture such as living room sofas and coffee tables, dining room chairs and bar carts, bedroom and bathroom vanities and mirrors, home office and entertainment essentials, as well as mattress and flooring options, and much more.
Brian and Brent said their secret to keeping the business going for a century is the consistency in family orientation, hands-on service, offering the best quality for the best prices and treating customers with respect.
“The owners are in the store every day,” Brent said. “So most of the time when someone calls, they will actually be talking to one of them.”
Brian explained that with every year comes new challenges, and it’s just about adjusting.
“Every year’s a new period; you just have to keep up to date on current items, adjust to hard times, and do what you have to do to get through them,” he said.
To show their appreciation for customers, until Saturday, customers can register to win 12-14 different weekly door prizes. Customers can also enjoy a cookout at the store on Saturday, from noon to 2 p.m.
“My hope for the future is to provide the same service and quality that we do now and have done since starting,” Brent said. “This is a huge responsibility for me; I am just trying to keep the same morals and values that they had before me.”

text:
Montana's new "I voted" sticker. (Secretary of State's Office photo)The Montana Secretary of State’s office has mailed out absentee ballots for the 2026 election.
More than 575,000 ballots have been mailed to registered absentee voters, according to Secretary of State Christi Jacobsen.
Absentee ballots must be returned by 8 p.m., on Election Day, Nov. 3. Voters are encouraged to return their ballots promptly and are reminded to follow the instructions provided by their county election office.
Around three-quarters of Montanans vote by mail.
“I encourage Montanans to visit VoteMT.gov to view their sample ballot, track their absentee ballot, and prepare to make their voices heard on Nov.3,” said Jacobsen. “The Montana election team is honored to serve our voters.”
According to the secretary of state’s website, which tracks absentee ballots sent and received and updates every morning, 1,236 Montanans had already returned their ballots as of Friday.

text:
Who will replace Republican Councilwoman Janet Kilpatrick? Here’s where Kira Alejandro and Melissa Brayman stand
This story is part of Delaware LIVE’s continuing coverage of the 2026 New Castle County Council races.
WILMINGTON, Del. — In August, Delaware LIVE introduced the two Democrats running to replace Councilwoman Janet Kilpatrick. Kira Alejandro won that Sept. 15 primary over Kyle Grantham. Now she faces Republican Melissa Brayman, and on Wednesday, Oct. 7, the two answered questions side by side at an in-person candidate forum hosted by the League of Women Voters of New Castle County at Limestone Presbyterian Church.
Kilpatrick, a Republican who has represented Hockessin, Yorklyn, North Star, Pike Creek and part of Newark for 16 years, is not seeking reelection. She was in the audience.
The seat is known as New Castle County Council District 3. County council votes on the county budget, property taxes and requests to rezone land for new development. According to the League of Women Voters of New Castle County, questions were submitted online before the forum and on note cards at the event.
The general election is Nov. 3. Six county council seats are on this year’s ballot, but only three have candidates from both parties, and this is one of them, according to the Delaware Department of Elections. A Delaware LIVE look at all six races is coming next.
What they have in common
Whoever wins, the seat will stay with a woman. Neither Democrat Kira Alejandro nor Republican Melissa Brayman has held elected office. Both attended the University of Delaware, both left Delaware for a time before coming back, and both bring an environmental background to the race: Alejandro through her work saving land from development, and Brayman through her University of Delaware studies in wildlife conservation.
Both named affordability as the county’s most urgent problem. Both said the state passes costs to the county without paying for them, and both said many residents don’t know what county council does.
Several questions asked about specific development proposals, including a McDonald’s on Limestone Road and a car wash in Hockessin. Delaware LIVE will report separately on the status of those projects.
The table below compares the two candidates in 10 areas, from their backgrounds to where they stand on taxes, development and data centers. The forum covered more ground than we could fit here. You can watch the full discussion on the League’s website.

Would allow more kinds of homes, including small starter homes and in-law suites


Data centers
Wants a pause on approving new data centers: “We don’t totally understand everything about data centers yet.”
Would not support a pause if defending it costs taxpayers money, but would “pump the brakes a little bit”; opposes data centers in any residential area


Money from developers
Takes none from developers, land use attorneys, corporations or corporate political action committees; will refund any developer donation she learns of
Has not accepted any from developers; did not say directly whether she would commit to refusing them



How to vote
The deadline to register to vote in the general election is Saturday, Oct. 10, at 11:59 p.m. Early voting runs Oct. 22 through Nov. 1, except Sunday, Oct. 25, at any early voting center in your county. Hours are 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. through Oct. 27 and 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. from Oct. 28 on. Polls are open 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3. Find early voting locations on the Delaware Department of Elections website, and check your registration or district at the state’s voter portal.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Restaurant inspection update: Three food trucks temporarily shut down
description: State, city and county inspectors have cited Iowa restaurants and stores for hundreds of food-safety violations during the past several weeks, including expired and moldy food. At least three food trucks were temporarily shut down due to issues uncovered by inspectors, with an inspector citing “imminent health hazard conditions” at one of three. The findings[...]
text:
The Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing oversees restaurant inspections in Iowa. (Photo via Getty Images; DIAL logo courtesy of Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing)State, city and county inspectors have cited Iowa restaurants and stores for hundreds of food-safety violations during the past several weeks, including expired and moldy food.
At least three food trucks were temporarily shut down due to issues uncovered by inspectors, with an inspector citing “imminent health hazard conditions” at one of three.
The findings are reported by the Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing, which handles food-establishment inspections at the state level.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Listed below are some of the more serious findings that stem from inspections at Iowa restaurants, stores, care facilities and other businesses between Aug. 10, 2026, and Oct. 1, 2026. (DIAL withholds from public disclosure all food-safety inspection reports for eight days past the date of inspection.)
The inspections department reminds the public that its reports are a “snapshot” in time, and violations are often corrected on the spot before the inspector leaves the establishment. For a more complete list of all inspections, along with additional details on each of the inspections listed below, visit the Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing’s website.
Izumi Japanese Steakhouse, 4901 Utica Ridge Road, Davenport — During a Sept. 2 visit, a Scott County inspector cited this establishment for 14 risk-factor violations, an exceptionally large number. “Three different employees were observed handling ready-to-eat tomatoes, salads and avocados with their bare hands,” the inspector reported.
Also, one worker, without gloves, was slicing ready-to-eat tomatoes directly alongside another employee who was butchering raw beef, the inspector stated, noting that this was a repeat violation. In addition, the facility did not have the required parasite-destruction records for sushi — another repeat violation.
The inspector also reported the restaurant was not properly date-marking food items to ensure freshness and safety. “Facility is not keeping any records for sushi rice, where time as a control for safety is being used,” the inspector added.
The inspector also noted issues with cleanliness, observing that stored knives had leftover food debris on them and the interior of one cooler had a buildup of grime.
“All rice makers have buildup of food debris,” he reported. “Wire shelving, flooring, and riser pallets in the walk-in cooler have a buildup of grime and food debris. Interior of the ice machine has a buildup of grime and dust. Rice bins in the dry storage area, have a buildup of grime on the lids.”
Employees were seen washing a bowl with soap and water without performing the required process of wash/rinse/sanitize — another repeat violation.
“Two cans of Raid found in the storage room, which are not permitted in a commercial restaurant setting,” the inspector reported, adding that “several food buckets” were being stored on the floor of a walk-in cooler. “Exterior of the fryers, rice cookers, sides of cooking equipment on the back cook line, and barbecue equipment have an excess buildup of grease and debris.”
The inspector also noted that the hot-water supply in the employee restroom had been shut off.
The visit was in response to a customer’s complaint that grease from the overhead ventilation hoods in the hibachi area dripped into their drink. The inspector deemed the complaint to be verified.
Hy-Vee Food Store, 2827 Hamilton Boulevard, Sioux City — During a Sept. 30 visit, a Siouxland District Health Department inspector noted that the equipment and utensils in the sushi-preparation area were being used for both raw and ready-to-eat food without being washed, rinsed and sanitized between uses. In addition, the magnetic strip used to store knives in the sushi-preparation area was visibly soiled, as was the wall behind the three-compartment sink in the sushi area.
Inside a retail cooler, the inspector found meal kits holding at 45 degrees and potato salad holding at 50 degrees, well above the 41-degree maximum, all of which had to be discarded. In addition, the dishwasher in the bakery department was not reaching 160 degrees as required, and multiple, small flying insects were observed in the dishwashing area. Also, single-service food containers were stored directly on the floor of the sushi area and the cooler-fan guards in the sushi and meat department were visibly soiled with accumulated debris.
Acapulco Mexican Bakery, 1937 Keokuk St., Iowa City — During a Sept. 29 visit, a Johnson County inspector cited this establishment for 11 risk-factor violations, an unusually high number, and determined the person in charge was not a certified food protection manager and did not demonstrate adequate control of food-safety practices.
Containers of raw meat and cooked foods were left uncovered inside the main walk-in cooler; numerous containers of hot food on the steam table had an internal temperature below 135 degrees and had to reheated to 165 degrees; a container of raw pork, measured at 51 degrees, was being stored at room temperature on a table outside the kitchen; a container of unspecified cooked meat, measured at 57 degrees, was being stored at room temperature near a grill and numerous food containers had no date-markings to ensure freshness and safety.
Also, a container of pork feet was thawing at room temperature on top of a three-compartment sink, and there was no probe-style thermometer available to measure the internal temperature of food.
Ampride Travel Center, 217 W. 3rd St., Peterson – During a Sept. 23 visit, a Siouxland District Health Department inspector observed a container of sliced turkey deli meat inside the walk-in cooler that showed “the presence of mold.” The meat was discarded. Also, sour cream, French onion dip, raw eggs, raw chicken, and lunch meat inside the cooler were all holding at 45 degrees or warmer and had to be discarded.
In addition, containers of lunch meat were not properly date-marked to ensure freshness and safety and had to be discarded, and the kitchen staff was not completing the sanitizing step when cleaning dishes and utensils. Because the walk-in cooler was unable to keep food at 41 degrees or colder, all of the temperature-controlled food inside was removed and discarded.
The inspection was in response to a non-illness complaint alleging improper holding temperatures. The complaint was deemed verified.
Dordt University, 700 7th St. NE, Sioux Center — During a Sept. 23 visit to the university’s food service, a Siouxland District Health Department inspector observed water leaking from the ceiling in front of the walk-in cooler, and noted that chicken wings cooked at 10:30 a.m. were holding at 71 degrees at 12:47 p.m. In addition, chicken wings in the hot-holding unit of the buffet table were measured at 115 degrees and had to be removed from the buffet. Also, grilled chicken breast in the buffet area was measured at 126 degrees and had to be reheated to 165 degrees. Marinara sauce holding at 130 degrees on the pasta buffet table had to be discarded, as did rice noodles that were holding at 123 degrees and cut cantaloupe that was holding at 43 degrees. The inspector also reported that cooking spoons that had been put away and stored were marred by a buildup of food debris.
Kimme’s Humboldt Country Store, 411 S. 13th St., Humboldt — During a Sept. 23 visit, a state inspector noted that gravy prepared that morning was holding at 53 degrees at 1:34 p.m. and had to be discarded. Also, various food items — including stuffed breadsticks, multiple types of cheese, chicken and ham — were measured at above 41 degrees and had to be discarded or moved to a walk-in cooler to rapidly cool.
In addition, multiple food items had no date-markings to ensure freshness and safety. The inspector found refried beans that were prepared 12 days earlier, on Sept. 11, and which had to be discarded, and the fountain beverage machine was marred by a buildup of syrup and debris. The inspector also noted that food items packaged for retail sale — including wraps, sandwiches, parfaits and bakery goods — were not labeled with their ingredients, food allergens, weight, or the place of production to ensure source traceability.
Pump & Pantry, 11925 University Ave., Clive — During a Sept. 21 visit, a state inspector noted there was no certified food protection manager on site during all hours of operation, as required. Also, the person in charge did not demonstrate adequate knowledge of holding-temperature requirements or date-marking procedures.
In addition to undated  food items, the inspector reported finding food items that were not sold or discarded within seven days as required. Those food items included pork dated Sept. 9, turkey dated Sept. 7 and Sept. 10, and ham that was dated Sept. 7.  Also, pizza slices that were not marked with the time at which they were expired had to be discarded.
Kinnick Stadium-East Concourse, Aramark Concessions, 825 Evashevski Drive, Iowa City — A Johnson County inspector conducted a series of inspections at the University of Iowa stadium during active food operations over two visits on Sept. 5 and Sept. 9, and then combined his findings into a single report.
The inspector visited a total of 23 concession stands over the two days, with each stand evaluated individually. However, the inspector’s published report identifies each concession stand only by a number rather than the stand’s common name.
Among the findings: Hot foods were not being held at 135 degrees or warmer as required, including cooked pork held at 120 degrees, hot dogs held at 118 to 121 degrees, burgers held at 121 to 129 degrees, and corn dogs held at 122 degrees. Foods that should have been held at 41 degrees or colder included cheese held at 54 degrees, pepperoni held at 51 degrees, and lettuce held at 52 to 61 degrees.
Also, debris buildup was observed on food-contact surfaces at two concession stands, and handwashing sinks were not maintained or accessible for use at five concession stands, with some of the sinks used for storage or blocked by other equipment.
In addition, the walk-in cooler at one concession stand had an ambient temperature of 57 degrees rather than 41 degrees or below. After two hours with the cooler’s door closed, the unit was able to reach 35 degrees.



Quotation







Imminent health hazard conditions were identified during the inspection and discussed with the person in charge. Following the discussion, the person in charge voluntarily ceased food service operations.


– Inspector's report for the Cactus 3 food truck in Iowa City 


Cactus 3, 245 S. Gilbert St., Iowa City — During an Aug. 27 visit, a Johnson County inspector cited this establishment’s food truck for 11 risk-factor violations, an unusually high number.
“Multiple ready-to-eat food containers that require temperature control were stored uncovered on an exterior table outside the mobile unit, exposing them to potential environmental contamination,” the inspector reported. “All seven containers of foods requiring temperature control — including prepared sauces, lettuce, cheese and other prepared foods — were observed at internal temperatures above 41 degrees … All commercially processed refrigerated foods requiring date-marking were observed without the required date-marking.”
In addition, the handwashing sink in the food truck had no soap, paper towels or hot-water supply at the time of the inspection, and access to the sink itself was obstructed by items stored in the basin. Also, the sink intended to wash equipment and utensils was instead being used to store cups, containers and bags, the inspector reported.
“Imminent health hazard conditions were identified during the inspection and discussed with the person in charge,” the inspector reported. “Following the discussion, the person in charge voluntarily ceased food service operations. Food service shall not resume until the conditions creating the imminent health hazard have been corrected.”
On Sept. 17, the Cactus 3 mobile food unit was allowed to resume business operations.
Hy-Vee Foods, 5050 Edgewood Drive, Cedar Rapids — During a Sept. 17 visit, a Linn County inspector noted that an employee preparing raw sushi was not washing their hands or changing gloves before moving onto other tasks.
Also, fried shrimp was being held at 67 degrees on the sushi preparation counter and had to be reheated to 165 degrees. In addition, sliced watermelon and cans of whipped cream were cold-holding at 45 to 48 degrees in an open-air retail cooler and had to be discarded.
“Several products were date-marked for eight days,” the inspector reported, suggesting the listed discard dates extended beyond the allowable maximum of seven days.
The inspector also reported that access to the handwashing sinks in the Market Grille dish room and the bakery were blocked by boxes or equipment, and the handwashing sink in the Hy-Chi area for Chinese food was not supplied with hand soap.
“There is a presence of flying insects in the bakery ware-washing room,” the inspector reported.
Two in-use knives were observed being stored in standing, room-temperature water in the sushi department, and unpackaged fish was being stored in direct contact with cloth towels, the inspector added. Also, a faucet in the bakery was leaking, as was the detergent basin used in the bakery’s dishwashing machine.
“Meat department walk-in cooler was observed visibly soiled,” the inspector reported, adding that the “bakery floor was observed visibly soiled.”
The visit was in response to a complaint concerning unprotected food items, lack of date-markings on food, the presence of pests and general sanitization and cleaning practices within the bakery department. The complaint was deemed partially verified with regard to flying insects and the soiled floor in the bakery area.
Good Samaritan Home-Timber Ridge, 2 Oak Ridge, Ottumwa – During a Sept. 14 visit to this assisted living center and care facility, a state inspector cited the business for 10 risk-factor violations, an unusually high number, and noted the person in charge appeared unable to fulfill their duties as evidenced by the extent of the violations.
Salsa in the care facility’s reach-in cooler “appeared to have mold growth,” the inspector reported, adding that some items in the cooler were holding at temperatures above 41 degrees, such as ranch dressing at 51 degrees, salsa at 52 degrees and milk at 53 degrees. All of the food items that were out of safe temperature ranges were discarded.
The inspector also reported that taco meat, lettuce and deli turkey inside the walk-in cooler had no date-markings to ensure freshness and safety. In addition, ground beef had been left in a pan of standing water to thaw, and food was being stored on the floor of the walk-in freezer and dry storage room. “Drawers, cupboards, and bottom of coolers in both kitchens not clean,” the inspector reported.
Gunchies, 2905 Telegraph Road, Davenport — During a Sept. 10 visit, a Scott County inspector cited this establishment for 10 risk-factor violations, an unusually high number, and reported seeing an employee using their bare hands to handle flour tortillas in the kitchen. Also, several opened products — such as ham, turkey and coleslaw — had been held for more than 24 hours without being date-marked to ensure freshness and safety.
One bottle of house-made ranch dressing had to be discarded as it had a preparation date of Aug. 30, beyond the seven-day limit. Also, a food slicer had a buildup of dried food debris along the blade, and the interiors of both cold-preparation tables in the kitchen were marred by a buildup of soil and required cleaning and sanitizing.
Pans being washed and rinsed without being sanitized, and there were no handwashing sinks located in the basement food-preparation area.  Also, some of the walls and kitchen floor fans showed a buildup of dust and food splatter, the inspector reported.
China Buffet, 2500 S. Center St., Marshalltown — During a Sept. 4 visit, a state inspector cited this establishment for maintaining sliced melon, fruit-salad mix, and puddings on the buffet line at temperatures of 50 to 56 degrees — well above the allowable maximum. The restaurant also had no date-marking system in place to ensure the food it served was fresh and safe.
“Foods like cooked meats, cooked vegetables, and cooked noodles in the walk-in cooler do not have a production or discard date,” the inspector reported. “Fruits and vegetables are not washed before preparation.”
The Bettplex, 4850 Competition Drive, Bettendorf — During a Sept. 3 visit, a Scott County inspector reported there were no date-markings on food items such as lettuce and cooked chicken breast. Also, expired food items — including sliced tomatoes dated Aug. 22, cooked chicken breasts dated Aug. 23, and homemade ranch dressing dated Aug. 7 — had to be discarded. In addition, the microwave ovens were marred by food debris and the cooler of one concession stand had water pooling in the bottom.
The Foundry Food and Tap, 5055 Competition Drive, Bettendorf — During a Sept. 2 visit, a Scott County inspector cited this establishment for 10 risk-factor violations, an unusually high number. The inspector noted that several food items — including homemade dressings and sliced tomatoes — were not date-marked to ensure freshness and safety. Also, a portion of the interior of a large ice chest had “spotted black spots on it,” and access to a handwashing sink was blocked by garbage cans.
In addition, bottles of oil, water and salad dressing were not labeled to avoid confusion, and “broken glass pieces” were found in the refrigerated cooler of the bar area. “Kitchen equipment has a grease buildup,” the inspector reported. “Wall behind prep cooler in the kitchen has excess food debris on it.”
El Maya Mexican Restaurant, 2351 Sunset Drive, Norwalk — During an Aug. 27 visit, a state inspector cited this restaurant for 12 risk-factor violations, an exceptionally large number. The inspector reported the person in charge was not a certified food protection manager and concluded there was a “pattern of non-compliance” with food-safety regulations.
The inspector reported that beans and queso made the previous day that had yet to cool to 41 degrees and had to be discarded. Also, rice and enchilada cheese that were out of acceptable temperature ranges was discarded, as was salsa that was “sitting out on the table” at 66 degrees. ‘
“Interior of ice machine unclean,” the inspector reported. “Soda nozzle at the bar unclean. Handwashing-only sink behind the bar had several cans of beer in the basin.”
The inspector also reported that employee medications were being stored with the bottled hot sauces. “Due to the large number of repeat violations, the inspection frequency of this establishment has been increased to every nine months,” the inspector reported.
Taqueria Leal, 2247 Hubbell Ave., Des Moines — After an Aug. 25 visit by a state inspector, the operator of this food truck, typically parked at the Hubbell Avenue location Monday through Saturday, agreed to shut down operations until the food truck could be brought into compliance with most food-safety regulations.
While the state inspector’s written report is devoid of any detail, it does recite the regulations violated at the time of the visit. “Food safety certificate is expired,” the report states. “Person in charge stated refried beans were made at home. Ready-to-eat foods not dated…  No sanitizer available. Establishment does not have functioning running water to sanitize dishes and food-contact surfaces. No hot water; ran out during inspection. No soap. No paper towels… Heavy food debris and grease buildup throughout unit. License not posted. Previous inspection not posted… Person in charge agrees to not reopen without approval from department.”
State records indicate the Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing authorized the reopening two days later, on Aug. 27, while also citing the business for two additional risk-factor violations.
Tacos Jalisciense, 1608 Grandview Ave., Muscatine — During an Aug. 24 visit, a state inspector cited this eatery for 11 risk-factor violations, an unusually high number. The inspector reported finding uncovered taco salad bowls “in storage” that then had to be discarded, and reported that cooked chicken inside a cooler, prepared the previous day, had cooled only to 60 degrees and had to be discarded. Also, “a couple containers of cooked meat (were measured) at 132 degrees sitting on a shelf” and had to be reheated to 165 degrees. “Microwave interiors soiled,” the inspector reported. “Knife not sanitized after cleaning.”
José’s Tacos, 2720 Holcomb Ave., Des Moines — During an Aug. 20 visit to this food truck, a state inspector cited the business for 10-risk-factor violations, an unusually high number. After the visit, the operator agreed to shut down the food truck until it could be brought into compliance with food-safety regulations.
While the inspector’s written report provides few details on the precise nature of the violations, it does include a recitation of the basic allegations, indicating that tomatoes, ham, chorizo and other food items that were out of safe temperature ranges had to be discarded.
“Ready-to-eat foods not dated,” the inspector reported. “No sanitizer available. No water at hand sink. No soap at hand sink. No paper towels at hand sink. Potatoes stored in hand sink… Owner agrees to remain closed until approved to reopen.”
State records indicate the Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing authorized the reopening of the food truck on Aug. 27 after citing the business for five additional risk-factor violations.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Cowbells and handshakes open Magaziner-Mellor debate, but little agreement follows
description: Clang clang clang went the cowbells as supporters of Republican congressional candidate Vic Mellor gathered outside WPRI 12’s studios Friday ahead of his first TV debate with incumbent Democratic U.S. Rep. Seth Magaziner, who had his own posse of fans congregating before his arrival. Inside was at first quieter, with Magaziner and Mellor shaking hands […]
text:
Democratic U.S. Rep. Seth Magaziner, left, and Republican challenger Vic Mellor exchange remarks during their first general election debate at WPRI 12's East Providence studios on Friday, Oct. 9, 2026. (Photo by Aaron Aguilar/WPRI 12)Clang clang clang went the cowbells as supporters of Republican congressional candidate Vic Mellor gathered outside WPRI 12’s studios Friday ahead of his first TV debate with incumbent Democratic U.S. Rep. Seth Magaziner, who had his own posse of fans congregating before his arrival.
Inside was at first quieter, with Magaziner and Mellor shaking hands before and after the taping. While cordiality reigned over their limited offscreen interaction, the televised back-and-forth was decidedly more acrimonious, with each man impugning the other’s character as much as his politics. 
“So he wants to abolish ICE,” Mellor, 56, said of Magaziner’s stance on the immigration enforcement agency at one point. “That’s basically what he said there. He just doesn’t have the gonads to say it.”
Magaziner, meanwhile, described his opponent as a fly-by-night opportunist.
“Vic Mellor is treating Rhode Island like a pit stop between Florida and Washington,” the 43 year-old congressman said, a reference to Mellor moving from Florida back to his native state and beginning his congressional campaign within the same month. 
“He hasn’t lived here since 1997,” Magaziner noted, and twice said that when Mellor last lived in Rhode Island, “‘Titanic’ was No. 1 at the box office.” 
The candidates also clashed over Iran, healthcare and stock trading.
And inevitably they engaged on Mellor’s embrace of the Jan. 6, 2021, march on the U.S. Capitol, a choice which he reiterated Friday came with “no regrets.”
“You know he tried to do a stunt, and that backfired on him,” Mellor said of Magaziner’s Sept. 10 press conference outside the Rhode Island State House, in which Magaziner enlisted police officers who had been harmed in the events of Jan. 6 to make the case that Mellor’s participation that day was repugnant and disqualifying. 
Magaziner calls a press conference to vilify his ‘J6er’ opponent. His opponent showed up.

“Rhode Islanders don’t care about Jan. 6,” Mellor said, then turned to his opponent, “What they do care about is the riots that happened here in Providence with the socialists, the DSA, and the defund the police movement, which you marched with in solidarity.”
“I have covered the criminal cases of those arrested for their actions on Jan. 6,” WPRI-12’s Tim White, who along with Ted Nesi moderated the debate, said at one point. “Mr. Mellor is not one of them. Are you simply lumping him in with the rioters for political gain here?”
Magaziner did not directly answer the question, but accused Mellor of being “lost in a sea of conspiracy theories” about Democrat-led puppetmasters manufacturing Jan. 6. 
Magaziner recalled the Capitol police officers who had traveled to Rhode Island for his press conference, saying: “It’s so serious that some of those Capitol police officers who bravely defended our Capitol on Jan. 6 came up here to Rhode Island to say, ‘Don’t vote for Vic Mellor.’”
Mellor also showed up to that presser — less than a day after his primary win against state GOP-endorsed candidate Dr. Stephen Skoly — and clarified to the media that he had never been charged or involved in any sort of legal action for his Jan. 6 participation. And while he stood less than 30 feet from Magaziner that day, he did not speak to the congressman. 
“I’m sure at some point him and I will have face-to-face conversations,” Mellor told reporters then.
Friday’s face-to-face saw the two men spar most sharply over President Donald Trump’s immigration enforcement strategies. Mellor defended the feds, parrying questions about federal agents’ shooting of civilians, illustrating them as something like a death wish.
“The people that were shot by ICE were for death,” Mellor said. “They were — they were causing death reasons for ICE agents, and they unfortunately got what they deserved.”
Magaziner’s reply: “Mr. Mellor just made a claim that everyone shot by ICE was doing death stuff, or whatever that means.”
He turned to the July fatal shooting of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Maine, and questioned whether federal agents were being held accountable for excessive force. Perhaps some of ICE’s immigration enforcement powers should be transferred to another agency, Magaziner suggested.
When Nesi asked Magaziner if he supported abolishing ICE, Magaziner replied, “I don’t think that ICE, as it is currently constituted, has the culture necessary to enforce the law while also upholding people’s civil rights and civil liberties.” 
That triggered Mellor’s assessment of Magaziner’s words as lacking fortitude.
“He’s got the political answer going on,” Mellor said. 
Supporters of Democratic U.S. Rep. Seth Magaziner and Republican challenger Vic Mellor gather outside WPRI 12’s East Providence studios ahead of the candidates’ first general election debate on Friday, Oct. 9, 2026. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)
Both candidates faced questions about their residential histories in the district they seek to represent. Nesi pressed the second-term Magaziner on his unfulfilled promise from earlier campaigning that he would move to the 2nd District. 
“I told you before, my family situation changed,” Magaziner said. “Specifically, my wife got a job that requires her to commute to Boston, so we had to be close to the train station, and I live in Providence, which is one of the 21 cities and towns that I represent.”
Both the 1st and 2nd Congressional District represent Providence, depending on which part of the city you live in. Magaziner technically lives in the part of the city that falls within the 1st District.
Mellor, meanwhile, is a Woonsocket native who lived in Florida for about three decades before moving to Warwick last year for his campaign.
“How can you represent a state in Congress that, until recently, you hadn’t lived in for several decades?” Nesi asked.
Mellor replied that he was “born and raised” in Woonsocket, by a single mom on welfare, and that a dearth of opportunities drove him out of the state.
“Nothing’s changed here in 30 years. It’s gotten worse,” Mellor said.
“Why not, though, run for Congress in Florida, where you have made your life for the last 30 years?” Nesi asked. 
“I can make a bigger, bigger, better impact here in Rhode Island than I can in Florida,” Mellor replied. 
The candidates also sparred over the war in Iran, which Mellor declined to describe as a war, and congressional stock trading, with Mellor accusing Magaziner of voting against his own proposed ban. Magaziner had actually voted against a Republican-led bill that combined the stock trading legislation with unrelated stipulations on voter identification requirements. 
On health care, Mellor advocated for the expansion of health savings accounts, while Magaziner called for the restoration of federal funding.
You can watch the debate online. It will also air Sunday at 10 a.m. on FOX Providence.
Early voting begins Wednesday, Oct. 14, ahead of the Nov. 3 general election.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: House Speaker Mike Johnson rallies with Miller-Meeks in contentious 1st District race
description: DAVENPORT — U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson asked Iowans at a Davenport rally Friday to send U.S. Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks back to Congress — telling the crowd, “I gotta have her,” as she runs in one of the nation’s most competitive U.S. House races in November. Miller-Meeks running for reelection against Democrat Christina Bohannan, who […]
text:
U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson, right,  and other House Republicans including Illinois U.S. Rep. Darin LaHood, left, joined by Iowa U.S. Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, center, for a rally in Davenport Oct. 9, 2026, less than a month before the 2026 general election where she is seeking reelection in what is expected to be one of the most competitive seats in the country. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)DAVENPORT — U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson asked Iowans at a Davenport rally Friday to send U.S. Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks back to Congress — telling the crowd, “I gotta have her,” as she runs in one of the nation’s most competitive U.S. House races in November.
Miller-Meeks running for reelection against Democrat Christina Bohannan, who also ran for Iowa’s 1st Congressional District in 2022 and 2024. While Miller-Meeks defeated Bohannan in those two elections, and political forecasters and polls predict the Democratic candidate could pull ahead in the Nov. 3, 2026 election.
Earlier Friday, Cook Political Report moved their race ratings for Miller-Meeks’ seat, as well as for Iowa’s 3rd Congressional District, currently represented by Rep. Zach Nunn, from “toss-up” to “leans Democrat.” The political forecaster’s move for these Iowa seats — as well as shifting Iowa’s 2nd Congressional District from a “leans Republican” to a “toss up” race — were three of 18 race ratings to shift in Democrats’ favor with less than a month before the election.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Cook Political Report editor Erin Covey wrote in an analysis about the race rating changes, “In the final weeks of the election, Republicans have hoped that a massive ad campaign effort could dent Democratic candidates’ images and shore up Republicans struggling to free themselves of the anchor of President Donald Trump. With less than four weeks to go, that heavy spending has yet to move the needle.”
Miller-Meeks and Johnson both noted the high amount of spending going into this year’s midterm elections, as well as the spending happening in Iowa alone — Punchbowl News reported Tuesday Iowa’s 1st District had reached $37.4 million in ad spending. Johnson said he believed the 1st District race “is going to be a $50 million dollar race” leading up to Election Day.
“This is not what the founding fathers intended, OK, but this is what we got,” Johnson said. “We have to put the resources onto it. We have to make sure that our warriors like Mariannette Miller-Meeks get reelected, because we’re in the battle for saving the future of the republic.”
The Davenport visit was one of Johnson’s many campaign stops leading up to Nov. 3 as he and Republicans aim to keep control of the U.S. House. The speaker said he had been to “40 districts, 22 states this month alone” supporting Republicans. He said Miller-Meeks’ district was one of the “top five districts” in the country that will determine which party gains majority control of the House.
There are several reasons why GOP candidates are facing tougher election odds in states like Iowa, which supported President Donald Trump and Republicans in 2024. High fuel costs driven in part from the war with Iran, the impacts of tariff policies and concerns about Medicaid cuts through the 2025 “One, Big Beautiful Bill Act” amid rising healthcare costs and rural hospital closures are all issues Democrats say are top concerns for Iowans on the campaign trail, and reasons voters are frustrated with GOP majorities.
While Johnson highlighted tax cuts, immigration enforcement and some of the “pro-growth” policies supporting U.S. businesses in his speech, he focused on Democrats running in the 2026 election, who he said were “radicals” and “communists.”
“The insurgent left is taking over the Democrat Party, and it is a very dangerous thing,” Johnson said. “The Marxists, the communists, the socialists are on the rise, and they are winning races all around America. They’re putting people like Bohannan in this race. … Now in the campaign right now, they’re trying to pretend like they’re moderates, but we all know the truth.”
Miller-Meeks claimed her opponent was “OK with the Socialist Party,” and said Bohannan’s voting record as a state politician and her work as a law professor at the University of Iowa on issues related to diversity, equity and inclusion shows her positions are out of touch with most Iowans. She contrasted this with her own support for the $15 billion Mesabi Metallics steel mill project announced by Trump earlier in October, which has a planned location in the 1st District.
“Would you rather have someone that delivered the largest tax cut in American history and the largest steel mill in American history, or would you rather have someone that’s perfectly OK with the Socialist Party before it even became hip to be elected as a socialist in the Democrat Party?” Miller Meeks asked.
Miller-Meeks and Republicans have linked Bohannan with movements like the Democratic Socialists of America. But a September campaign event, when Bohannan was asked if she supports or is a member of DSA, she responded, “I’m not a socialist. I don’t support that.”
“It’s a laughable charge,” Bohannan campaign manager Dan Driscoll said in a statement responding to Johnson’s visit.  “Christina criticized President Biden for failing to secure the southern border and disagreed with him on college loan forgiveness. She’s an advocate for small business, innovation and competition, and she has worked extensively in rural economic development.
“What’s out of touch with voters is Rep. Miller-Meeks’ record of siding with billionaires, corporations, special interests and party bosses like Speaker Johnson, who is stumping in Iowa in a sad attempt to rescue her flailing campaign.”
Johnson had also come to Iowa in support of Miller-Meeks, as well as Nunn, during the 2024 election cycle as they were expected to face tight reelection races. The House speaker said Miller-Meeks’ victory in 2024 by less than 800 votes after a recount — as well as her initial 2020 win by a margin of six votes — shows the importance for Republicans to get out the vote.
“This district, more than any in America — when we say close election, we mean close election,” Johnson said.

title: Man taken into custody in Vermont faces murder charge in his mother’s death in Massachusetts
description:
Court records made public Friday revealed that an argument about cats between the mother and son preceded the fatal shooting.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Man taken into custody in Vermont faces murder charge in his mother’s death in Massachusetts.
text:
Ryan Hanafin appears on a video conference from Northeast Regional Correctional Facility in St. Johnsbury on Friday, October 9, 2026. Screenshot by Alan J. Keays/VTDigger

A Massachusetts man wanted in connection with the death of his mother in the Bay State appeared in a Vermont court Friday after he was taken into custody a day earlier in Warren.
Ryan Hanafin, 22, agreed during a brief hearing Friday afternoon in Washington County criminal court in Barre to be extradited to Massachusetts. MassLive.com reported Friday that Hanafin faces charges of murder and assault and battery with a dangerous weapon in Massachusetts in the fatal shooting of his mother, 49-year-old Andria Hanafin.
VTDigger was not able to confirm the charges Hanafin faces in Massachusetts. The Middlesex County District Attorney’s Office in Massachusetts could not immediately be reached Friday for comment. 
Vermont Superior Court Judge Michael Kainen asked Ryan Hanafin if his decision to return to Massachusetts was voluntary.
“Yes, sir,” Hanafin said, appearing by video for the proceeding from the Northeast Regional Correctional Facility in St. Johnsbury where he has been held without bail since he was taken into custody Thursday afternoon in Vermont. 
Washington County State’s Attorney Michelle Donnelly told the judge that she expected authorities in Massachusetts to come to Vermont and transport Hanafin back to that state “pretty quickly,” though she added she did not have exact timing. 
Kainan set the case for another hearing next week to check on the status of Hanafin’s return to Massachusetts.
According to court filings made public Friday in Vermont following his hearing, Massachusetts authorities had early on in the investigation termed Hanafin a “person of interest” in the shooting death of his mother in a home where they both lived in Reading, Massachusetts, a suburb of Boston. 
Massachusetts State Police had contacted authorities in Vermont on Thursday reporting that they believed Hanafin was in Vermont, and that he was known to have a “prior connection” to Powderhound Road in the town of Warren, according to police and court filings.  
Hanafin was spotted by police in Vermont driving a Dodge Charger on Route 100 south of the Sugarbush Access Road in Warren around 2:30 p.m. Thursday and troopers pulled him over and took him into custody on an arrest warrant out of Massachusetts, according to the court filings. 
Andria Hanafin, a mother of three, was also an “animal rescuer/fosterer” of cats and worked as a veterinary technician, the court filings stated. Inside the home, the filings added, there were 20 to 30 cats and kittens roaming.
Matthew Hanafin, Ryan Hanafin’s father, who had discovered his wife’s body in the home when he returned home from work early Thursday morning, told investigators that his son and his son’s Dodge Charger were missing, court filings stated.
“Matthew told investigators he noticed that and thought it was strange because Ryan had not left the house in several days,” according to the court filings.
The father reported to police that he had last spoken to wife Wednesday evening. “They spoke briefly about an argument with their son Ryan about the cats in the household,” the court filings stated, adding, “During that conversation, the victim told Matthew she wanted Ryan to move out of the house.”
The father also reported to police that the last time he saw Ryan Hanafin was around 11 a.m. Wednesday when he recalled “yelling at Ryan that he needs to get a job and do something with his life,” the court filings stated. 
Police also spoke to a friend of Ryan Hanafin’s who reported that he received a Snapchat message from Hanafin at 6:44 p.m. Wednesday about a conversation Ryan Hanafin had earlier with his cousin. “Told him I blew madre to pieces and he believed me” the message from Hanafin stated, according to the court filings, using the Spanish word for mother.
Avi Springer, an attorney who represented Hanafin in the Vermont court proceeding Friday, could also not immediately be reached Friday for comment.
