name: Mississippi Today
title: Curtis Flowers battled diabetes during his wrongful imprisonment
description: Curtis Flowers, center, stands with his attorneys Henderson Hill, left, and Rob McDuff at his bail hearing in Winona, Miss., Monday, Dec. 16, 2019.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
As the cause of Curtis Flowers‘ death is under investigation, an attorney who represented him during multiple appeals, eventually leading to his exoneration and release from death row, said his former client struggled with diabetes the entire time he knew him – a condition that isn’t easy to manage in prison.
Flowers, 56, was found dead Wednesday at his family home in Winona, leaving behind siblings, a daughter and grandchildren. Family members were not immediately available for comment Friday. 
Flowers was convicted of four counts of capital murder but maintained his innocence through the string of trials that led to a landmark U.S. Supreme Court case about racial bias in jury selection. Decades of legal work led to his release from prison in 2019. 
State Public Defender Andre de Gruy, who was part of the team that represented Flowers during his third through sixth trials, said Flowers enjoyed meeting law school students and interns and talking about the relationship between a client and their attorney. 
“He had more experience in the courtroom and legal system than they will ever have,” de Gruy said. 
De Gruy said he talked with Flowers a few weeks ago. They were laughing together and catching up about life. They have kept in touch over the years after Flowers returned home. 
When they last spoke, Flowers was trying to find a job. He wasn’t sure what type of work he could pursue, de Gruy said, because Flowers didn’t have access to vocational training while on death row.
De Gruy said he and Flowers talked about the possibility of Flowers doing clerical work at the State Public Defender’s Office, but Flowers would have had to relocate to Jackson. He didn’t seem interested in moving, de Gruy said. In Winona, Flowers was close to family and was able to care for his father until his death last year. 
“He felt like he was able to pay back some of the love his family had shown to him,” de Gruy said. 
In July 1996, Flowers was accused of fatally shooting four people at Tardy Furniture in Winona. Then-Montgomery County District Attorney Doug Evans spent nearly two decades prosecuting Flowers six times, each time resulting in a hung jury or a guilty verdict later overturned by the Mississippi Supreme Court.
The sixth trial resulted in a death sentence. The state court heard and denied appeals twice, and Flowers’ case went to the U.S. Supreme Court. 
In 2018, the American Public Media podcast “In the Dark” investigated Flowers’ case and presented evidence of a history of racial bias in jury selection by Evans and evidence that suggested someone else may have committed the shootings.
Flowers’ case went before the U.S. Supreme Court twice, and in June 2019, the court decided 7-2 to overturn Flowers’ conviction, finding that Evans intentionally struck Black people from serving on the jury that convicted Flowers, who was Black. 
Afterward, Evans recused himself and the state attorney general’s office stepped in. Months later in December 2019, Circuit Judge Joey Loper dismissed Flowers’ capital murder charges with prejudice on a motion by the attorney general’s office.
Flowers left death row and the Mississippi State Penitentiary at Parchman, but he spent some time in other jails and prisons before he was released and returned home.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Supreme Court denies request to extend deadline for skill games
description: In a letter to the court late Thursday, Chief Deputy Attorney General Susan E. Affronti noted the request from three state lawmakers came only two business days before the deadline after which the slot machine-like games will become illegal.
text:
A skill games parlor in Williamsport, Pa. (Photo by Peter Hall/Capital-Star)(This article was updated at 3:30 p.m., Friday, Oct. 9, 2026, to include the Supreme Court’s decision.)
The state Supreme Court on Friday denied requests to extend the deadline Tuesday to remove skill games from establishments across the commonwealth.
In a pair of one-page orders, the court denied petitions asking the court to allow the slot machine-like games to remain in operation until Feb. 10 while state lawmakers work to pass a regulatory and taxing scheme for the industry.
The decisions followed Attorney General Dave Sunday’s office asking the court to reject a request from a trio of state lawmakers who want to delay enforcement of the court’s decision that the machines are subject to the state Gaming Act and Crimes Code.
In a letter to the court late Thursday, Chief Deputy Attorney General Susan E. Affronti noted the request from three state lawmakers came only two business days before the deadline after which the slot machine-like games will become illegal. 
That deadline is the result of a 120-day stay the Supreme Court placed on its June 15 decision that resolved more than a decade of ambiguity over the machines, which the state argued are functionally equivalent to casino slot machines. As a result, the machines and operators must be licensed by the state Gaming Control Board.
“Because this petition comes too late, because these three legislators lack standing to obtain the relief they seek, and because the equities weigh against them, the Court should deny the King’s Bench petition,” Affronti wrote.
As the state’s high court, the Supreme Court may use its extraordinary King’s Bench power – derived from English courts – to take immediate, direct control of a case or legal issue in a crisis.
State Sens. Gene Yaw (R-Lycoming) and Anthony Williams (D-Philadelphia) and Rep. Jonathan Fritz (R-Wayne) filed, withdrew and refiled a petition this week asking the Supreme Court to use its emergency powers to extend the Wednesday deadline so the Pennsylvania General Assembly can  pass legislation legalizing skill games. One of the companies involved in the manufacturing of skill games is in Yaw’s district.
Friday’s orders denied the lawmakers’ request and one made by 20 charitable organizations that host skill games.
In its June decision, the high court said it’s up to the General Assembly to determine whether the machines should be legal. It stayed the effect of its decision to give the legislature time to act and avoid the upheaval an immediate ban would cause. 
Pace-O-Matic (POM), which produces the software at the heart of the machines, and a group called the Skill Games Business Consortium have also made filings in support of extending the stay.
Skill games are commonly found in small businesses such as taverns, restaurants, convenience stores and fraternal organizations such as Veterans of Foreign Wars posts and volunteer fire companies. Proprietors of those establishments say banning skill games will take away revenue that keeps them financially afloat.
The attorney general’s office argued the Georgia-based company should have requested a reargument before the court if it believed the four-month stay was too short. 
Affronti noted that the lawmakers did not explain why they waited to ask for an extension. The General Assembly has known since the court agreed to hear the case in June 2024 that it might result in a ruling declaring the machines illegal.
She also argued that lawmakers lack standing to request that the court reopen its ruling. The Supreme Court has ruled previously that individual lawmakers have standing only when their ability to participate in the voting process is impaired or they’re deprived of their official powers as legislators.
“While petitioners wish to propose legislation, there is no allegation, or any other reason to believe, that failing to extend the stay will block their ‘ability to participate’ once the ruling takes effect,” the letter said.
Skill games have been the subject of several court rulings as they proliferated across the commonwealth in the last decade. The Supreme Court’s ruling overturned a lower Commonwealth Court precedent that the machines were distinct from gambling devices.
POM and the Lycoming County business that produces the Pennsylvania Skill machines that run the software, Miele Manufacturing, argued in the Supreme Court that skill games differ from gambling machines because skill game players have an opportunity to win back their bets.
The attorney general’s office said, in practice, few players bother to go through the lengthy, laborious process of completing the skill portion of the game. Most simply make another bet in hopes of winning a jackpot.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Flathead County judges make their pitch for the Montana Supreme Court
description: Two judges, both alike in current roles, are making the case for why they are best to ascend to the state’s highest bench.  At a series of forums around Montana in recent weeks, Flathead County District Court Judges Amy Eddy and Dan Wilson have sought to distinguish their legal bonafides, their campaign strategies and approach […]
text:
Flathead County District Court Judges Amy Eddy and Dan Wilson are facing off in the race for an open seat on the Montana Supreme Court. (contributed photos)Two judges, both alike in current roles, are making the case for why they are best to ascend to the state’s highest bench. 
At a series of forums around Montana in recent weeks, Flathead County District Court Judges Amy Eddy and Dan Wilson have sought to distinguish their legal bonafides, their campaign strategies and approach to impartiality as candidates for the Montana Supreme Court. 
The most common thread was how to keep politics out of the courtroom, an issue Montana voters will also weigh in on with a ballot initiative, I-132, that could preserve the state’s nonpartisan judicial elections.
During a Bozeman event sponsored by the Gallatin County Bar Association, Eddy said that despite a new Montana law allowing political parties to donate to judicial campaigns, she is not accepting campaign donations from parties nor speaking at political gatherings. 
“We do not want our judges swearing loyalty oaths to political party platforms before a judge makes a decision,” Eddy said. “We don’t want them considering whether that will jeopardize a political party endorsement or ongoing political party campaign contributions.”
Her decision to remain nonpartisan presents one of the clearest examples of where the two candidates differ, as Wilson has taken the opposite approach. 
He has accepted campaign contributions from both the Montana Republican Party and county GOP committees, was the keynote at the state GOP winter campaign kickoff event this year, and the party has endorsed him as the “conservative candidate” in the race. 
Wilson has said personal politics shouldn’t play a role in the courtroom, and in a Bozeman forum, he said the players making arguments before the bench certainly matter, and he has not sought out endorsements or donations from attorneys. 
“As a judge, you know who those lawyers are who contributed funds to your campaign,” Wilson said, adding that it’s not hard to imagine they might expect a favorable ruling in return.  “I made the decision early on that I wasn’t going to solicit money from attorneys.”
Both candidates have donations from lawyers listed on their campaign financial disclosures.


Wilson has endorsements from the Montana Chamber of Commerce, Montana Stockgrowers Association, Montana Mining Association, Montana Association of Realtors and Montana Contractors Association. 
Eddy lists endorsements from eight current and former supreme court justices and more than two dozen district court judges, as well as from the Montana Federation of Public Employees, Montana AFL-CIO, Nurses for America, Montana National Organization for Women, Montana Conservation Voters, Montana Sportsmen’s Alliance and Big Sky 55+. 


 The jurists

Eddy grew up in Stanley, Idaho, which has a population generously reaching 100 during peak season. She skied to and from the bus stop to get to her K-8 school, early lessons in grit and perseverance she says have propelled her throughout her professional career. 
She attended law school at the University of Montana and had a private practice before she was appointed to the district court bench in 2015 by Democratic Gov. Steve Bullock. She has twice been reelected to the position. 
Eddy was also selected by the state Supreme Court to preside over the newly formed asbestos claims court in 2017 which dealt with hundreds of personal injury and wrongful death lawsuits stemming from vermiculite mining around Libby. 
Wilson is a fourth-generation Montanan with family homesteading roots near Malta. His grandfather also wore judicial robes, serving as a Phillips County judge, which Wilson said gave him values of fairness and respect for the law. 
Wilson also went to the University of Montana Law School and worked as a prosecutor in Great Falls, Chinook and Kalispell before moving into private practice. He was a Justice of the Peace in Flathead County before voters selected him for the district court bench in 2016. 
Wilson has run for the supreme court before, losing by 14 points to current Justice Katherine Bidegaray. In the same election cycle, now-Chief Justice Cory Swanson, one of the court’s more conservative voices, won his own race by eight points. 
This year, the two judges are competing to replace retiring Justice Beth Baker, who is sometimes seen as a swing vote on a bench that is characterized as having a moderate to leftward tilt which the state GOP has said Wilson will counteract if elected.  
According to a 2026 Montana Law Review article, the Treasure State’s Supreme Court tends to be in agreement more often than not, even with two new justices joining the court last year. 
Of 291 opinions authored by the court, only 30 dissents were written — led by Bidegaray, at nine — and 80% of opinions were unanimous. 
That is in contrast to the federal Supreme Court, according to Constance Van Kley, a constitutional law professor at the Blewett School of Law at the University of Montana, which rarely approaches 50% unanimity.  
During a forum hosted by the Yellowstone County Farm Bureau, Wilson said having a supreme court that is predictable benefits rural communities, by helping avoid hidden costs in “unnecessary complexities.”
“It’s vitally important that the Montana Supreme Court keep and maintain a rule of law in these cases that is predictable, that is common sense, and that people can rely on,” Wilson said. “The Montana Supreme Court is very predictable and very emphatic in its ruling. That, to me, is the ideal situation.”
He added part of a predictable supreme court comes from giving “weight and respect” to laws, with a presumption that they are constitutional, derived from the idea that power comes from the people. 
“When the people elect their legislatures and send them to Helena to enact our laws, the outcome of their wrangling, arguing, voting … ultimately the laws they pass are entitled to tremendous respect,” Wilson said. “The law … is the product of thoughtful people who take time out of their lives to go to Helena for 90 days every two years and do the people’s business.”
Eddy emphasized the constitution maintains a clear separation between the three branches of government, which needs to be preserved. She said justices should respect the roles of the other branches of government, understand limits of judicial authority, but also prevent overreach by the legislative and executive branches. 
“We are not elected to be the policymakers, and when we strike down a law, we are impacting policy sometimes in ways that we cannot even begin to anticipate,” Eddy said. “For that reason, we have a very high burden in establishing a law that is unconstitutional.”
Both Wilson and Eddy have broadly aligned on their views of the state judiciary. 
Both judges advocate for more transparency at the state’s high court, with Eddy saying it will come as part of the new judicial performance and evaluation commission, which the 2025 Legislature formed to better show the public how judges operate.  
Wilson has urged opening up more Supreme Court operations, such as holding more oral arguments in venues other than the Supreme Court chambers, as well as letting the public access normally closed-door conference discussions. 
Voters have already had a chance to cast votes for Eddy and Wilson, during the state’s June Primary, though it was inconsequential as both were already set to advance to the general election regardless of the outcome. In the primary, Eddy earned more than 51% of the vote.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Debate about Kansas law incentivizing data center construction charges up governor’s race
description: Republican Ty Masterson and Democrat Cindy Holscher share perspectives on intense Kansas debate about boundaries for mega-data centers popping up in Kansas.
text:
Sen. Ty Masterson, an Andover Republican, is defending a 2025 state law outlining the 20-year tax break for large data centers that is a key issue in the 2026 campaign for governor. Overland Park Democratic Sen. Cindy Holscher, Masterson's opponent, wants to pause data center develop to allow adoption of stronger financial and environmental guardrails. (Photo by Jill Hummels for Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Cindy Holscher and Ty Masterson sat about 20 feet apart on the floor of the Kansas Senate on the final day of the 2025 legislative session as they voted for the bill granting a 20-year state and local sales tax exemption to developers of massive data centers.
In 18th months since a bipartisan coalition of 101 members of the Legislature and Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly embraced the bill championed by artificial intelligence and information technology lobbyists, public skepticism about Kansas’ welcome mat for data centers became a flashpoint in the 2026 race for Kansas governor. The blowback was reflected in a Gallup poll showing 71% of Americans didn’t want to live near a data center.
Holscher, the Democratic nominee for governor, and Masterson, winner of the Republican gubernatorial primary, responded differently to scrutiny of their April 11, 2025, votes for the bill granting incentives to data centers.
Holscher said the groundswell of criticism prompted reconsideration of her vote and led to her decision to seek a freeze on data center projects until more meaningful financial and environmental boundaries were in place. She criticized the IT industry’s expenditure of about $1 million to support Masterson’s gubernatorial campaign. She highlighted Masterson’s dinner meetings and acceptance of political contributions from the trade association representing Google, Meta, Amazon, X, OpenAI, eBay, Netflix, Kalshi, StubHub, Airbnb and TikTok.
“This is just more of the same corrupt, pay-to-play politics that people are so sick of,” Holscher said. “Ty Masterson works for his wealthy donors and their lobbyists, not for regular Kansans. Meanwhile, the rest of us pay the price as the cost of living goes up and our budgets are stretched thinner and thinner.”
Masterson defended Senate Bill 98 and argued the state law contained restrictions that would protect communities and that, ultimately, local elected officials possessed authority to decide whether data center projects came to town. Barber County, which approved a Google-affiliated project in August, should be free to link its economic future to a data center, he said.
He denounced Holscher as a political flip-flopper on an issue important to Kansas voters.
“However the winds blow. She was for it before she was against it,” Masterson said. “My position has never changed. It is about growth and opportunity for our kids.”
The tax break was created to benefit companies investing at least $250 million over five years in a Kansas data center project that would serve growing demand in the United States for artificial intelligence. For a quarter-billion dollars, investors in Kansas could avoid sales tax on construction, equipment and maintenance of data centers. That lure was available on the condition data center investors created 20 jobs within two years, bought electricity from local utilities for 10 years and committed to conserving water used to cool systems in data centers
The House voted 85-37 for SB 98, and the Senate concurred 26-8. Kelly signed the bill in April 2025. The package was designed to serve as a magnet for hyperscale data centers based on the assumption no data center would locate in a state without the sales tax exemption. The bill began its legislative journey as Senate Bill 51, which was introduced at the request of the powerful trade association NetChoice.
Sen. Cindy Holscher, an Overland Park Democrat and candidate for governor, says robust guardrails need to be in place before Kansas presses ahead with building massive data centers. She says her rival, Republican Ty Masterson of Andover, cannot be trusted to restrain data centers given the $1 million investment the technology industry is making in Masterson’s campaign. (Photo by Jill Hummels for Kansas Reflector)
 
Masterson’s pledge
Masterson, the Republican serving as Senate president, was embroiled in a caustic primary campaign for governor when he issued his “Kansas Ratepayer Protection Pledge.” The document was a response to public dissatisfaction with emergence of at least a dozen data center proposals in Kansas.
He said data centers wouldn’t blend well in some communities, but the opportunity to secure new property tax revenue might be a good fit elsewhere.
“There’s places that don’t make sense, and there’s places that do make sense,” he said.
In the campaign pledge, Masterson said he would make certain as governor that data center developers paid the full cost of electricity necessary to operate the energy-sucking facilities. He pointed to a section of SB 98 prohibiting data centers from making use of a 40% discount on the price of electricity typically available to companies making huge investments in the state’s economy.
Masterson promised to oppose the use of eminent domain to acquire land for data centers and vowed to protect the state’s water resources.
He said he supported the Kansas law requiring a special review to prevent data centers from deploying technology from China and other countries that might want to harm U.S. national security. That piece of the puzzle echoed a requirement backed by President Donald Trump, who endorsed Masterson’s campaign for governor.
“President Trump is right, America wins the AI race or we hand it to China,” Masterson said. “But folks build here on our terms, or they don’t build here.”
In terms of data center reform, Masterson said he would urge passage of legislation requiring back-up power to be built to strengthen the grid in an emergency. He would place in statute a mandate that the Kansas Corporation Commission confirm in every utility rate case that data centers were paying the full cost of electricity used to operate.
 
Holscher’s perspective
Holscher said she proposed a pause on data center development projects because it was evident the “beautiful picture of economic growth” presented in 2025 by IT lobbyists and organizations didn’t take into account the contrary views of some Kansans.
“Since that time, things look a lot different,” she said. “I’ve done about 80 town halls across the state where I listened to people. The people are worried. they don’t want their water depleted. They don’t want their utility rates going up. Farmers don’t want viable land taken out of production.”
Holscher said Kansas could be a player in the data center development boom, but protections must be in place to prevent projects from depleting or polluting the water supply. The details of electricity consumption by data centers had to be revisited to guarantee regular consumers’ utility bills didn’t surge, she said.
In other parts of the country, she said, jobs promised by data center developers never materialized. The Kansas data centers should be constructed with union labor, she said. Local governments are open to a statewide reset to rules on data centers, she said.
“What I’m hearing is that they want help from the state,” Holscher said. “I believe in local control, but they want help from the state in terms of helping to find these guardrails.”
She said Masterson accepted an $8,000 campaign donation from Steve DelBianco, president and CEO of NetChoice, four months after the Kansas data center bill passed. The NetChoice firm later delivered an $8,000 check to Masterson’s campaign for governor.
That was part of nearly $1 million that IT and AI interests invested in Masterson’s campaign for governor, she said.
“His campaign was fueled by, you know, these big tech companies pushing him through that primary,” Holscher said. “You cannot count on Ty Masterson to put guardrails in place when these big tech companies essentially bought his campaign.”

name: WyoFile
title: Authorities use chemical irritant grenade to arrest former Wyoming journalist
description:
The encounter involved law enforcement firing gas to compel April Morganroth to surrender. She now faces another charge for interfering with peace officers. 
The post Authorities use chemical irritant grenade to arrest former Wyoming journalist appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
A former Wyoming journalist accused of perjury and forging documents faces a new interference charge after Laramie County authorities say they needed to use chemical irritant projectiles to take her into custody on an outstanding warrant.
April Morganroth, formerly known in Wyoming by her alias Marie Hamilton, was arrested Tuesday following an altercation at her residence that involved Laramie County Sheriff’s deputies firing chemical irritants to compel her to surrender. Morganroth was wanted for allegedly forging documents to enroll her child in Laramie County School District 1 and obtain special education services. 
That charge was in addition to 20 other forgery and perjury charges Morganroth faces in Platte County. The 41-year-old has pleaded not guilty to those charges. Her attorney in those matters has requested that the criminal cases against her be suspended while she undergoes a mental evaluation. 
Morganroth worked as a journalist in multiple states including Nebraska, Colorado and Wyoming. The Denver Post reported she was fired by the Boulder Daily Camera in 2021 after editors there acknowledged in a retraction that she fabricated quotes in a story about local residents reflecting on the Sept. 11 terrorism attacks.
Morganroth moved to Wyoming and worked as a reporter for the Platte County Record-Times, the Guernsey Gazette, the Torrington Telegram and the Newcastle News Letter Journal. She later launched her own publication, 307 Wyoming Sentinel, and also freelanced for Oil City News.
Following Tuesday’s altercation, Platte County Prosecuting Attorney Douglas Weaver requested that the court revoke Morganroth’s $20,000 “personal recognizance” bond, which allowed her to remain free as long as she appeared in court and didn’t violate any law. 
An affidavit connected with the request details the Tuesday law enforcement encounter that ended in Morganroth’s arrest. The document, written by Laramie County Sheriff’s Office Det. Ryan Mershon, describes his efforts to locate Morganroth. He had previously contacted Morganroth’s attorney and requested that she turn herself in. 
“Her public defenders in Platte County advised me that she would not turn herself in and would be unlikely to comply with us,” Mershon wrote. Another detective, Keith Huebner, had also tried to contact Morganroth, but “she became uncooperative with him and hung up.” 
Mershon “searched for local contacts” for April’s husband and found a call from a family member who was concerned about the husband’s well-being and had provided a Cheyenne address for the family, the detective wrote. 
Huebner asked Det. Miles DePrimo to go to the address and conduct surveillance. Shortly after he arrived, DePrimo saw Morganroth and a child arrive in a Ford pickup, park in the address’s driveway and enter the home. 
Mershon and Huebner arrived at the address. Mershon knocked on the door while Huebner and DePrimo watched the side yard and back of the residence. The child answered the door. Mershon asked the juvenile if Morganroth was home. He said she wasn’t. Mershon told him that a detective had seen her enter the house. The minor “began to lie and stated it was his older sister who was thirty years old,” Mershon wrote.  
“Detective Huebner stated that would mean your mother gave birth to your ‘sister’ at ten years old,” Mershon narrates. “The minor did not have an answer for this factual inaccuracy.” 
Mershon told the boy to “tell his mother that she needs to come outside.” When he returned, the boy stated that Morganroth “was inside, but wouldn’t come out.” 
“We asked the minor to step outside and confirmed that now his mother April Morganroth, was the only one in the home and that they reside at the residence,” the affidavit states. 
The child was “temporarily secured” in a patrol vehicle “to keep him safe and away from the residence while attempting to contact April.” The detectives announced their presence, yelling “April Morganroth this is the Laramie County Sheriff’s Office with an arrest warrant, step outside with your hands up now.” But Morganroth didn’t comply, authorities say. 
DePrimo requested support. Mershon moved his truck to the front lawn and turned on his emergency lights. He made “several announcements” with a loudspeaker commanding April to come out of the house. “It was loud enough to bring most of the neighbors out of their house to investigate,” Mershon wrote. 
Mershon then turned on his siren, stating again over the loudspeaker, “April Morganroth this is the Laramie County Sheriff’s Office with an arrest warrant, exit the residence with your hands up and empty, failure to comply with my orders may result in the use of force, deployment of chemical agents, less lethal munitions or being bit by a police k-9.” He repeated the command three times “with no response from April,” according to the affidavit. 
Cheyenne police officer Benjamin Vapenik and his K-9 arrived at the residence. Vapenik “gave three rounds of announcements at the front door ordering April to come out with her hands up.” She didn’t comply. 
After about 30 minutes “of commands being given to April with no response,” the officers decided to enter the house. Huebner entered the rear living room door, removing dogs from the house to the backyard “where they were secured.” Vapenik, Huebner, DePrimo and Mershon entered the first floor “while announcing our presence as law enforcement.” 
The officers “cleared the first floor and did not encounter April.” They say they found a ballistic plate carrier and a loaded AR rifle in the bedroom. 
DePrimo “heard movement coming from the basement.” The basement had a 90-degree turn at the bottom of the stairs, and the officers determined that “moving down the stairs to encounter April would be unsafe, especially given the new information that she may be armed,” the affidavit states. 
Huebner “gave April commands to come upstairs with her hands up” and informed her that she had a felony arrest warrant. She didn’t comply, authorities say. He then fired about five rounds of chemical irritant at the basement floor. “The rounds caused April to begin to cough from the basement,” Mershon wrote. 
After waiting about 10 minutes and continuing to order April to come out of the basement, DePrimo gave her a “loud warning.” She still didn’t comply, the affidavit states. 
Mershon put on a gas mask and deployed a chemical irritant grenade into the basement, which dispersed a chemical powder. He then “transitioned” to his taser, but never fired it. Huebner yelled to Morganroth that the powder wouldn’t go away, and that she needed to “come upstairs to decontaminate.” 
“After several minutes, April began crawling up the basement stairs,” the affidavit states. 
The officers moved April to clean air. The detectives took her into custody, placing handcuffs on her. They moved her outside, where medics assessed her. 
Morganroth was booked into the Laramie County Detention Center. The criminal cases against her are ongoing, and she has not yet been formally convicted of any crimes.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Trump administration cuts environmental reviews to fast-track Alaska oil exploration
description: Seismic surveys, well drilling, ice road construction and other wintertime oil exploration activities on federal lands on the western North Slope will no longer be subject to case-by-case environmental evaluation, under a new rule the Trump administration announced on Thursday. The U.S. Bureau of Land Management issued the rule for exploration activities in[...]
text:
Light from the setting sun on March 21, 2008 is reflected on the surface of an ice road in the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska. Under a new Trump administration rule, new ice roads and other oil-exploration projects in the reserve will no longer have to undergo case-by-case environmental analysis. (Photo by Wayne Svejnoha/U.S. Bureau of Land Management)Seismic surveys, well drilling, ice road construction and other wintertime oil exploration activities on federal lands on the western North Slope will no longer be subject to case-by-case environmental evaluation, under a new rule the Trump administration announced on Thursday.
The U.S. Bureau of Land Management issued the rule for exploration activities in the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska.
The BLM said it is granting a “categorial exclusion” to streamline permitting for most activities that would otherwise require individual environmental analysis under the National Environmental Policy Act, or NEPA. Up to now, such activities have had to be examined through environmental impact statements or environmental analyses — formal studies that adhere to federal law.
The exclusion from NEPA requirements means that past environmental studies of exploration and development activities are considered sufficient to guide future exploration work, according to the agency.
“The BLM has decades of experience analyzing the effects of exploration in the Petroleum Reserve and permitting responsible exploration,” Kevin Pendergast, the agency’s Alaska state director, said in a statement. “This categorical exclusion builds on that record to allow developers to more nimbly locate energy resources in the Petroleum Reserve, ultimately increasing domestic energy supply, leading to stable energy costs and more revenue for Alaskan communities and the American public.”  
There is no public comment period on the new rule, which went into effect on Friday.
Oil and gas development backers welcomed the rule, while environmentalists criticized it.
The Alaska Oil and Gas Association, in a statement, thanked the administration “for moving this common-sense action forward.”
“Decades of environmental review and operating experience demonstrate that these activities can be conducted responsibly under well-established safeguards. BLM’s analysis of the last 28 years of winter exploration activities in the Petroleum Reserve and the judicial record are clear and decisive: winter seismic and exploratory drilling activities in the Petroleum Reserve are consistently found to cause no significant impacts,” the statement said.
“Responsible development in the Petroleum Reserve creates good-paying Alaska jobs and strengthens America’s energy and national security,” they said.
Environmental groups said the rule is part of a pattern of giving oil companies free rein to exploit public lands without regard for the consequences.
“It is no secret that the Trump administration will ignore impacts to public lands and our nation’s laws if it benefits resource extraction corporations, but recent efforts to remove any and all public review of Arctic oil extraction are particularly egregious,” Andy Moderow, senior director of policy for Alaska Wilderness League, said in a statement. “This drill first and discover the impacts later approach puts Arctic lands, waters, and wildlife at risk.”
“The administration is handing oil companies a free ride to drill and develop the Western Arctic while blocking Americans from having a say in the process or even effectively knowing about destructive oil and gas activities on our public land,” said Matt Jackson, Alaska senior manager for The Wilderness Society. “The Western Arctic is not a uniform landscape, and these are not small, routine activities. Where companies operate, how much ground they cover and what conditions exist on the tundra all matter. That’s precisely why environmental review and public engagement are important.”
The announcement about the categorial exclusion for exploration work in the petroleum reserve comes a month after the BLM announced a similar new rule for permitting development projects. That categorical exclusion for development projects had been requested in a petition submitted by the Alaska Oil and Gas Association. The public comment period is open until November 9. 
In the BLM notice about the exploration categorial exclusion published in the Federal Register on Friday, the agency said the relevant winter exploration activities in the reserve “normally do not significantly affect the quality of the human environment.” Additionally, those activities “do not produce significant or lasting environmental impacts,” the notice said.
However, several scientific studies have found that North Slope exploration activities do have negative and sometimes llating environmental impacts.
University of Alaska Fairbanks scientists have found that seismic surveys can cause lasting damage to permafrost terrain. A 2022 UAF study warned that areas of the North Slope, including the petroleum reserve, may lack sufficient water in some years to support ice road networks, and that withdrawals of water from lakes to build those roads could harm fish populations.
A 2022 study by Chinese scientists found that the suitable season for building ice roads had diminished substantially since the late 1970s. And a 2020 study led by scientists at the Institute for Conservation Research at the San Diego Zoo found that denning polar bears are disturbed up to a mile away by noise from aircraft, “thumper” trucks used to conduct seismic surveys and other industrial equipment employed for exploration.
The new rule streamlining permitting for exploration is the latest Trump administration step aimed at vastly expanding oil drilling in the Indiana-sized reserve.
The administration replaced an Obama-era management plan that protected about half of the reserve with a new plan opening up more than 80% of it to oil leasing. Areas the Trump administration opened to development include Teshekpuk Lake and its surrounding wetlands. The lake, the largest in Arctic Alaska, and its adjacent lands had been off-limits to oil development for decades because of the region’s importance to migratory birds, caribou and other wildlife and to Indigenous subsistence food-gathering traditions.
The Trump Department of the Interior also overturned an agreement to protect Teshekpuk-area caribou habitat that had been struck between the Biden administration and the tribal and city governments and Native corporation in Nuiqsut, the Inupiat village closest to reserve development. That action triggered a lawsuit by the Nuiqsut parties and a U.S. District Court decision against the Trump administration. The administration appealed that ruling in June.
In March, the administration held a record lease sale in the petroleum reserve, drawing $163 million in high bids for territory that included territory in and around Teshekpuk Lake that is currently the subject of legal dispute.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: A rural Oklahoma hospital is bringing back maternity care. Can it survive healthcare cuts?
description: On the last day of August, Julie Schroeder was one day away from giving birth to a baby girl. The 25-year-old Arnett resident didn’t know it, because she wanted to go into labor naturally and deliver with the provider she saw during pregnancy. But that meant planning for a nearly two-hour drive southeast to Weatherford […]
text:
Newman Memorial's CEO Tom Vasko and Amy Calhoun-Vasko stand in Newman Memorial Hospital's future labor-and-delivery unit on Aug. 31. (Photo by Jillian Taylor/StateImpact Oklahoma)On the last day of August, Julie Schroeder was one day away from giving birth to a baby girl. The 25-year-old Arnett resident didn’t know it, because she wanted to go into labor naturally and deliver with the provider she saw during pregnancy. But that meant planning for a nearly two-hour drive southeast to Weatherford Regional Hospital.


Schroeder had seen Amy Calhoun-Vasko at Newman Memorial Hospital up until 26 weeks. The certified nurse midwife is about 20 minutes away in Shattuck. After that timeframe, Calhoun-Vasko can continue seeing her patients at Weatherford Regional, where she delivers babies. It’s one way she has adapted to Newman Memorial not having labor and delivery.
The hospital’s last delivery was in 2015. Several physicians retired around that time, and when only one remained, it was “too much to handle,” Calhoun-Vasko said.
Today, only 27% of Oklahoma’s rural hospitals offer labor and delivery services amid workforce shortages and financial pressures. In 2024, about half of Oklahoma’s counties had zero obstetric clinicians. And according to the Center for Healthcare Quality and Payment Reform, payments from private insurance plans and Medicaid programs often don’t cover the cost of delivering safe, high-quality maternity care.
About four years ago, Calhoun-Vasko and her husband, Tom Vasko, left Virginia to work in rural Oklahoma. In a job interview before Vasko became Newman Memorial’s CEO, he was told the critical access hospital wanted its next leader to meet a seemingly insurmountable goal: bring labor and delivery back.
Since then, the couple has worked to obtain a few million dollars to get started. Vasko said the door has been slammed in their faces many times. But that is about to change.
The Northwest Oklahoma hospital plans to restore this service next year, using money from a five-year, $50 billion federal investment meant to transform rural healthcare across the U.S.
Newman Memorial hopes the model it’s building can sustain access despite nearly $1 trillion in looming reductions to federal Medicaid spending over a decade, signed into law last year alongside the dollars fueling its project.
Restoring maternity care

	Oklahoma received more than $223 million from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services for its first year of funding under the Rural Health Transformation Program. The state’s plan features 29 initiatives, including the Rural Regional Reorientation Program, under which Newman Memorial is receiving $1.4 million, Vasko said.
It’s intended to improve access to local and specialty care, and reduce disease and avoidable hospitalizations.
Vasko said the dollars will go toward infrastructure like beds, monitors, equipment and surgical needs. Because it’s reimbursement-based, the critical access hospital has applied for additional opportunities to secure upfront funding. The goal is to have infrastructure in place by January and launch sometime next year, Vasko said.
“If you’d asked me three and a half years ago, I wanted to walk in the door and deliver a baby the next day,” Calhoun-Vasko said. “Three and a half years later, I now realize that we were not ready for that, and we needed this time period to build up to that.”
The hospital has implemented lactation and mental health services for maternity care and hired a doula.
Once Newman Memorial opens its labor-and-delivery unit, Calhoun-Vasko will handle low-risk births. She said about 85% of pregnant patients fall into the category appropriate for her care. A group of OB-GYNs will rotate weekly and cover high-risk deliveries and gynecological surgeries, bringing a needed service to Northwest Oklahoma and revenue to Newman.
Dr. Zach Wohlgemuth hopes to be one of those OB-GYNs. He is a medical director at a hospital in North Carolina and Calhoun-Vasko’s former coworker. His facility has implemented a similar midwifery-forward model, including several midwives and physicians. He said this structure helps clinicians work at their maximum capacity to serve patients.
Wohlgemuth said he appreciates that the physician team Newman Memorial is assembling won’t rely on a staffing company. Instead, several consistent, core doctors will work alongside Calhoun-Vasko in the town of 1,212 people.
“People care who deliver their babies, and they want continuity in that care. And that’s important to them,” Wohlgemuth said. “Especially in small towns.”
Newman Memorial is set to become Oklahoma’s second critical access hospital to deliver babies. Darin Farrell, CEO of Weatherford Regional Hospital, said his critical access facility isn’t the first to offer the service, but it is the only one remaining.
Medicare pays critical access hospitals based on cost. Because of that, Farrell said it can be financially counterproductive for them to deliver babies. In 2025, Medicaid covered around half of Oklahoma births, and about 42% were paid for by private insurance, according to data from the State Department of Health.
But Farrell said the service has always been a priority in Weatherford.
“Even in very, very lean times, financially speaking, the hospital leadership and the medical community, the physicians, have seen it as a vital component of what we do at the hospital,” Farrell said.
The hospital has benefited from a steady group of physicians to help maintain labor and delivery. Farrell said its partnership with certified nurse midwife Calhoun-Vasko is a first. But he’s seen how the setup can be beneficial.
A Weatherford patient went into labor during Calhoun-Vasko’s first weekend covering labor and delivery. While she handled the delivery, the patient’s physician got to continue coaching his child’s soccer game.
The physician told Farrell the patient might have been one he would have taken into C-section earlier than Calhoun-Vasko would have. The patient ended up delivering vaginally.
“That model is something that now we will continue to do in the future and be much more open to it than we had been in the past,” Farrell said.
Growing midwifery care

	Farrell, a registered nurse, said he didn’t have experience working with certified nurse midwives before Calhoun-Vasko. The providers hold graduate degrees and are advanced-practice registered nurses who specialize in primary, sexual and reproductive care.
“I’ve come to realize that even if nurses have a nursing background or physicians have gone and received their education, they still have a lack of knowledge in regards to certified nurse midwives,” said Priscilla McFolling, the program director of The Midwifery Project.
The Oklahoma Perinatal Quality Improvement Collaborative program works to expand the state’s midwifery capacity. According to the March of Dimes, midwifery care can reduce interventions and health care costs, and increase patient satisfaction.
Oklahoma had 86 certified nurse midwives as of August, and McFolling said they aren’t being used to their full potential.
Only 12 of Oklahoma’s 41 birthing hospitals have integrated the providers, she said. A report from the State Department of Health notes that midwifery care is well established in tribal facilities, and it can be a viable option for low-risk pregnancies in areas with provider shortages.
“I feel like midwives are definitely a part of that solution for how we can ensure that our women of reproductive age, pregnant women, can have that high-quality care from a provider,” McFolling said.
Barbara O’Brien, director of the Oklahoma Perinatal Quality Improvement Collaborative, said she hopes Newman Memorial’s model will succeed and can be replicated in other hospitals.
“For example, can McCurtain County start providing obstetrical services again? Could one of the hospitals out in the Panhandle provide obstetric services again, so that their people don’t have to drive all over?” O’Brien said. “Or could they bring midwives out there at least that have prenatal care that they can provide? So [there are] different options that might be available in the future for the different communities in rural Oklahoma.”
Cuts to Medicaid

	As Newman Memorial prepares to launch maternity care, CEO Tom Vasko said it will also be fighting against federal Medicaid cuts, which will impact Oklahoma’s directed payment program. It helps bring hospital reimbursements for serving certain Medicaid patients closer to private insurance rates.
Oklahoma Hospital Association President and CEO Rich Rasmussen said in an email the cuts are designed to begin hitting states on Jan. 1, 2028. Because Oklahoma’s directed payment program was reduced this year, he said the actual cuts will now begin Jan. 1, 2029.
Payments will be phased down by 10% every year until they reach 100% of the Medicare rate.
“That’s what really enables critical access hospitals to keep OB care going and alive is to offset that loss of being underpaid by Medicaid to kind of true up to at least get us to break even. And that’s what DPP does,” Vasko said. “I think it’s also very important that, as we have a change of command and governorship this coming year, that both our candidates really give that some thought.”
Farrell said the Rural Health Transformation Program is a great opportunity for hospitals like Newman Memorial to bring back labor and delivery services that they stopped providing years ago. But to sustain access, he said providers need better Medicaid payments.
“It eventually becomes a decision of, ‘Do we keep the hospital open? Do we continue to provide an emergency room for the community?’ And, for many of the hospitals over the years that close their OB services, that’s the decision it came down to is, ‘We can’t afford to do OB anymore,'” Farrell said.
Despite all of the challenges Vasko and Calhoun-Vasko faced to get to this point, they said nothing has made them want to give up. They’re sustained by passion and stories like that of Jean Foreman and her daughter, Nancy Brookshire. This year, Brookshire celebrated her 70th birthday with Foreman at Newman Memorial, where her mom welcomed her into the world.
“It shows just how the hospital impacts a family across multiple generations – from birth through the entire lifespan,” Vasko said.
Now that they have funding behind them, Vasko said he has no doubt they’ll accomplish their goal, and newborn cries will echo through their halls once again.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: A survived execution in Tennessee exposes the grim science of lethal injection
description: It took Christa Pike nearly a week to regain consciousness after the Tennessee Department of Corrections failed to kill her with two doses of the barbiturate pentobarbital, a drug used to put animals to death and to execute humans by lethal injection in Tennessee and other states. She was confused and angry. She couldn’t eat […]
text:
Randy Spivey and Luke Ihnen, lawyers for Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike, update a gaggle of local and national media on her condition after a Sept. 30 botched execution. (Photo: John/Partipilo) It took Christa Pike nearly a week to regain consciousness after the Tennessee Department of Corrections failed to kill her with two doses of the barbiturate pentobarbital, a drug used to put animals to death and to execute humans by lethal injection in Tennessee and other states.
She was confused and angry. She couldn’t eat because of damage to her throat, she couldn’t move her arms, and her hands were swollen to where they looked like “surgical gloves,” according to one of her attorneys. It was noted during and immediately after the execution attempt that skin on her arms was chemically burned by the high alkalinity of the drug. 
But by Oct. 8, she was “walking with assistance,” according to a memo circulated by her attorneys to federal defenders around the country on Thursday, “and her arms — which sustained significant injuries during the execution attempt — are healing and regaining movement and strength. Her lungs are clear, and she has started to eat a regular diet. Physicians are encouraged by her physical recovery.”
Pike’s attorneys and medical advisors had warned that Pike had a blood disorder, and that it had always been difficult for medical staff to draw blood from her veins, let alone insert IV lines. During the execution, after several failed attempts, the technicians placed a needle that most likely collapsed the vein. The bulk of the killing drugs likely went into the tissue around the needles placed in her arms.
Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike receiving medical care after failed execution

“I think Christa didn’t die because most of the pentobarbital didn’t get into her brain,” said Dr. Joel Zivot, an Emory University anesthesiology professor who consulted with Pike’s legal team. “It ended up in her arms, so she never had a high enough blood level to kill her. That was the reason — not that she has some capacity to resist pentobarbital. It’s because it just never got into her brain.”
At least not enough to kill her.
The email to federal defenders cautioned that Pike “continues to experience cognitive challenges with concentration and memory. Her physicians have cautioned that it may take months to fully understand whether she sustained lasting cognitive injuries.”
And the burning on her arms belies another frequent problem with pentobarbital used in executions: It is highly caustic. When the drug does flow properly through the veins, the dying prisoner may appear to be sleeping, but in the majority of cases, studies have found that the pentobarbital solution is disintegrating the prisoners’ lungs, burning them apart, causing the condemned prisoners to literally drown in their own body fluids. 
That all happens before the drug has a chance to kill the way it is intended to.
“It’s supposed to stop your breathing,” Zivot said. “But it’s supposed to stop it in your brain. This is different. I think the caustic nature of the solution is separate from what’s killing you. The pentobarbital works on the brain and the heart, and that’s killing you. But it’s what it’s cut with that I think is burning your lungs.”
The syndrome is called flash pulmonary edema, and it theoretically produces a sensation similar to waterboarding. In a deposition in federal court in 2019, Gail Van Norman, a researcher at the University of Washington, called it “one of the most powerful, excruciating feelings known to man.” Van Norman studied 27 autopsies of executed prisoners and found evidence of pulmonary edema in 20 of them.
Some researchers posit that the dying prisoners may still be able to feel the pain, even if they are too sedated to react. Of course, no one has lived to confirm that theory. And there is no news yet whether Pike experienced it.
Zivot’s own research found pulmonary edema in 33 of 43 executions carried out with pentobarbital or midazolam. The identifying symptoms in autopsies are lungs that are up to three times normal weight and the presence of a pink, frothy liquid in the respiratory tree. The froth, Zivot said, is an indication that the person is still struggling to breathe at the point of onset.
What is pentobarbital?
Pentobarbital is used in clinical settings to treat epileptic seizures and also as an anesthesia. It is made by a European pharmaceutical company and marketed under the brand name Nembutal. But the manufacturer will not sell it for use in executions, so corrections departments buy it on the gray market as pentobarbital salts, which then have to be converted into an injectable liquid form by a compounding pharmacy.
In January 2025, during the final days of the Biden administration, the U.S. Department of Justice issued a warning about pentobarbital in executions, citing multiple studies about pulmonary edema. Outgoing Attorney General Merrick Garland had ordered its use stopped.
But in April 2026, the Trump DOJ countered those warnings. After a long preamble about misguided Biden policies, it declared them “wrong on the standard” and “wrong on the science,” and quoted its own expert who said the pulmonary edema didn’t matter because the prisoners were already brain dead, a claim that has not been scientifically settled.
When lethal injection was first used to replace the electric chair and the gas chamber in the 1970s, it used a three-drug process: the anesthetic sodium thiopental to render the prisoner unconscious, followed by a paralytic drug to ensure the prisoner didn’t breathe or show any signs of discomfort, and a final killing dose of potassium chloride that stopped the heart.
But by 2010, thiopental was no longer manufactured in the U.S. and could not be imported. It had been largely replaced in clinical settings by newer drugs. 
Then the pharmaceutical companies balked at selling pentobarbital for use in executions, and corrections departments had to look elsewhere. 
After botched execution of Christa Pike, Tennessee correction chief steps down

A long road back
When Katie Hobbs took the Arizona governor’s office in 2023, she engaged David Duncan, a retired federal magistrate judge, to conduct a study of execution procedures, which had been problematic under long-time prisons director Charles Ryan and his successor, David Shinn. Shinn’s deputy director, Frank Strada, oversaw those three executions in which medical technicians struggled to insert catheters into the arms of condemned prisoners.
Strada left Arizona to become director of the Tennessee Department of Corrections. Pike’s was the second failed execution in Tennessee, and the first failed because they also couldn’t set lines in that prisoner’s arms. Strada resigned nearly a week ago.
Pike likely has a long road back to health.
Even if there was not enough pentobarbital in her bloodstream to kill her, 
“The whole body has been exposed to this serious blood flow,” Zivot said. “If it affects the brain, it could affect the kidneys, the liver, the intestines, the lungs — all of it. I think it will be revealed soon enough.”
Corinna Lain, a University of Virginia Law professor who has extensively researched lethal injection, suggested that perhaps the secret was in knowing how to push the drugs.
Zivot, the anesthesiologist, discounted that theory and questioned whether the secret lay in the preparation of the raw pentobarbital salts into an injectable liquid form, “some way of adjusting the pH so it’s not quite so alkaline.”
But Michaela Almgren, a professor of pharmacology at the University of South Carolina, says that there is little leeway there.
“The catch is that there is a specific pH range in which it has to stay to meet the drug quality,” she said. “We don’t really have clinical evidence, but we don’t study it.” 
There’s the rub.
What kind of doctor takes money to kill people?
“The medical scientists operate under the same Hippocratic oath as doctors,” Lain said.
“We’re experts in non-killing,” Zivot said. “Anesthesiologists know about drug toxicity and other things. These are dangerous substances, and when mishandled, they can cause dangerous outcomes. But it’s not the practice of medicine in any way.”
What kind of doctor takes money to kill people on behalf of the state, anyway?
“The state may want to use these people,” Zivot said, “but that’s clearly not medicine.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: John James introduces bill to use tariff revenue for manufacturer relief
description: U.S. Rep. John James, the Republican gubernatorial nominee, introduced legislation in the U.S. House Tuesday to use tariff revenues to help American manufacturers harmed by the increased costs and supply chain disruptions stemming from tariffs levied by the Trump administration on other countries and retaliatory tariffs imposed on the United States. “Michiga[...]
text:
U.S. Rep. John James, R-Shelby Twp., speaks to reporters at the Michigan Capitol in Lansing, Mich., after Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer's eighth and final State of the State address on Feb. 25, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)U.S. Rep. John James, the Republican gubernatorial nominee, introduced legislation in the U.S. House Tuesday to use tariff revenues to help American manufacturers harmed by the increased costs and supply chain disruptions stemming from tariffs levied by the Trump administration on other countries and retaliatory tariffs imposed on the United States.
“Michigan is disproportionally affected by the trade war, so it’s reasonable to use tariff revenue to reduce the effect on Michigan businesses and workers,” the Shelby Township Republican said in a press release from his office. “Our country needs to push back on unfair trade practices, but states like Michigan should not have to shoulder that burden alone.”
According to the text of the bill, H.R. 10759, to receive assistance, applicants must conduct “substantial production, manufacturing, agricultural, processing, or related productive activity in the United States,” and must meet a number of requirements around keeping production and manufacturing activity within the United States.
The legislation would establish several types of aid, including a refundable tariff impact credit, tariff working-capital loans for those “experiencing short-term liquidity constraints,” and rapid relief for “critical employers” in the case of imminent risk of closure of a domestic manufacturing facility or substantial layoffs. 
U.S. Customs station at the Blue Water Bridge in Port Huron, Michigan. (Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance)
It would also establish an “American investment credit” to fund actions to expand or establish domestic production, reshore supply chains, or substitute U.S.-made products for tariff-affected foreign inputs.
At least 35% of the assistance would be required to go to small or midsize businesses, meaning those up to twice the industry size standard set by the Small Business Act. 
The relief would be financed through the “Tariff Relief for American Development and Employment Fund” or “TRADE Fund,” using “net additional customs duties attributable to covered tariff actions, after refunds, drawbacks, and administrative adjustments.”
Tariffs have been a top concern for voters in Michigan and across the country as affordability becomes a central issue ahead of the November general election. James’ Democratic gubernatorial competitor, Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, has attacked James repeatedly for supporting GOP leadership in levying the tariffs. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Michigan Smart Trade Alliance is tracking an estimate of the financial impact of tariffs under the Trump administration on Michigan households. The tracker, as of Oct. 9, shows a statewide tariff impact of more than $27.2 billion in Michigan since January 2025, or about $6,667 per household.
“The costs on Michigan families is taking a toll in the form of higher costs and frustration with trade policies and tariffs that are holding our economy back,” Michigan Smart Trade Alliance spokesperson John Sellek said when the tariff tracker was announced. “It’s time to end the trade war with Canada, get both sides to the negotiation table, and find a solution that will end this affordability crisis in Michigan.”
In Michigan, tariffs against Canada — and those levied in retaliation by the Canadian government — have been especially prominent due to the state’s proximity to Canada and a historically strong trade relationship between Michigan and its neighbor to the north.
For example, disputes over tariffs delayed the opening of the Gordie Howe International Bridge between Detroit and Windsor, Ont., and conversations escalated to the point that Canadian leaders hosted a grand opening celebration without any American officials present. 
The Gordie Howe International Bridge, seen from Windsor, Ontario. July 24, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
“I fought with Canadians in Iraq. We have a deep and abiding bond that will not extinguish. I’m committed to making sure we continue to improve and deepen our relationships, and making sure our differences are resolved in a civil manner, quickly,” James said. “Our countries need to work out a reciprocal, fair, and mutually beneficial arrangement so we can bring back jobs and protect our industry.”
The House is not expected to hold any votes until after the November general election, and the current legislative session ends in late 2026. However, Congress is expected to return to Washington after the election for a lame duck session that will include voting on appropriations bills for 2027, as funding expires in mid-December under the current funding package.
James referenced the bill in both a Tuesday debate with Benson and in a conversation at the Detroit Economic Club in September, though details of the bill were only just made available Friday.
The bill has been referred to the House committees on Financial Services and Ways and Means.
Michigan Democrats criticized the timing of the legislation — Michigan Democratic Party spokesperson Derrick Honeyman called the bill “nothing but a desperate political stunt from a flailing D.C. politician,” citing the fact that Congress is out of session until after the election. 
And a spokesperson for Benson’s gubernatorial campaign similarly called the bill “a last minute political stunt designed to distract from his record of making life more expensive.”
“The timing tells you everything. After voting to continue Trump’s tariffs and getting called out for the $6,400 John James Tax he saddled on Michiganders’ backs, John James introduced this bill only after the House had ended its session and sent members home. If he was serious about passing this legislation he would’ve introduced it when the House was in session and secured even one cosponsor for it,” Benson’s press secretary Rajan Srinivasan said.

title: Trump appoints committee to revive quest to remove Lisa Cook from Fed board
text: President Donald Trump has formed a White House committee to investigate Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook, escalating even further a lengthy feud with the Federal Reserve Board member.The three-member committee will seek evidence that Cook made false statements in obtaining a mortgage and will hold a closed-door hearing at the White House on Nov. 5, two days after the midterm elections, according to a presidential memorandum. The memorandum is dated Oct. 7 but was published to the White House website Friday.Trump tried to fire Cook last year after Bill Pulte, then the director of the Federal Housing Finance Agency, alleged she lied on a mortgage form to obtain a more favorable rate. A U.S. Supreme Court decision in June found Trump did not have cause to remove Cook from the independent board. The president tasked the committee with finding enough evidence of wrongdoing to meet the court’s standard for firing. “As President, it is my job to ensure the laws are faithfully executed, including by firing subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law,” Trump wrote.Attorneys for Cook said Trump’s record of trying to fire Cook raised major concerns that the process would be illegitimate.The committee will be composed of Assistant to the President for Economic Policy Kevin Hassett, Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Chair Andrea Lucas and acting Director of the U.S. Office of Government Ethics Keith Sonderling. They are permitted to “consult with appropriate personnel from executive branch departments and agencies, including the Department of Justice.”The memorandum calls for Cook to be present for questioning at the Nov. 5 hearing. She is also permitted to submit a written statement to the committee. The memorandum also calls for Cook to comply with the committee’s requests for documents or other evidentiary material.Cook can also submit another written statement up to five days after the hearing.The committee will then write its own report with a recommendation to Trump on “whether there is cause to remove Governor Cook.” Cook’s attorneys Abbe Lowell and Norm Eisen said in a statement that an objective investigation would show no wrongdoing, and that Cook looked forward to clearing her name.“In light of the President’s repeated statements that he has already decided to fire Governor Cook – regardless of the facts and evidence -  we have grave doubts that this ‘hearing’ is a legitimate one that would conform to the law,” they wrote. “But if it is anything close to objective, the conclusion will be that Governor Cook did not commit mortgage fraud, leaving no cause to remove her from the Federal Reserve Board.” Trump has squabbled with Cook and former Fed Chair Jerome Powell, whom he appointed and who still serves on the board, over interest rates that the president believes should be lower to stimulate the economy. He has used legal investigations to pressure Cook and Powell, including a probe into Powell’s oversight of a Fed headquarters renovation.

title: Measles cases reach 4,080 for the year — the highest in decades
description: Measles cases for the calendar year surpassed 4,000 for the first time in decades, with as many as five deaths in Pennsylvania, as the federal government steps in with financial help for states but also fans vaccination fears and skepticism.  A weekly report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention showed 4,080 cases this […]
text:
A sign at a University of Utah health clinic warns visitors about the spread of measles. The state has had 535 reported cases this year, among the largest counts in the country. (Photo by McKenzie Romero/Utah News Dispatch)Measles cases for the calendar year surpassed 4,000 for the first time in decades, with as many as five deaths in Pennsylvania, as the federal government steps in with financial help for states but also fans vaccination fears and skepticism. 
A weekly report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention showed 4,080 cases this year as of Oct. 8, up 192 cases in a week. 
Pennsylvania, which has reported five confirmed deaths from measles, alone had 142 new cases for the week — for a total of 1,105 for the year. The CDC has recognized just two of the state’s reported deaths.
Measles cases have reached a 35-year high

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a Democrat, has protested the CDC’s death count; his state’s five deaths would be more than the three deaths reported in 2025 for the entire nation.   
Other states with large numbers of cases, more than 200, did not see their case numbers change for the week: South Carolina (670 for the year), Utah (535) and Wisconsin (207). States with more cases included New York, which declared a measles emergency, with 19 new cases for a total of 103 this year; and Iowa, up 17 cases to 39. 
Kentucky reported separately on Friday that cases there had reached 104, up 10 from last week. 
Pennsylvania, which has become ground zero for this year’s outbreaks, reported this week that a new awareness and pop-up vaccine clinics are leading to more measles vaccinations.   
All but five states have had at least one measles case this year. The last time the United States had this many cases was in 1991, reaching 9,643 cases as the nation still struggled to roll out vaccinations for the disease, amid budget cuts that hit programs in big cities. 
Pennsylvania’s health department this week announced “a surge of interest” in vaccinations as more residents become aware of the outbreak — more than 56,000 doses were given out in September, more than twice the usual monthly volume. The state has added pop-up clinics in the most affected areas.  All but four of the measles cases were among unvaccinated people. 
The Lewistown Sentinel reported that an 18-year-old woman there died in September from brain swelling as a result of the measles virus after two of her brothers survived the disease. 
While the federal government has offered states more funding to combat measles, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy moved forward this week on plans to emphasize vaccine injury, announcing a new clinic and work to strengthen a database that tracks problems after a vaccination. 
“We must listen to patients and families who report vaccine injuries — not dismiss or gaslight them,” Kennedy said in a statement. 
Stateline reporter Tim Henderson can be reached at thenderson@stateline.org.
