title: North Carolina records first reported flu-related death of the season
description: The North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services announced on Thursday its first reported flu-related death of the 2026-2027 flu season. The case involved an adult in the central part of the state who died due to complications of the virus during the first week of October. “This is a heartbreaking reminder of how […]
text:
With the start of the respiratory virus season, state health officials say now is a good time to schedule a flu vaccine. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)The North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services announced on Thursday its first reported flu-related death of the 2026-2027 flu season.
The case involved an adult in the central part of the state who died due to complications of the virus during the first week of October.
“This is a heartbreaking reminder of how serious the flu can be,” said Health and Human Services Secretary Dev Sangvai in a statement.
Dr. David Wohl, a professor of medicine in the Division of Infectious Diseases at UNC’s School of Medicine, said people often try to “find the sweet spot” for timing their flu shot.
“They don’t want the vaccine to run out of steam towards late winter,” said Wohl in an interview with NC Newsline. “I do generally tell people that around October is a good time to get it.”
While the level of virus circulating now is low, Wohl said people shouldn’t wait until flu is more prevalent to protect themselves.
During last year’s respiratory virus season, North Carolina reported 335 flu-related deaths, including 10 children.


Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline
North Carolinians can also help limit the spread of respiratory illnesses by:

Staying home when sick and avoiding close contact with others
Washing hands frequently with soap and water.
 Covering coughs and sneezes.
 Frequently cleaning high-touched surfaces.

 Source: NC DHHS


“We see the flu really comes on after the winter vacation, where we see a lot of mixing of people and college kids are all over the place,” said Wohl. “Again, you want to be covered through the first of the year, do it in October.”
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends everyone six months and older should get a flu vaccine every season to reduce the risk of serious complications or hospitalizations.
One addition to the vaccine line-up this year is a new mRNA flu shot. The Food and Drug Administration approved Moderna’s mFlusiva in May for people 50 and older. The mRNA flu vaccine is produced using the same technology as the COVID vaccines, allowing it to be produced much more quickly than a traditional vaccine. Early research shows that it may also offer slightly longer-lasting protection than the traditional shot.
Combating COVID
While the 2020 pandemic may seem like a distant memory, Wohl said there are still summer and winter surges of COVID cases. It peaks in different regions of the country at different times, which can be helpful to know if traveling, said Wohl.
“The older you are, the more I’m going to suggest that you get an annual COVID shot,” Wohl recommended.
Wohl said there is also a new oral antiviral medication that can help prevent COVID after a known exposure. The FDA approved Xocova in June for adults and adolescents 12 and older for use after being exposed to COVID. Experts say the treatment could be especially helpful in households where one person has COVID and another family member is trying to avoid getting sick.
“We didn’t have that before,” Wohl said. “So, there are things we’re doing, not only vaccines, but also medicines that I think people need to be aware of.”
According to the state’s respiratory disease dashboard, as of the first week in October, just 1.9% of the statewide population has received a COVID-19 shot this year, with 6.6% receiving the flu vaccine.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: How opposition to Flock cameras took flight in CT
description: Towns like South Windsor, Windsor, Killingworth, Ledyard, Milford and Newtown have ended or suspended use of license plate readers in 2026.
text:
Without public notice, the unblinking eye of Flock Safety came to South Windsor in April 2025 to begin its 24/7 mission of uploading images of every vehicle passing by a few chosen spots. Artificial intelligence cataloged license plates and other details into a searchable, privately-controlled database. 
The unheralded arrival of Flock’s automated license plate readers, or ALPRs, was typical of a company that had rapidly, and mostly quietly, amassed a network of 120,000 cameras in 49 states. Eighteen months later, the ground has shifted, and Flock is Exhibit A in a reckoning over AI and surveillance. 
Kristian R. Lindstrom, the police chief who brought Flock’s cameras to South Windsor with an informal endorsement by the previous town council, glumly watched Monday night as the current council passed a resolution directing him to cease their use immediately and arrange for removal within 60 days.
South Windsor, a suburb of 26,000 with a crime rate nearly 90% lower than the national rate, is at least the sixth Connecticut community to end or suspend the use of ALPRs this year, following Windsor, Killingworth, Ledyard, Milford and Newtown.
The story of Flock in South Windsor follows a narrative seen elsewhere: A backlash erupts over the realization Flock is in their community, followed by a debate over risk vs. reward: Is sacrificing a measure of privacy for a promise of greater public safety a fair or Faustian bargain? 
“There’s a trade-off between freedom and security, and everyone decides individually where they fall in that trade-off,” Lindstrom, a South Windsor cop for 29 years and the last six as its chief, told the council at a hearing last month. “I know where I fall.”
It is how Garrett Langley, the chief executive and co-founder of Flock, framed the issue in an upbeat TED talk recorded six months ago, when his company was growing and contract terminations still were rare. It was titled, “Can a camera on every corner make us safer?”
Langley told the story of an 11-year-old girl kidnapped from her grandmother’s home in Tennessee in the middle of the night, and how a detective recalled the Flock camera near the woman’s house. Only one car had passed, headed towards I-75 and Georgia. The tag was on a car registered to a sex offender.
“Now that girl is alive today because the detective had two things: he had a license plate and he had a direction to travel,” Langley said. “This, for me, is one of thousands of stories I sadly hear about every day in America.”


Langley described his 9-year-old company as the answer to what he sees as a simple data problem, a means to strip the anonymity of movements across the nearly 18,000 law enforcement agencies in the U.S. by creating a sortable, searchable record.
“This is the problem,” Langley said. “You literally can commit a crime in city A and drive to city B, and they’re like, ‘Oh, who are you?’ You leave state A to state B, and they’re like, ‘Oh, we have no record of you.’ This entire problem is a data problem.”
The data problem is solved. In much of America, there is a record of people now. Three-quarters of Connecticut law enforcement agencies report they have deployed, collectively, 1,564 fixed ALPRs. Flock is the biggest supplier in the state, providing about 40%.
“I’m not saying that it’s not a choice,” Langley said. “I’m just saying that for me, the trade-off is I don’t know how many more 11-year-old girls need to be kidnapped, or human trafficking rings, or Silver Alerts, or Amber Alerts we have to go through before we say, ‘Enough is enough.’ Now, the beauty of America, though, is that every city, state, county gets to pick. It’s not my choice.”
Grumbling over what is the right choice grew louder as the summer progressed, prompting Gov. Ned Lamont on August 7 to urge a moratorium by municipalities on new Flock installations and to request the Police Officers Standards and Training Council recommend standards for their deployment and use.
Bipartisan concern
In South Windsor, it was the choice of a town council that Democrats flipped last year, winning a 6-3 majority. The vote to turn off Flock’s cameras was partisan, with every Democrat in favor and every Republican opposed. But the issue blurs party lines in ways unlike most issues. 
In Milford, a Republican alderman pushed a permanent ban, backed by a DeFlock Milford movement organized by a Democratic activist. Instead, after a number of raucous hearings and meetings, the Board of Aldermen voted Monday to pause their use, pending further study by a technology committee.
The Republican governors of Texas and Florida have moved against ALPRs, with Florida banning them from state highways and Texas pausing state spending on them.
Last month, at a U.S. Senate subcommittee hearing titled, “Always Watching: Flock’s Nationwide AI Surveillance Network,” observers were treated to the rare sight of the conservative Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., and liberal Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., on the same side of an issue.
Both expressed alarm at how quickly a private company had managed to construct a network that records 20 billion images each month with little regulatory oversight as to their storage or use.
“It’s unlike anything we’ve ever seen in this country before,” Hawley said.
Blumenthal told the committee the issue is a source of near-daily headlines in Connecticut. In an interview this week, he said Flock has become a catalyst for larger concerns over big tech in general and AI and more specifically.
“The controversy about the Flock cameras has struck a nerve. It’s like an existential dread of loss of privacy, abuse of systems to surveil, and big government, big corporations somehow tracking people,” Blumenthal said. “If the controversy with  these cameras had occurred five years ago, it would not have inflamed the kind of emotions that it has.”
Flock declined to send a representative to the hearing, and the company declined comment for this story.
Artificial intelligence technology
The debate over license plate readers often is conflated with concerns over cameras used to ticket motorists for speeding or running red lights. The systems are separate, and civil libertarians see a significant difference between an image triggered by a specific act versus images recorded over every passing vehicle.
ALPRs are old technology. What’s new is the AI that allows Flock to rapidly sort and catalog billions images of license plates, make and model of cars, roof racks, bumper stickers and other identifiers. 
“This is all supercharged by AI,” said Alasdair Whitney, a legislative counsel for the Institute for Justice, which has proposed federal standards for their use. “A couple of years ago, you couldn’t possibly sift through 20 billion images with just a few officers, or even a hundred or a thousand officers.”
Subscribers essentially can go back in time, tracking a vehicle’s movements by ALPRs over previous hours, days or weeks. The technology was used last week to track a murder suspect from Middletown to West Hartford within hours of the crime. He was arrested after a chase and exchange of gunfire.
Eric J. Weiner, who sparked an examination of Flock in Windsor, addressed the South Windsor council before its vote on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026. Credit: Mark Pazniokas / CT Mirror
It also allowed a sheriff’s deputy in Johnson County, Texas, to search last year in Connecticut for a car belonging to a woman who had an abortion, a discovery by a retired tech executive, Eric J. Weiner of Windsor, through a Freedom of Information Act request to his local police department.
Weiner’s FOI request was a match that lit a fire over Flock in Connecticut.
The inspiration for Weiner’s request was a story posted May 29, 2025 by 404 Media, a news site that focuses on technology and its impact on society. The headline: “A Texas Cop Searched License Plate Cameras Nationwide for a Woman Who Got an Abortion.”
Weiner was curious if images from Windsor were part of the search. Windsor responded to his FOI request within 48 hours, producing a log of Flock searches for about two months, from April 1, 2025 through June 9,  2025, when he filed his request.
“And surprise, surprise: There were 590,900 records in that data dump, illustrating that across the country, Windsor’s data had been searched that number of times,” Weiner said. “And 150,000 of those searches were just from Texas, and of those, about 100,000 were from Houston, and that was just bizarre.”
One drew his eye. Under reason for search, it stated: “had an abortion, search for female.”
Weiner took his finding to the Windsor police chief, Donald Melanson. They had spoken in the past about ALPRs, and Weiner found him responsive. Melanson discovered his cameras unknowingly had been configured to be accessible nationally, Weiner said.
Melanson, who did not respond to a request for an interview, began tightening the parameters on who could see data derived from images in Windsor, Weiner said. Houston? Off limits. Eventually, only police agencies in Connecticut had access.
“And this was all self-driven by him,” Weiner said. “He wasn’t getting outside pressure at this point, but this did catch the attention of our town council and many members of the public. It got kicked over to the town council, which has a health and safety committee made up of three town councilors.”
What followed in Windsor was something missing when Flock arrived there and across the Connecticut River in South Windsor: A long and belated public discussion about the pros and cons of automated license plate readers.
Don Bell, a senior policy counsel to the Project on Government Oversight who watched the unfolding drama as vice chair of the town council in neighboring East Hartford, said the introduction of ALPRs without notice was the industry’s “original sin.”
“I think most Americans have an expectation that if a technology as powerful as an automated license plate reader is going to be deployed in their community, that they’re at least going to get some heads up about it,” Bell said. “And in many instances, not only was there no heads up, there was no public process, there was no vote, there was no discussion on any of the issues that a community would want to think about with using these kinds of technologies.”
South Windsor
In South Windsor, according to documents the town provided to The Connecticut Mirror, the police chief signed a memorandum of understanding with Flock on March 30, 2023. Lindstrom said it was a preliminary step that gave his department access to Flock data from neighboring Manchester.
After a review and recommendation from the sergeant in charge of his investigative unit, Lindstrom took the next step in November, briefing the council in executive session of his plans to use money from a grant to contract with Flock. No public vote was needed or sought.
“I went to them, really not looking for permission, but rather seeking endorsement, because I knew or felt that it could drift towards some type of a political hot potato, right?” Lindstrom said. “So I wanted their endorsement. I wanted them to know what we were doing, and again, I tried to walk the line between permission versus endorsement.”
On Nov. 28, 2023, the sergeant overseeing the investigations unit signed a one-year lease for Flock to install and operate six “Flock Safety Falcon” cameras with “Vehicle Fingerprint technology to capture vehicular attributes” at a cost of $19,400.  They later added two cameras. The eight provided bidirectional coverage at four locations.
In a town where the starting pay for a police officer is $87,000, Lindstrom would call them a cost-effective “force multiplier.”
The cameras did not become operational until April 2025, a delay Lindstrom attributed to getting the state Department of Transportation to sign off on installing the devices on Route 5, a state right of way. 
Two months later, Weiner would get his FOI data and begin a yearlong public debate in Windsor that eventually would spill across the river.
Windsor moved deliberately, listening to residents. On Jan. 5, 2026, the council adopted a policy for ALPR data use and security — and quickly discovered that its contract with Flock did not comport with the new policy. The next month, the council voted 8-1 to turn off the cameras and renegotiate with Flock.
In June, the council’s health and safety committee sent a motion to the full council to turn the cameras back on under new rules. It was rejected on a 5-4 vote, ending Windsor’s relationship with Flock. The cameras began coming down in September, as South Windsor held its first hearing.
None of this occurred in a vacuum. On August 19, the Washington Post published a story detailing how police officers used the Flock data base to track wives and former romantic partners, exposing a glaring weakness: In some departments there were no regular audits on usage.
Secure Justice, a nonprofit tracking surveillance, reported that Flock lost more than 100 contracts, mainly for its ALPRs, in August and a similar number again in September.
More regulation 
Responding to Lamont’s request in August, the Police Officers Standards and Training council, POST, issued a 59-page report last month recommending stringent standards for Connecticut beyond a limited law that took effect Oct. 1. It is likely to be the basis of legislation drafted after the General Assembly returns in January. 
Recommendations included limiting retention of data collected by license plate readers and other sources to seven days, further tightening the 21-day limit set in the new law. They also called for greater oversight on access to the data, including two-step logins, tracking of usage by case numbers and monthly audits, as well as standards for how many cameras are deployed and the rationales for their locations.
The conservative Manhattan Institute made similar suggestions, saying the technology is worth saving the backlash was “overhyped.” Flock itself already was installing similar safeguards on its system.
But the momentum was against them, and their crisis communication strategy seemed geared too heavily at legislative bodies, not a broader public that polling found to have turned against the company over the summer.
“What they’ve done is actually some good things, but their narrative hasn’t changed,” said Doug Johnson, a crisis communication consultant who has written about the controversy. “You know, it’s the trial by media that’s killing them right now.”
On Oct. 2, an Oklahoma federal judge generated a fresh round of damaging headlines, ruling that a Tulsa County deputy’s warrantless, monthlong search of a driver’s travel history through Flock’s data base violated the Fourth Amendment.
“No doubt, ALPR technology comes with remarkable benefits that the court cannot ignore. But the Fourth Amendment requires courts to draw a line when the cost is too great,” wrote U.S. District Judge Sara E. Hill. She called the tracking “a type of indiscriminate mass surveillance.”
Elected officials at various levels of government, from the town council in South Windsor to the U.S. Senate, said the company has a crisis of credibility, not technology. Weiner told the POST council he admired the thoughtfulness behind the recommended safeguards, but he had chilled to the idea of effective regulation.
“I came into this with a very strong belief in regulation and that we can find a path through to address the civil liberties concerns and, at the same time, allow the good technology to move forward,” he said. “My view is completely changed in the last six months.”
The audience at public hearing in South Windsor on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, was asked to indicated if they supported turning off Flock’s cameras. Credit: mark pazniokas / CT Mirror
South Windsor Mayor Craig Zimmerman, a voting member of the town council, said he had come to the same conclusion, abandoning his initial belief the cameras could be kept and used under stricter rules. Michael Ouellette, a Republican councilor, asked for more time to assess Flock’s impact in town.
“I haven’t heard anything about the use of Flock in South Windsor, Ouellette said. As for the problems, he said, “It’s everywhere else.”
Lindstrom, the police chief, made one last effort to turn sentiment around. 
On Oct. 2, Lindstrom had activated Flock’s transparency portal, an optional online tool that had gone unused in South Windsor. It provides data on usage — and who has access to its images. In some communities, the portal allows the public to examine a monthly log of searches and the reason for the inquiries.
Lindstrom gave the council a memo stating, as of Oct. 1, that South Windsor only shared its Flock data with law enforcement in 53 communities, all in Connecticut, and there were only 77 searches of the data in the previous 30 days.
“Seventy-seven known searches,” Zimmerman said.
He clearly did not trust Flock, a problem that could not be reconciled in South Windsor.
Lindstrom’s prior effort before the council in September had not gone well. Lindstrom said there was no expectation of privacy on a public road, and the Flock system was a useful tool that could be safely used by his officers.
Deputy Mayor Andrew Paterna told Lindstrom he respected and trusted the police department, but not Flock. 
“I’m not going to argue,” Lindstrom said sharply. “You guys want to shut it off, that’s on you. But when your wife goes missing, or something happens —” 
Lindstrom did not finish the sentence. Instead, he asked, “What’s the value of my mother when she goes missing?”
He did not speak at the most recent hearing, which was held on Oct. 5, the same night the council voted. All 10 people who spoke urged the council to turn off the cameras. Zimmerman called for a straw vote, asking those in the audience their preference, regardless of whether they had testified.
Opposed to Flock?
Eighteen raised their hands.
In favor of Flock?
One woman in the last row raised her hand. Zimmerman scanned the room, seeing if there was anyone else in favor. 
From a seat in the front row, the chief of police raised his hand.
Police Chief Kristian Lindstrom signifying his support for Flock cameras at a meeting on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026. Credit: mark pazniokas / CT Mirror

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Judges reinstate Roselle police chief’s firing over use of anti-gay slur
description: The court ordered Roselle Police Chief Stacey Williams be fired, reversing an administrative ruling that suspended him for 30 days.
text:
New Jersey’s Appellate Division on Friday, Oct. 9, 2026, reinstated the firing of Roselle Police Chief Stacey Williams. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)New Jersey’s Appellate Division on Friday reinstated the firing of a Roselle police chief accused of using a homophobic slur in front of an openly gay officer and in reference to other police officers.
The court’s non-precedential decision reinstates the borough’s termination of Roselle Police Chief Stacey Williams after the New Jersey Civil Service Commission in April tamped down his punishment to a 30-day suspension.
“In his actions, Williams discredited himself and the Borough and negatively impacted the public’s respect and confidence in RPD. The reinstatement of Williams to his leadership position is contrary to the Borough’s and RPD’s interest in maintaining safety, discipline, order and morale within RPD and in retaining the public’s trust and confidence,” the appeals court said.
An email seeking comment from Williams’ attorney and from the borough were not immediately returned.
The court’s reversal comes more than a year after Williams is accused of using the word fa**ot while telling a story about a personal friend to an audience that included an openly gay police lieutenant.
When confronted over the slur by a police captain who noticed the lieutenant’s distress, Williams said he would “make a big deal out of” the times the gay lieutenant discussed fellatio. A separate captain testified he had never heard the gay officer discuss his sex life at work.
Williams disputed the first captain’s recollection of that exchange and said it was “possible, absolutely” that he used the slur when telling the story.
He did not deny directing the phrase “a bunch of fa*s” at officers who became ill at the site of a badly decomposed body approximately 10 years ago.
Though the borough had pushed for Williams’ removal, the Civil Service Commission instead imposed a 30-day suspension, which was recommended by an administrative law judge. The commission then reinstated the police chief with back pay.
In its decision, the commission said Williams had not intended to offend anyone and opined removal would be inappropriate for an official who had not experienced other progressive disciplinary measures.
The appeals court disagreed. Williams’ intent was irrelevant because the commission had found he violated local regulations barring use of derogatory language and sustained a charge of conduct unbecoming a public employee. The commission’s review should have been limited to what the proper penalty was, the court said.
Progressive discipline — an employment practice that sees escalating punishments for subsequent violations — was also unneeded because some infractions were severe enough to justify immediate removal, the court said, noting the commission had called Williams’ language “abhorrent.”
“We cannot discern the difference between abhorrent language and egregious misconduct to support the CSC’s rejection of the Borough’s penalty of termination other than it acted in an arbitrary and capricious manner”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC legislator arrested on charge of pulling gun at polling place
description: Rep. Michael Rivers, a Democrat from St. Helena Island who lost his reelection bid, called the accusation "politics at its worst."
text:
Rep. Michael Rivers, D-St. Helena Island, was arrested Friday, Oct. 9, 2026, on charges of pointing a gun at another person. (File photo by Getty Images)COLUMBIA — Police arrested a state representative Friday on accusations he pointed a gun at his primary opponent’s relative following an argument outside a polling place.
Rep. Michael Rivers, a Democrat from St. Helena Island who lost his reelection bid, was booked in the Colleton County jail Friday morning before his release on a personal recognizance bond, according to court records. That means he signed a promise to return to court without needing to pay cash.
The charge carries up to five years in prison, plus a fine left up to a judge to decide.
2 SC legislators ousted in primaries include GOP sponsor of redistricting bill

Rivers, who was first elected in 2016, denied any wrongdoing.
“I’m innocent and feel this accusation from my political opponent represents politics at its worst,” Rivers told the SC Daily Gazette on Friday.
The pastor and Air Force veteran, who turns 68 next week, is accused of drawing a weapon June 9 after an argument broke out at Green Pond Community Center, a polling place for the statewide primaries, according to an arrest warrant from the State Law Enforcement Division.
According to the warrant, the charge was based on video from the parking lot as well as witness statements.
Rivers got into an argument with the uncle of Shannon DeLoach, the Democrat who successfully challenged Rivers’ re-election. DeLoach brought his uncle to help greet voters when they ran into Rivers, he previously told the Gazette.
After a brief conversation with DeLoach, Rivers got in his car, DeLoach said. When DeLoach’s uncle approached, Rivers brandished a gun before driving off, he said.
Rivers did not elaborate on what happened, adding only that he considered himself a good representative of the people in his district, which spans portions of Colleton and Beaufort counties.
“I ask that people withhold judgment until this matter is settled in a court of law,” Rivers said.
DeLoach, a pastor and owner of two funeral homes, defeated Rivers in the primary with 54% of the vote. He faces Republican Shelley Gay Yuhas in the Nov. 3 general election.

name: VTDigger
title: John Rodgers sought to tie Molly Gray to ‘mistreatment of migrant workers.’ Here’s what records show
description:
Molly Gray is not involved in the operation of Four Corners Farm, according to her brother, farm manager Peter Gray.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  John Rodgers sought to tie Molly Gray to ‘mistreatment of migrant workers.’ Here’s what records show.
text:
The Vermont Occupational Safety and Health Administration, within the Department of Labor, issued two citations to Four Corners Farm that were settled in 2025. Photo by Liam Elder-Connors / Vermont Public
Carly Berlin covers housing and infrastructure for Vermont Public, in partnership with VTDigger.
Republican Lt. Gov. John Rodgers launched a new line of attack against Democratic challenger Molly Gray at Vermont Public’s debate on Tuesday, accusing the farm operated by Gray’s family of “mistreatment of migrant workers” and suggesting Gray should have spoken out.
Gray, who served as lieutenant governor between 2021 and 2023, often references her childhood at Four Corners Farm in Newbury on the campaign trail, as well as her work supporting immigrants in Vermont as the director of the Vermont Afghan Alliance. But she is not involved in the farm’s operation, according to her brother, farm manager Peter Gray. She immediately denounced Rodgers for implicating her family.
The issue, which involved housing quality for seasonal laborers on federal H-2A visas, had not previously been reported. Hundreds of pages of records released by Rodgers’ campaign present a series of investigations beginning in 2024 into housing at the farm, one settlement in 2025, and regulatory actions that exasperated Gray’s brother to the point of appealing to the governor’s office for help. 
Gray does not appear in the records compiled by Rodgers’ campaign, and she told Vermont Public on Thursday that she learned of the housing issue from her brother in early 2025 when he was working to resolve it. 
Accommodations provided to the over 500 seasonal H-2A workers in Vermont are held to specific federal standards – which is somewhat unique in the world of farmworker housing. The state Department of Labor partners with the Agency of Agriculture, Food and Markets to conduct inspections before workers arrive. State monitors routinely visit workers during the growing season.
During the summer of 2024, state agriculture and labor agents visited Four Corners Farm and noted several potential violations related to the quality of housing provided for 10 migrant workers there. Those concerns included livestock being kept too close to the workers’ kitchen area, a lack of insulation in the living quarters, and holes in window screens that let in bugs, among other issues.
After a referral, the Vermont Occupational Safety and Health Administration sent its own inspector to the farm, who determined that the issues weren’t as widespread as the other state agents had alleged. 
VOSHA ultimately cited the farm for failing to provide “an adequate sanitary food preparation area” for workers and for failing to keep certain documents of workplace injuries and illnesses. The records show that the Gray family paid a settlement in early 2025 and fixed the issues, and VOSHA closed the case.

READ MORE

Right around the same time, state employees initiated another round of inspections at Four Corners ahead of the 2025 growing season, this time with a state fire safety inspector. Workers were not living at the farm at the time.
An Agency of Agriculture staffer noted a lack of running water, and the fire inspector noted that the units needed handrails, different smoke detectors and their own bathrooms, among other code issues. The farm would need to resolve the problems in a matter of days in order to get their worker visas approved for the upcoming season, according to an account by farm manager Peter Gray. 
Peter Gray was surprised by the results of the inspection and began reaching out to state officials. In a January 2025 email to Gov. Phil Scott’s office, Peter Gray wrote that the farm had already poured thousands of dollars into fixing up the farmworker housing the prior year. The results of the latest inspection meant that the farm needed to comply with a new and different standard for the housing, essentially “‘mov[ing] the goal post’ just months before the start of the growing season.’’
“At this point, we have concerns that the goal of this process is not to help us succeed, but rather to see us fail, and shut down as a Vermont family farm,” Peter Gray continued.
Soon after, state officials met with the farm staff and helped determine a path forward. 
At Tuesday’s debate, Rodgers asked Molly Gray whether she used her influence to direct the investigation into the farm. She refuted any suggestion that she helped sway the situation. She did not hold elected office at the time of the inquiries included in the records.
According to Kendal Smith, commissioner of the Vermont Department of Labor, the department does not have any current or active cases with the farm, and the housing units used for the 2026 season passed inspection. The records indicate that a separate federal inquiry into farmworker housing was closed in March 2025.
Smith said H-2A housing complaints aren’t especially commonplace. 
“Like any program that we administer in state government, from time to time, there are complaints and things come up. But I would not say this takes up an inordinate amount of capacity for us,” Smith said in an interview on Wednesday. 
In an emailed statement, Peter Gray emphasized that the farm worked quickly to bring the housing into compliance and up to code when issues arose. 
“We care deeply about our employees, they are like family to us and we could not farm without their help,” he wrote. “What was said and done by John Rodgers not only hurts our farm but the many other Vermont farmers who depend on the H2A program and value their employees as deeply as we do.”
Molly Gray echoed that sentiment in her own written statement. “Our family farms are what make Vermont special and for John Rodgers to attack them, particularly when all issues were promptly addressed in this case, shows more about him than anyone else,” she wrote. 
Recent Vermont Public polling has shown Gray edging ahead of Rodgers in the race for the state’s second highest post. Election Day is Nov. 3.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: A political blogger sent an explicit meme of Shrek to Ohio lawmaker. Now he’s on trial.
description: WILLOUGHBY, Ohio — An Ohio political blogger had his first day in court Thursday, facing charges of harassment after sending a powerful state lawmaker an explicit picture of the cartoon character Shrek. Watch scenes from the courtroom below:   D.J. Byrnes, who also goes by his pen name “The Rooster,” is known for his outlandish […]
text:
State Sen. Jerry Cirino, left, and D.J. "The Rooster" Byrnes, right. (Photos by WEWS.)WILLOUGHBY, Ohio — An Ohio political blogger had his first day in court Thursday, facing charges of harassment after sending a powerful state lawmaker an explicit picture of the cartoon character Shrek.
Watch scenes from the courtroom below:
 






 
D.J. Byrnes, who also goes by his pen name “The Rooster,” is known for his outlandish antics, “busting up” legislators and lobbyists at the Ohio Statehouse. He is often found with a camera or microphone in hand, cornering politicians to get answers.
He’s amassed more than a hundred thousand followers on his social media and 15,000 on his Substack account. He’s described in court documents as “anti-power — if you are The Man, he’s going after you.”
‘The Man,’ according to Byrnes in his jury trial, is Senate Finance Chair Jerry Cirino (R-Kirtland), a high-ranking leader. Byrnes and Cirino have some history.
“Cirino, you threw in the towel, brother,” Byrnes can be heard in a video posted on his social media.
The blogger claims his reports played a role in Cirino losing his bid to become Senate president. After Cirino officially dropped out, Byrnes is accused of sending him two taunting messages, as well as a digitally altered explicit image of the cartoon character Shrek holding his genitals.
“It was an image that I found extremely offensive. I would consider it to be pornographic in nature — that I didn’t ask to have seen,” Cirino said.
Cirino testified he directly called the local police chief, saying he wanted charges to be filed.
“I’ve had it with this,” Cirino said, remembering the call. “Let’s pursue something here because I am being harassed.”
A local judge signed the warrant, and Byrnes was arrested publicly at the Statehouse. Despite paying his bond, records show the blogger was held in custody overnight.
“That should not happen in America,” the defense attorney said. “You might ask yourselves, why did it happen in this case?”
Byrnes pleaded not guilty to telecommunications harassment, a first-degree misdemeanor. If convicted, he faces up to six months in jail and a $1,000 fine.
“The image made the exact same point he texted. Cirino had exposed himself,” defense attorney William Livingston said, adding that this was political speech. “One message and a meme and one reply, all about a single subject: the Senate race that Cirino had just lost.”
Byrnes argued he has free speech and that Cirino is jailing a political opponent. The defense claims Cirino used his influence with the police to punish him.
Public records show Cirino called the judge who signed the arrest warrant a ‘good friend’ in late April and donated at least $2,500 to her political campaign in 2016. A different judge is presiding over the case.
“What’s important in this case is that DJ was engaging in a political speech to a politician,” Livingston said.
Byrnes may take the stand when the jury returns Friday, his attorneys told the judge. Byrnes was unable to do an interview, as he may testify.
Cirino did an interview with us following the hearing, and we referenced the defense’s line of questioning, asking if there was a conflict of interest between his status as a lawmaker and contacting the police and courts.
“There is no conflict of interest here,” Cirino said. “I have a right as a private citizen not to be harassed.”
Byrnes has previously texted the Shrek photo to other politicians, such as Republican candidate for governor Vivek Ramaswamy and Sec. of State Frank LaRose. Back before his X account was permanently suspended, he would respond to lawmakers with the image.

text:
Born: 12/7/1949
Montpelier, Vermont
Died: 10/01/2026
Northfield, Vermont
Details of service:
There will be no public services for Michael. He will be interred at the Graves Cemetery in Duxbury next to his mother and father.


Michael Charles DeForge, 76, of Morrisville passed away on October 1, 2026 at Mayo nursing home with his daughter Jasmine, his best friend Pete Jones, and his son-in-law Jonathan by his side.

He was born to Marjorie (Bailey) DeForge and Robert DeForge in Montpelier, and was the eldest of four children.

Michael graduated from Spaulding High School in Barre, VT in the later 60’s. He attended Vermont College of Norwich University where he majored in Psychology.

In the 70s Michael joined the United States Marine Corp during the Vietnam Era. He was very proud to have been a Marine (once a Marine, always a Marine).

Michael worked very hard at his sobriety of more than twenty-five years, and his daughter Jasmine was proud of him. Easy does it! He was deeply committed to AA; he was a long time member and sponsor to many.

He held positions within the mental health field including working at the Vermont State Hospital and in the Lamoille Valley. But, his favorite job was working at Big Lots in Morrisville, assembling furniture. He got great joy from his work there and spoke very fondly of the friends he made.

An avid outdoorsman, Michael could often be found hunting and fishing the woods and waters of East Montpelier, Calais, and Woodbury. He built an off the grid home with his own two hands in the woods of Hardwick, VT.

Michael enjoyed listening to jam bands, and even played bass guitar in his own band during the 90s. One of his favorite bands was Dire Straits and he also enjoyed The Grateful Dead and of course wearing tie dye t-shirts.

Michael was preceded in death by his father Robert DeForge and his mother Marjorie DeForge.

He is survived by his daughters, Jasmine Boucher and her husband Jonathan, Nova DeForge and her husband Bert Johnson, and their children Gibson and Maddilynn, Angela Martin, Tauni Martin, and Sonia Macie. He is survived by his siblings Valerie, Frank, and Tom, his best pal Pete Jones, several grandchildren, nieces, nephews and good friends.

For those who would like to honor and celebrate Michael, please consider being kind to those who are a bit different, who don’t quite “fit in”, who have caring hearts, and just want to belong.

For anyone wishing to donate in Michael’s memory please consider donating to Mayo Healthcare at VT Residential Care Nursing Home & Rehab Facility | Mayo Healthcare or mail to Mayo Healthcare 71 Richardson St. Northfield, VT 05663 or the Montpelier Food Pantry at https://www.justbasicsvt.org/hunger-free.  
Arrangements are entrusted to des Groseilliers Funeral Home, 97 Church Street, Hardwick, VT.
Michael’s daughters Jasmine & Nova would like to extend a special thank you to Mayo Nursing Home in Northfield, VT for taking such good care of him. We understand it is not an easy job. Also, a special thank you to des Groseilliers Funeral Home (Nicole and Doug) in Hardwick, VT for their compassion, caring and understanding. Thank you to Nina and David Witham for helping with the move to Montpelier and the endless support and caring over the years. Last but not least, thank you to the Montpelier Food Pantry for keeping Mike’s belly full & delivering wholesome foods to him while he was living in Montpelier.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Lindstrom reports $50 spent in 2026 NE gubernatorial campaign. The total is likely higher.
description: OMAHA — Former state Sen. Brett Lindstrom of Omaha twice petitioned this summer for the 2026 ballot for Nebraska governor, but he reported Thursday he only spent $49.50 this year so far. That number is likely to change. Lindstrom has said his initial nonpartisan bid for Nebraska governor, from July 13 until he turned in 5,765 […]
text:
Former state Sen. Brett Lindstrom of Omaha, newly registered member of the America First Party, talks with reporters outside the Nebraska Secretary of State's Election Division after filing paperwork to be the gubernatorial candidate for the new political party on Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026, in Lincoln. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)OMAHA — Former state Sen. Brett Lindstrom of Omaha twice petitioned this summer for the 2026 ballot for Nebraska governor, but he reported Thursday he only spent $49.50 this year so far. That number is likely to change.
Lindstrom has said his initial nonpartisan bid for Nebraska governor, from July 13 until he turned in 5,765 signatures Aug. 3, included paid signature gatherers. It was on Aug. 14 that Lindstrom’s nonpartisan bid fell flat as 2,407 signatures were rejected. Many of those were flagged as possibly fraudulent, the largest portion in Lancaster County. He needed 4,000 valid signatures.
Two new political parties also petitioned to get on the ballot — the Nebraska Working People Party and America First Party — and Lindstrom on Sept. 1 became America First’s gubernatorial nominee. In that effort, he needed just 25 signatures from new party members.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen of Columbus, a Republican, top left, is running for reelection against former Democratic state Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont, top right, Rick Beard of Omaha, the nominee for the Legal Marijuana NOW Party, bottom left, and former state Sen. Brett Lindstrom of Omaha, the nominee for the America First Party, bottom right. (Photos courtesy of the candidates/campaigns | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Lindstrom now faces Republican Gov. Jim Pillen, former Democratic state Sen. Lynne Walz and Legal Marijuana NOW’s Rick Beard. Each has selected a running mate. A campaign disclosure committee is required after a candidate raises or spends $5,000. 
The latest reporting period was June 17 through Sept. 29, the first for the general election.
In that period, gubernatorial candidates reported the following:

Pillen: $2.4 million raised, $4.4 million spent and $7.5 million cash on hand.
Walz: $2.2 million raised, $2 million spent and $860,464.44 cash on hand.
Lindstrom: $12,154.90 raised, $49.50 spent and $12,105.40 cash on hand.
Beard: No campaign filings (less than $5,000 raised or $5,000 spent).

Between Jan. 1, 2025, and Sept. 29, Pillen and Walz have raised a combined $14.7 million and spent $9.9 million. More than 70% of that is from Pillen’s campaign. The 2026 election is already the third most expensive governor’s race in state history and appears on track to take the second-highest spot. For just general election spending alone, 2026 is the most expensive.
The 2022 GOP primary, which featured Pillen, Lindstrom, Falls City agribusinessman Charles Herbster and six other Republicans, exceeded $26 million in funds raised and $25 million in funds spent. Pillen would go on to spend $2 million in the general election. Then-state Sen. Carol Blood, a Democrat, spent $635,000 in the whole 2026 election.
The Nebraska Accountability and Disclosure Commission, which is similar to the Federal Election Commission for federal candidates, confirmed that virtually all spending toward the goal of being elected is considered a campaign expense. That includes signature gathering.
“There are a couple specific exceptions in statute, but this is not one of them,” NADC deputy director David Hunter said in an email to the Nebraska Examiner.
He added: “We have had a few candidates and committees lately that are unaware certain expenses like that should be reported as campaign expenditures, so we may need to better publicize that these types of expenses would qualify. I imagine that the Lindstrom campaign will report them when we let them know. That filing and others are currently being reviewed.”
Lindstrom said Friday: “I’m currently getting clarification from the NADC on what I need to update on my form.”
Nebraska Lt. Gov. Joe Kelly of Lincoln, a Republican, top left, is running for reelection alongside Gov. Jim Pillen. The Republican ticket faces Ben Steffen of Humboldt, top right, and former state Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont for the Democratic Party; Keenya “Ruby” Barnes of Omaha, bottom left, with Rick Beard of Omaha for the Legal Marijuana NOW Party; and Michael Picard of Omaha with former state Sen. Brett Lindstrom of Omaha for the America First Party, bottom right. (Photos courtesy of the candidates/campaigns | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Part of Lindstrom’s first petitions went up in smoke over his work with the signature-gathering firm On The Ballot. That firm also ran the Lincoln petition effort this summer to amend the Lincoln City Charter. Good Government Lincoln at first failed due to significant allegations of fraud. The Lincoln petitions restarted and supporters qualified for the Nov. 3 ballot.
A total of seven circulators have been arrested who allegedly gathered fraudulent signatures on the Lincoln effort. A few of those circulators also worked on Lindstrom’s campaign.
State and county election officials are now considering banning paying per signature, a method Lindstrom voted in favor of legalizing in 2015 after a seven-year ban. In September, Lindstrom said he learned firsthand how a pay-per-signature-collected system could backfire.
Good Government Lincoln spent $390,000 on signature gathering via Vanguard Field Strategies. Vanguard subcontracted work to On The Ballot on June 8, July 1 and July 27, each time at $108,000.
Hunter said all campaign statements that come into the NADC are thoroughly reviewed. They are normally spot-checked in the order received and later reviewed more thoroughly. He said some filings could still be coming in for the Oct. 5 due date as they only need to be U.S. Postal Service postmarked by the due date. Agency staff then enter those filings.
There are two more state reporting periods for Nebraska’s 2026 general election: Sept. 30 through Oct. 19 (due Oct. 26) and Oct. 20 through Dec. 31 (due Jan. 12).

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas Gov. Laura Kelly rallies Iowa educators for Sand’s campaign
description: Kansas Gov. Laura Kelly joined Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand in Des Moines on Thursday, saying her tenure shows it is possible to be an effective Democratic governor while working with a GOP-controlled state Legislature. Joining Sand in person at the Iowa State Education Association headquarters, Kelly said when she was first elected in 2018, [[...]
text:
Kansas Gov. Laura Kelly joined Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand in Des Moines on Thursday, saying her tenure shows it is possible to be an effective Democratic governor while working with a GOP-controlled state Legislature.
Joining Sand in person at the Iowa State Education Association headquarters, Kelly said when she was first elected in 2018, Kansas faced a “very similar situation” to Iowa as the state experienced budget problems — including public schools being “chronically underfunded.” Since then, she said, Kansas has “fully funded our schools now for eight years in a row,” alongside making additional investments in public education and special education services.
“None of this has been easy, and none of it happened because one party got its way,” Kelly said. “It happened because we worked across the aisle and stayed focused on our schools. After two terms, I am proud to say we did get things back on track. We balanced our budget, we funded our schools every year, and we built records for business investment and job creation. … What does that prove? That with the laser focus on the issues that matter, you can turn things around. And Rob Sand is that leader.”
At the event, educators asked Sand, the current state auditor, what he would do to better support students and staff in Iowa’s public school system. They also asked Sand how he would address changes made in recent years to the state’s Area Education Agencies, which providing services for special education students. While he has said he would support a 5% increase to K-12 funding in his first year as governor, Sand also warned that he would not have the ability to reverse measures passed into law by GOP majorities, under the assumption that Republicans will continue to hold legislative majorities in Iowa.
“I’m not going to be able to unilaterally undo things, and I’m not the kind of person who’s going to stand in front of you and make promises that I know that we have a constitutional system of self-governance that won’t let me keep that promise,” Sand said. “… I know that might sound disappointing, but it’s the truth. Here’s the piece that’s really easy to say that is exciting. More bad bills that hit my desk, I can veto.”
Kelly also said Sand may be in a more advantageous position than herself if elected governor in the Nov. 3, 2026 election. While Kansas has Republican supermajorities in both chambers, Iowa currently has a supermajority in the House and a majority in the Senate. She said working across the aisle in her state became more difficult as “moderate Republicans” were replaced by “MAGA”-affiliated Republicans, but said she has still been able to build relationships across the aisle to accomplish common goals.
“It’s not been easy to get things done, but if somebody knows where they want to go, there are ways and there are people that you will find if you’re willing to talk and be willing to listen … and now you will be able to find those legislators who can modify their approach or their vote to get where you want to go,” Kelly said. “You know, it may have to be transactional. You have to make some deals, and do really what they want over here, so that you can get what you really need over her. But there are ways to do it, and I have no doubt, given Rob’s history as your auditor … the fact that many people have been willing to work with him bodes well.”
She criticized Iowa’s GOP gubernatorial candidate, Zach Lahn, for his approach to state education, while pointing to a regular criticism from the campaign trail that he “still has a home in Kansas” and frequently travels to the state.
Earlier in the week, Kelly had released an advertisement supporting Sand in the 2026 gubernatorial campaign, in which she said though she generally supports Kansans, “in the Iowa governor’s race, I’m supporting the Iowan.”
“Zach, there are no hard feelings, but it is time to come back to Kansas,” Kelly said in the video. “As they say, there’s no place like home.”
Sand and Democrats have regularly criticized Lahn over his Iowa residency status, pointing to reports showing he lived and was a registered voter in Kansas prior to the 2024 election cycle. His residency changed in time to qualify him to run for Iowa governor in 2026. He also regularly travels to Kansas using his private plane – trips Lahn said are because some of his children are located in Wichita.
The two candidates faced off Monday at a debate hosted by KWQC in Davenport, where Lahn addressed some concerns about his residency and travel to Kansas. He said criticisms of his travel and time spent in Kansas were criticisms of his family.
“I’m gonna tell you this right now, this issue is about one thing. It’s about my children. That’s it,” Lahn said. “I have a blended family, and they split time. … I am not going to be intimidated on this.”
The Lahn campaign did not immediately return a message seeking a response for this article.
Kelly also said Lahn’s work in Kansas private schools shows he would not be the best choice for Iowans hoping to improve the state’s K-12 school system. In 2018, Lahn helped launch a private pre-K through 12th-grade school in Wichita, Kansas on the campus of Wichita State University called Wonder. The Kansas governor referenced a report from the Kansas Reflector that found Wonder owned Lahn and his wife Annie Lahn approximately $4.5 million in 2025, and that its expenses exceeded revenues in five of six years of operation.
“His plan for Iowa schools is to model them after the private school he started in Wichita, Kansas. That school is now $4.5 million dollars in debt. Iowa already has a $1.4 billion dollar budget hole. You don’t fix that by importing a failed model.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Why this candidate for SC attorney general doesn’t want donations
description: COLUMBIA — The Democrat seeking to be South Carolina’s next attorney general is operating a campaign with zero cash flow, and that’s on purpose. “When you owe no one, you can fight for everyone, and that’s the whole point,” attorney Richard Hricik told the SC Daily Gazette this week. That includes owing himself. Beyond refusing […]
text:
Richard Hricik, who owns a law firm in Mount Pleasant, is the Democrat running for attorney general on Nov. 3, 2026, ballots. (Photo courtesy of Richard Hricik's campaign)COLUMBIA — The Democrat seeking to be South Carolina’s next attorney general is operating a campaign with zero cash flow, and that’s on purpose.
“When you owe no one, you can fight for everyone, and that’s the whole point,” attorney Richard Hricik told the SC Daily Gazette this week.
That includes owing himself. Beyond refusing to accept donations, he also won’t dig deep into his own wallet.
Back in March, he loaned his campaign $8,420 — enough to open a bank account, pay the $8,320 candidate filing fee and launch a website. He officially forgave the debt June 30, according to campaign filings.
That may seem an odd strategy for flipping a statewide office last won by a Democrat 36 years ago.
But Hricik, who owns a law firm in Mount Pleasant, said his refusal to fundraise allows him to be an “authentic defender” of South Carolina uninfluenced by donors with their own agendas. He’s also banking on his decision appealing to voters who believe there’s too much money in politics and who are tired of the barrage of campaign ads, texts and mailers.


For more on our 2026 election coverage and information on voting in South Carolina, check out our Voter Guide.


As of his last campaign filing, his account had a balance of just $94.
Compare that to his Republican opponent, 8th Circuit Solicitor David Stumbo, who had more than $43,000 cash available June 30 after spending more than $800,000 in a contested GOP primary and runoff.
Neither Hricik nor Stumbo has filed a third-quarter report yet.
The two are competing Nov. 3 to replace Attorney General Alan Wilson, the GOP nominee for governor.
Hricik said the advertising “blizzard” for other races, including governor and U.S. Senate, make word-of-mouth campaigning the most effective way to reach voters for the down-ballot contest.
Eighth Circuit Solicitor David Stumbo officially launched his bid for South Carolina attorney general Tuesday, Sept. 16, 2025. (Photo provided by Stumbo campaign)
In response, Stumbo told the SC Daily Gazette he respects his opponent’s “right to run his campaign however he chooses.”
However, he said, “it is very misleading to imply that a candidate who receives financial campaign support is incapable of faithfully serving and impartially seeking justice for the people of South Carolina.”
That incorrectly implies nearly every elected officeholder is unqualified, Stumbo said. The chief prosecutor for Abbeville, Greenwood, Laurens and Newberry counties added that it “defies logic” to believe candidates can reach voters statewide without raising money to share their message.
Hricik, a native of Cleveland, Ohio, moved to Mount Pleasant in 1997 to teach criminal justice and constitutional law at Charleston Southern University, then started his law firm. He continues to teach part-time at the Charleston School of Law and online for William and Mary Law School, his alma mater.
He decided to run for attorney general, he said, because no other Democrat had signed up, and he believed the “rule of law needed an authentic defender.” He turned in his candidacy paperwork toward the end of the two-week filing period in March and was unopposed as the Democratic nominee.
Hricik said he believes his experience as a trial and appellate attorney representing clients statewide better qualifies him to be the state’s attorney general than a solicitor responsible for prosecuting criminal cases in a judicial circuit.
His notable cases include reaching a $2 million settlement with the Columbia Housing Authority in 2023, four years after a carbon monoxide leak from a faulty furnace in public housing killed two men. Hricik represented the family of one of the residents of Allen Benedict Court, which has since been demolished.
Beyond his experience in personal injury and wrongful death cases, Hricik’s wins in court include a 10-day extension for voter registration in October 2024 following Helene’s path of destruction through South Carolina as a tropical storm. In that case, he represented the state Democratic Party.
Hricik argues the attorney general’s office functions like a law firm, similar to his own. He contends the role is less focused on criminal prosecutions.
But Stumbo called it “puzzling” that a non-prosecutor would seek the job, saying his experience as a solicitor for the last 14 years and, before that, an attorney in private practice make him the better qualified candidate.
The attorney general is considered the state’s chief prosecutor. The duties of the office include representing the state in all appeals of criminal convictions, including death penalty cases. It also oversees the State Grand Jury, the Human Trafficking Task Force and the Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force, which prosecutes crimes related to child sexual abuse material.
What happens behind the scenes when SC joins a multi-state GOP lawsuit

The office also defends the state from lawsuits and participates in national lawsuits.
Hricik said Wilson’s administration has done far too much of the latter.
Throughout his four terms, Wilson has regularly led and signed onto lawsuits with other GOP attorneys general to challenge the Obama and Biden administrations while filing briefs backing the Trump administrations from Democrat-led lawsuits.
Hricik said that’s inappropriately using the office to take political stances. A spokesman for Wilson declined to comment.
“The attorney general is supposed to be the people’s attorney, and I’m going to be the people’s attorney,” Hricik said.
If elected, he said, he’ll “go after all the bad guys, and that means the polluters too.” That includes looking into the environmental and financial impact of data centers and pollution by plastic pellets.
