name: Virginia Mercury
title: Constitutional: The amendment that could permanently protect reproductive rights in Virginia
description: Kacia Kriener Putman credits abortion access with her ability to grow her family.  Three weeks before first pregnancy’s due date, the Alexandria resident developed pre-eclampsia, a potentially life-threatening high blood pressure condition that occurs in some pregnancies and can cause organ damage. She also developed HELLP, a syndrome that affects blood clot[...]
text:
Kacia Kriener Putman, who supports Virginia's proposed reproductive rights constitutional amendment, stands outside the Bank Street entrance to the Virginia State Capitol with her children in January 2026. (Photo courtesy of Putman)Kacia Kriener Putman credits abortion access with her ability to grow her family. 
Three weeks before first pregnancy’s due date, the Alexandria resident developed pre-eclampsia, a potentially life-threatening high blood pressure condition that occurs in some pregnancies and can cause organ damage. She also developed HELLP, a syndrome that affects blood clotting and liver function. 
Doctors rushed her into an emergency cesarean section. The joy of bringing her son Malcolm into the world was marked by the terror she and her husband experienced, Putman said. 
It taught her firsthand how quickly things can go awry in pregnancies, and why complications sometimes require terminations to save a mother’s life. 
When Putman and her husband decided to have a second child, they talked about the risks at length with her doctors. 
She felt safe to try to become a two-time mom only because she knew she could get an abortion if she needed one to save her life, Putman recalled. 
“It’s scary that (my daughter) might not have existed … if I didn’t have the freedom (to get an abortion),” she said. 
Abortion is legal in Virginia through the 26th week of pregnancy. After that, three doctors must certify that the procedure is needed to save the life of the mother in order for the abortion to be granted. 
A proposed amendment on Virginia voters’ ballots this fall could cement abortion access and other reproductive rights into the state’s constitution. It’s among three pending measures to enshrine same-sex marriage protections and restore voting rights to former felons who’ve completed their prison sentences. 


Proposed Constitutional Amendment 1
Question: Should the Constitution of Virginia be amended to (i) protect the freedom to make personal decisions about prenatal care, childbirth, postpartum care, birth control, abortion, miscarriage management, and fertility care; (ii) protect doctors, nurses, and patients from being punished for these decisions; and (iii) allow for restrictions on access to abortion during the third trimester of pregnancy except when the patient’s health is at risk or the pregnancy cannot survive?


 What the amendment would do

If approved, the amendment would remove the three-physician threshold for late-term abortions. Beyond abortion, the measure would also protect contraception access and fertility treatments like in vitro fertilization (IVF). 
IVF allowed Albemarle County resident Casey Oakley to become a surrogate for friends. Before that, an abortion saved her life when she experienced a “missed miscarriage” during one of her pregnancies. 
Her body had stopped producing hormones to continue the pregnancy, but weeks later, it had not expelled the contents of her uterus.
“I was going into sepsis,” Oakley said in an interview with The Mercury this summer. “The abortion saved my life.”
State lawmaker Del. Cia Price, D-Newport News, has emphasized how contraception treats her polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) — a disorder which can cause irregular menstrual cycles, chronic inflammation and pain.
Democratic lawmakers pushed for contraception’s inclusion in Virginia’s proposed amendment because reproductive rights could be limited in the future, Price said. 
After the Supreme Court struck down abortion protections in 2022, Justice Clarence Thomas expressed interest in reconsidering cases that uphold contraception access. 
The amendment only advanced thanks to Democratic majorities in the state legislature. Every Republican state lawmaker voted against advancing it to ballots, largely due to their stance on abortion. 
They argued it could override existing state law that requires parental or guardian consent for minors to have surgeries including abortion. They also aired concerns that the amendment could enable infanticide.
Federal court cases have upheld parental consent and infanticide is illegal at the state and federal levels. 
 Varying views on third-trimester abortion

Christian advocacy group Family Foundation has a pending lawsuit that seeks to strike down the amendment if the majority of Virginians approve it.
The lawsuit argues  that the ballot language is misleading and that legislative procedural steps for the amendment were not properly followed. A related case was dismissed over the summer but will be further deliberated by the Court of Appeals of Virginia. 
Proponents suggest that removing the three-physician standard for late-term abortions would be helpful in emergencies and for rural patients who travel further for care. 
But opponents, including VCU Health OBGYN Dr. Edward Springel, counter it would make it too easy to get an abortion. Springel also said that survival rates increase for fetuses born after 25 weeks of pregnancy and onward. 
With no uniform definition of fetal viability, doctors handle pregnancies on a case-by-case basis with patients as they move through their second trimester. 
Casey Oakley, who needed an abortion after an unsuccessful IVF embryo transfer. She and her husband have two biological children and she has been a surrogate mom for two families. The couple has also foster parented four girls. (Photo courtesy Casey Oakley)
Springel said that’s when parents who develop life-threatening conditions may more likely have the option to have a premature birth rather than an abortion procedure. 
“The baby could be delivered alive, and then you would have two living patients,” he said. 
The Richmond doctor typically doesn’t wade into politics, he said, but the pending amendment’s language spurred him to participate in the Virginia Medical Professionals For Women’s Safety campaign. 
The group is an offshoot of The American Association of Pro-Life Obstetricians, a national organization that opposes abortion. 
Dr. Kimi Chernoby, a Northern Virginia emergency medicine doctor who supports the amendment, emphasized that each pregnancy is different and complications vary widely. 
Life-threatening conditions like the ones Putman experienced typically emerge in the third trimester, close enough to due dates that parents and doctors usually opt for an early or emergency birth, but other factors could lead to abortions beyond the second trimester.
“People are not getting third-trimester abortions for preeclampsia,” Chernoby said. “People are getting third-trimester abortions for things like fatal fetal anomalies, where they know that the fetus does not have a chance of survival.”
And while developing preeclampsia earlier in pregnancy is rare, it does happen. 
“No one,” Chernoby said for example, “is doing an induction at 17 weeks and thinking that there is going to be a survivable birth.” 
As a fetus cannot survive outside the mother’s body at that point of gestation, she likened it to “ending the condition of pregnancy without the intention of producing a live birth.”
Third-trimester abortions, which make up about 1% of abortions nationwide, are usually due to a late-developing, critical condition of the fetus or the pregnant person, a 2022 National Institutes of Health study indicated.
When third-trimester abortions do occur, an American Medical Association study found they’re most often performed closer to the start of the third trimester than well into it. 
Though fetal anomalies are usually detected within the second trimester, some severe or lethal defects may not be apparent until the third trimester, according to another NIH study. 
This year, Putman has volunteered with the Virginians For Reproductive Freedom campaign, a coalition of medical and reproductive rights groups that have banded together to boost the amendment.
She plans to vote yes to all three amendments and, as she knocks on doors to drum up support for the reproductive rights measure, she encourages others to do the same. 
Though opponents argue the amendment is too broad, Putman said it ensures people will be able to maintain their bodily autonomy, no matter what kind of pregnancy complications may arise. 
“We can’t legislate around every exception,” Putnam said. 
Early voting runs through Oct. 31. Election Day is Nov. 3.

title: Proposed Head Start changes would eliminate slots for Virginia children experiencing homelessness
description: Pending changes to Head Start initiated by President Donald Trump’s administration could make it harder for Virginia families to utilize the program, including those whose families lack permanent shelter.  A U.S. Department of Health and Human Services proposal would eliminate a rule that allows Head Start centers to reserve admission spots for homeless stud[...]
text:
A U.S. Department of Health and Human Services proposal would eliminate a rule that allows Head Start centers to reserve admission spots for homeless students and those in the foster care system. Virginia Head Start workers and advocates oppose the change. (Photo by Getty Images)Pending changes to Head Start initiated by President Donald Trump’s administration could make it harder for Virginia families to utilize the program, including those whose families lack permanent shelter. 
A U.S. Department of Health and Human Services proposal would eliminate a rule that allows Head Start centers to reserve admission spots for homeless students and those in the foster care system. Currently, about 3% of slots are reserved for such families. 
Additionally, families would lose the ability to self-affirm they are homeless.
Lawrence Howerton, an outreach coordinator and Medicaid application assistant at the nonprofit Virginia Organizing, didn’t realize he was technically homeless during part of his childhood. 
His mother and siblings had been living in “a back room” in his uncle’s house. 
“We didn’t have a key, we had to be let in,” he said. 
The family wasn’t living on the streets or sleeping in shelters, but they lacked a stable home. Instability in his formative years, he believes, is what contributed to his juvenile incarceration. 
Now as an adult, he helps similarly struggling families and is concerned the proposed rule could harm children already living in tough circumstances. 
Virginia Head Start Association director Dawn Ault is also worried about the proposed rule, including how it would eliminate self-affirmation of homelessness. She said there’s no clear way for such families to prove their circumstances. 
“I don’t understand what kind of flexibility they’re going to allow programs in determining if someone’s homeless if they’re not allowed to self-identify that,” she said. 
Ault suggested that programs could still utilize the McKinney-Vento definitions of homelessness, which stems from a 1987 law Congress passed to ensure housing-unstable children could enroll in schools despite lacking a fixed address or certain paperwork. 
The measure is meant to aid children sleeping in cars, homes of friends or family — like what Howerton experienced — living in motels, campgrounds, homeless shelters or sleeping in public spaces. 
“It does say it allows programs flexibility in documenting how they’re homeless, but they don’t give any specific information on what it is that families would have to produce,” Ault said. “If this were to be placed as in the final rule, then we need to seek more guidance on what exactly is the ‘flexibility’ in documenting homelessness.”
Though the rule would drop the requirement to reserve slots for homeless families, she added that providers could still choose to reserve space. 
“We still hope and want all programs to still function under the current regulations because that’s what’s been proven and with our data to be in the best interest for children and families,” she said.
Head Start programs occupy a multifaceted role in public service to families. The early childhood education program starts ahead of formal K-12 school and functions as a childcare option for working parents.
Head Start also exposes children to healthy habits, and staff serve as what Howerton calls “identifiers.” 
Instructors can spot children that show early signs of learning disabilities, behavioral health problems, underlying health conditions, or side effects of unstable home lives and offer them specialized attention and support. 
The proposal would also remove regulatory references to health, mental health, dental care and developmental screenings. 
Howerton said if he’d been part of Head Start as a youth, it might have helped deter him from the “school to prison pipeline.” His experience drives his efforts to assist families around the South Boston area of Virginia, where he is based. 
“It’s poor communities that are being attacked,” he said. 
With 11,000 funded Head Start and Early Head Start spaces for children under five in Virginia, the program supports families whose earnings fall below the federal poverty line (which is currently around $30,000 per year for a family of four).
The program also supports families undergoing sudden life transitions. 
Nottoway County mother Amanda Daugherty relied on Head Start after the death of her husband while she worked to support her family. 
“Our local agency … wrapped their arms around me. I had no family here, nothing,” Daugherty previously told The Mercury. 
Beyond adjustments to how families without stable housing access the program, the Trump administration’s proposed rule pares roughly 130 pages of Head Start regulation down to 10, Ault said. 
Broadly, it would eliminate classroom ratios and group-size limits, reduce requirements for serving children with disabilities and multilingual learners, as well as cap administrative spending for the program. 
With the homeless population one piece of the “mammoth puzzle,” Ault said that providers are watching closely for how to navigate changes. 
Public comment for the proposed changes closed on Oct. 6, with over 40,000 submissions from people and organizations nationwide. Many comments either expressed opposition to the proposed changes or offered praise for the support the program provides. 
“When given early access to therapies and services, it significantly reduces the overall healthcare and government spending because families have what they need right away,” a Pennsylvania-based occupational therapist wrote. 
“Families benefit from this care and are less likely to need services when they’re done with us, because they feel prepared and educated on what to do without support.” 
The deluge of feedback is a good thing, Ault said. 
Still, she said, “the question is about funding down the line, because if things are no longer required, will the administration continue to fund  what we currently have?”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana BMV deserves kudos — with one big caveat
description: It was a good week for the Indiana Bureau of Motor Vehicles. The agency is hauling in money from a popular “blackout” plate design and received top rankings nationwide in an analysis of branch Google reviews. I still have a bone to pick with BMV. But first, let’s focus on the good stuff. We reported […]
text:
Indiana Bureau of Motor Vehicles Commissioner Kevin Garvey speaks during the unveiling of the state's new blackout license plate on Monday, July 21, 2025, at the Indiana Government Center in Indianapolis.(Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle) It was a good week for the Indiana Bureau of Motor Vehicles. The agency is hauling in money from a popular “blackout” plate design and received top rankings nationwide in an analysis of branch Google reviews.
I still have a bone to pick with BMV. But first, let’s focus on the good stuff.
We reported that a review of Google ratings landed Indiana in the top spot. The average score nationwide is 3.8 stars, but the 84 Indiana offices scored highest — averaging 4.16 stars.
The Scottsburg branch came out tops in the state at 4.60. Here are a few reviews I found complimenting the site:

“Took me nine minutes from car door to car door to renew my license, outstanding!”
“Love, love this branch!!! All the ladies are so helpful and very friendly!! Thanks for all you do for our community ”
“Went in to register a vehicle on Saturday morning and the service was phenomenal. In and out in less than 30 mins. Grateful that this office is here…”

This is a long way to come for an agency that really went through it in the early 2000s.
In 2006, Joel Silverman resigned as commissioner of the BMV after closing 20 license branches with little to no community or legislative input. And he oversaw a computer overhaul that was fraught with failure. He also removed the clocks from branches to try to downplay how long transactions were taking.
While Silverman’s tactics were unpopular, eventually the network change was completed and he started customer satisfaction surveys. I contend he laid the groundwork for where the agency is today.
That doesn’t mean there still isn’t room for improvement. But even Indiana’s lowest-rated branch — Batesville, at 3.53 — scored higher than 694 offices elsewhere in the country.
A few Batesville reviews:

“Staff needs training. I still can’t believe they kept this branch open and not Versailles.”
“Worst DMV I’ve visited. They tell you that you need 1 paper then they tell you they didn’t need that paper and it is a different one. The people there do not try to help you but make you go through hoops trying to figure it out yourself. The place sucks overall, and I would rather go all the way to Lawrenceburg or Greensburg. Would give it zero stars if I could.”

But there was another review that brings me to what’s really wrong with BMV:
“I recently tagged a vehicle. As soon as I did, I started getting junk mail that listed my new car. They sold my data and you can’t opt out. So, they are sharing private data that you have to register to drive. Great Government at its best. Make as much money as you can from your citizens.”
Indeed, the BMV has been selling your data for years, including your name, address, date of birth, make and model of vehicle, plate number, VIN, purchase date, driver record, license type and more. The data is sold to attorneys, towing services, debt collectors, insurance companies and auto dealers. The practice brings in about $26 million a year.



Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



Lawmakers in recent years have done a lot to protect Hoosiers’ data in the private sector. But they have refused to do the same with BMV data. Other states have allowed an opt-out provision.
Which brings me to the revenue from the blackout plate.
The BMV announced this week that the agency has sold more than 380,000 “blackout” license plates in the year since the minimalist design launched, generating $12.9 million. The black plates with white numerals are all the rage.
The agency plans to use the revenue toward a five-year modernization program that includes an AI chatbot, digital driver’s licenses and improved tracking software.
What they should do is dedicate at least half of the money to covering the $26 million in data sharing revenue. Then ask the Legislature to do the right thing and ban the practice in 2027.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Cyanobacteria, and their toxins, are incredibly diverse. How can risk be measured?
description: When a greenish cloud, surface scum or other suspicious algae appears in a previously clear lake, the message is clear: Stay away. As cyanobacteria blooms become more common in New Hampshire, that precaution has become common practice across the state. The reason? Cyanobacteria, an ancient single-celled organism that multiplies to excess when nutrients and h[...]
text:
Cyanobacteria and algae flourish in a pond in Concord. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)When a greenish cloud, surface scum or other suspicious algae appears in a previously clear lake, the message is clear: Stay away. As cyanobacteria blooms become more common in New Hampshire, that precaution has become common practice across the state.
The reason? Cyanobacteria, an ancient single-celled organism that multiplies to excess when nutrients and heat are plentiful, can produce toxins harmful to the skin, liver, nervous system, stomach and more. Effects range from mild illness and rash to, in rare instances, death; therefore, authorities like the New Hampshire Department of Environmental Services and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention urge would-be swimmers, paddlers and pets to stay away from water that shows signs of a bloom.
The effects of cyanotoxin exposure are widely documented. But not all cyanobacteria are toxic and beneficial cyanobacteria are much more common, filling an important ecological role at the base of the food chain. Yet differentiating the two, and determining when and to what extent the organisms pose a threat to health, is a significant scientific challenge. 
There are thousands of known species of cyanobacteria and at least hundreds of variations of the dangerous chemicals the bacteria can produce, called cyanotoxins. But scientists have yet to characterize many of those specific molecules, according to Anyin Li, associate professor of chemistry at the University of New Hampshire.
That lack of knowledge is a major hurdle in efforts to understand how toxins differ, how they affect us and how they travel through ecosystems, Li said.
“It’s one of the reasons, in fact, that a lot of the information you’ll find about cyanotoxins is very general, and focused on sort of potential risk,” he said in an interview. 
Li and other researchers have focused their work on that knowledge gap, turning to molecular techniques they hope will help create an information-rich library of cyanotoxin profiles. Ultimately, researchers said, they hope the work will contribute to efforts to create evidence-based safety regulations while helping people enjoy the water bodies they love without fear. 
Protein detectives
One technique scientists tend to use more than others to test for the presence of cyanotoxins is a molecule-tagging technique called ELISA (short for enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay). The tags tell scientists whether the toxins are present, but the technique has some limitations, Li said. It is vulnerable to false positives — such as when the toxin molecule has broken up but the test still reads it as present — and does not provide the level of detail researchers said would be most useful. 
Within one class of cyanotoxins called microcystins, for example, there are 400 possible subtypes, Li said. ELISA on its own is not enough to differentiate among all of them.
This is emblematic of the challenges associated with other tests scientists have at their disposal to assess cyanotoxins, he added. 
“At this point, many of these tools to look at these toxins, they are too general,” he said. They do not differentiate subtypes, and they do not always allow researchers to estimate the amount of toxin present in a sample. The error rate, he said, is as high as 40%. 
When separate toxin subtypes have the potential to affect the human body very differently, that matters.
In Li’s laboratory, UNH researchers are refining a method of identifying those molecules based on a different molecular technique called mass spectrometry. This technique allows researchers to take minute measurements of the matter in a molecule, yielding information so precise they can be analyzed to identify specific toxin subtypes. 
So far, the technique has allowed Li’s lab to identify those subtypes with more precision than other methods. 
Cyanobacteria genes
Another way to learn more about what a bloom may be producing is to get specific about the types of organisms it contains, said molecular biologist and algae expert Robin Sleith and microbial ecologist Pete Countway, both researchers at Bigelow Laboratory for Ocean Sciences in Boothbay, Maine. 
Because cyanobacteria are single-celled and incredibly diverse, defining species boundaries between them is difficult, Countway said. 
Regarding single-celled organisms in general, “that’s something we’ve been struggling with, you know, for my entire professional career,” he said. 
Instead, he said, it helps to consider the organisms’ entire genetic sequences. Determining whether the organism may pose a risk to human health, then, requires the scientists to work forward along the path from DNA to protein building blocks to finished toxins. Decoding genes is the first step.
Sleith and Countway analyze DNA collected from the environment, also known as eDNA, and DNA from cyanobacteria samples, as well as other potentially harmful microorganisms, looking for the genes that could allow the creatures to make toxins. 
Just the presence of a toxin gene doesn’t mean it’s being produced, however, so another test, like ELISA, may follow. 
While this method can help identify harmful toxins when they are present, it can also be a way to alleviate concerns. In a paper published this September in the journal Harmful Algae, Sleith, Countway and their co-authors demonstrated that the toxin-producing genes were not present in one species of cyanobacteria that can appear in lakes. 
Multiple species of duckweed and algae are visible on the surface of Horseshoe Pond, in Concord, on Aug. 27. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Cyano knowledge is power
Learning more about the diversity of cyanotoxins is crucial because, by their nature, cyanobacteria are all around us, said Amanda McQuaid, a professor of water quality and ecotoxicology at UNH and director of the university extension’s Lakes Lay Monitoring Program. 
The tiniest cyanobacteria can be airborne, for instance, making their way into people’s lungs, while others are found nearly anywhere there is water, she said. But in most cases, this is normal and not cause for alarm. 
Yet, there are also circumstances where precautions against health impacts are necessary. Scientists haven’t yet pinpointed exactly what level of toxin exposure is dangerous, but McQuaid said she hopes more precise research would help. 
This is Li’s goal, too: He hopes to see more precise evidence aid the development of federal exposure guidelines.
“Better quantitative methods will allow us to define more specific guidelines,” he said. “Right now the EPA guidelines are very general.”
Making these measurements more widely available is also important, said Sleith and Countway. That would require development of accessible, fast water tests using some of these techniques. 
“Basically, we’d need to see it become as standard as, like, home COVID tests,” Countway said.
More precise testing will also allow scientists like Anna O’Brien, UNH assistant professor of molecular, cellular and biomedical science, to track toxins as they cycle through ecosystems, she said.
As an example, O’Brien pointed to duckweed, a small aquatic plant that absorbs nutrients from pond water as it grows. By adding the plant to soil, farmers could access a readily available source of “green” fertilizer, O’Brien said. But scientists must first ensure that they would not also be plying their croplands with cyanotoxins, something O’Brien hopes a better understanding of the toxins will rule out. 
With climate change contributing to hotter summers and warming water bodies in the Northeast, cyanobacteria blooms are likely to remain prevalent. 
“What I see on the horizon is that these blooms are getting, especially in the Northeast, it’s probably going to get a little bit worse before it gets better,” Sleith said. 
But with the right tools and increased knowledge, he’s hopeful people will be able to navigate the coming years safely.
“What I want is for people to feel safe about enjoying their time in the water,” he said. 
Aquatic insects and duckweeds skim the surface of Horseshoe Pond in Concord on Aug. 27. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: ‘We are seen as disposable’: Rural residents fight a proposed gas pipeline
description: This story was produced by KFF Health News. CHATHAM COUNTY, N.C. — Despite being in one of the nation’s fastest-growing states, this rural county of roughly 85,000 people is still brimming with red foxes, coyotes, white-tailed deer, and wild turkeys. But in recent months, Enbridge Gas North Carolina’s proposed plans for a natural gas pipeline […]
text:
A 28-mile natural gas pipeline Enbridge Gas North Carolina has proposed for a rural stretch of Chatham County has prompted protests from small farmers and others. Some residents are worried the pipeline would fuel more of the population and business growth that is already threatening their way of life. (Photo: Fred Clasen-Kelly/KFF Health News)This story was produced by KFF Health News.
CHATHAM COUNTY, N.C. — Despite being in one of the nation’s fastest-growing states, this rural county of roughly 85,000 people is still brimming with red foxes, coyotes, white-tailed deer, and wild turkeys.
But in recent months, Enbridge Gas North Carolina’s proposed plans for a natural gas pipeline have exposed how population growth, here and across the nation, is driving a divide between wealthy newcomers and longtime residents.
Chatham has grown into one of North Carolina’s most affluent counties, fueled by an influx of new residents in its northeastern corner. Yet the pipeline would run from Moncure to Siler City, two communities where the per capita income is roughly $25,000 a year, or about half the income typical for the region.
And it’s raising familiar concerns. A 2020 report from the Chatham County Public Health Department stated that “unjust, unfair, and uneven distribution of social and economic resources” in the county, including exposure to environmental hazards, limited people’s “ability to achieve optimal health.”
In September, the Chatham County Board of Commissioners unanimously voted to oppose the project, saying that “protecting public health, safety, environmental resources, and private property rights remains a priority.” The resolution states that the proposed pipeline could affect areas occupied by vulnerable, low-income residents. Under state law, Enbridge could still attempt to take land through eminent domain, and low-income communities affected would have fewer resources available to fight back.
The state Department of Environmental Quality typically would review applications for permits to build a natural gas pipeline. That department has not yet received a permit application for the pipeline, said Onotse Omoyeni, senior press secretary for the office of Gov. Josh Stein. The North Carolina Utilities Commission declined to comment.
Enbridge says the 12-inch-diameter pipeline is needed to meet growing energy demands in the area, including Chatham, where the population has soared 21% since 2016, as well as neighboring Lee County.
Yet the proposed pipeline has set off protests at public meetings and attracted hundreds of people to a Facebook group to express their opposition, many of them small farmers, retirees, or their relatives. They argue the pipeline would pose an environmental threat to wells used for drinking water and expose people in less affluent areas to toxic pollutants that could increase the risks of cancer, preterm births, and asthma — all for the benefit of people who live nowhere near the proposed route.
“Nobody wants to be next to a pipeline,” Dorasue Burns Christian, a retired dental hygienist, told KFF Health News. She said the proposed route cuts across the roughly 22-acre farm where she has lived for more than 50 years. “I’m stressed and I can’t sleep at night. I have been pushed as far as I can be pushed.”
Enbridge Gas has promised to prioritize safety during the construction and operation of a proposed natural gas pipeline in Chatham County, N.C. But residents point to other communities in which Enbridge has operated where government reports say oil spills and a natural gas pipeline rupture led to evacuations, injuries, and at least one death. (Photo: Fred Clasen-Kelly/KFF Health News)
Enbridge Gas North Carolina is a subsidiary of the Canadian energy company Enbridge. Residents point to other communities in which Enbridge has operated — such as Marshall, Michigan; Romeoville, Illinois; and Danville, Kentucky — where oil spills and a natural gas pipeline rupture led to evacuations, injuries, and at least one death.
Enbridge declined an interview request to answer questions about the location of the North Carolina pipeline and the company’s safety record. In a statement, spokesperson Persida Montanez said the pipeline is needed to accommodate population and business growth in Chatham and neighboring Lee County.
A company website says safety will be prioritized during construction and operation, including monitoring, maintenance, and compliance with regulatory rules.
Many residents believe the company is attempting to profit from a proposed data center, which many also oppose. The company website says that Enbridge does not intend to use the pipeline for that purpose and that serving a data center would require a pipeline at least twice the size of the one planned for Chatham.
The pipeline would connect to existing natural gas infrastructure in Siler City and near Moncure, the company said.
Still, pipeline opponents say they are fed up.
“They chose this route because they probably thought people would not fight back,” said Amanda Clark, a protest organizer who grew up in Chatham. Her family roots in the county date to the 1700s. “In rural communities, we are seen as disposable.”
‘Collateral damage’
Chatham County’s fight comes amid a construction boom in the natural gas pipeline industry and the Trump administration’s promises of “American energy dominance.”
The U.S. produces more natural gas than any other country, about as much as China, Russia, and Iran combined.
Research shows natural gas pipeline leaks are concentrated in low-income and minority communities where people experience higher rates of poverty and physical disabilities and have fewer means to respond to crises.
Nationwide, there were nearly 2,600 pipeline incidents between 2010 and 2021 that were serious enough that they were required to be reported to the federal government, including fires and explosions that killed 122 people and injured more than 600.
In 2019, one person died and six were injured in Kentucky when an Enbridge natural gas pipeline ruptured, according to a federal government report.
Enbridge reached a $177 million settlement with the federal government after the 2010 oil spills in Michigan and Illinois. In the Michigan spill, a pipeline discharged 1 million gallons of oil into Talmadge Creek, in one of the largest inland oil spills in U.S. history.
More than 300 people attended a Chatham County Board of Commissioners meeting in Pittsboro, North Carolina, in early August, many wearing T-shirts to protest a proposed natural gas pipeline. Speakers said they feared the pipeline would pose an environmental threat to the community, including to farms, waterways, and wildlife. (Photo: Fred Clasen-Kelly/KFF Health News)
“No Pipeline. No Compromise,” read the red T-shirts worn by some of the more than 300 people who attended a Chatham County Board of Commissioners meeting in Pittsboro, North Carolina, in early August. Outside the building, they displayed signs that said “People NOT Pipelines” and “Save Our Farms.”
Under North Carolina law, private utilities and pipeline companies can obtain property easements, which give them the right of way to construct, operate, and maintain pipelines without outright taking ownership.
Enbridge will propose the final route for the pipeline based on field surveys, environmental studies, and engineering analysis, Montanez said. “The utility is also focused on delivering safe, reliable natural gas service that supports long-term economic vitality,” Montanez said.
Some residents, like Clark, argue that while the pipeline would power more housing and business development in wealthier parts of Chatham, it would create a public health risk in rural, poorer areas.
Clark, who works as the drug and injury prevention manager for the public health office in nearby Guilford County, said her great-grandparents were full-time farmers and passed down land near Siler City where her grandparents, dad, aunt, and cousin live.
Her grandfather retired from a hosiery mill and farmed part-time. He gave land to his children when they married, Clark said, because it was the only major asset he owned.
Clark said she is now in line to inherit land from her family and wants to protect the legacy of people who worked as farmers, mechanics, and schoolteachers from profit-taking by a company.
“We’re the collateral damage,” Clark said. “It makes people feel like they don’t have value.”
A class divide
Northern Chatham — which is an easy drive from major universities and Research Triangle Park, home to more than 250 companies — has seen a rush of newcomers.
Many have settled into places like Fearrington Village, a community with boutique shops, gardens, and homes that can cost nearly $1 million. Another master-planned community nearby, Chatham Park, is expected to bring up to tens of thousands of new residents over the next 20 years.
Not far outside the county’s borders are Chapel Hill, home to the University of North Carolina; the state capital of Raleigh, home to North Carolina State University; and Durham, home to Duke University.
As those places have grown more crowded, Chatham has become a cheaper alternative.
But prosperity is fleeting in many parts of the county. A quarter of residents are considered low-income, and on average there are 24 candidates for every job opening, according to a report released this year by the NC Budget and Tax Center.
Christian, an 85-year-old widow who lives a few miles south of Pittsboro, spends her days on her farm, raising hay and caring for chickens, birds, dogs, and cats. She has received letters from Enbridge saying the company wants to survey her property, where she lives with her 66-year-old son, who has a disability.
Christian said she needs money to care for her son and worries that she may one day need to move to a nursing home because of declining health. She said she has been diagnosed with macular degeneration, an eye disease that blurs straight-ahead vision, making it difficult to recognize faces or read.
She had planned to make ends meet by selling multiple parcels of land, but she said potential buyers backed out once they heard about the pipeline. At the Board of Commissioners meeting in August, she pleaded for local officials to try to stop Enbridge.
“They should be ashamed of themselves,” she told KFF Health News. “It’s disheartening. They are stealing from poor people.”
KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

name: National
title: Cornell case highlights the patchwork of state laws governing intoxication, sexual consent
description: A Cornell University student’s allegations of gang rape in 2024 have renewed attention on a difficult area of sexual assault law. A person can be awake, responsive and even able to move during a sexual encounter while still being so intoxicated or impaired that they cannot understand what is happening or make an informed decision […]
text:
The Chi Phi fraternity house at the center of a rape allegation stands on the campus of Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y. Nineteen states, including New York, limit mental incapacity under sexual assault law to cases of involuntary intoxication, such as being drugged against one’s will. (Photo by Ryan Murphy/Getty Images)A Cornell University student’s allegations of gang rape in 2024 have renewed attention on a difficult area of sexual assault law.
A person can be awake, responsive and even able to move during a sexual encounter while still being so intoxicated or impaired that they cannot understand what is happening or make an informed decision about sex.
But whether that person is considered legally incapable of consenting can depend on the state and, in some cases, on how the person became intoxicated. 
“There are a lot of very good laws on the books,” said Renée Williams, CEO of the National Center for Victims of Crime. “The problem is that nobody knows how to enforce them, including district attorneys, and enforcement varies from jurisdiction to jurisdiction, even within the same state.”
In New York, where Cornell is located, criminal law distinguishes between mental incapacitation caused by a substance administered without a person’s consent — such as being “roofied” — and other forms of intoxication. That can leave prosecutors relying on other provisions of the state’s sexual assault laws when someone voluntarily drinks alcohol or uses drugs and later becomes severely impaired.
More states are tracking rape kits. But key support for survivors may be slipping away.

The legal debate comes amid years of scrutiny over sexual assault and safety on college campuses, particularly around fraternity and sorority life, where alcohol and drugs are often part of the social environment. The Cornell case has brought those broader concerns back into focus while New York state lawmakers consider changes to the state’s sexual assault laws.
Across the country, sexual assault statutes vary in how they define incapacity, what level of impairment can make someone legally unable to consent and what prosecutors must prove about the accused person’s knowledge of the victim’s condition. 
Nineteen states, including New York, currently have statutes that limit the definition of mental incapacity in sexual assault law only to cases of involuntary intoxication, such as when someone is drugged against their will, according to experts. 
More than half of states also set time limits for prosecuting sexual assault. But those statutes of limitations vary by state and offense, and they can make prosecution more difficult when a case is reported years after an alleged assault, according to a review of state laws by NBC News.
Legislation on the issue has been before New York lawmakers for years, but the Cornell case has renewed attention on proposed changes to the state’s sexual assault laws. Two measures that passed the state Senate unanimously earlier this year would broaden how the law addresses intoxication and incapacity, and change the definition of “physically helpless.” 
The legislature has already adjourned for the year, but both measures were stalled in the Assembly after they failed to garner enough support for passage. Since the case came to light, the Assembly has formed a 15-member working group to examine the state’s sexual assault laws ahead of the 2027 session.
Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul, who has assigned the state’s attorney general to investigate the case independently, has said lawmakers could consider changes to state law early next year. . 
Some possible changes have drawn pushback from some criminal defense attorneys, including the New York State Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers, who have raised concerns about whether the proposed language would provide enough guidance about when someone is too intoxicated to legally consent. 
“Claims that a loophole exists are not supported by the law, and proposals based on that premise risk creating confusion while eroding fundamental due process protections and increasing the risk of wrongful convictions,” the organization said in an emailed statement to Stateline. 
What happened at Cornell
The allegations date to October 2024, when the young woman, identified in court documents as Jane Doe, was a student at Cornell. She alleged that she was sexually assaulted by members of the Chi Phi fraternity, naming seven men in connection with the incident.
She said in her lawsuit that she drank alcohol at a local bar, then felt pressured by two of the defendants to snort ketamine while at a party at the fraternity chapter house, and that it was her first time doing the drug. She also wrote that she was “plied” with marijuana and “Jamaican Liquor.”
All of the men have denied the allegations, according to hundreds of pages of confidential investigative files obtained by The New York Times. Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit in September naming the fraternity members, the fraternity, Cornell University, a local bar and her sorority, Tri Delta, as defendants. A Snapchat screenshot in the lawsuit shows a message to all Chi Phi fraternity members encouraging them to join the encounter.
Jane Doe reported the alleged assault to Cornell police in November 2024. In an interview with police, she described being severely intoxicated and said she was confident she had been raped. The subsequent criminal investigation did not result in charges.
Tompkins County, New York, District Attorney Matthew Van Houten has defended his office’s decision, saying the evidence available to prosecutors did not establish a prosecutable case under New York law, and that his office had not received the full transcript of the woman’s interview with police. The New York Times reported last week that a condensed version of the police statement sent to the DA’s office omitted that she reported being raped.
Under Cornell’s disciplinary process, two of the men were expelled, two suspended, two given lesser sanctions and one, a graduate, barred from campus. The Chi Phi fraternity chapter was closed in 2024.
But university proceedings and criminal prosecutions operate under different standards. For prosecutors, the issue is whether they can establish the elements of a specific sexual offense under New York’s criminal statutes.
That makes the state’s definitions of consent and incapacity central to the case.
Defining incapacity
The details of New York’s penal law offer a window into how seemingly narrow distinctions in legislative language can have significant implications for the outcome of a sexual assault case. 
The state’s criminal code identifies several circumstances in which a person is considered incapable of consenting to sexual activity.
One is physical helplessness. A person is physically helpless when they are unconscious or otherwise physically unable to communicate unwillingness to an act.
Another is mental incapacitation, which New York defines as being temporarily incapable of appraising or controlling one’s conduct because of an intoxicating substance administered without the person’s consent.
Those definitions can create challenges in cases involving intoxication. Erin Murphy, an expert on sexual assault laws and a law professor at New York University, said the physical-helplessness standard can be difficult to apply to someone who is severely intoxicated but still conscious.
“The failure to express unwillingness continuously means that they were not physically helpless,” Murphy said, describing current law. “Someone can kind of fall through the cracks.”
New York law also raises questions about what the person accused of the crime knew about the other person’s condition. And a defendant’s own intoxication can also be relevant.
One of the men accused in the Cornell case said he was “a victim of sexual misconduct” because Jane Doe had performed oral sex on him when he was “too incapacitated” to consent, according to the university’s investigative files obtained by The New York Times.
Voluntary intoxication
One of the most significant distinctions in New York’s law is that its definition of mental incapacitation only applies when an intoxicating substance was administered without the person’s consent, such as when someone is unknowingly drugged. 
That does not make sex with a voluntarily intoxicated person automatically legal. Other provisions of New York’s sexual assault laws address forcible compulsion and cases in which a person clearly expresses that they do not consent.
It’s hazing season on college campuses. State safeguards are uneven.

Still, the distinction has fueled what some lawmakers and victim advocates call a “voluntary intoxication loophole.” But others, including the New York State Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers, deny there is a loophole.
“Proposed legislation that would brand someone a rapist if their partner is voluntarily intoxicated and later claims a crime was committed because they were “incapable of appraising or controlling their conduct” is simply too vague to be fairly enforced,” the association said in an emailed statement.
Murphy said the challenge for lawmakers is drawing a line between someone who is intoxicated but still capable of making consensual decisions and someone whose impairment leaves them unable to consent.
“Any indication they were conscious or unwilling kind of works against them under physical helplessness,” Murphy said, referring to how New York’s laws are currently written.
That line can be particularly difficult to establish when a person has little or no memory of a sexual encounter. Alcohol, marijuana and ketamine — substances Jane Doe said she consumed before and during the alleged assault — can affect memory, judgment and perception. 
Prosecutors will likely have to rely on text messages, photographs, videos, witness accounts and other evidence to establish Jane Doe’s condition, Murphy said.
Dr. Chinmoy Gulrajani, a psychiatry professor at the University of Minnesota who has studied intoxication and consent laws across the U.S., said a person’s effort to reconstruct an incident afterward can also introduce another complication. Talking with friends or other witnesses about what happened may help fill gaps in memory, but those conversations can also influence how a person remembers or interprets the encounter, and, in turn, how they report it to authorities.
“To actually figure out what actually went down and what the exact facts were can be a challenge for the legal system,” Gulrajani said.
Because a person’s condition can change during an encounter, prosecutors and juries may have to assess the evidence moment by moment, including what the accused person knew about the other person’s condition.
Varied approaches across the states
New York is also not the only state wrestling with this issue.
A national comparison is complicated because states define consent, incapacity, intoxication and sexual offenses differently. Some statutes focus on whether the victim was “mentally incapacitated.” Others use terms such as “incapable,” “impaired” or “unable to resist.” Some expressly address intoxication, while others rely on broader definitions or case law.
Sexual assault survivors can now track their rape kits in most states

A 2022 research article published in the Journal of the American Academy of Psychiatry and the Law found significant variation among state statutes and cautioned that courts can interpret similarly worded laws differently.
In 2021, when the review of state statutes was conducted, 21 states appeared to limit mental incapacity to involuntary intoxication only — though two states, Michigan and Texas, have since changed their laws. 
Another 25 states now recognize incapacity from either voluntary or involuntary intoxication. And six states address the issue through case law rather than statutory language, according to the research article.
“Lawmakers need to understand that a person who is mentally incapacitated due to intoxication is a vulnerable person,” said Gulrajani, the Minnesota psychiatry professor and an author of the research article. “It does not matter whether they ingested the chemical of their own volition, or it was forced on them, or they were deceived into taking it.”
Minnesota changed its law in 2021 after its Supreme Court overturned a sexual misconduct conviction involving a victim who had voluntarily become intoxicated. 
The state legislature amended the law so that the victim’s intoxication could establish incapacity regardless of whether the alcohol or drugs had been voluntarily consumed. 
Michigan adopted similar language in 2023, following years of pressure to pursue other major legislative changes to better support survivors of sexual violence.
In Texas, lawmakers added a provision in 2025 that expressly defines as sexual assault a situation in which a person knows someone is so intoxicated or impaired by a substance that they are incapable of consenting.
Stateline reporter Amanda Watford can be reached at awatford@stateline.org.

title: All nine Indiana congressional seats are contested. Here’s who’s running.
description: All nine Indiana members of the U.S. House are defending their seats this fall, with challengers offering competing plans for healthcare, household costs and federal spending as voters help decide control of Congress. Seven Republicans and two Democrats are up for reelection under the same district boundaries lawmakers approved in 2021. The Indiana Senate re[...]
text:
Hoosier voters will help determine control of the U.S. House as they choose representatives in all nine congressional districts. (Photo by Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom)All nine Indiana members of the U.S. House are defending their seats this fall, with challengers offering competing plans for healthcare, household costs and federal spending as voters help decide control of Congress.
Seven Republicans and two Democrats are up for reelection under the same district boundaries lawmakers approved in 2021. The Indiana Senate rejected a proposed replacement map last December that was designed to help Republicans win all nine.
The general election pairs veteran lawmakers with challengers from local government, education, business and other professions.
Perhaps the most competitive of the contests is in the 5th district, where Democrat J.D. Ford is trying to move from the Indiana Senate to Congress. But he first has to get past GOP U.S. Rep. Victoria Spartz.
Early voting began Oct. 6. Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3, when polls will be open from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. local time. Voters can find their polling places and ballot information at IndianaVoters.in.gov.
Here is a look at each congressional race.
1st District: Mrvan faces Porter County commissioner Regnitz
Democratic U.S. Rep. Frank Mrvan faces Republican Barb Regnitz in Northwest Indiana, where Republicans are again seeking to capture one of the state’s two Democratic-held congressional seats.
Mrvan, a Hammond native and former North Township trustee, is seeking a fourth term. Regnitz is a Porter County commissioner whose professional background includes software engineering and financial planning. The National Republican Congressional Committee added her to its MAGA Majority program in July as part of an effort to support candidates aligned with Trump’s agenda.
Democratic U.S. Rep. Frank Mrvan, left, and Republican challenger Barb Regnitz are running for Indiana’s 1st Congressional District. (Courtesy photos)
Mrvan’s campaign platform emphasizes federal investment in the region, union jobs and reproductive rights. He supports putting the abortion protections of Roe v. Wade into federal law and points to infrastructure funding and Medicare prescription-drug price negotiations as parts of his record.
Regnitz’s platform calls for stronger border enforcement, reduced federal spending and debt, and greater support for law enforcement. She also proposes limiting mail-in ballots to rare, verified exceptions and using watermarked paper ballots for in-person voting.
The candidates offer different prescriptions for affordability: Mrvan emphasizes federal investment and healthcare savings, while Regnitz argues that spending restraint and curbing inflation would strengthen families’ purchasing power.
2nd District: Yakym draws Democratic and Libertarian challengers
Republican U.S. Rep. Rudy Yakym faces Democrat Jamee Decio and Libertarian William Henry in the north-central Indiana district that includes South Bend, Elkhart, Goshen and Warsaw.
Yakym has held the seat since 2022 and is seeking another term on a platform of limited government, lower taxes and reduced regulation. In a September social media post displayed on his campaign website, he highlighted border security and safe communities alongside keeping the House under Republican control.
“I firmly believe that government should be accountable, transparent, and focused on its core responsibilities,” his campaign website says.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates and tools you need to cast your vote.]
Decio is a South Bend lawyer and former Elkhart County deputy prosecutor. Her campaign emphasizes lowering everyday costs, protecting Medicaid and Social Security, and requiring data center developers to bear their own costs. She also supports local control and greater community input before those projects are built.
Henry, an Elkhart communications professional and military veteran, advocates reducing federal spending and regulation, improving veterans’ care and protecting medical privacy.
The region’s manufacturing economy is another concern. Decio has criticized tariffs’ effects on the recreational vehicle industry, while Henry supports workforce training and economic diversification to help communities weather downturns.
3rd District: Stutzman faces contractor Thompson
Republican U.S. Rep. Marlin Stutzman faces Democrat Kelly Thompson in northeast Indiana.
Stutzman, a farmer and business owner from Howe, returned to Congress after winning election in 2024. He previously served in the Indiana House and Senate and held the congressional seat before his unsuccessful 2016 U.S. Senate bid.
His campaign platform emphasizes reducing federal spending, strengthening border security, protecting gun rights and limiting federal involvement in education. He told the Capital Chronicle that small-business growth and limiting the reach of the federal government are among his priorities.
Thompson, a concrete contractor and nonprofit founder from North Webster, is campaigning on wages, housing, healthcare and government accountability. Her website calls for Medicare for All, a ban on stock trading by members of Congress and the president, and greater accountability for corporate polluters.
The candidates also divide over congressional boundaries. Stutzman told the Capital Chronicle he supports another redistricting effort. Thompson opposes it and argues that lawmakers should focus on delivering for their existing constituents.
4th District: Baird seeks fifth term against Purdue instructor Cox
Republican U.S. Rep. Jim Baird faces Democrat Drew Cox in west-central Indiana, including the Lafayette area, Crawfordsville and Greencastle.
Baird is seeking a fifth term after defeating state Rep. Craig Haggard and John Piper in the Republican primary. A farmer, small-business owner and Vietnam veteran, he previously served as a Putnam County commissioner and Indiana state representative.
In an April questionnaire published by Based in Lafayette, Baird identified lowering costs and securing the border as priorities. He proposed reducing federal spending and regulation, supporting energy independence and strengthening immigration enforcement.



Quotation







I’ll support policies that empower patients and providers while strengthening rural healthcare systems so families can access quality care close to home.


– Republican U.S. Rep. Jim Baird


On healthcare, Baird advocated competition, telehealth and fewer regulatory barriers.
“I’ll support policies that empower patients and providers while strengthening rural healthcare systems so families can access quality care close to home,” he told Based in Lafayette.
Cox is a Purdue University music instructor from Lafayette. His campaign emphasizes healthcare access, workers’ rights, veterans’ services and reducing the influence of money in politics. He says his campaign refuses corporate political action committee donations and supports overturning Citizens United, the Supreme Court decision that struck down restrictions on independent political spending by corporations and unions.
5th District: Spartz faces state Sen. J.D. Ford
Republican U.S. Rep. Victoria Spartz faces Democratic state Sen. J.D. Ford in a district stretching from Hamilton County’s suburbs to communities including Anderson, Muncie, Marion and Kokomo.
Spartz, first elected in 2020, is seeking a fourth term. Born in Ukraine, she worked in accounting and business before serving in the Indiana Senate. Ford has represented Senate District 29 since 2018 and became the General Assembly’s first openly gay member.
The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has designated it as a target district “in play” for the election, and the candidates have sparred over having a debate and television ads Spartz called inaccurate.
Republican U.S. Rep Victoria Spartz, left, speaks with Democratic state Sen. J.D. Ford following a news conference about flooding damage in Carmel, Indiana, on Aug. 31, 2026. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Both candidates emphasize healthcare costs and government accountability, but their platforms offer different approaches.
Spartz supports spending reductions to balance the federal budget, changes to legal immigration and work visas, and greater transparency and competition in healthcare.
“Our healthcare costs are unsustainable and destroying the middle class,” her campaign website says.
Ford’s platform calls for restoring and protecting Medicaid funding, preserving rural hospitals and protecting reproductive freedom. He also proposes restricting home purchases by large corporations and international investors, requiring data centers to cover their own water and utility expenses, and holding regular town halls.
The candidates were on opposite sides of last year’s redistricting fight. Spartz supported the effort, and Ford voted against it in the state Senate.
6th District: Shreve and Wirth meet again
Republican U.S. Rep. Jefferson Shreve faces Democrat Cynthia “Cinde” Wirth in a rematch of their 2024 election.
Shreve won that contest with 63.9% of the vote. He is seeking a second term representing the central and eastern Indiana district that includes communities south of Indianapolis and extends to Richmond.
Before Congress, Shreve built a self-storage business, served on the Indianapolis City-County Council and ran unsuccessfully for Indianapolis mayor in 2023.
His campaign priorities include affordability, border security, reduced government spending, infrastructure and support for farmers and small businesses. He also supports abortion restrictions and gun rights.
Wirth, a Columbus-based small-business owner, scientist and former high school teacher, is campaigning on stronger public education, affordable healthcare, environmental protection and support for working families.
Her website highlights her experience teaching biology and environmental science and serving as a congressional fellow. Her proposals include federal investment in childcare and addressing housing costs.
7th District: Carson faces McAuley and Sceniak
Democratic U.S. Rep. André Carson faces Republican Patrick McAuley and Libertarian James Sceniak in the Indianapolis-based district.
Carson, Indiana’s longest-serving current U.S. House member, has held the seat since winning a 2008 special election following the death of his grandmother, U.S. Rep. Julia Carson. He defeated three challengers in this year’s Democratic primary.
From left: Democratic U.S. Rep. André Carson, Republican Patrick McAuley and Libertarian James Sceniak, candidates for Indiana’s 7th Congressional District. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Indiana Capital Chronicle; provided photos)
Carson told the Capital Chronicle that affordability, infrastructure and equality are among his top priorities. He criticized Trump’s tariffs and cuts to Medicaid and food assistance, and pointed to his work securing transportation funding.
McAuley works in commercial real estate and previously interned for U.S. Sen. Todd Young. His campaign platform focuses on public safety, housing and homelessness, and career opportunities. He proposes expanding housing supply, returning vacant properties to productive use and increasing access to trades and apprenticeships.
Sceniak, a behavior therapist and previous Libertarian congressional candidate, told WFYI that his priorities include privacy protections, lower taxes and better veterans’ care. He supports giving veterans more choices within their health care system.
8th District: Messmer faces Evansville councilor Allen
Republican U.S. Rep. Mark Messmer faces Democrat Mary Allen in southwest Indiana, where Republicans have held the congressional seat since 2010. Although once known for close contests and changes in party control, the district is now reliably Republican.
Messmer is seeking a second term after moving to Congress from the Indiana Senate. He previously served in the Indiana House and was the Senate’s majority leader.
His campaign website emphasizes economic growth, individual liberties and constitutional protections, and presents him as a pro-Trump conservative. He is a small-business owner from Jasper.
Allen is an at-large Evansville City Council member, small-business owner and Army Reserve veteran who previously worked as an occupational therapist.
Her campaign platform calls for protecting and expanding Medicaid and Medicare, preserving rural hospitals, increasing affordable housing and reducing the cost of essential goods.
Allen also told the Capital Chronicle she wants to limit families’ childcare costs to 7% of their income.
“Nobody should lose their life because they can’t afford to see a doctor or don’t have a hospital in our county,” she said.
9th District: Houchin faces Meyer and Hudson
Republican U.S. Rep. Erin Houchin faces Democrat Brad Meyer and Libertarian Tonya Hudson in southern Indiana.
Houchin, a Salem resident and former state senator, is seeking a third term. Her campaign platform emphasizes border security, support for Israel, reduced federal spending, abortion restrictions and parental involvement in education.

Meyer is a Bloomington electronics engineer whose career includes manufacturing and civilian engineering work for the U.S. Navy. His campaign advocates Medicare for All, higher wages, stronger collective bargaining rights and lower housing and education costs.
Meyer told the Capital Chronicle he would propose making the first $20,000 in wages tax-free and expanding eligibility for overtime pay. He also identified protecting Social Security as a priority.
Hudson, a real estate broker from Mitchell, previously ran for Congress and lieutenant governor. Her platform calls for abolishing the Internal Revenue Service and moving toward a sales-tax-based system, balancing the federal budget and reducing regulatory burdens on businesses and farmers.
The district includes Bloomington and communities along the Ohio River, including New Albany. Houchin and her challengers are offering voters sharply different approaches to federal taxation, health care and the government’s role in household affordability.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Trust fall: ads for Kansas candidates address voters’ slumping faith in almost everything
description: I watched 52 Kansas campaign commercials today so that you don’t have to.  Actually, for the next few weeks you will still be watching them. Whether you want them or not, they will still be on during the nightly news, college football games and re-runs of “Everybody Loves Raymond.”  If I can’t do you the […]
text:
Campaign ads this Kansas political season have seized on our low-trust environment — both when promoting and attacking candidates. (Photo illustration by Eric Thomas for Kansas Reflector)I watched 52 Kansas campaign commercials today so that you don’t have to. 
Actually, for the next few weeks you will still be watching them. Whether you want them or not, they will still be on during the nightly news, college football games and re-runs of “Everybody Loves Raymond.” 
If I can’t do you the favor of vaporizing the ads from your channels, let me give you a new way to think about them.
Let’s divide them into two buckets. The division won’t be about Democrat vs. Republican or state vs. local. The distinction will be about trust, because trust seems like an essential political ingredient  this election. 
One variety of ads uses “real people” — or the appearance of people who appear to be ordinary Kansans, even if they are paid actors. These ads use nearly anonymous cardboard cutouts of folks because we have otherwise become so skeptical of everything except for the apolitical people around us.
The second bucket uses political celebrities to do the exact opposite: sow distrust and animosity. Through messages packed with Washington elites or well-known Kansans, campaigns and PACs are trying to tear down their opposition.   
To find the ads, I visited the Kansaspolitics YouTube channel, which has archived ads for state house, attorney general, governor and U.S. Senate races. Some gain trust in subtle ways, while others are screechingly obvious.
Most of the ads were standard fare. For 30 seconds, we hear a campaign, candidate or PAC argue for your vote. Usually, these ads would run on broadcast TV, but they likely appear on streaming platforms like YouTube. 
(The Kansaspolitics channel also documents a political phenomenon that was new to me. A few ads extended past two minutes, notably Adam Hamilton’s response to an attack from the right that was posted to the channel at the end of September. There was also a 3 minute 14 second ad titled “Protecting our Farmers from Data Centers.” Call them what you will. Ads? Mini-docs? Campaign announcements? Social media content?)  
 
The distrust election
At the end of last month, one national political reporter urged us to think about the 2026 election as the “distrust” election. Sabrina Tavernise of the New York Times described how American trust in institutions has meaningfully eroded. Backed by longstanding polling from Gallup, Tavernise argues that our slumping faith in many things — the medical system, banks and Congress — will steer election results in November. 

Combine that with our recent increased skepticism of national political candidates. Even loyally conservative Kansas has lost trust in President Trump, allowing a fall of 20 percentage points in his approval rating in the state as compared with his first term. 
When Kansas threatens to elect its first Democratic senator since 1932, Republicans are experiencing a once-in-a-lifetime crisis of trust. 
The idea of 2026 as a distrust election echoes through the ads I watched. While Tavernise hears distrust from the voters she met throughout the country, I saw it coloring Kansas political ads. 
 
The good stuff
With Americans reluctant to trust, how do you conjure positive feelings in a possible Kansas voter for a candidate? 
The answer, over and over again in the ads I watched, was surrounding the candidate with “real people.” When Americans trust few other things, we are left with, well, just folks. 
Gallup polling reaching back to 1973 shows we trust fewer institutions. The ones that we do trust are barely hanging on. Big business is favorable among only 8% of Democrats and 32% of Republicans. So, no use boasting of the fortune you, the candidate, made as a business person.
Only 13% of Democrats and 22% of Republicans trust the criminal justice system a great deal or quite a lot. Grab your resume and cross off your work as a lawyer, judge or prosecutor. 
Trust in organized labor has eroded to only 32% — and that is among Democrats. During the 1970s, a greater share of all Americans trusted labor unions than Democrats do now. No use appealing to union membership in your commercial. 
The church, banking, police and public schools are the same: Less than 30% of either Democrats or Republicans nationally trust those institutions. With that, a political campaign has few visual symbols they can use to build a candidate’s image. 
Nameless and often faceless people are the standard B-roll of almost every positive political advertisement. (The Kansaspolitics YouTube channel helpfully labels these as “pro-”, as in pro-Kris Kobach.) The goal is clearly to build trust with these anonymous, briefly seen maybe-Kansans.
A candidate walks and talks with a couple in their 60s. One sits down next to an older woman — seemingly clutching her property tax bill. Another candidate struts his way through a manufacturing business flanked by two normal guys dressed in red and blue. Over and over, candidates huddle with people who refer to candidates by their first names and who are meant to represent everyday Kansans.
Often, the locations are just as vital. The ads brag: “Our candidate finds real people everywhere!” At the library and walking the dog. At a backyard dinner table and at the playground. On their front porch and at the hospital. Downtown and on the farm.
Often, it’s the kitchen table as the epicenter of trust. The ads ask you to imagine how these candidates squirm their way past a Kansan’s front door only to sit at an empty kitchen table for a chat. No drinks. No snacks. No clutter at all. Who has a kitchen table so pristine? It’s an alien landscape, so staged and antiseptic, for most families. 
The other home interiors also suggest a family of orderly, wealthy, suburban Kansans who we can trust. Yes, even the couch behind Tricia Sinclair, a Republican candidate for the Kansas House, was uncannily reassuring. “You can trust my beige, overstuffed cushions and decorative throw pillow with a pattern of blue scrolls,” the couch said to me from the background. 
That’s when I realized, “Wait. I have seen that trustworthy couch before!”

It was also sitting behind GOP House candidate Alex Bergman in his ad. And those downright respectable folks talking to Bergman in the front yard of his ad? They were also chatting with Sinclair in her ad. The kitchen table chat? Bergman and Sinclair were talking to the same couple at the same kitchen table in their two different ads. 
So much for “real people” developing trust. 
Sometimes, campaigns took the extraordinary steps of choosing people because they actually are connected to an institution. The workplaces chosen as locations for a few ads suggest small businesses. Gallup polling suggests such businesses are a smart electoral choice in terms of building trust. No other institution — not even the military — had higher cumulative trust ratings than small businesses.
Adam Hamilton’s campaign took a riskier swing in this way. They chose doctors for a recent campaign testimonial. In addition to endorsing Hamilton, the physicians in the ad remind voters of both the medical system and higher education, both of which are seen as overwhelmingly untrustworthy by Americans. (Democrats and Republicans trust the medical system at a rate of only 26% and 30%, respectively. Higher education has only 23% support from Republicans.) 
Even so, the message was an effective roast of Roger Marshall’s aggressive handling of his patients’ medical bills, as reported recently. Sometimes you need to ignore the numbers and bow to the political narrative.
The masterclass in rallying the visual of “real people” for a positive message comes from the campaign of Cindy Holscher, who is the Democratic candidate for governor. In 33 seconds, we see Holscher with Kansans in what believably appear to be candid, informal situations. Who knows, maybe they actually were!
Fourteen different shots feature Holscher in a meeting, a brewery and a gymnasium, always smiling, always listening and even dishing out a few hugs. Cultivating trust looks natural for Holscher, and that’s the point.
 
Art of darkness
The counterpoint ads bring bleakness. 
Conventional political wisdom apparently says that injuring the image of an opponent is as simple as associating him or her with distrust. And what is less trusted than Congress? (Spoiler alert: nothing.)
Gallup reports that the least-trusted American institution of all those they polled is Congress. I can’t even describe my embarrassment, on behalf of journalism, that newspapers and television news are only a few cumulative percentage points higher.
Nevertheless, Congress resides in the basement with less than 15% of all Americans, whether Republicans, independents or Democrats, trusting it a great deal or quite a lot. The distrust of national politicians becomes a cudgel against your opponent.
Attack ads exploit this by showing a rival candidate next to the most extreme personalities in Congress. In one ad, resembling a deranged art project, Adam Hamilton’s face is combined with one Democratic leader after another: Hillary Clinton, Kamala Harris and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. “Two-Faced,” the ad concludes. “Too Extreme For Kansas.” It’s blunt — if bluntly untrue — but likely effective for some voters swayed by hinting at Hamilton’s associations with “extremists” and “radicals.”
To drain humanity from your rivals and their alleged political allies, the producers of the commercials de-saturate every Congressional or political face we are meant to loathe. This dark and gritty styling, when combined with selecting the least flattering moment possible, makes people look sinister.
An ad for Democratic Attorney General candidate Chris Mann does exactly this to his opponent Kris Kobach. Curiously, an ad supporting Kobach gives his image — along with a family walking down the street — the same bleak, stylized treatment. 
Trump’s approval rating has slumped recently, and he was absent from every ad I reviewed from the past few weeks. This is despite the “presidency” being the most trusted branch of the federal government, according to the Gallup polling. Republicans likely see him as a liability when persuading Kansans for the general election. Democrats seem reluctant to use him as a weapon in ads because of lingering, if reduced, statewide support among conservatives.   
Standing out from the herd of ads this week was a 30-second ad for Don Coover, a Democrat running against Derek Schmidt for the US House of Representatives. His ad pokes Schmidt without all of the overprocessed gloom and darkened images of his rival. 
Instead, standing in front of cattle, Coover repeatedly almost says, “Bull****” before being interrupted by a cow’s moo. “Protecting DC insiders? That’s just bull…” 
Moooo. (Even the cow knows how little trust Americans have in Congress.)
Clicking through these 52 ads, I found either menacing attacks on Congressional trust or polished candidates with real people. During the last few weeks of campaigning before the mid-term election, there will likely be few ads in between. 
In other words, there will be little viewers can trust.
