name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Terrebonne tackles removal of hundreds of sunken boats from its bayous
description: Parish officials are working to clear the castaway and derelict vessels from the bayous to improve environmental and safety conditions on the water.
text:
Abandoned boats sit in Bayou Petit Caillou in Terrebonne Parish, Louisiana. The Parish was granted a portion of National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration funds to remove boats that sank and became environmental and safety hazards. (Photo by Elise Plunk/Louisiana Illuminator)Along the twisting network of bayous in Terrebonne Parish lie hundreds of boats, many of them submerged in hurricanes, others accidentally run aground or simply abandoned. Several vessels have sat for years with no one and no money available to move them.
But now parish officials, aided by federal funding via a national boater safety nonprofit, are working to clear the castaway and derelict vessels from the bayous to improve environmental and safety conditions on the water. 
Terrebonne Parish was one of 10 locales the BoatUS Foundation picked in 2023 to receive grants funded by National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration to remove sunken boats from coastal waterways. The parish matched the $1 million award with its own money. 
Noah Lirette, Terrebonne Parish chief administrative officer, said the derelict vessel removal campaign started last year. To date, he said the parish has pulled out about 100 vessels from Terrebonne bayous during the campaign, expecting to remove about 134 vessels in all. 
“Hopefully we can remove more as other people pull out their boats that belong to them and we can extend those dollars,” he added.
Crews remove an abandoned boat that sank in Bayou Petit Caillou in Terrebonne Parish, Louisiana. (Photo by Elise Plunk/Louisiana Illuminator)
In 2024, the parish identified 232 sunken or ditched vessels that needed to be removed, said Lirette. Many sank during Hurricane Ida, a category 4 storm that hit Louisiana in August 2021 and caused $75 billion in damage, according to the NOAA. 
“A lot of people abandoned them. We had a problem we had to deal with,” Lirette said, adding that many people who dealt with damage from Ida have moved away permanently.
Abandoned watercraft have become a problem across the country, according to the BoatUS Foundation. The mass production of recreational boats with fiberglass hulls has made it easier and cheaper to own a boat, but it has also increased the number that need to be disposed of. 
“There are more boats coming to end of life now and, unlike the old wooden boats, fiberglass doesn’t just deteriorate and go away or go back into nature,” said Alanna Keating, director of outreach for the BoatUS Foundation. “It is continuing to sustain in the environment, and so the disposal of it becomes more challenging.”
Abandoned and derelict boats pose an array of hazards, including environmental and boating safety concerns. 
“It does leach out paints and chemicals and things like that when it’s just sitting there for years and years,” Keating said. “But beyond that, they can become a navigational hazard, especially in places … where there’s not a large channel for boats to go and pass.”
In Chauvin, where two boats were extracted from the bayou Tuesday, Lirette said “a ton of commercial fishermen” traverse the bayou daily to go work.
“They need to be safe for those guys,” he said.
Sunken boat removals can be expensive. While every job is different, Keating said the cost to extract a 25-foot vessel averages around $25,000. The longer an abandoned boat sits untouched, the more expensive it is to remove, she said.
“It’s not like picking up tires on a beach or a waterway cleanup,” she said. “These need barges and cranes and lift bags and licensed captains and divers and really specialized skills and equipment and knowledge to be able to do this.”
Keating said the remains of the abandoned boats are being disposed of at a landfill.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Chris Murphy says he was denied access to largest US military base in Middle East
description: During a multi-day trip to the Middle East, U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy said he was denied entry to the largest U.S. military base in the region.
text:
U.S. Senator Chris Murphy (D-CT) is back from spending several days in the Middle East.
While on the trip, he was denied entry to the largest U.S. military base in the region — and blamed Department of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
“There is an active cover-up going on right now,” Murphy said. “It is absolutely ordinary for members of Congress to travel to areas of conflict and get to talk directly to the military leaders and the soldiers that are involved in the conflict, and see for ourselves the damage that has been done to our bases and equipment.”
The third-term Senator cited past trips to active war zones, including Afghanistan and Iraq.
In a statement, a Senior Department of War official told WSHU that Murphy had been told he would be denied access before he left for the trip.
“Senator Murphy’s office was informed before his trip to the Middle East that he would not receive Department of War support to access Al Udeid Air Base, consistent with the Secretary of War’s directive on travel restrictions in the region ordered on March 3, 2026,” the official said. “That decision was communicated in advance by the Office of the Secretary of War for Legislative Affairs. The Department applies the Secretary’s guidance evenly.”
In a press briefing on Thursday, Murphy reaffirmed the Pentagon’s statement: he had been told before his travels that he would not have access to the base. However, he said, he left the U.S. under the impression that he may have been able to receive a briefing from military officials during the trip.
No such briefing was provided.
Murphy claims he is the first Senate Democrat to travel to the region since the war in Iran started. He met with leaders in Qatar and Saudi Arabia, conversations he described as difficult but productive.
They included talk about business deals between the country’s leaders and the Trump administration and family.
“I told the Qataris that no matter how much pressure they got from Donald Trump to gift that plane, they should have said no, because it is obvious what’s happening here: the plane is going to be in U.S. hands for a matter of years, and then Trump is going to take it with him,” Murphy said. “Knowing that this was a corrupt deal, the Qataris should have said no.”
“I also spoke very candidly to Mohammed bin Salman, told him that his investments in Jared Kushner’s private equity fund and his invitation to Trump and his business entities to partner on projects in Saudi Arabia was an enormous problem for the U.S.-Saudi relationship in the long run,” he continued.
Murphy is a member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.
This story was first published Oct. 8, 2026 by WSHU.

name: VTDigger
title: Universal primary care is at the center of the race for governor. How would it work?
description:
Democratic challenger Amanda Janoo has proposed an income tax on the wealthiest Vermonters to fund primary and preventive care for all state residents. The idea has been met with support, skepticism and questions.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Universal primary care is at the center of the race for governor. How would it work?.
text:
Hospital staff tend to a patient on a gurney. Photo via Adobe Stock

Proposals for universal primary care have become a central platform point in the race for Vermont’s top state office. 
The Democratic candidates for governor and lieutenant governor, Amanda Janoo and Molly Gray, tout free publicly funded primary care as their chief healthcare policy proposal leading into the Nov. 3 general election. 
Proponents of the policy say it can reduce costs by keeping people healthier in the first place, while skeptics worry it does not target the most expensive parts of healthcare and bring true affordability. 
Republican Gov. Phil Scott “supports the concept of universal access to primary care,” said Emma Shouldice, a representative for his reelection campaign. She noted that the incumbent signed a bill into law in June that would commission an exploratory report on the feasibility of universal primary care. Scott is “committed to exploring the details” of that report, she said. 
“We should be very clear, though, there is no such thing as ‘free’ healthcare,” Shouldice added, “and campaign promises that offer as much should be met with the highest level of scrutiny.”
Scott has advanced a largely deregulatory view of health insurance, to allow for age-varying premiums and plans for small businesses. He advocates working directly with hospitals to lower healthcare costs and wants to move away from relying on regulators to maintain healthcare affordability. 
The momentum that universal primary care proposals, and the candidates who support it, have gained underscores just how hungry Vermonters are to tackle healthcare affordability, said Alex Garlick, a professor of health policy at the University of Vermont. 
He thinks Vermonters are tired of incremental progress in curbing hospital costs and keeping insurance premiums from rising too steeply. At the same time, Scott “has not been proactive” on healthcare issues, he said, instead vetoing a bill that would have capped hospital prices for certain insurers this year.
“I think Amanda Janoo’s success in the Democratic primary over the summer shows there might be an appetite for newer, bolder ideas,” Garlick said. 
“But,” he continued, “I am not convinced that this particular idea would have a major return on investment that would justify raising taxes and increasing spending on healthcare.” 
So how would universal primary care work?
Higher taxes for some, care for all
Janoo proposes levying a “fair share tax” on the income of the wealthiest Vermonters in order to build a network of small-town primary care doctors across the state and pave the way toward eventual full universal healthcare.
Proposals for a tax on high earners estimate that Vermont could raise between $114 million and $344 million in annual revenue. Janoo has supported these proposals and said she hopes her administration could bring finer granularity and analysis to determining this figure to fund a universal primary care program if she’s elected. But she says the basic principle is “ensuring that no matter what, everybody has access to a primary care provider that they’re able to see for free.”
Janoo hopes to finance local community health teams, modeled after the municipally run and funded community nursing programs in the Upper Valley, where nurses are public employees.
Janoo estimates that by increasing free access to primary care providers, mental health professionals and other local healthcare coordinators, Vermonters can reduce emergency room visits and more expensive hospitalizations enough to save the state up to $300 million a year. 
But she acknowledges that it’s a rough estimate intended to gauge whether an ambitious plan for primary care would be feasible and financeable. She is open, she said, to exploring an array of options for funding the program, knowing that Vermont could raise a significant portion of revenue to fund this through an income tax, like the one on wealthy Vermonters that she advocates.
“The point for me was less like ‘it has to be funded by this specific revenue stream’ as much as I wanted to feel confident, if I was going to come out and advocate for a policy, that it was going to be something we could realistically pay for,” Janoo said. 
She called her current calculation of the revenue and cost of a universal primary care proposal a “sense check.” It’s important, she said, that it fundamentally shifts the state’s primary care away from a fee-for-service model to one where primary care providers are paid to keep people healthy, whether that’s through a salary or other types of per-patient, per-month payments.
In 2015, on the heels of then-Gov. Peter Shumlin’s failed effort for single-payer healthcare across Vermont, state analysts estimated how much it would cost to roll out a universal primary care program.
Those authors set an understanding of universal primary care as publicly financed primary care for all Vermonters, regardless of their insurance coverage. They estimated that, by 2017, universal primary care could cost the state $281.9 million in annual claims — if patients paid nothing out of pocket to share the cost of care — plus $12.2 million to $34.7 million in administrative costs. They figured that Medicaid, which is jointly funded by the state and federal governments, could pay nearly $107.4 million of those claims, with a special waiver to reroute federal Medicaid funds for primary care into this type of program.
But a decade after that report, Janoo thinks Vermont can cover the cost with a new income tax — and avoid requesting a Medicaid waiver for now.
Still, she wants an even more refined picture of how many primary care doctors or nurses or physician assistants Vermont needs to care for the entire population. To fully understand the cost requires combining that estimate with an estimate of the annual salaries for those doctors and nurses, she said. Would that include relocation incentives for rural pockets of the state? Would it also take student loan repayments into account? 
As governor, Janoo hopes she could leverage the state government’s analytical arm to find answers.  
“When I first started, there was hesitancy to talk about anything related to universal healthcare because there was some PTSD, I think, from the Shumlin administration,” she said.
But the climate has changed since 2014, Janoo and fellow advocates said.
Things are “fundamentally different now,” said Dr. Jack Mayer, a retired primary care provider and staunch advocate for universal primary care. “At that time, our hospitals were not facing bankruptcy, and our primary care system was not collapsing, and our costs were not going through the roof. Now what’s different is that every Vermonter is appreciating the personal impact that the decline of our healthcare system is having on their personal finances.” 
Starting with primary care
Mayer is now part of a group of citizen activists calling for universal primary care in Vermont who go by the name the “Little Seeds,” but he said he has been advocating for universal care since he was a medical student 50 years ago. This moment is “as close as we’ve ever gotten” to having real legislation for publicly funded health care, he said. 
He’s not alone in feeling like this year could be different: An Oct. 6 poll from the health policy group KFF found national support for a publicly funded healthcare program is the highest it’s been in the 10 years since the group started polling on the topic, with 66% of people favoring some kind of Medicare for all.
Across the U.S., midterm elections in states like Michigan, New York and Washington have similarly revived the question of state-sponsored, single-payer healthcare. 
It makes sense, to Mayer, to start with publicly funded primary care. The cost of investing in preventive care — a pill for hypertension, say — is low compared with the cost of hospital care that it can avert, such as a trip to the emergency room for a stroke. 
Also, having the state pay a set amount for primary care could be important for expanding access to rural areas.
As a young pediatrician, Mayer worked in a clinic near the Canadian border, in the rural Franklin County town of Enosburg Falls. Nearly all of his patients were uninsured or on Medicaid — which generally pays less than the cost of care, and most clinicians make up the difference by charging more from commercial insurers. 
“It’s unsustainable,” Mayer said of practicing in places like Enosburg Falls today. “Any young physician who wants to go into primary care will look at that and say it’s impossible.”
Advocates say a statewide budget could allocate funds evenly for primary care practices to remain solvent, regardless of its patient population’s insurance.
Mayer is open to the flexibility that Janoo’s proposals allow. To him, even having a high-profile candidate call for these proposals is an amazing first step.
“We need to let 1,000 flowers bloom here. We need to get lots of ideas about how we could implement this system,” he said. 
Too little or just right?
Some others say that not thinking big or broadly enough could risk leaving behind some of the most vulnerable Vermonters.
Dr. Elizabeth Hunt, a primary care physician with Timber Lane Pediatrics in Burlington, who ran for state Senate this summer, worries about specialty care becoming a luxury if Vermont transitions to universal primary care without considering how people will afford costly other care. She said cash-strapped Vermonters might drop their insurance, banking on the fact that they could access primary care without it, and then be left high and dry when they need expensive care. 
“How do we handle their catastrophic coverage if any Vermonter gets cancer or is in a terrible accident?” she said. “The costs are enormous and unforeseen, and I would be concerned that more and more people would go without.”
Garlick, the UVM professor, is skeptical about how much return on investment tackling just primary care — instead of the much bigger slices of the healthcare spending pie, like hospital care or pharmaceuticals — might yield.  
He drew parallels between the call for universal primary care and Vermont’s faltered attempt at running an accountable care organization in the wake of proposals for a single-payer model. The accountable care organization paid providers fixed amounts per patient, regardless of how much care the patient received, as a way to incentivize keeping patients healthy. Still, when the rest of the healthcare system relied on a fee-for-service model, all the preventive care in the world did not change the fact that eventually and inevitably people would need costly medications, emergency room visits or hospital care, Garlick said. There is little evidence that Vermont’s accountable care organization contained healthcare costs at all. 
“When I think about cost containment, I think there are two ways to do it,” Garlick said. “You can reduce the number of services that are consumed, or you can reduce the price of those services. (Universal primary care) would get at the number of services, reduce utilization by making people healthier, but I have not seen a lot of evidence that that would then lead to markedly fewer expensive specialist visits or emergency room visits.”
To others, the fact that primary care is a small slice of the pie is exactly the point. Ethan Parke has been a citizen advocate for universal healthcare for decades, since he worked as an independent dairy farmer trying to figure out ways to insure his family, he said.
One reason, among many, that he thinks Shumlin’s plan for wider universal care folded in 2014 was that it would cause “too much economic dislocation all at once.” 
“Why not bite off a smaller piece?” he asked. “Primary care is so much smaller, and it pays the biggest dividend in terms of disease prevention, early detection, fewer trips to the emergency room, fewer appointments with specialists. You can catch things early; people are up to date on their immunizations; they’re getting regular checkups.” 
Still, Parke worries that the scale of an undertaking like this might be too big for Vermont’s citizen Legislature to wrap its arms around in the short, monthslong clip of a legislative session. 
He hopes the state can follow the example of Oregon, where in 2023 the Legislature created a panel tasked with envisioning a plan for state-funded healthcare for every resident. Lawmakers are expected to vote on that plan in the coming legislative session or put it to a ballot vote in 2028, according to reporting from KFF Health News.   
In Vermont, an analogous outside panel could dig into the questions that Janoo has raised — on payment mechanisms, funding, delivery type and quality assurance metrics.
But regardless of who is elected to the governor’s office in November, Vermont is on track to have yet another state analysis of universal primary care, along these lines. The primary care bill that Scott signed into law in June established the Legislature’s intent to establish a program of universal primary care. It tasked the state treasurer’s office and the Agency of Human Services with working with other Northeastern states to figure out how to establish a universal primary care program across the region. Their report is due to the Legislature by mid-January. 
To Parke, as long as the basic principles remain, Vermont is on the right track: “To really achieve the savings, you have to get rid of private insurance with all its administrative cost and profit seeking. You really have to have public financing. You really have to cover everybody. If you do that, you can make it affordable and you can make it high quality.”

title: Invasive freshwater jellyfish found near Canyon Ferry Reservoir
description: The Treasure State is being invaded by aquatic jellyfish from parts unknown, and while Montana Fish, Wildlife and Parks said they’re not dangerous, it’s an introduced species, not native to the state. “It’s not something we’re really alarmed about,” said Tom Woolf, who coordinates FWP’s  Aquatic Invasive Program. “It’s an awareness kind of thing. They […]
text:
A freshwater jellyfish captured in Montana. (Montana FWP photo)The Treasure State is being invaded by aquatic jellyfish from parts unknown, and while Montana Fish, Wildlife and Parks said they’re not dangerous, it’s an introduced species, not native to the state.
“It’s not something we’re really alarmed about,” said Tom Woolf, who coordinates FWP’s  Aquatic Invasive Program. “It’s an awareness kind of thing. They don’t harm people or anything, and their impacts on the environment appear to be small, but they’re not a desirable thing.”
The jellyfish, Craspedacusta sowerbii, known as “a common freshwater jellyfish,” was discovered in a pond near Canyon Ferry Reservoir this summer by Vivi Veitch, a 10-year old who reported the sighting to her dad, according to the FWP. The father then called FWP, which sent a team to find the jellyfish.
Invasive plants and animals can have a wide range of impacts on the state lands and waters, ranging from incredibly bad to relatively harmless. The jellyfish fall into a relatively harmless category, but since they’ve been introduced, they can’t easily be removed and now essentially join the ecosystem.
“I thought I was seeing lots of plastic, so I tried to pick it up because you don’t want plastic in the lake,” Veitch told FWP. “But it was really hard to pick up because it was slimy.”
The common freshwater jellyfish is native to the Yangtze River area of China and is now found in most states across the U.S. The first time it was ever noted outside of China was in England in 1880, according to FWP documents. The same species was noted 17 years ago in Montana, at a pond at an abandoned golf course near Great Falls.
It’s tiny and spends most of its life attached to underwater surfaces in microscopic polyps that go dormant in the winter. The free-floating (medusa) phase of its life cycle is only around for a short time in the summer. 
Montana Fish, Wildlife and Parks documents following the initial discovery say the average size of those collected in 2009 were about 29 mm across (or, a little bigger than one inch). Freshwater jellyfish feed on zooplankton, an important foundational component of aquatic food webs on which other creatures also depend.
Officials say it’s unclear how the jellyfish got there, and could have been moved in a variety of ways. 
Woolf said they’re common in the Midwest, and could have entered via a boat, but can also live in ornamental potted plants and occasionally get in scuba gear as well.
There’s a reason one of FWP’s main public advertising campaigns is “Clean, Drain, Dry” —  aquatic species can attach themselves to boats, floats, tubes, inflatable kayaks and paddleboards, as well as any other item that touches the water. And FWP needs the public’s help both to prevent the spread of invasive species — and reporting them when they see them.
“If you see something strange, report it, so we can verify it,” Woolf said. “If it was something like an invasive plant or invasive crayfish or something like that, there’s a potential for us to get in and do a response. If the population is small and we detect it early enough with some of these species, we can go in and take them out.”
Montana has boat checks throughout the state and officials say anyone, even if their paddleboard or float is folded up in their car, is legally required to stop for an inspection. All out-of-state boats are also required to stop for inspection.
FWP and contracted staff have performed 114,000 inspections so far this year at 17 watercraft inspection stations, Woolf said. They’ve intercepted 600 boats carrying weeds this year, 31 stops that found either zebra or quagga mussels, and more than 1,000 inspections that found boats with standing water in them.
A picture of a sailing boat on Canyon Ferry Reservoir on Jan. 15, 2026. (Courtesy photo)
One of the biggest worries is zebra and quagga mussels, which can cause algae blooms, take food from native species and can clog water and hydroelectric systems.
Both quagga and zebra mussels are found throughout the eastern and midwestern U.S. Quagga mussels have been creeping closer to Montana and are present in California, Arizona, Nevada, Utah and Idaho. There have been detections of mussel larvae in two Montana reservoirs, but the state responded, and Montana is still considered free of both mussels.
There’s also additional worries about a newer invasive species, golden mussels, which is native to eastern Asia.
Collaboration between government agencies, tribal governments, and the public is incredibly important to tackle invasive species issues, Woolf said. The issue has also led to the creation of the Montana Invasive Species Council, which recently turned 10 years old and has a biennial summit, which this year will run from Nov. 4-5 in Helena at the Heritage Center.
The positions on that council are appointed by the governor and cover a wide range of stakeholders and invasive species, which also includes insects, weeds and feral hogs.
“The cost of more effective prevention, detection, response, and mitigation will not be insignificant,” the MISC’s website says. “But if we were to fail, the costs would be many times greater: Enormous economic damage, unending costs of mitigation, and most of all, the priceless destruction of the natural and cultural heritage entrusted to us.”

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont school districts scramble to cover the increased cost of diesel
description:
Typical school buses run on diesel fuel. With prices at the pump remaining steadily high since September, districts are considering how to come up with the extra money.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont school districts scramble to cover the increased cost of diesel.
text:
School buses line up to drop off students at the Allen Brook School in Williston in September 2020. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

With diesel prices hitting record highs, Vermont school districts are taking on unexpected costs to bus students to school. The spike is forcing districts to consider cutting other spending or tapping their reserves.
Champlain Valley School District expects to spend $200,000 over its budget on diesel fuel if prices remain at current levels, according to Meghan Metzler, chair of the district’s school board. 
The district is spending about $40,000 a month on diesel, she said, up 60% from what it spent on average last year. 
Champlain Valley owns and operates about 60 buses, meaning district officials are immediately confronting the increased costs. Districts that outsource their busing anticipate added costs in the future, but haven’t yet felt the effects. 
Lamoille North Supervisory Union faces that added layer of uncertainty. It contracts with a local transportation agency to run 11 buses. The supervisory union enrolls about 1,600 kids from Belvidere, Cambridge, Eden, Hyde Park, Johnson and Waterville. 
In its busing contract, the supervisory union pays a set price for fuel, plus a surcharge if fuel rises above $4.33 a gallon, according to Deborah Clark, the supervisory union’s business manager. Costs have clearly surpassed that amount, Clark noted. 
“It’s too early in the year to see how big of an impact this is going to be,” Clark said. 
If the price of diesel holds steady throughout the school year, the district would be looking at spending an extra $41,000 to $42,000 in fuel costs, Clark said. Any unbudgeted costs will be difficult for the supervisory union to manage, and it’s going to have to adjust other spending accordingly, she said. 
“Where those shifts will come from? We don’t know yet,” Clark said.  
Retail diesel prices have remained steadily high since hitting a national record of $6.53 per gallon late last month. Districts often pay a lower price for diesel than what’s at the pump, but they’re still seeing unusually costly fuel. The increase is driven by the U.S. and Israel’s war against Iran and by Ukraine’s attacks against Russian oil refineries, which have made less diesel available on the global market. 
“Diesel fuel is only one of many costs that have gone up,” Champlain Valley’s Metzler said, citing healthcare and food prices as well. The district enrolls about 3,600 kids from Charlotte, Hinesburg, St. George, Shelburne and Williston. 
District administrators are closely tracking the district’s finances and could decide to freeze spending later on, Metzler said. The district also has reserve funds, where it has set aside money that went unspent in previous budget years, she added. 
“It is something that we could go into if we need to, but obviously we prefer not to,” she said. 
Meanwhile, Otter Valley School District — which has about 1,100 students from Brandon, Goshen, Leicester, Pittsford, Sudbury and Whiting — is in an unusually fortunate position. 
The district operates about 30 of its own buses and has its own diesel storage tanks, according to Laurie Bertrand, the district’s school board chair. At the end of the previous fiscal year, the district used some extra funds to buy up diesel before the price skyrocketed, she said. 
Since buying diesel months ago, the district hasn’t needed to refill its supply, meaning it’s been able to stay sheltered from rising fuel costs, according to Bertrand. But when it does have to buy again, it expects to pay 50%-75% more than it budgeted, she said. 
“If the price remains that high, we’re going to have to look at other places to cut in order to not go over budget overall,” Bertrand said. 
President Donald Trump issued an executive order Monday that aims to lower costs by suspending federal enforcement of taxes for the on-road use of red-dyed diesel, which is usually reserved for agriculture and construction.
However, Vermont fuel taxes still apply to the use of red-dyed diesel for most vehicles on public roads. The federal order doesn’t change states’ laws, only encourages them to follow suit. 
Amanda Wheeler, Gov. Phil Scott’s press secretary, said in an email Tuesday that the governor was working to understand the recent order. 
“The Governor is always looking for ways to lower costs for Vermonters, but we will want to understand what the change means, as well as any unintended consequences, to make sure the good outweighs the bad,” Wheeler said.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont school districts scramble to cover the increased cost of diesel.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: DMV review confirms Rhode Island voter registration safeguards
description: Rhode Islanders can’t be offered the opportunity to register to vote at the state’s Division of Motor Vehicles (DMV) unless they first provide proof of citizenship, a review of Rhode Island’s voter registration procedures has found. Both Secretary of State Gregg Amore and House Minority Leader Mike Chippendale confirmed the results this week, two months […]
text:
A review of Rhode Island’s motor voter system found noncitizens can’t access registration. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)Rhode Islanders can’t be offered the opportunity to register to vote at the state’s Division of Motor Vehicles (DMV) unless they first provide proof of citizenship, a review of Rhode Island’s voter registration procedures has found.
Both Secretary of State Gregg Amore and House Minority Leader Mike Chippendale confirmed the results this week, two months after they met with DMV and Board of Elections officials to review the motor voter registration system which relies on the same software vendor responsible for a glitch in New Jersey revealed in July that led to 6,600 noncitizens being registered to vote.
“The DMV’s conclusions, as well as our participation in a systems review alongside the Minority leaders of the House and Senate, affirmed that only individuals who present the appropriate citizenship documentation at the DMV are offered the opportunity to register to vote,” Amore said in a statement Wednesday to Rhode Island Current.
Amore on July 24 requested that the DMV audit its records covering the first two years of the state’s contract with Idemia Identity & Security USA LLC. At the time, Amore said the review was intended to help maintain Rhode Islanders’ trust after a malfunction at New Jersey’s Motor Vehicle Commission mistakenly registered noncitizens to vote when they applied for driver’s licenses and identification cards between June 2023 and June 2024.
Amore requests DMV audit after New Jersey mistakenly registered noncitizens to vote

Chippendale, a Foster Republican, called for an independent audit of the state’s voter rolls the same day.
Idemia has been a Rhode Island DMV vendor for credentialing and software services since June 2002, with a number of extensions and amendments since then, the latest through June 2027.
Amore’s audit request covered 2017 to 2019, the first two years of the DMV’s motor voter transaction system after the state adopted automatic voter registration. Since 2019, the DMV has conducted a regular audit of a randomized selection of driver records to ensure that database entries match paper records.
Two weeks after Amore’s request, on Aug. 7, the Democratic secretary of state met with Republican House and Senate leaders at the DMV’s Cranston headquarters, where DMV and elections officials presented how the system prevents people who identify as noncitizens from registering to vote.
Chippendale described the meeting as a relief in this midterm year.
“The way that our system operates, it simply isn’t possible for anyone who clicks ‘non-citizen’ to even access the voter registration portion of the system,” he said in a statement Thursday. “That’s a strong safeguard.”
But the meeting raised a separate issue for Chippendale: that the DMV’s system does not distinguish Driver Privilege Cards (DPC), which noncitizens can obtain, from standard driver’s licenses. 
“Even more concerning, is that once an individual leaves the DMV – not even the DMV can distinguish between the DPC and a real Driver’s License,” he said. “There is no record kept of DPCs issued – they simply mix in with all the Driver’s Licenses in the system.”
Chippendale said he later learned the Rhode Island Board of Elections gets a separate list of Driver Privilege Card recipients and checks it against voter records after elections.
“What was concerning to me, was that this was the first time I was hearing of this,” he said.
Chippendale, who is running unopposed for an eighth term representing House District 40, said he plans to introduce legislation next year aimed at strengthening safeguards and penalties for people who cast ballots despite being ineligible to vote.
A spokesperson for Idemia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Rick Scott makes the case for Byron Donalds as poll shows him tied with David Jolly
description: LARGO — When it comes to winning close statewide elections, no one has been more successful in Florida than Rick Scott. The senior Republican U.S. senator won three straight contests for governor and senator in the 2010s by a single percentage point before enjoying a rare blow-out reelection victory by 13 points two years ago. […]
text:
Florida Republican U.S. Sen. Rick Scott speaking in Largo on Oct. 8, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix).LARGO — When it comes to winning close statewide elections, no one has been more successful in Florida than Rick Scott.
The senior Republican U.S. senator won three straight contests for governor and senator in the 2010s by a single percentage point before enjoying a rare blow-out reelection victory by 13 points two years ago.
Scott appeared Thursday with GOP gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds in Pinellas County. He urged the crowd to vote as soon as possible, just as a new public opinion survey showed Donalds in a dead heat with Democrat David Jolly.
“If you have your mail-in ballot, get it in today. You know why? Because this campaign has to spend money to make sure you get your mail-in ballot in. The earlier you vote, they’re going to stop bugging with all of those texts and the phone calls. And you’re going to save them money, the campaign money,” Scott said at Veterans Metal, a finishing and manufacturing company  in Largo.
A St. Pete Polls survey of the governor’s race released Thursday of 836 likely Florida voters shows the race in a statistical tie with Donalds at 44.7% and Jolly at 44.6%. The survey has a margin for error of +/- 3.4%.
That’s in contrast to an NBC6/Telemundo Station Group poll of 625 registered Florida voters conducted by Mason-Dixon Polling & Strategy released Wednesday that shows Donalds up 48%-41% over Jolly, with 1% supporting an independent candidate and 10% undecided. The margin for error with that poll was +/- 4%.
 The Black vote
Two campaign ads for Donalds have been airing this week touting his endorsements by Donald Trump and Gov. Ron DeSantis. But he modulated that partisan pitch Thursday, saying his message is for all Floridians.
“As a Republican, so much is made about, ‘Oh, these Republicans, they only care about big business,” he said. “In Florida, we know that there is no economy without our environment. You have to protect the environment if you’re going to have a viable economy. The two work together.”
He pivoted to saying he had recently spoken with a reporter who asked him why he was working so hard to court Black voters.
“I said, ‘Typically, Republican campaigns don’t do the amount of work we’ve been doing talking to Black voters,” he said. “Honestly, most political consultants are only concerned about getting the candidate to 50% plus one, because 50% plus one is all you need to win the seat. But I’m not interested in 50% plus one. I’m interested in 100%.”
The Jolly campaign began the day by announcing former North Florida Democratic U.S. House member and state lawmaker Al Lawson has announced his support for Jolly. Lawson was the first Black politician since Reconstruction to win a North Florida legislative seat in a predominantly white district when he was elected to the Florida House in 1982.
“I’m proud to support David Jolly for Governor because David believes everyone who works hard deserves more than a daily struggle to survive. They deserve a home they can afford and a fair chance to build a better life,” Lawson said in a press release.
“And to those who in the Black community who think Byron Donalds has changed, don’t fall for it,” he added.
Lawson called on Black voters to look closely at Donalds’ voting record before casting their ballots, noting that he voted against the John Lewis Voting Rights Act and called the recent U.S. Supreme Court ruling undoing a section of the Voting Rights Act a ‘major win.’”
“Byron Donalds is one of Donald Trump’s biggest sycophants, and there is no daylight between the two,” Lawson said. “Let’s be clear — if you support Byron Donalds, you support Donald Trump.”
If elected, Donalds would make history as the first Black Republican elected governor in the United States. Three Black Democratic governors have been elected — Doug Wilder, Deval Patrick, and Wes Moore).

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming lawmakers take steps to further restrict online gaming
description:
Select Committee on Gaming advances proposed ban on online sweepstakes games. 
The post Wyoming lawmakers take steps to further restrict online gaming appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Facing another record-breaking year for money wagered at Wyoming gaming establishments, lawmakers are mulling new measures to regulate the industry. 
In a unanimous vote this week, lawmakers on Wyoming’s Select Committee on Gaming sponsored draft legislation that would ban online sweepstakes games — drawings where prizes are awarded purely by chance. Under the proposed bill, operating online sweepstakes games would become a felony offense. 
Currently, state law bars online casinos, although online sports wagering and participation in fantasy sports contests is legal in the state. The law isn’t as clear when it comes to online sweepstakes. And regulators face confusion as to what entity — Wyoming’s Consumer Protection and Antitrust Unit or the Wyoming Gaming Commission — should handle complaints arising from such games. Consumer protection is tasked with protecting consumers by enforcing the state’s Consumer Protection Act, while the Wyoming Gaming Commission deals with gaming laws. 
When consumer protection gets complaints about online sweepstakes, “they look at it as gambling,” Nicholas Larramendy, who heads the Wyoming Gaming Commission, explained to lawmakers. 
“They give it to us. We look at it. Then we get the argument that this is under consumer protection,” Larramendy said. The gaming commission then sends it back to consumer protection, creating a “constant cycle.”
“So this bill definitely makes it very clear that this is illegal gambling,” Larramendy concluded.  
Online sweepstakes games are often designed to look like online casinos, which has led to some of the confusion. “Online casinos and online sweepstakes can look almost identical when you play them online,” explained former Republican state Senator Affie Ellis, a Cheyenne-based attorney representing Bally’s Corporation, which recently took majority ownership of a Cheyenne horsetrack and has plans to open gaming facilities in the city. “They look like maybe the same slot machine, same blackjack table, same jackpot animations, but they are two fundamentally different products.”
Whereas online casinos take real money and pay out cash, online sweepstakes are free to play and currently are legally treated as promotional advertising under Wyoming’s Consumer Protection Act. 
Some argued that online sweepstakes should remain legal. “This is over broad and it does conflict with the idea that a sweepstakes in connection with a purchase of a good or service is currently valid in Wyoming and should remain valid in Wyoming,” Bill Gantz, an attorney for VGW, a gaming company, said. Although entering a sweepstakes can be connected to a purchase, under federal law, people must be given what’s called an “alternative method of entry” — a way to enter the sweepstakes without making a purchase. 
Gantz noted that VGW has been operating online sweepstakes games in Wyoming since 2012. 
“If this language were adopted, Wyoming would be virtually the only state that I can think of that would not allow a free entry to be used in a game that is resulting in the award of a prize,” he said. 
Gambling activity has risen precipitously in Wyoming over the last decade. Last year, about $2.7 billion were wagered in Wyoming across all forms of legalized gambling, according to Larramendy. He said 2026 is shaping up to be another record-breaking year, exceeding $3 billion in wagers. 
That proliferation has drawn the attention of lawmakers, who have taken steps to strengthen regulations around the industry. In 2025, the state formed a legislative task force — the Select Committee on Gaming — to address gaming issues in the state. 
In addition to the proposed measure to ban online sweepstakes games, lawmakers sponsored legislation to update fingerprinting requirements for certain people regulated by the Wyoming Gaming Commission.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas measles cases grow to five; community transmission not seen
description: TOPEKA — Five measles cases reported in Kansas are related to out-of-state travel, health authorities said Thursday. “As of right now, we are not seeing the larger community transmission we saw back in 2025, but we will refrain from venturing a guess as to whether that will change,” said Kansas Department of Health and Environment […]
text:
Measles, which was considered eradicated more than 25 years ago, continues to reappear across the United States. Kansas is reporting five measles cases, all associated with out-of-state travel. This is a three-dimensional representation of the measles virus particle. (Photo by Alissa Eckert/Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)TOPEKA — Five measles cases reported in Kansas are related to out-of-state travel, health authorities said Thursday.
“As of right now, we are not seeing the larger community transmission we saw back in 2025, but we will refrain from venturing a guess as to whether that will change,” said Kansas Department of Health and Environment spokesman Preston Webb in an email.
The state’s Infectious Disease Dashboard is updated on Wednesdays, and cases rose from two last week to five. 
Last year, the state experienced measles outbreaks, many associated with unvaccinated individuals and communities where vaccination rates decreased.
“The best way to protect individuals and communities from measles outbreaks is through vaccination,” Webb said. “We encourage everyone to talk to their local health department or other trusted healthcare providers about any questions they may have about the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine.”
As of Oct. 1, 3,887 confirmed measles cases were reported in the United States in 2026, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama officials urge residents to prepare as Hurricane Isaias nears
description: Montgomery officials and members of Alabama’s congressional delegation urged residents Thursday to be prepared for Hurricane Isaias, expected to bring heavy rain, strong winds and the threat of tornadoes. Mandatory evacuation orders are in place for the west end of Dauphin Island in Mobile County. Gov. Kay Ivey Thursday ordered all visitors south of the […]
text:
Montgomery Mayor Steve Reed and U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures speak about Hurricane Isaias on Thursday, Oct. 8 in Montgomery, Alabama. The storm is expected to make landfall in Mobile late on Friday. Officials urged residents to prepare for the severe weather and to continuously monitor notices for updates. (Ralph Chapoco/Alabama Reflector)Montgomery officials and members of Alabama’s congressional delegation urged residents Thursday to be prepared for Hurricane Isaias, expected to bring heavy rain, strong winds and the threat of tornadoes.
Mandatory evacuation orders are in place for the west end of Dauphin Island in Mobile County. Gov. Kay Ivey Thursday ordered all visitors south of the Gulf Intracoastal Waterway – on Dauphin Island in Mobile County and Gulf Shores and Orange Beach in Baldwin County – to evacuate immediately.
“We often hear in emergency management: Hope for the best. Prepare for the worst,” Ivey said in a message. “That is the approach we need with this particular storm system.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Voluntary evacuations were set for Baldwin County residents who live in flood prone or low-lying areas.
Montgomery Mayor Steven Reed and U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Mobile, pleaded with residents during a news conference to not only gather supplies and fully charge their cell phones before the arrival of the storm but to also closely monitor city and county notices.
“There are lots of ways to receive emergency warnings,” Reed said. “Every household needs more than one way to receive weather warnings. That is very, very important.”
He directed people to enable weather alerts on their cell phones and to continuously watch the television and radio for any updates on the severe weather.
Both Reed and Figures also recommended people limit their driving, to check on older adults who need assistance receiving emergency notifications, and to have an emergency plan that is understood by members of the household.
Emergency management officials said at the news conference that they have been monitoring the developing severe weather since Monday. As of Thursday morning, Isaias was classified as a Category 1 hurricane, according to the National Weather Service in Birmingham. It is situated just off the coast of the Yucatan Peninsula and was characterized as a fast-moving system headed northeast.
“The latest forecast calls for it to continue to be a hurricane as it approaches the Alabama and west Florida portions of the central Gulf Coast Friday, probably making landfall Friday night and into the day Saturday,” said Jason Holmes, meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Birmingham.
Isaias is expected to be downgraded from a hurricane to a tropical storm when it reaches central Alabama. The storm is expected to travel west of Selma with tropical storm-force winds that will be more than 39 mph. Later Saturday, the weather system will be in northwest Alabama, the Florence and Muscle Shoals area, before it moves on to Tennessee Saturday evening and into Sunday.
“It is typical with tropical systems making landfall, there is a tornado risk generally on the east side of the tropical system,” Holmes said. “With this track into the western portion of the state, it is going to put much of the central and eastern portion of the state at risk for tornado activity in those bands.”
Montgomery Emergency Management Agency Director Wade Lyles said the city is opening a tornado shelter at 360 Williams Drive, but it is unclear when it will open.
Ivey declared a state of emergency for 40 counties in south and central Alabama. She announced Thursday that state offices in Baldwin, Coffee, Covington, Dale, Escambia, Geneva, Henry, Houston and Mobile counties will close at noon on Friday.
Figures said at the news conference that his office has prewritten a declaration disaster request in case it is needed once a survey of the storm damage is complete.
“First and foremost, we want everyone to remain safe,” Figures said. “This is not meant to serve as any sort of overexaggeration of what is about to come. What is coming is a Category 2 hurricane. With it will come wind, will come rain, the potential for flooding and for tornadoes as well.”
The University of Alabama said in a statement Thursday afternoon that Saturday evening’s football game against Georgia was still scheduled, but will only allow uncovered tailgating after noon on Saturday and moved ESPN’s “College Game Day” by ESPN into Coleman Coliseum. President Donald Trump is expected to attend the game.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan Supreme Court hears arguments in discrimination case involving former Calvin professor
description: The Michigan Supreme Court heard oral arguments Thursday in a case where a former Calvin University professor, Joseph Kuilema, alleges that he was the subject of associational discrimination when he was fired in 2022 after officiating a wedding for a same-sex couple. The Supreme Court will rule on whether that associational discrimination claim — the […]
text:
Michigan Supreme Court Justices Kimberly Thomas and Elizabeth Welch listen to oral arguments on Oct. 8, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)The Michigan Supreme Court heard oral arguments Thursday in a case where a former Calvin University professor, Joseph Kuilema, alleges that he was the subject of associational discrimination when he was fired in 2022 after officiating a wedding for a same-sex couple. The Supreme Court will rule on whether that associational discrimination claim — the fact that he was fired over his association with LGBTQ+ individuals — can proceed in a trial court.
Charissa Huang, Kuilema’s lawyer, argued to the justices that court precedent on associational discrimination on the grounds of sex discrimination “would ask not whether Joe was fired because he’s a man, but whether he was fired because of the sexes of the people in the wedding. This claim is not clearly unenforceable.”
For Huang, the question in front of the court is broader than just Kuilema’s case — she argued to the justices that, if a prior Court of Appeals ruling stand, it will “misdirect courts across the state and leave people who are discriminated against because of a protected characteristic without recourse.” 
“Allowing this Court of Appeals holding to stand that it must be because of the plaintiff’s own sex, that would have a chilling effect upon people of different races and cultures and sexism, sexual orientations, they could be fired for associating with one another with no recourse,” Huang said.
Charissa Huang, a lawyer representing Joseph Kuilema in his associational discrimination claims against Calvin University, presents at oral arguments at the Michigan Supreme Court on Oct. 8, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)
The Court of Appeals, in its ruling that Kuilema appealed, argued that, because the decision to fire Kuilema had no bearing on his own sex — it would have been the same if he were a woman or a man — his argument of associational discrimination is invalid. 
“Kuilema’s sex is irrelevant to Calvin University’s decision to terminate his employment. The university’s decision to terminate his employment was based upon his decision to officiate a same-sex wedding,” the appellate court’s decision read. “Based upon the allegations in the complaint, the discriminatory action would have occurred regardless of Kuilema’s sex.”
Huang, however, argued that the appellate court misinterpreted the intention of Michigan’s Elliott-Larsen Civil Rights Act, and that though it does not explicitly include discrimination of associates of people of a protected class, it does implicitly include those associations.
“The Court of Appeals read a limitation into the Elliott-Larsen Civil Rights Act that the Legislature never wrote, in holding that associational discrimination must be because of the plaintiff’s own sex. That holding contradicts the act’s plain language and its purpose. ‘An employer shall not discharge an individual because of sex.’ That language is unambiguous, and it should be enforced as written. Calvin University fired Joe Kuilema because he officiated a wedding for an LGBTQ couple.”
Stephen J. Vanstempvoort, the attorney for Calvin University, disagreed about that interpretation of the state’s civil rights law. 
“I think the plain text of the statute is actually pretty clear that it has to be the individual who’s experiencing discrimination,” he said. “It has to be their protected characteristic that’s at issue.”
Vanstempvoort also said that, because the individuals in the wedding officiated by Kuilema were not directly harmed by Calvin’s action to fire Kuilema, then court precedent involving race-based associational discrimination should not apply in this case.
“If a plaintiff says, well, somebody else experienced illegality, and then I suffered damages as a result, well, then that plaintiff has a claim under the plain text of the statute, right? So that’s how Miller works. But that’s not what the claim is here,” he said, referring to Miller v. Michigan Department of Corrections, a 2024 court case. 
Stephen J. Vanstempvoort, a lawyer representing Calvin University, presents at oral arguments at the Michigan Supreme Court on Oct. 8, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)
In response to questions from Chief Justice Megan Cavanagh, who asked if performing an LGBTQ+ marriage is different than other hypothetical claims, based on the fact that sexual orientation is a protected characteristic in Michigan’s civil rights law, Vanstempvoort said that distinction would be difficult to only protect association with groups deemed “inclusive.”
“Having an anti-discrimination statute hinge upon ideology, I think, is very problematic from a First Amendment perspective. But second, I think, in practical terms, it may be very difficult to implement,” he said. “For example, consider somebody who opposes or who disapproves of affirmative action, like a race-based affirmative action program. I don’t know what camp that falls in.”
Huang noted that any discrimination in that hypothetical would be viewpoint discrimination. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“The questions that were asked about viewpoint discrimination really helped to clarify that this is not about viewpoint discrimination,” Huang said after arguments concluded. “In fact, Joe expressed all kinds of viewpoints throughout his career at Calvin for many, many years, and he was not fired for those viewpoints. He was fired after he officiated the wedding for these people, his friends.”
Kuilema, now a professor at Grand Valley State University, sued his former employer for both retaliation and associational discrimination under Michigan’s Elliot-Larsen Civil Rights Act.
He told Michigan Advance after the oral arguments, “I was encouraged by the justices’ questions. I think we made our case effectively and persuasively, and I think this is an area that’s been clarified around issues of race, and it’s just time to clarify what it means for issues related to sex. It’s high time that the court does that.”
Kuilema and Huang both said that they were glad to continue fighting a case that they said will “clarify some aspects of the law that will benefit a lot of people, especially LGBTQ people, but lots of other people too,” Kuilema said.
“We wouldn’t even be here if this couple had been a heterosexual couple,” Huang said in her final remarks during oral arguments.

title: Florida taking next step against Instagram after rejecting nationwide settlement
