The motion for temporary injunction is part of larger, nationwide legal wrangling between state attorneys general and Meta, the company that owns […]
text:
The parent company of Instagram and Facebook agreed to settle a nearly nationwide lawsuit by paying up to $17.1 billion and implementing safety features on its platforms to protect children. Florida wants additional concessions. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)Florida’s attorney general is asking Facebook and Instagram to tighten their platforms to deny access to its “addictive features” for children, as the state pressed it legal battle against the tech giant Meta.
The motion for temporary injunction is part of larger, nationwide legal wrangling between state attorneys general and Meta, the company that owns the two social media platforms. 
Florida and New Mexico were the two states that did not join an otherwise nationwide, $18 billion settlement earlier this year with Meta in response to allegations the company intentionally created and profited from developing for young users “addictive features” like infinite scrolling, persistent notifications, and like-counts on posts.
“Sources ranging from the United States Surgeon General to lawsuits to independent studies to Meta’s own research demonstrate that Meta caused Young Users extensive harm, including anxiety, depression, self-harm, sleep deprivation, eating disorders, exposure to unwanted sexual advances, and tragically, suicide,” Uthmeier argued in an 85-page motion filed Wednesday.
The document is part of a case the state filed in Pasco County Circuit Court against Meta. 
“Meta engages in unconscionable acts by prioritizing its own growth over the safety of the vulnerable Young Users it targets,” Uthmeier wrote, invoking the argument that started the national action against Meta.
Uthmeier was not satisfied with the settlement other states took, which he said “does not go far enough to protect children from the consequences of Meta’s deceptions and exposure to the products designed to addict them.”
Meta to pay 47 states up to $17.1B in landmark child safety settlement

The state seeks three things in the temporary injunction: “prohibit Meta from making further deceptive statements and omissions in Florida;” require Meta to verify ages and remove users under 14 years old; and eliminate addictive aspects of the platforms.
“There is no end in sight to the harm Meta has caused Florida’s children,” the motion says.
Uthmeier pointed to a case in New Mexico that resulted in Meta imposing restrictions on its apps for minor account holders. The New Mexico case shows Meta can “protect Florida’s children through changes Meta has already shown are feasible.”
New Mexico Department of Justice rests case in second phase of Meta child safety lawsuit

In 2024, Florida passed a law prohibiting children under 13 from using social media and 13- to 15-year-olds from using platforms without parental consent. Specifically, the law banned use of platforms with the “addictive features” listed above.
That law went through an extensive federal challenge brought by a group of social media companies.
Uthmeier said in November he would “aggressively enforce” the social media ban for minors after the preliminary injunction on the law is lifted. 
He filed suit against Tik Tok in St. Lucie County Court for not complying with the law earlier this year.  
In 2023, former Attorney General Ashley Moody joined the federal suit that claims Meta deployed features that encourage kids to spend more time on the apps and that it violated Florida’s Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act. 
“Meta has told Congress and the public repeatedly that children under 13 are not allowed on Instagram or Facebook — that it does not market to them, that it screens for them, and that it removes their accounts,”  Uthmeier’s motion argues.
“Behind the scenes Meta’s documents say the opposite: ‘We lack a U13 classifier, insufficient means to detect and remove u13s at scale,’” it claims. 
Uthmeier cites various statistics about how Instagram has harmed young people and alleges Meta has turned a blind eye to problems created by its products. 
He called for Meta to make the changes in Florida that it made in New Mexico and to be prohibited from targeting young people with advertisements about Instagram and Facebook. 
The state believes Meta should be required to report to the court its progress in implementing these changes. 
Florida wants a “quiet mode” that blocks use of anything but settings in the app between 9 p.m. and 8 a.m.
New Mexico imposed a monthly limit of 90 hours of use across Facebook and Instagram. Florida wants 60. 
Meta did not respond to a request for comment before publishing deadline but issued a written statement to Politico.
“This agreement won’t succeed until our industry peers join us. We know that restricting one platform simply causes teens to migrate to others. The Attorney General should be using taxpayer resources to get YouTube and TikTok to empower parents and protect teens in Florida,” it reads.
“We regret that he has chosen instead to pursue a meritless preliminary injunction years into the litigation. The state cannot both claim the benefits of a settlement Florida declined to join while continuing to sue us.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: ‘We are in the new nuclear age.’ Swisher and Lack meet in Jackson to discuss the future of AI
description: Kara Swisher and Andrew Lack discuss artificial intelligence during the "All In On Mississippi" summit at the Two Mississippi Museums in Jackson on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
The impacts of artificial intelligence are, in many ways, contingent on the decisions of a small, powerful group of tech elites, but ordinary people have a central role to play in demanding reasonable regulation of the technology, Kara Swisher told Andrew Lack on Thursday.   
“We are in the new nuclear age, and you need to understand what that means,” Swisher told a crowd at the Two Mississippi Museums in Jackson at Mississippi Today’s 10th Anniversary Celebration. “And demand that your public officials do their job.”
Lack, a journalist and media executive, and Swisher, one of the nation’s most prominent technology journalists, delved into how AI could reshape the world. Lack is the executive chairman and founder of Mississippi Today and Deep South Today and the former chairman and CEO of NBC News. Swisher hosts the podcasts “On with Kara Swisher” and “Pivot”
The talk came at a time when the rapid rise of AI has ignited both excitement and concern around the globe about the ripple effects of the fast-advancing technology across society. In the American news industry, outlets of every size are working to make sense of what AI will mean for the journalism they produce, their business models and their relationships with the public. 
Swisher cut her teeth covering the technology industry — for outlets such as The Washington Post, The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times and Vox — as it came to dominate nearly every aspect of American life. During that time, she developed relationships with many of the world’s most powerful tech titans, including Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, Sam Altman, Sergey Brin and Dario Amodei.
She has since fallen out with many of them, most notably Musk. The world’s richest man and President Donald Trump mega donor has called her an “asshole.” Swisher, for her part, has called Musk a “one-man wrecking ball” and a “professional adult toddler.”
Back when they were on speaking terms, Swisher said on Thursday, Musk was an early figure to raise the alarm about the potential risks of AI. 
But he has since raced to join the AI arms race and, along with his competitors, has thrown caution to the wind, Swisher said. That is why it’s important to remember that AI is not yet a technology with a life of its own, but one with humans at the helm.
“The tool is not the problem, and one of the ways it’s being pushed by tech people is, you know, there’s a 10% chance AI will kill the human race,” Swisher said. “Actually, it’s not AI that will kill the human race. It’s the people making AI that will kill the human race, and so we take the technology and blame the technology instead of blaming the person.”
In Mississippi and nearby states, the proliferation of data centers, including those pushed by Musk, has stirred a wave of private investment and public backlash. 
Tech leaders, Swisher said, are running “into a buzzsaw of anger,” necessitating more public input into how AI is regulated. But these same tech leaders have poured money into the political apparatus of Trump, who has returned the favor by vowing to avoid regulating AI, she added.
Swisher and Lack have ridden the tides of a changing media landscape over their careers, but AI might present more potential to disrupt the news industry than any technology in history.
Lack quoted an Axios report on a shadowy political polling firm that warned of the rise of an “AI-enabled flood of outright fabricated content” that is “wreaking havoc on reality, poisoning the signals that most people rely on to understand just basic politics, business, and culture.” 
Despite the threats and challenges posed by AI, Swisher said, it was still important to remain optimistic about the positive potential of the technology, such as in medical research, while staying clear-eyed about its risks if left unregulated. 
“The deli on my corner has more regulation than a tech company,” Swisher said. 
The discussion served as the keynote session at the “All In on Mississippi” summit, an event hosted by Mississippi Today featuring conversations about the forces shaping Mississippi’s future. The summit event is the second of a two-day event celebrating Mississippi Today’s first decade of reporting.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: State, CSX agree to rail upgrades in the Berkshires
authors: Colin A. Young I State House News Service
description: MassDOT has agreed to fund improvements and additions that would support permanent seasonal weekend Berkshire Flyer service and lay the groundwork for expanded passenger rail in Western Mass.
text:
AN AGREEMENT STRUCK between the Department of Transportation and railroad company CSX will reduce conflicts between freight trains and the state’s desire to further expand passenger rail service in the Berkshires, the Healey administration said Thursday.
MassDOT has agreed to fund construction of a new siding and other track improvements around Pittsfield to increase rail capacity, and to consider the feasibility of a new platform at Pittsfield Station, work the governor’s office said “will provide the infrastructure needed to support permanent seasonal weekend Berkshire Flyer service and lay additional groundwork for expanded passenger rail in Western Massachusetts.” CSX owns the tracks and MassDOT says the work will benefit freight as well as passenger trains, but the administration did not specify what CSX committed to under the agreement.
The Berkshire Flyer service has operated summer weekend passenger rail service between Pittsfield and New York City since 2022. Amtrak runs the trains, supported by MassDOT. At the same time, the state has been inching toward expanding passenger service from Boston, through Worcester, Springfield, and Pittsfield to Albany, New York, via the long-discussed East-West Rail project. All are part of the state’s “Compass Rail” vision for intercity passenger rail throughout Massachusetts.
“The Berkshire Flyer has already shown what better transportation connections can mean for a region — more visitors, stronger local businesses and another reliable option for residents,” Lt. Gov. Kim Driscoll said. “Now we’re taking the next step by making the infrastructure investments needed to sustain this service for the long term while continuing to move our broader passenger rail vision forward for Western Massachusetts.”
Pittsfield Mayor Peter Marchetti said the rail connection to New York City is “an important asset” for his city. But MassDOT says the service’s “on-time performance has been hampered by conflicts with freight trains,” and notes that there are long stretches of single track on the CSX-owned corridor between Albany and Pittsfield.
MassDOT included $31 million for the Pittsfield track capacity project in its most recent capital plan. A year ago, the department said its planning showed “that adding a 3-mile siding track (second track for passing trains) in Richmond near the Pittsfield border and a new track switch in Pittsfield would bring operational benefits by increasing corridor capacity.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Ladapo: Eliminating vaccine mandates isn’t about science, it’s about parents’ rights
description: Florida State Surgeon General Joseph Ladapo is a well-known vaccine skeptic. But on Thursday he said the state’s drive to change its rules to eliminate four vaccines children are required to take to enter school or daycare centers has nothing to do with science or the efficacy of the vaccines. It is about putting parents […]
text:
Gov. Ron DeSantis speaks at a press conference in Orlando on June 3, 2022. Florida Surgeon General Joe Ladapo stands behind him. (Photo via DeSantis Facebook page)Florida State Surgeon General Joseph Ladapo is a well-known vaccine skeptic.
But on Thursday he said the state’s drive to change its rules to eliminate four vaccines children are required to take to enter school or daycare centers has nothing to do with science or the efficacy of the vaccines.
It is about putting parents in charge of their children’s healthcare.
“You know, this isn’t about the scientific effectiveness of one vaccine or the other, the safety of one vaccine or the other,” Ladapo told a crowd attending a rule workshop in Lake Mary. The DOH, he said, is “open to hearing about that.”
But he said the pursuit of public health “cannot supersede the right of a parent to make a decision about what’s best for their child. Period. It’s not complicated. It’s very simple in that respect. Those are very important concerns.”
Eimear Roy, a parent and self-described healthcare community advocate from Orange County who suffers from long-term COVID, disagreed.
“So, I’d really love the Department of Health to be about health. Health is not intuition. Health is not parent rights. I’ve seen parent rights, parent right movement. The parent rights, my rights as a parent, do not exceed the rights of other humans to exist,” she said. 
“And this is fundamentally it. No one wants to take away the choice. Every parent should decide for their child about vaccines, but what you can’t decide is my right to exist,” she said.
She testified that once vaccines are eliminated insurance companies will no longer cover them and poor people with health problems who are uninsured or don’t qualify for Medicaid would be placed at greater risk.
“So, absolutely, the choice is the parents.’ But with that choice comes the effect, and the effect is maybe then you can’t go to public school,” she said.
DOH authority
Florida law requires children at a minimum to be immunized for poliomyelitis, diphtheria, rubeola, rubella, pertussis, mumps, and tetanus to attend school but allows exemptions for valid medical and religious reasons.
The DOH holds authority under statute to also require vaccinations for “other communicable diseases as determined.” Under that authority, the DOH has required children to also be immunized for haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib), hepatitis B, varicella (chickenpox), and pneumococcal conjugate.
The health department has moved to change its rules to eliminate the four vaccines that aren’t included in statute.
Supporters praised Ladapo for having the tenacity to tackle vaccine mandates and promote what they called “medical freedom.” One woman said she hopes Ladapo’s reign as state’s healthcare czar and secretary of the Florida Department of Health transcends DeSantis’ term as governor, which comes to an end in January. 
Another woman, the last to testify during the meeting, wrapped up her comments by requesting a selfie with Ladapo.
And even though allegations that the measles/mumps/rubella vaccine was linked to autism — a theory initially espoused in 1988 by a British physician but debunked by several large studies since then — some proponents of the changes mentioned autism in their public testimony.
Allison Euker was one of them.
Euker, who testified that her child was injured by a vaccine, thanked Ladapo for “being the light in the darkness of the captured medical system,” and blasted organized medicine for “pushing the narratives” that she said financially benefit the pharmaceutical industry.
“The doctors and medical professionals fall in line. If they don’t, they suffer career-ending recourse,” Eucker said. “But if they do, they profit from injecting kids, and who suffers? The child, the families, left with gaslighting from most doctors who will never mention that the tics, the autism, the speech impediments, the ADHD are all serious side effects from the multiple vaccines they push at every visit.”
Several people who testified in favor of the change were people new to Florida who said they moved here because of changes being made to vaccine policies.
 That was Suzanne Moanco’s story, who moved to Winter Springs from Oregon following experiences in the Oregon Capitol trying to beat back vaccine mandates.
“That taught me medical freedom shouldn’t be political,” she said.
She added: “It makes sense to remove these vaccine requirements. When it comes to my kids, that decision belongs to me as their parent, not the state, not my nosy neighbor, and not a politician.”
The process
DeSantis and Ladspo last year announced they wanted to eliminate all vaccine mandates from Florida statutes.
The state last year published a proposed rule to eliminate mandates for vaccines required through administrative rule and to add moral or conscientious to the medical and religious exemptions already allowed.
The DOH held a public meeting in Panama City Beach in December. 
Florida school, daycare vaccine tussle kicks off in Panama City Beach

The administration in the beginning of the year started working with the Legislature to accomplish its goal. 
After the proposals died in the regular legislative session and subsequent special legislative session, the DeSantis administration vowed to work on the issue long as he remains governor.
DeSantis’ resolve to pass his vaccine policies strengthens as measles cases continue to rise

 To that end, his administration returned its focus to making the changes administratively. 
It republished the proposed rule it first introduced in 2025 and later published a change to the rule that eliminated conscientious and moral objections as valid. It also scheduled the Lake Mary rule hearing.
Because Thursday’s meeting was a rule hearing, the questions being asked of the DOH weren’t limited.
(A rule hearing is one step under Florida’s Administrative Procedures Act. Following a rule hearing, an agency can address any concerns raised and revise the proposal. Any changes made to a proposed rule must be published by the state within 21 days.)
Or the agency can go ahead and adopt the rule.
The APA also gives any affected party an opportunity to file a rule challenge with the state Division of Administrative Hearings and request that it be heard by a administrative law judge.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: ‘It’s time to make us essential,’ EMS responders tell NJ lawmakers
description: EMS leaders urged lawmakers to pass a bill to make their work an essential service in New Jersey, like fire and police, during a legislative hearing Thursday.
text:
EMS leaders urged lawmakers to pass a bill that would make their work an essential service in New Jersey, like fire and police, and called for other changes during a legislative hearing Thursday. The Senate committee took no votes, but leaders promised action. (Photo by New Jersey Monitor)Emergency responders urged state officials at a legislative hearing Thursday to make basic lifesaving ambulance service an essential requirement under state law, create a statewide plan for responders, expand funding, and make it easier for people to volunteer.
The Senate Legislative Oversight Committee took testimony in the Trenton Statehouse from nearly a dozen people, almost all of whom encouraged lawmakers to act on legislation to require local communities to provide certain emergency medical services, a bill that had initial votes by committees in both the Senate and Assembly in May. Some said the bill needs amendments to ensure volunteer squads would satisfy the requirement.
Witnesses also called for the state to adopt a statewide EMS plan, lift the $125,000 annual cap on local tax contributions for ambulance squads, and make other changes. The committee did not vote on any of the measures Thursday.
Statewide EMS task force faces shutdown amid funding crisis

Sen. Andrew Zwicker (D-Middlesex) pledged to tweak and advance some bills and introduce others to address planning, training, funding, oversight, data collection, and more.
“In the end, we want to capture everything needed for providing that first response when someone is in critical, critical need,” Zwicker said.
Advocates for change say New Jersey’s emergency response system is increasingly fragile, a patchwork of volunteer and paid squads  — associated with hospitals, fire departments, and private companies — that face growing challenges involving vehicle crashes, opioids, natural disasters, and more. While volunteerism has been declining for some time, the trend accelerated in recent years, witnesses said.
Jennifer McCarthy, a vice president and board member of the statewide EMS Task Force, a nonprofit that coordinates large-scale responses, said modernizing these services is “paramount” to protecting patients, public health, and emergency response in general. Currently, there is no law requiring communities to have emergency response providers in place.
“It’s 2026. It’s time to make us essential,” McCarthy said.
Such a change would make for more consistent responses, improve outcomes, and boost volunteer participation, she added.
McCarthy also urged lawmakers to adopt a second bill that would have the state study the current landscape and create a statewide plan that considers regional coordination of emergency response.
“We need to reverse-design the system, where volunteers and career personnel can work together to meet the needs of the public,” McCarthy said.
The EMS Task Force depends on a mix of paid and volunteer staff from 60 local agencies, although nearly one-third retire each year, she said.
Ari Meisel, executive director of Princeton First Aid and Rescue Squad, said people continue to want to volunteer, but the state’s process of training, credentialing, and onboarding them is far too slow. Lawmakers should “make the on-ramp faster,” Meisel said.
“Every week of delay is a week we lose a good person,” he said.
Sen. Robert Singer (R-Ocean) described the benefits Lakewood and surrounding communities have seen from the local volunteer Hatzalah service, an organization based in some Jewish neighborhoods that responds to emergencies for people of all backgrounds and faiths. The group currently has a waiver that enables higher-ranking responders to have cars stocked with medical equipment so they can travel directly to the site of the emergency, he said, reducing delays.
Singer said he would introduce legislation to allow other communities to have a similar structure with high-ranking responders.
“Here’s something that works well and is on a waiver, but should become permanent if any other squad wants to use it,” he said.
Corry Van Elsland, with Paramedics for the Advancement of New Jersey Emergency Medical Services, a nonprofit that represents paid paramedics, questioned the continued reliance on volunteers, given the growing complexity and requirements of emergency response.
He underscored the call for a statewide study and plan to better determine response times and outcomes across all 21 counties, but said the future will require more professional staff.
“Are we preserving a system because it works, or because it’s a system we’ve always known?” Van Elsland said, adding that “gratitude in the past can’t substitute planning for the future.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: FEMA confirms $17.9 million in disaster aid for four Wisconsin counties, provides application info
description: The Federal Emergency Management Agency confirmed $17.9 million in disaster aid is being made available for Wisconsinites in Forest, Outagamie, Vilas and Winnebago counties to assist with damage caused by a tornado and severe storms on July 27.  President Donald Trump announced via a post on Truth Social on Wednesday that he would be approving […]
text:
A Madison Gas & Electric truck drives past downed powerlines in Menasha after a July tornado. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)The Federal Emergency Management Agency confirmed $17.9 million in disaster aid is being made available for Wisconsinites in Forest, Outagamie, Vilas and Winnebago counties to assist with damage caused by a tornado and severe storms on July 27. 
President Donald Trump announced via a post on Truth Social on Wednesday that he would be approving the money after speaking with U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany, who is running for governor. The aid is meant to help communities after a tornado and severe storms hit parts of Appleton and Menasha in July, destroying and damaging homes.
Gov. Tony Evers, who had issued a call for aid in August, said Wednesday that he had not heard from the federal administration, cast doubt on when the money would be available and accused Trump and Tiffany of playing politics. Evers initially sent a request for federal aid to Trump in August, after assessments found more than $8.2 million in damage to more than 2,300 residential properties and more than $13.8 million in public sector damage. The request had so far gone unfulfilled and in the absence of aid, local communities had turned to fundraising efforts.
Evers’ office did not respond immediately Thursday to a request for comment about whether they have yet heard directly from the federal government.
In a press release Wednesday evening, FEMA said that individuals who sustained losses in the four counties should first file claims with their insurance providers and then apply for assistance through FEMA online at www.DisasterAssistance.gov, by calling 1-800-621-3362 or by using the FEMA App. 
The assistance will support grants for temporary housing and home repairs, low-cost loans to cover uninsured property losses and other programs to help individuals and families recover from the effects of the disaster. 
State, tribal and eligible local governments as well as certain private nonprofit organizations will also be able to access public assistance federal funding “on a cost-sharing basis for emergency work and the repair or replacement of facilities damaged in Vilas and Winnebago counties.” 
According to Troy Christensen, a FEMA public affairs specialist, the $17.9 million in assistance for Wisconsin reflected preliminary damage assessments in the affected communities. He said in an email to the Examiner that the amount is a “projected initial figure that may change as recovery costs are finalized.”
Christensen said that staff will help each applicant to “navigate their unique situation and specific needs.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico cybersecurity leader calls for quantum safeguards while state inks deal with major player
description: New Mexico cybersecurity officials told state lawmakers Thursday to prioritize updating digital security systems across state agencies before other countries develop a high-tech quantum computer. The admonition came the same day Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham announced a partnership with Japan-based tech company Fujitsu to establish a quantum computing research[...]
text:
From left to right, New Mexico Economic Development Department Secretary Rob Black, Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham and Fujitsu Chief Technology Officer Vivek Mahajan on Oct. 8, 2026, announced a partnership to create a quantum computing research center in New Mexico. (Photo by Matt Mondschein/Source NM)New Mexico cybersecurity officials told state lawmakers Thursday to prioritize updating digital security systems across state agencies before other countries develop a high-tech quantum computer.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The admonition came the same day Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham announced a partnership with Japan-based tech company Fujitsu to establish a quantum computing research center in New Mexico. The timing of both meetings emphasized how quickly quantum computing is developing in government and business.
Government agencies typically store sensitive data — such as birth and death records, juvenile records and health records — in encrypted systems. Standard encryption typically deters hackers by requiring a computer to solve a series of complex math problems one at a time. Experts believe that quantum computers, however, will be able to solve several complex math problems at once, rendering standard encryption useless.
Officials in the U.S. and China, in particular, for years have been locked in a race to beat the other to a quantum breakthrough and gain an edge in obtaining the other nation’s state secrets.
State lawmakers this year have often discussed how New Mexico, which has attracted several high-profile quantum companies in recent years and is home to multiple national laboratories, can lead the country’s efforts. The Quantum World Congress in September recognized just two states — New Mexico and Illinois — as national leaders in quantum technology investment.
Todd Baran, general counsel for the New Mexico Office of Cybersecurity, on Thursday spoke to state legislators on the interim Science, Technology and Telecommunications Committee in Los Alamos. He said it’s critical to create security systems that could fend off a hostile country with quantum computing technology as soon as possible.
“The malicious actors are going to harvest this data today and then, four or five years from now when the tool becomes available to decrypt it, they’re going to decrypt it,” he said.
Baran added that the federal National Institute of Standards and Technology has set deadlines for adopting newer encryption methods. By Dec. 31, 2030, many federal systems and federal contractors must make the switch. The goal, he said, is to have all federal systems updated and to “retire” the old encryption methods by 2035.
Baran told lawmakers that the Legislature will need to pass a bill in the upcoming legislative session that gives his office the authority to mandate these changes across state agencies. Currently, he said, his office doesn’t have that power.
While Baran was speaking in Los Alamos, Lujan Grisham was inking a memorandum of understanding in Santa Fe with Fujitsu. The corporation has worked with New Mexico State University since 2025 and will now work with the state to build the state’s capacity for quantum computing hardware and software and to support education and workforce programs.
Under the agreement, Fujitsu’s center would focus on training scientists and engineers in addition to creating internships and research opportunities for students.
The governor said the partnership is a key step in ensuring New Mexico continues to lead the nation’s quantum efforts.
“I want New Mexico to be a leader in quantum. I’m banking that that is the future of innovation and investment in the state,” Lujan Grisham said at a news conference in the Roundhouse Thursday morning. “There are only two states in the World Quantum Conference that are identified as leading and ready, and that’s Illinois and New Mexico. And I’m bullish about us winning.”
Fujitsu Chief Technology Officer Vivek Mahajan, speaking alongside Lujan Grisham, said he believed New Mexico’s universities and national labs made the state the natural choice for such a partnership.
“You have world-class labs here, really good university talent,” he said. “And I think the government here has created an excellent ecosystem.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: ‘There will be impacts,’ DeSantis warns as Hurricane Isaias approaches North Florida
description: Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said Thursday that state emergency planners are preparing for Hurricane Isaias to make landfall as a Category 3 storm near the Florida Panhandle. The National Hurricane Center (NHC) said at 11 a.m. Eastern Time that Isaias is expected to strengthen as it moves towards the Gulf Coast and had reached an […]
text:
Graphic from the National Hurricane Center as of 2 p.m. ET on Oct. 8, 2026.Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said Thursday that state emergency planners are preparing for Hurricane Isaias to make landfall as a Category 3 storm near the Florida Panhandle.
The National Hurricane Center (NHC) said at 11 a.m. Eastern Time that Isaias is expected to strengthen as it moves towards the Gulf Coast and had reached an intensity of 85 mph. The center of Isaias was about 500 miles south-southwest of Pensacola at that time.
The NHC expects Isaias to become a Category 2 storm Friday morning, with most models showing it peaking as a high-end Category 1 to a low-end Category 3 hurricane.
Speaking from the State Emergency Operations Center in Tallahassee at 2 p.m., DeSantis said  the state was expected to experience wind impacts as early as Friday afternoon, with landfall projected for late Friday night into early Saturday morning.
“It’s moving quickly,” he said. “There will be impacts all across the Florida Panhandle.”
The way the storm was tracking, DeSantis said, most of the hurricane models place landfall somewhere between Mobile Bay in Alabama and Navarre, in the western Florida Panhandle.
Florida Department of Transportation Secretary Jared Perdue said storm surge from Isaias is forecast to range from five to seven feet.
Mandatory evacuations have already begun in Franklin County, and for residents in Fort Walton County who live in zones A, B, and C began as of noon Thursday Central Time.
The Division of Emergency Management was prepared for the storm, DeSantis said. It has assembled more than 1,000 generators that are either being loaned or staged; 500,000 gallons of gasoline; 1 million gallons of diesel, and 35,000 gallons of aviation fuel. More than 1.1 million bottles of water are available to be distributed.
More than 6,000 utility linemen and restoration personnel were standing by to restore power as quickly and as safely as possible.
Residents in northwest Florida who want to know the most up to school closures can go to https://www.fldoe.org/em-response/storm-info.stml.
For road closures, they can go to https://fl511.com/region/Panhandle.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Legislative staffer sues Nebraska Legislature for response to sexual harassment report
description: LINCOLN — A legislative staffer filed a complaint against the Nebraska Legislature, accusing lawmakers of violating their workplace harassment policy in their response to an alleged groping incident last year. The complaint, filed in Lancaster District Court Wednesday, centers on an end-of-session party in 2025, where a legislative staffer claims former stat[...]
text:
State Sen. Dan McKeon of Amherst, left, and State Sen. Dave Murman of Glenvil. Jan. 9, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — A legislative staffer filed a complaint against the Nebraska Legislature, accusing lawmakers of violating their workplace harassment policy in their response to an alleged groping incident last year.
The complaint, filed in Lancaster District Court Wednesday, centers on an end-of-session party in 2025, where a legislative staffer claims former state Sen. Dan McKeon of Amherst made a sexually charged remark, saying “he hoped that she wasn’t going to Hawaii to ‘get lei’d’” and then touched her buttocks. McKeon denied any inappropriate conduct.
McKeon has since resigned from the Legislature as a result of the accusation and faced a Class III misdemeanor charge for disturbing the peace. His criminal case was dismissed in August after he successfully completed a court diversion program.
The plaintiff in the complaint is labeled Jane Doe, and court documents note that she fears “retaliation, retribution, and harassment” if her identity is exposed. The Examiner is not publishing her name because it is the policy of States Newsroom and the Examiner not to identify people who say they have been abused unless they wish to talk publicly.
In the complaint, the staffer alleged that even prior to the sine die party on May 29, 2025, McKeon would regularly visit the office she worked in and make sexual jokes to her co-worker loud enough for her to hear, which she said were unwelcome and interfered with her work.
After the interaction at the sine die party, the staffer told her boss about the incident the following Monday, June 1, and filed an informal sexual harassment complaint to the Legislature’s Executive Board on June 2. Board members instructed McKeon to have no further contact with the staffer during their investigation, according to the complaint.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Despite this instruction, the complaint alleges that McKeon attended a legislative party that the staffer helped coordinate that same day and continually positioned himself to sit facing her. The complaint described his conduct as “threatening, harassing, intimidating and retaliatory.”
On July 29, the staffer filed a formal sexual harassment complaint to the Executive Board.
According to the Legislature’s workplace harassment policy, the board must respond to a harassment complaint no later than 45 days after the report is submitted, or 45 days after the date a formal investigation begins following an unsuccessful effort at an informational resolution, whichever is later. If the alleged harasser is a member of the Legislature, the chair must promptly appoint a special panel made up of three lawmakers plus the chair to determine the appropriate action.
In early September, the staffer learned that the panel had not yet met and had not conducted an investigation into her report, which would violate the policy. After learning this, she filed a report with the Nebraska State Patrol, which charged McKeon with misdemeanor public indecency on Oct. 31. Those charges were later downgraded to disturbing the peace.
Nebraska state senator cited for ‘public indecency’ during session-ending party

The special panel’s report, which found that McKeon had violated the Legislature’s workplace harassment policy, was not issued until Oct. 28, nearly 45 days late, according to the complaint. The report directed McKeon to take several corrective actions, including prohibiting him from having any communication with or about the staffer.
Despite this, the complaint alleges, McKeon and his attorney Perry Pirsch made several false and defamatory statements about the staffer, both in the media and in private. The complaint further alleges that Executive Board members were aware of these statements and were aware of McKeon’s inappropriate conduct prior to the sine die party, and failed to take appropriate remedial action — another violation of the policy.
The staffer claims she was subjected to gender-based discrimination and a hostile work environment through this process. Among her requests are that the Legislature pay her past, present and future compensatory damages, and that the Legislature be prohibited from “any further discrimination or retaliation” against her.
State Sen. Ben Hansen of Blair, who chairs the Executive Board, declined to comment on the pending litigation.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Mother of Secoriea Turner urges Jackson to stop using her daughter’s name, image in campaign ads
description: The family of an 8-year-old girl who was killed during a period of civil unrest in Atlanta is urging Republican candidate for governor Rick Jackson to stop using her name and image in campaign material, calling the ads “deeply hurtful.” Secoriea Turner was fatally shot in 2020 while riding in a vehicle near a Wendy’s […]
text:
Mawuli Mel Davis (left) and Shean Williams (right), attorneys for Secoriea Turner's family, speak at a press conference on Thursday, Oct. 8. Maya Homan/Georgia RecorderThe family of an 8-year-old girl who was killed during a period of civil unrest in Atlanta is urging Republican candidate for governor Rick Jackson to stop using her name and image in campaign material, calling the ads “deeply hurtful.”
Secoriea Turner was fatally shot in 2020 while riding in a vehicle near a Wendy’s where a man had been killed earlier by police. The fast food restaurant had become the site for demonstrations against police brutality and calls for social justice during Democratic nominee for governor Keisha Lance Bottoms’ tenure as mayor of Atlanta. Secoriea Turner’s death was part of a wave of violence occurring at the time that prompted the governor to call in the Georgia National Guard. 
Jackson has used photos and news coverage of the event as part of his campaign rhetoric, arguing that Bottoms failed to keep Atlanta residents safe.
Last week, Secoriea’s mother Charmaine Turner publicly urged Jackson to stop using her daughter’s name and image in campaign materials and sent his campaign a cease and desist letter. But attorneys who represent Turner’s family said that instead of honoring the request, the campaign doubled down, releasing a new attack ad featuring Charmaine’s screams as she called 911 after Secoriea was shot.
“Today we stand making it very, very clear that Secoriea Turner, that her death, that her image, that who she was as a beautiful 8-year-old, is not a part of any campaign property,” attorney Mawuli Mel Davis said during a Thursday press conference. “She should not be part of any political or campaign stunt. This is real pain.”
Turner’s mother declined to attend Thursday’s press conference, but she said in a statement provided through her attorneys that she would continue to fight for her daughter. In 2021, she filed a lawsuit against Bottoms and the city of Atlanta over their handling of the protests, which is still pending.
Rick Jackson, the Republican nominee for governor. Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder
In a statement released ahead of the press conference, Jackson campaign spokesperson Garrison Douglas defended the use of Turner’s story in the campaign ads.
“We cannot imagine the immense pain the Turner family has gone through,” he said. “They are not a political talking point. They are one of the major reasons why Rick is running — so that another family does not have to experience such a devastating tragedy as a result of Keisha Lance Bottoms’ abdication of her duty.”
Shean Williams, another attorney who represents the Turner family, condemned the campaign ads as “morally irresponsible,” adding that Jackson never attempted to contact the Turner family before using Secoriea’s image.
“If it’s not a political point and he really cares about Secoriea Turner, her legacy, her image, then why hasn’t he even reached out before today, before he ran for governor?” he said. “It tells me it’s a political talking point because this is all political.”
The Bottoms campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment Thursday.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Racial disparities persist in North Carolina schools, new report finds
description: Black students in North Carolina were 3.7 times as likely as their white peers to receive a short-term suspension during the 2024-25 school year, even as the overall number of suspensions continues to decline, according to an analysis of state education data by the Southern Coalition for Social Justice.  The disparity in short-term suspensions was […]
text:
Black students accounted for more than 55 percent of all out-of-school suspensions (OSS), but made up only a quarter of the student population. (Image: Adobe Stock)Black students in North Carolina were 3.7 times as likely as their white peers to receive a short-term suspension during the 2024-25 school year, even as the overall number of suspensions continues to decline, according to an analysis of state education data by the Southern Coalition for Social Justice. 
The disparity in short-term suspensions was largely unchanged from the previous year. 
Black students made up about 25% of traditional K-12 enrollment during the school year but accounted for 51% of all short-term suspensions and 54% of school-based juvenile delinquency complaints, according to the report. 
The report also found that white students were 2.4 times as likely as Black students to be considered career and college ready in grades 3-8, and 2.5 times as likely in grades 9-12. 
In 82 of the state’s 110 reporting districts, white students were at least twice as likely as Black students to be considered career and college ready, according to the report. 
In some districts, the gap is much wider, and it’s growing. 
At Asheville City Schools, 57.6% of white students in grades 3-8 were considered career and college ready. For Black students, the figure was 4%. White students were 14.4 times as likely as Black students to meet that standard, up from 8.6 times the year before.
The district had the state’s largest gap in short-term suspensions, too. Black students were nearly 11 times as likely as white students to receive a short-term suspension. 
Legislation to clarify NC school suspensions finds initial bipartisan support

Some of the largest school districts in the state also saw growing disparities this past school year. Black students were 8.4 times as likely as white students to receive a short-term suspension in Charlotte-Mecklenburg Schools, up from 7.5 times the year before. In Durham Public Schools, they were 7.7 times as likely, up from 7 times. 
The report found that 9,514 of the state’s 36,356 juvenile delinquency complaints in 2024-25 originated in schools, or about 26%. 
Nine districts had no Black teachers during the 2024-25 school year, according to state data cited in the report. 
In Asheville, where 18% of students are Black, 4.5% of district employees were Black, according to the report. 
“Every year we publish these numbers hoping to report progress, and every year we see racial disparities worsen,” said Jake Sussman, chief counsel for Justice System Reform at SCSJ.
“North Carolina’s constitution promises every child an equal opportunity at a sound basic education,” Sussman said. “When a Black student in this state is nearly four times as likely to be suspended and less than half as likely to be counted college or career ready, that promise is being broken, and the failure belongs to the system, not the students.” 
NC Newsline reached out to the Department of Public Instruction, Asheville City Schools, Charlotte-Mecklenburg Schools and Durham Public Schools for comment. None had responded as of publication.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: ‘Historic’ grant will help West Virginia State University build Agriculture Complex
description: INSTITUTE, W.Va. — West Virginia State University has received a $26.5 million federal grant that will help the school build a new, 40,000 square foot Agriculture Complex.
text:
West Virginia State University President Ericke Cage speaks during an announcement Thursday of a $26.5 million federal grant to help expand its agriculture program in Institute, West Virginia. (Photo by Lori Kersey/West Virginia Watch)INSTITUTE, W.Va. — West Virginia State University has received a $26.5 million federal grant that will help the school build a new, 40,000 square foot Agriculture Complex. 
The new complex will house lab space for the West Virginia Department of Agriculture and the school’s Purdy School of Agriculture, Food and Natural Resources.
“As a proud 1890 land-grant institution, West Virginia State University has a long-standing responsibility to advance agriculture education, research and service,” West Virginia State University President Ericke S. Cage told reporters Thursday. “This new agricultural laboratory will significantly expand our ability to fulfill that mission. 
“It will strengthen our capacity for agricultural research, education and assistance to producers across the state. It will support critical work in food safety, microbiology, shelf life studies and value-added agricultural development,” he said. 
The grant from the U.S. Department of Agriculture represents the largest competitive grant in the school’s 135-year history. WVSU is getting the second-highest amount of the 36 schools that are getting grants from the program, school leaders say. 
“That, ladies and gentlemen, is an extraordinary achievement for this university,” Cage said. “It demonstrates something that we have known for a long time here at West Virginia State, and that is that our institution can compete and win at the highest levels. We may not be the largest institution in the country or in the state, but we have the talent, the expertise, the vision and determination to compete with the very best.”
A mockup of West Virginia State University’s Agriculture Complex. (Courtesy photo)
The grant comes from the USDA’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture’s Research Facilities Act Program, a $121 million investment nationwide. 
“For 164 years, USDA has partnered with America’s great land-grant and agricultural universities to produce the discoveries, service and education needed to keep the nation fed and to fuel U.S. agricultural progress around the world,” NIFA Director Dr. Jaye L. Hamby said in announcing the program in June. “This investment reaffirms our commitment to that valued partnership and to the next generation of agriculturists. We are excited to see the tremendous impact this program will have to accelerate research from the lab to the marketplace and the fields to improve profitability for our farmers, ranchers, and producers and secure our nation’s food supply.”
Located in Institute, West Virginia State University is one of two historically black colleges and universities in West Virginia. 
Former Gov. Jim Justice announced the project during his 2024 state of the state address. The state Legislature approved $50 million in state funding for the project during a special legislative session in May 2024. 
The school held a groundbreaking ceremony for the project in November 2024. 
When the $50 million state award was announced, leaders said West Virginia State University was the only land-grant university in the country without its own agricultural program. The Purdy family gave $2.5 million to help develop the new school. 
WVSU leaders say the school leveraged the $50 million state funding allocation to get the federal award. 
“That is a significant return on the state’s initial commitment and a demonstration of what is possible when state investment and federal opportunity come together,” Cage said. 
Construction on the complex is expected to start in early 2027. Leaders expect the building will be completed and occupied in 2029. 
Perkins&Will is leading the project’s design and PJ Dick and Pray Construction will be construction manager, the school said in a news release. 
The agricultural facility will have food science laboratories for food safety, microbiology and shelf-life studies; a commercial kitchen, flexible agriculture and natural resources laboratories, agricultural artificial intelligence computing and teaching space for the agriculture school, WVSU said in a news release.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota measure campaigns pull in large group donations
description: Millions of dollars from national and in-state groups have gone into campaigns telling North Dakotans how they should vote this fall on whether to make it harder to change the state constitution and provide free meals to school children. Campaign finance reports recently filed with the secretary of state brought into better focus who is […]
text:
Michelle Wagner, left, carries boxes of signed petitions for a proposed ballot measure to make public school breakfasts and lunches free in North Dakota on April 9, 2026, at the Capitol. To her right are Amy Jacobson and Ashley Gaschk, other members of the measure's sponsoring committee. Together for School Meals has reported nearly $1.1 million in monetary support for the measure. (Photo by Mary Steurer/North Dakota Monitor)Millions of dollars from national and in-state groups have gone into campaigns telling North Dakotans how they should vote this fall on whether to make it harder to change the state constitution and provide free meals to school children.
Campaign finance reports recently filed with the secretary of state brought into better focus who is spending money to support or defeat the general election’s two statewide ballot measures. Both are constitutional amendments. Measure 1 would require at least 60% of voter support to amend the state constitution. Measure 2 would provide free school meals to K-12 students.
Together for School Meals, the group behind Measure 2, reported nearly $1.1 million in monetary contributions this year. There does not appear to be organized financial opposition to Measure 2.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The info you need to cast your ballot.]
Protect the North Dakota Constitution, which opposes Measure 1, has reported more than $1.2 million of donations. StrongND Fund, a group aligned with Gov. Kelly Armstrong, has spent $978,000 in support of Measure 1.
National groups such as the Fairness Project and the National Education Association have given to both groups. The Fairness Project has spent more than $1.12 million against Measure 1 and $600,000 to support Measure 2. The National Education Association gave $50,000 to Protect the North Dakota Constitution and $250,000 to Together for School Meals.
Supporters of Measure 1 say the state constitution needs a higher threshold than a simple majority to change it. Opponents say the measure takes power away from voters to enact changes they want. Measure 2 backers say free school meals would ease costs for parents and keep kids fed and focused during the school day. Opponents say the mandated spending should not go into the state constitution.
Both measures are part of national movements, but in the context of other states, $1 million is paltry, said Mark Jendrysik, a professor of political science and public administration at the University of North Dakota.
“A million dollars in North Dakota goes a fair way,” he said. It’s not a huge amount of money, but “it’s enough to get certain things done,” such as mail and television ads, he said.
The Fairness Project “fights for policies voters want when politicians fail them,” and provides funding and expertise to help measure campaigns, Executive Director Hannah Ledford said in emailed comments. 
The D.C.-based organization lists measures in Michigan, Missouri, Montana and Virginia on its website among campaigns it supports, in addition to North Dakota’s Measure 2. Some of those other measures deal with protecting reproductive rights in Virginia, cementing Montana judicial races as nonpartisan and redrawing Missouri congressional districts.
The Fairness Project supports Measure 2 because “politicians in Bismarck failed three times” to enact free school meals, leading supporters to drive the ballot initiative, a power the organization doesn’t want Measure 1 to weaken, Ledford said.
“Our work brings us together with local organizations and advocates who want to improve their communities through ballot measures. Together for School Meals and Protect the North Dakota Constitution reflect both parts of that mission: helping voters deliver policies their families need and defending their right to do so,” Ledford said.
Free school meal ballot measure debated at North Dakota policy summit

Together for School Meals is spending money on in-person events and digital and mail ads, Measure 2 spokesperson Amy Jacobson said. She said the campaign has been funded by “a lot of different organizations who are value-aligned with us” or worked with partners in the state for years.
“Really it’s about feeding kids and making sure kids get breakfast and lunch at school at no cost to families, and we are working with national groups as well as locals to make sure that that happens,” Jacobson said.
Jacobson is executive director of Prairie Action ND, a progressive policy group. She said she has worked with the Fairness Project for many years on different projects. “Grassroots groups” approached the Fairness Project for assistance to get Measure 2 on the ballot after the Legislature “had rejected it multiple times,” she said.
“We knew that ballot measures require quite a bit of investment, and so we used those longtime partnerships to help make this a reality for us,” Jacobson said.
The measure’s biggest in-state donor appears to be North Dakota United, the state’s teachers and public employees union, at $135,000.
All of the monetary donations to Protect the North Dakota Constitution have come from outside of the state, according to a North Dakota Monitor analysis of filings. Nearly all of the group’s $1.22 million of contributions, but for $100,000, has come from the Fairness Project. 
“Most average North Dakotans don’t have the personal wealth to reach every voter or educate them on critical issues. Measure 1 is a threat to North Dakota’s future, and we welcome support from all who value democracy and protecting our constitution,” Protect the North Dakota Constitution Chair Sargianna Wutzke said in emailed comments. Wutzke lives in Bismarck.
She noted two other groups, ProtectND and Respect ND Voters, that have similar aims. Only ProtectND appears to have raised any money – none since June and not at the same level as Wutzke’s group, according to filings.
Sponsor, opponent debate need for North Dakota ballot measure to change constitution

Wutzke blasted StrongND Fund, which supports Measure 1, as a “dark money group” that has funded ads “to support politicians’ power grab and to rip up our constitution all without disclosing the source of a single dollar.” 
StrongND Treasurer Nick Hacker said, “We just don’t think special interests should have that much ability to effectuate constitutional change. We’re not arguing against ballot measures. That’s not it at all.”
StrongND’s video ads urge voters to vote yes on Measure 1, citing California’s constitution as “a grab bag of spending mandates and special-interest carveouts.” 
North Dakota’s foundational document needs more than a simple majority vote to be amended, said Hacker, who lives in Mandan and has served in the North Dakota Senate and on the State Board of Higher Education. North Dakota has a cheap media market and an easy process to change the state constitution, he said.
StrongND is following the law, and its donors are not required to be disclosed, he added. The vast majority of donors are in the state or have interests in North Dakota, he said.
Hacker called the Fairness Project “a far-left leaning organization” and “a pro-abortion group” with “fingerprints all over far-left causes.” 
Both measures need a simple majority to pass.
Reach North Dakota Monitor reporter Jack Dura at jdura@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Invasive zebra mussels have made their way to the Utah portion of the Colorado River
description: Biologists have discovered a live adult zebra mussel below the Westwater Recreation Area in the Utah side of the Colorado River, raising the risk of the invasive species spreading in the state. The discovery was made Sept. 22, about a month after testing detected zebra mussel DNA in the water in Utah, according to a […]
text:
The Colorado River is pictured near Moab on Sunday, Feb. 18, 2024. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Biologists have discovered a live adult zebra mussel below the Westwater Recreation Area in the Utah side of the Colorado River, raising the risk of the invasive species spreading in the state.
The discovery was made Sept. 22, about a month after testing detected zebra mussel DNA in the water in Utah, according to a news release from the Utah Division of Wildlife Resources. The division received confirmation Wednesday that it had in fact found a live mussel downstream of the infestation near Loma, Colorado. 
Utah’s Division of Wildlife Resources has ramped up testing for zebra mussels in the Colorado River between the state line and Moab after the Loma infestation was detected in 2025. Once an invasive species is detected, concerns of outbreak are elevated as the risk grows of people recreating in the river and then unknowingly transporting organisms to other waterbodies on their watercraft, the division warned.
Tiny zebra mussels pose an outsized threat to rivers and lakes. (Amy Benson, Wetland and Aquatic Research Center)
Utah law requires that all vessels going into the water in the state — from boats and jet skis to kayaks and paddleboards — must be cleaned, dried and drained when they leave. That includes water and mud on trailers transporting them, according to the news release.
Recreators must also complete a mandatory mussel-aware boater program course, pay the state’s aquatic invasive species fee and remove drain plugs while transporting their watercraft.
Inspection and decontamination sites to check for zebra mussels and other invasive species like quagga mussels and Eurasian watermilfoil are set up around the state. Over Labor Day weekend, state agencies inspected 9,418 watercraft.
Invasive mussels are a particular threat in irrigation-dependent Utah. They can spread to water lines, clogging pipes and costing millions of dollars to remove, and damage boat engines. They remove plankton from water, disrupting food supplies for fish. 
Though small, zebra mussels are known for covering beaches with razor-sharp shells and damaging ecosystems. Meanwhile, quagga mussels have been found for a fourth year in Idaho’s Snake River, though in fewer numbers after years of aggressive treatment.
More information about invasive species can be found at Utah’s STD of the Sea website, which includes a list of decontamination stations around the state and requirements for watercraft.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Another South Dakota Republican lawmaker is facing a criminal charge
description: A South Dakota state senator was cited for driving under the influence this week, marking the third time criminal charges for a state lawmaker have come to light in the space of four months.  Leola Republican Mark Lapka, 45, was cited for driving under the influence between Tuesday night and early Wednesday morning, McPherson County […]
text:
Sen. Mark Lapka, R-Leola, speaks in the South Dakota Senate on March 4, 2025, at the Capitol in Pierre. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)A South Dakota state senator was cited for driving under the influence this week, marking the third time criminal charges for a state lawmaker have come to light in the space of four months. 
Leola Republican Mark Lapka, 45, was cited for driving under the influence between Tuesday night and early Wednesday morning, McPherson County State’s Attorney Austin Hoffman confirmed to South Dakota Searchlight. Lapka was cited, not arrested, Hoffman said, “due to the circumstances of the situation.”
He declined to offer further details, citing the ongoing investigation. No charges have been filed yet, Hoffman said, because the clerk of courts for McPherson County was not immediately available to file them.
Sheriff David Ackerman said the incident occurred near the edge of town in Leola, but also declined to elaborate due to the ongoing investigation.
A first offense of driving under the influence is punishable by up to a year in jail and a $2,000 fine. Lapka has no criminal record in South Dakota beyond the pending charge and a speeding ticket, according to a search of the state’s court record database.
Lapka is running uncontested for reelection to his seat in District 23, where he represents all of McPherson and Edmunds counties and parts of Brown, Campbell, Faulk, Hand, Potter and Walworth counties. He did not return a call or text from Searchlight.
December trial date set for South Dakota lawmaker facing election-related felony charges

Sioux Falls Republican Sen. Chris Karr, one of the chamber’s top leaders as president pro tempore, did not immediately respond to a call and a text seeking comment. 
Two other Republican lawmakers were charged criminally in June. Newell Rep. Travis Ismay was charged with felony damage to a road, but the charge was reduced when he agreed to plead no contest to a misdemeanor version of the same crime. Ismay agreed to pay back the county for the cost of re-grading the gravel road he’d graded himself.
Ismay is running unopposed for reelection to his seat in District 28B. That district includes Butte and Harding counties and parts of Perkins County.
Sen. Tom Pischke, R-Dell Rapids, awaits trial on two felony counts of attempting to file a false or forged instrument. That case accuses Pischke of signing and submitting nominating petitions for county party precinct positions without those candidates’ knowledge. The Minnehaha County Republican Party chairman has alleged that Pischke was motivated by a dispute within the party, and wanted to add committee members to make it more difficult for county party meetings to achieve a quorum.
A December trial date has been set for Pischke, who dropped out of his reelection race in July after saying he’d be unable to be “transparent” during the campaign while his criminal case is pending.
Pischke serves in District 25, which includes northern Minnehaha and all of Moody County. 
Former Republican lawmaker Bryan Breitling is running for Pischke’s seat as an independent. The Minnehaha County Republican Party chose Bart Sample, of Flandreau, to replace Pischke on the Republican ticket. Sample finished third in a three-way primary race on June 2 for two Republican nominations for the district’s state House seats.
